description: This work is five short movements that utilizes graphic notation and explore the different sounds a flute can make through a wide variety of tone colours, extended techniques and ensemble combinations. None of the movements have descriptive titles but rather a metronome marking. The first movement “Slowly eighth note equals 80” is a dialogue between the two instruments centered around fragmented motifs that are in response to one another. In the opening the motifs are repeated in an aleatoric manner creating thicker texture. The second section of the movement “con moto eighth note equals 160” is more disjunct with an eighth note being passed around the ensemble in different register, which undergoes an accelerando. As it progresses the eighth note becomes larger motifs that are in dialogue. The second movement “Eighth note equals 138” contains eight different aleatoric sections based on different patterns of sixteenth notes that the two instruments switch to at different times creating a very busy texture. The following movement “Quarter note equals 72” is in ternary form and begins with an oscillation between the notes B, C, and C♯ in the low register of the flute, which lead to a long frullato note. This is overtop of prepared piano techniques creating different unique combination of textures and sounds between the two instruments. The B “Rapido quarter note equals 104” are disjunct passages of sixteenth notes that are weaving between one another, which eventually develop into aleatoric sections. The fourth movement “Eighth note equals 116” has two main motifs (the piano one played by plucking the strings while wearing thimbles) that are in response with each other. At the start they are playing alone in alternation between the two instruments. As it develops the flute motif becomes a whole phrase, while the piano motif becomes an ostinato in a regular rhythm with the same amount of rests in between each statement. The final movement “Eighth note equals 152” features an ascending and scalar passages of eighth notes in the flute. As it develops it becomes sixteenth notes with fragmentation that becomes less scalar and more disjunct before returning to the opening material. This is all overtop of various extended techniques in the piano. Then as an interlude the piano responses with the scalar motif to set up the return of the flute’s original material.

premiere: July 26th, 2022 in France by Pascale Oberlé (fl), Oksana Krupenya (pno)
description: This is a one-movement work in ternary form that takes inspiration from Ukrainian folk songs and music. The work is a melancholic song in a somber character depicting a bird arriving with unfortunate news to share. Musically, the A section begins with an ostinato motif of undulating eighth notes alternating between the intervals of minor third, perfect fourth and perfect fifth. The flute then enters with a vocal-like melody singing around F minor tonality utilizing the intervals introduced in the piano’s ostinato. The melody begins in the middle register then proceeds to the lower register to create a more mournful tone. As it progresses the piano adds chordal accompaniment in the right hand and bass line in the left hand. The B section includes an arpeggiated bass line in the left hand and a chordal accompaniment in the right hand of the piano underneath a melody based on scalar motion that has quintuplet neighbouring motion ornamentation. As it develops grace notes are added in to make it even more active. The return to the A section features a counter melody line of eighth notes in the right hand of the piano added into the texture to conclude the work.

description: This is a short one-movement work that features a folk-like and lyrical melody in the flute that mainly utilizes stepwise motion with occasional arpeggiation. Rhythmically, it consists of sixteenth, eighth, quarter notes with dots and ties and the occasional triplet eighth and sixteenth notes. Harmonically, it uses scales and harmony from Ukrainian folk music to create a melancholic and nostalgic character. The piano mainly has an arpeggiated eighth note bass line or chords in the left hand and fragmentation of the melody often echoing the flute in the right hand.

description: This is a one-movement work that stylistically includes elements of American avant-garde and neoclassicism. The piece opens with a declamatory “Adagio ma non troppo” section of accented staggered entrances in dialogue between the instruments. After this short introduction a slow and dolce piano solo introduces the theme in a mysterious and ominous character. Eventually, the oboe and bassoon take over this melody in a contrapuntal manner overtop of an accompaniment piano part. Next, a “rubato” section occurs where the tempo quickens with the bassoon having a solo and more improvisatory line overtop of an arpeggiated-like accompaniment. Then the music returns to an “A tempo” that features the oboe and bassoon in dialogue of a sixteenth quintuplet motif and a triplet eighth with sixteenth motif, while the piano continues its arpeggiated-like accompaniment. A short “Lontano” section with a long cantabile line in the oboe and bassoon leads in the final section of the piece. This includes a quasi-aleatoric line that is slow and lyrical in the oboe and bassoon that gradually rallentando until the very end while the piano continues an accompaniment in a “tempo guisto” manner.

description: As described by the composer the title of the work is “a play on words, a puzzle. This word can be read as affair — in English, it means a dispute, a reason, or an event. Alternatively, it can be broken down into components: “A” — the first letter of my name, “ff” — fortissimo, symbolizing strength and energy, and also a frequent dynamic in this piece, and “air” — the air that is essential for playing the bassoon. This piece reflects my journey toward overcoming the fear of disputes. In the past, I used to bottle up negativity, afraid to express disagreement. Now, I have learned to freely enter discussions, even conflicts, and this has become an important milestone in my personal transformation. Affair also means “a reason,” and my composition plays with a variety of states and emotions that ultimately transform into something very powerful, even slightly defiant.” A-ff-air is a one-movement work that musically begins by exploring the contemplative and lyrical nature of the low register of the bassoon, which gradually accelerandos and becomes more virtuosic with each successive section climaxing with a virtuosic sequential passage of sixteenth notes in the high register of the bassoon. The opening section is marked quarter note equals 93 and consists of short motifs often embellished with grace notes leading to longer note values that crescendo systematically from pianissimo until an arrival at the desired fortissimo dynamic representing the opening up and overcoming fear through the “air” increasing and expanding on the bassoon. The metre through this section changes frequently creating instability by not allowing a consistent pattern to form, which can be interpreted as a representation of the fear and being unsure that the composer initially felt in their journey. The following section marked quarter note equals 107 introduces a couple motifs: 1) six eighth notes that weave around the perfect fifth interval and 2) arpeggiated motion. The arpeggiated motif is first introduced as incomplete skipping over notes in the chord, seen in its first introduced in measure 16 that skips over the third and seventh of the chord, only playing the root, fifth and ninth on the ascend with the flat seventh being introduced on the descend. As the work develops, the arpeggiation becomes more filled in and stabilized representing the answers and confidence that is being built in the composer’s journey. This section continues expanding upon these motifs becoming more virtuosic and aggressive with accents being added into the articulation being used. The next section quarter note equals 82 becomes more disjunct as the intervallic relationships expand creating large jumps between the high and low register of the bassoon. Multiphonics are also introduced into the texture to assist in the intensification of the music. The subsequent section quarter note equals 77 recalls material from the opening in a rubato and recitative character but quickly brings back the arpeggiated motif to lead into the next section quarter note equals 80 that begins the sequential development of the material that consists of full arpeggiated triplet passages with rests in between creating a dialogue texture representing the composer’s back and forth battle with herself and confrontation in her journey. The material continues developing in this manner as the tempo increases next to quarter note equals 93. Eventually, it develops into sixteenth note passages leading to longer note values with the crescendo motif from the opening material in between statements to signify the two worlds coming together slowly to reach a compromise of a virtuosic display of extended sixteenth note passages in a sequential manner. This is a musical representation of the composer finding their confidence and how to deal with conflict. This than leads into a section quarter note equals 127, which brings back the eighth note motif from earlier reimagined that gets developed and variated as a way to reflect on the progress in the composer’s journey. This leads into a section marked quarter note equals 133 that takes the perfect fifth interval from the motif in an accented sixteenth note followed by an eighth note and eighth rest that sequentially builds to the high register. Once this arrival is achieved disjunct arpeggiated motifs take over, but this time in a syncopated manner with rests inserted to throw off the pattern. Overtime, it builds back to an extended and virtuosic display of constant sixteenth notes in the high register of the bassoon. To conclude the piece the various variations on the sixteenth motifs are combined together working its way back down to a final resolution in the low register of the bassoon leading to a fermata quarter note rest to convey the change in the character in the composer’s journey and a moment of silence to reflect on the growth.

description: This is a short one-movement work in a neoromantic style reflecting the harmonic language, sweeping accompaniment, and long lyrical melodic lines. The work opens with a lyrical slurred melodic line in the bassoon overtop of an eighth note arpeggiated bass line on the left-hand and chordal eighth notes in the right-hand of the piano. As it develops the bassoon becomes rhythmically more active incorporating sixteenth notes combined with syncopated motifs such as the last sixteenth of the beat being tied over. Eventually, the bassoon part relaxes back to the original material to conclude the work.

description: This is a one-movement work in a quick tempo that has an unbalanced dance character due to the constantly changing meter and accents throughout. The piece opens with an “Allegro con fuoco” which is a bright and accented section with the instruments trading sixteenth notes to create a larger cohesive phrase. This leads into the second section “scherzando” that continues elements of the previous section, except now the flute has all of the sixteenth notes while the other instruments weave in and out of the line. This continues until a cantabile line in the flute, oboe, and horn emerges from the texture over the constant sixteenths that is now has triplets competing against it creating and consistent rhythmic syncopation in the accompaniment. The rest of the piece continues in this manner until it ritenuto into a F minor chord with a fermata. This allows for a shorten reprise of the first two sections of the piece that is cut short by unison sixteenths on the pitch “F♯” crescending to triple fortissimo to end the piece.

description: This is a short one-movement work that has three main sections. The first section “Improvizatione” is a contrapuntal duet between the flute and bassoon that weaves in and out briefly coming into homorhythmic moments before quickly changing. The second section “Adagio” begins with a pickup by the piano imitating the opening section with a large interval motif in dialogue between the two hands which the flute and bassoon respond in cannon through a polytonal texture. This develops and then fades away into glissandos in the flute and piano that the bassoon responds with a quasi-cadenza featuring the use of a multiphonic. The flute takes over with a passage of harmonics with short interjections from the bassoon and piano to conclude the piece.

This work consists of five short movements in contrasting characters. The first movement “Adagio” has a dolce espressivo melody first presented in the oboe overtop of a long tone accompaniment motif in the clarinet. The melody passes around the ensemble as the texture gets more contrapuntal as more voices enter. There is a middle section that presents a eighth note and rests motif that is homorhythmic in texture. The movement concludes with fragments of the main theme, accompaniment motif, and eighth note motif all combined in the flute, oboe, and clarinet. The next movement “Allegro non troppo” has three main components that are combined together: 1) a repeated sixteenth motif, 2) a syncopated sixteenth note and rest motif, and 3) a lyrical line of long notes. The third movement “Tempo di marcia” opens with the clarinet solo imitating a bugle call playing arpeggiated triplet eighth notes. Accompaniment figures in the ensemble take over leading into the main theme in a march-like style built around a dotted eighth and sixteenth note motif presented in the horn. The theme is fragmented and passed around the ensemble and combined with a lyrical line. There is a brief interrupting middle section “Tempo di polka” consisting of a melody in the flute and offbeats in the other voices. The following movement “Largo espressivo” consists of different ad libitum solos often in a virtuosic manner in dialogue throughout the ensemble. The final movement “Allegro” is centered around a main theme that passes around the ensemble with accompaniment figures. As the movement progresses the texture becomes more active and contrapuntal, developing into a sixteenth scalar ostinato combined with a chorale-like melody leading to a final two chords to conclude the work.

description: This is a one-movement work with two main sections that alternate between energetic and lyrical with moments of virtuosity throughout. The first section “Allegro moderato” features passages of sixteenth notes in the flute that often begin on the second sixteenth of the beat after reacting to a chord in the harp. The harp mainly plays rhythmic chords or passages of arpeggiated sixteenths underneath. As the section develops the flute theme incorporate longer note values as the harp becomes more active and a repeated note motif while the harp plays long note values or has silences. The second section “Andante” has a lyrical and vocal-like melody in the flute mainly built on eighth notes leading to a longer note value, while the harp has an ostinato of quarter notes in the left hand and eighth notes that highlight the harmonies. As it develops it becomes syncopated to rhythmically displace the theme against the harp’s ostinato.The return to the “Allegro moderato” is much more virtuosic with longer passages of sixteenth notes that traverse a larger portion of the flute’s register. The return of the “Andante” adds in embellishments into the flute’s theme. The piece continues alternating between the two sections with each restatement being a shorter fragment of the material until the final statement of the “Allegro moderato” material is the flute playing alone to conclude the work.

description: The title represents the two instruments with Air denoting the flute and glass denoting the accordion. The composer describes that for this work he “tried to imagine a confrontation of elements that really have no serious differences. Antagonism without difference, confrontation without visible contradictions. Alien elements are replaced by stable, gradually capturing the entire musical space, constantly striving for continuum balance.” Musically, this work is a hostile dialogue between the two instruments that are constantly competing to be heard and the focus of the listener. The two instruments often have small fragments that continue to intensify and develop to over take the over for a brief period before starting over or being contrasted by periods of agreement. The work begins with two different disjointed passages between the two instruments that achieve some sort of unification through the introduction of trills and glissandos for a brief moment. However, a return to conflict occurs with triplets in the flute fighting against sixteenth and quintuplet figures in the accordion. This is all framed within changing meters of unconventional types such as 5/4+1/12 with extra beats added on to create extra instability. Eventually, some of the trills begin to line up between the instruments to achieve some moments of clarity within the disagreement and chaos. This climaxes to a very disjointed dialogue between the two instruments leading into a virtuosic display of the accordion taking over. Afterwards, a brief agreement occurs with homorhythm occurring between the instruments in a disjunct string of sixteenth notes. Next, unconventional notation of black noteheads with a line leading to the next note occurs to mimic an improvisatory conversation that wanders around. The work continues in this manner bringing back material and introducing new motifs that alternate between musical disagreement and homorhythm clarity to depict a tumultuous conversation and relationship between two instruments or people.

description: This is a one-movement work that the title takes inspiration from the ancient architectural monument Akkerman Fortress in Odesa dating back to the thirteenth-century that has a rich history of withstanding many sieges and attacks from other various forces. The work begins with a motif of two sixteenths leading to four repeated eighth note in the bassoon. The rest of the ensemble responds to this with fragmentation, while the bassoon slowly develops this motif. As each instrument's fragment or motif expands into ostinato figures it creates a contrapuntal texture with the lines weaving in and out of one another. After the material climaxes the bass clarinet and clarinet trade off a one-measure melodic fragment that leads to a whole note with each successive fragment undergoing a ritardando to set up the next section. This section begins with longer note values that are changing independently in their own pattern in each instrument. The use of frullato is introduced into the texture to explore the different timbres possible throughout the ensemble. A quarter note theme that dynamically swells emerges from this texture in a perfect fifth interval in the alto saxophone and bass clarinet. This develops by the clarinet joining into this theme, while the longer note value texture disappears allowing room for an arpeggiated bass line to take over in the bassoon. As the section is climaxing the bassoon’s bass line rhythmic diminution becomes sixteenth notes to create more energy that leads into a trilled fermata dissonant chord that dies away. The next section is homorhythmic in a more march-like character achieved through either dotted or triplet sixteenth note rhythms. This texture is interrupted by virtuosic cadenza moments by the clarinet. Afterwards, the alto saxophone plays a new theme that incorporates motifs from the march-like section that prompts a contrapuntal treatment of this theme and its fragments in the ensemble before being interrupted by the original homorhytmic march and virtuosic clarinet line. The next section consists of disjunct articulated sixteenth notes that pass around the ensemble creating a interwoven texture. Eventually, the quarter note melody from earlier returns prompting a synthesis of different material and fragmentations from throughout the work to be recombined together creating new textures. This leads into a final brief four-measure chorale-like phrase of half notes that undergoes a ritardando allowing for an accented motif from earlier in homorhythm to surprise the listener to conclude the work.

premiere: never performed
description: This is a short one-movement work in a lively character. It opens with a syncopated three staccato eighth note motif leading to a long note in the flute, followed by two in the bassoon, and then one leading to a beat of triplet eighth notes in the oboe. The second half of the phrase is a homorhythmic statement of an eighth note slurred to a long note. The next section features staccato sixteenths leading to eighth notes that get passed around the instruments. When the bassoon passes the theme to the oboe it introduces a bass line underneath. This leads to fragmentation. Next, the bassoon introduces an ostinato consisting of a disjunct eighth note followed by three triplet eighth notes leading to three eighth notes that are followed by an eighth rest. Overtop of this ostinato are elements from the opening section return. The section continues developing these motifs and recombining different elements. Eventually, a constant line of staccato eighth notes are passed around the ensemble, which the lyrical line from the opening returns overtop of. The various motifs from throughout the piece return to conclude the work.

description: This is a one-movement work with various short sections that are attacca each exploring a different character while employing a variety of extended techniques. The piece combines elements of traditional sound production and harsher, unconventional modern techniques and aesthetics. The opening section “Distant light from the depth” consists of a single repeated note motif that begins as one long tone with rests and evolves overtime to become more rhythmic. Over time various extended techniques and audible exhaling and inhaling from the musicians is incorporated into the texture. This leads into “Windy” that incorporates air noises with small fragments and the one note motif that is now transformed into a note that glissandos stepwise alternating around the ensemble. The next section “Soft and vicious” returns to a thinner texture and calmer character consisting of long tones throughout the ensemble. In the next section “Annoying” the glissando motif is rhythmically shortened and repeated in closer succession to create a more joking character. Then “With gloomy obsession” returns to the previous character and motifs. Next, “Leggierio” utilizes the technique quasi ricochet to create a busy and active texture that allows the piece to climax into an “Like an improvisation” that is a contrapuntal-like texture with multiple motifs that are interacting in a cohesive manner. This then returns to another “With gloomy obsession” section. Next, “Anxious fatality” utilizes extended techniques to develop the single note motif. This develops into “Crystals” where we get a section similar to the opening but with more dissonance. The rest of the piece continues to expand upon the motifs established by different combinations of extended techniques, instrumentation, and combination of motifs to explore the various textures that an ensemble can produce through three main sections: “Interludio I”, “Hidden light”, and “Interludio II”. The final section creates the most active and busiest texture that climaxes with musicians grabbing and throwing a book. Overall, the piece experiments with how a single note can be developed in an ensemble through a variety of short character changes.

description: This piece is a metamorphosis on themes from the musical “Fiddler on the Roof” by Jerry Bock. Anatevka is a fictional shtetl (town) that the characters lived in and eventually were forced out of. In 2014, during the Russian invasion of Ukraine, a town of the same name inspired by the film was established on an empty plot of land near Kyiv as a refuge for thousands of Jewish-Ukrainian people. The piece begins with a grand maestoso section that introduces the first main theme that is developed through slight variations, which eventually leads into a waltz section with a new theme that undergoes development. The final new theme is presented in a Scherzando section. Eventually, the music arrives at the ending Giocoso section that brings back and combines material from throughout, which climaxes into a bassoon cadenza that finishes off the piece.

description: This piece is composed of five short contrasting movements that provide a quick overview of a variety of characters a woodwind trio can achieve. However, none of the movements have been given any titles to denote the character. Overall, the piece is in a style reminiscent of French twentieth-century wind chamber writing similar in style to Eugène Bozza. The first movement is an allegro that has a sneaky character with writing that either has clear melody and accompaniment or unison amongst the members. The second movement is a typical vivace tempo movement with staccato eighths and slurred 16th motifs. The third movement is in a pastoral character with an often lazy feel from the quarter followed by an eighth motif throughout. The fourth movement is another allegro tempo that features trading sixteenths in the flute and clarinet that is combined with a very stereotypical bassoon accompaniment figure of staccato eighth notes in a big interval. As the piece continues the bassoon becomes more melodically involved and the roles in the ensemble switch. The final movement is a bright vivace featuring elements from throughout the piece combined with a repeated sixteenth motif.

description: This work takes inspiration from sacred music and is based on two melodies from the Canon of Sunday on the Week of 5th Holos from the All-Night Vesper, which is an Evening Orthodox Service. Musically, the work is homorhythmic in a chorale style featuring quarter, half and whole notes. It utilizes accents to show where to place the emphasis and slurs to depict a melisma to imitate a vocal-like phrasing to the material. Overall, the work follows principles of voice-leading of a traditional Soprano, Alto, Tenor, and Bass vocal ensemble having each instrument represent a voice type in score order. The voices often move in contrary motion, for example the two clarinets are often in thirds and the bass clarinet and bassoon are in fifths and octaves. As the work develops the material undergoes variations such as displacing a note within the phrase to a different octave, revoicing of chords from closed to open positions, pauses, and the intensification of harmony through the additions of seventh of chords being added. The score is organized through rehearsal letters and numbers to display each row of text and which melody.

description: This is a work that requires the flutist to double and alternate between regular concert C flute and alto flute. Overall, the composer describes the work as “Nature sounds, the fragile 'pizzicato' of a music box, and echoes of Georgian folklore come together in an oneiric mosaic of memories of the composer and his homeland in a whimsical mosaic of memories of the composer and his homeland.” (Tarnopoloski via email 2026) Giya Kancheli was a 20th and 21st century Georgian composer who often combined “the polyphonic melos of traditional Georgian chants with modern components of the Western avant-garde, often shaking the listener to their core.” (Boosey & Hawkes, “Giya Kancheli”), which this work takes inspiration from. The work opens with a “Largo” section starting with a quasi wind chimes motif through long grace note figures consisting of seven or more notes. The alto flute then enters alone using breath noise and color changing from dark to light and back. The flute continues entering on the piano’s rest utilizing other extended techniques to create other nature-like textures. Next, the piano begins to experiment with a variety of extended techniques to get unusual combinations to create a unique sound world. Then a contrasting section has a more mechanical quality as it has a very rhythmically intricate dialogue between the two instruments. The instruments alternate between playing normally and utilizing extended techniques. A return to the opening texture and material follows. Afterwards, a “Lento” section that is more lyrical occurs with half and whole notes in the flute that incorporates extended techniques that alter the pitch such as bisbigliando and multiphonics, while the piano plays open fifths. This is followed by a “Lentamente” section consisting of triplet eighth notes that are disjunct arpeggios overblown while the piano does extended techniques. The next section “Vivace” brings back the rhythmic interplay and has a repeated note sextuplet sixteenth motif. As it progresses the motif intervallically expands. Eventually, a return to the previous section returns briefly to interrupt. The work continues alternating between the different sections and textures established with new variations until a virtuosic flourish nontuplet 64th notes are introduced that are in a dialogue passing back and forth between the two instruments. This continues developing and becoming more contrapuntal and overlapping with other rhythmic values added to conclude the work.

extended_techniques: quarter tones (bsn I, II), singing & playing (bsn I, II); Prepared piano: damping strings with fingers, strike the strings with fingers in thimbles, pluck strings with finger tips, insert cork in specified spots, scratch strings with nails, hit a stick across the frame, metal stick on metal plate, metal stick on strings, rub edge of metal plate on strings,  use palm on the strings, glissando on strings, drawing a figure eight on the strings with your nails
performace_considerations: some score instructions in Russian, aleatoric sections, some graphic notation used, notation used at times where only a note head is given with a black line until performer changes notes, 5:4 note groupings
description: This piece is three movements inspired by the Greek painter El Greco from the Renaissance era. He is known for his dramatic and expressionistic style that featured elongated figures and phantasmagorical images that married Byzantine traditions with Western painting. The first movement “Tempo sostenuto” has a mysterious character featuring prepared piano creating an eerie effect while the bassoons playing legato phrases in their lowest registers. As the movement progresses the movement intensifies to a faster agitated character depicting what the listener initially perceived was not exactly as it appeared on first glance, common in El Greco’s painting. The second movement “Tempo ad libitum, eccitando” is a much more exciting character with the rhythmic energy being a key feature as majority of the movement has constant eighth notes occurring. This movement is structured around the dialogue and passing of these eighth notes throughout the ensemble. The third movement “Tempo ad libitum, drammatico” is a very energetic and passionate character. The movement opens with sforzando prepared piano motifs responding to dramatic short fragments in the bassoons. This evolves into busy aleatoric accompaniments under short fragments in a call and response texture in the bassoons. This section ends abruptly to allow for the contrasting”sostenuto, religious” ending section to be an effective surprise that features long tones moving in canon reminiscent of renaissance music in a modern re-interpretation.

premiere: 1994 by Members of the Finnish Radio Symphony Orchestra: A. Piipponen (fl), J. Metsäpelto (ob), Kullervo Kojo (cl), Olavi Ojanperä (bsn)
recordings: CD “Compositions by Fridrich Bruk: Lyrical Images” self-released (FBCD-1994)
description: This is a three-movement suite that combines elements of folk music such as melody, rhythm, and harmony. This work was written prior to his immigration to Finland. The first movement “The Endless Wintry Steppe” opens with an “Andante” section that consists of a vocal-like melody that gets passed around the ensemble overtop of chords. This is starkly contrasted with an “Allegro” section that has ominous eighth note chords followed by an eighth rest in the ensemble underneath weaving triplet eighth notes in the flute. As it develops it becomes sixteenth notes in the flute and more lyrical lines are presented in the ensemble consisting of eighth, quarter, and half notes. A two measure return of the opening material occurs with a caesura that is followed by an open fifth whole note chord of the pitches “Bb” and “F” in the ensemble. The following movement “Spring Flow” is in an allegro tempo with an energetic dance-like character. It features a playful theme first presented by the flute that gets fragmented and passed around the ensemble. This is overtop of offbeat staccato eighth notes and half note trills. The final movement “Morning on the Steppe” has a pastorale character with a semplice theme of quarter followed by either an eighth or two sixteenth notes leading to a trill dotted quarter note that is first presented by the flute. This is overtop of dotted quarter note chords and a countermelody comprised of eighth notes with two sixteenth grace notes in the middle. The movement continues developing these motifs until arriving back at the original material to conclude the work.

premiere: July 16th, 2025 in Latina Italy by Giuseppe Brancaccio (bsn)
description: This is a short one-movement work in a neoclassical line that features weaving lines between the two voices. The first bassoon often has a melodic role while the second bassoon provides a countermelody line playing in between the first bassoon’s notes. Often the music is grouped into two measure units that are extended by the other voice entering in the middle connecting into longer phrases. The use of hair pin dynamics occurs frequently throughout. Rhythmically the work consists of only quarter, dotted quarter, eighth and half notes with half, quarter and eighth note rests. The piece begins and often returns to F major with brief tonicizations throughout to arrive at a cadence in D major to conclude the work.

date_written: 1997 in the city of Cherkasy, Ukraine
premiere: 1998 in Cherkasy at Cherkasy Music College for the “Young Composers’ Competition” by Oleh Komlach (fl), Iryna Lisun (pno)
description: This work won the second prize at the Young Composers’ Competition in Cherkasy, Ukraine. It is a short one-movement work that has three contrasting characters in the form of ABCA. Overall the work has a nostalgic feel to it, which one could imagine strolling through the streets of Paris observing the beauty all around. The A section marked “Andante cantabile” features a lyrical and expressive melody consisting of eighth notes often in scalar or small intervals leading to a longer note value. Throughout there are elegant embellishments such as grace notes or sixteenth note pickups. This is overtop of the piano accompaniment consisting of half note chords and a walking bass line on beats 2 and 4, which rhythmically gets flipped when a countermelody of eighth notes is introduced in the top voice. The following B section “Tempo di menuetto” has a lighter and more playful character with a waltz-like feel. The flute plays a melody of primarily eighth and quarter notes overtop of a dotted quarter walking bass line in the left hand and arpeggiaged eighth notes in the right hand of the piano. Next, the C section “Allegretto” is much lively with lots of forward momentum as if depicting a flowing river. The flute has oscillating neighbour tone slurred sixteenth notes, while the piano plays a lilting melody comprised of a quarter followed by an eighth motif overtop of an ostinato waltz-like accompaniment. Eventually, the left hand becomes more active shifting to sixteenth notes, which prompts the flute to expand upon their motif adding in little variations. A final return to the opening material occurs to conclude the work as if the listener is returning to their starting location of their stroll through Paris.

premiere: December 8th, 2024 in Latina, Italy by Arianna Bisceglia (fl), Raffaele Gaizo (cl), Giuseppe Brancaccio (bsn)
key: A major, Eb major, E major
description: This is a one movement work that uses elements of structure and phrasing combined with more modernist and jazz influence harmonies throughout. The piece explores a variety of key areas by constantly shifting around searching for a key area to call home depicting nature settling in before the sun rises for the day. The texture of the piece often features a clear melodic line overtop of accompaniment figures that interweave all together. It opens with a quarter note theme in the flute with an eighth note motif being traded between the clarinet and bassoon. As it develops the bassoon begins to expand the eight note into a longer cohesive bass line that weaves around using arpeggiated and scalar motion, while the clarinet becomes a countermelody line that eventually morphs into a lower harmony of the flute theme. This texture change prompts the bassoon to play syncopated eighth notes to create rhythmic energy into the first of many key changes. As the music goes through the various key changes the material from the opening section continues to develop and be varied to create different characters and texture for each key change until finally arriving back in the opening key area of A major with the original material. However, the final cadence is abruptly interrupted by the second key area of Eb major to end the piece in an unstable condition still searching for their home key area. This leaves the listener in anticipation like someone waiting to watch the sunrise right before it is going to happen.

published: Counterpoint Music Library Service in 2009 [score in concert pitch]
recordings: CD: Aeolian Woodwind Quintet, CBC Records, catalog #1142 at Glenn Gould Studio (1996)
performace_considerations: aleatoric sections, some acting instructions “remain motionless”
description: This is a six-movement suite with no intended order or combination of movements. However, the composer suggests that a good mix of slow and fast movements is ideal. There is also the option to perform the work spatially with the clarinet on stage because they control the flow of the piece, and the other performers distributed around the hall with them ideally hidden from view. At the very end they should come onto the stage. Each of the movements were written separately over a twenty-year period without the titles they now have for various purposes. The titles were added once all of them were completed, revised, and combined together for The Aeolian Winds in 1993. The titles are inspired by American writer Ambrose Bierce’s “The Devil’s Dictionary” which is a satirical dictionary with common words accompanied with a humorous or satirical definition. Therefore, the titles of the movements give clues and insight about the interpretation of each movement’s character and the role they play within the suite and ensemble. “The "Dictator" is the clarinet, who initially inspires his people into action, then stomps them into the ground when they grow too independent. Who is the "Idiot.," the clarinet or the bassoon? The "Cynic" is mocking and angular. The clarinet finds himself "Alone" as his companions, the horn and the bassoon, drift away into the meaninglessness of the universe - he eventually leads the whole group to his point of view, but reality drifts back to equilibrium. "Eulogy" is a strange lament. "Reality" is illusory and elastic, rhythmically unpredictable.”53 Musically “Dictator” is in an allegro tempo and features a prominent clarinet line mainly consisting of sixteenth notes overtop of accompaniment figures in the ensemble derived from the clarinet’s opening rhythmic motif. Eventually, it leads into an aleatoric section combining the different motifs from throughout the movement. This then returns to the original texture. The “Idiot” is in a molto moderato tempo and features an improvisatory-like line in the clarinet overtop of rhythmic accompaniment. As it develops the ensemble fragments the clarinet line in a dialogue-like texture. The “Cynic” is in an allegro tempo presents a theme consisting of large intervals in the oboe with accented interruptions from the ensemble. The flute then presents a more compact theme while the accompaniment is now occurring simultaneously underneath. The movement continues with different variations and fragmentations in a contrapuntal texture before returning to material similar to the opening. “Alone” is in an andante tempo consisting of a weaving chromatic eighth note line in the flute and oboe that becomes more syncopated with the introduction of sixteenth notes and ties. Eventually, the entire ensemble joins in on this in a canon-like texture switching from their original accompaniment texture. “Eulogy” is in an adagio tempo consisting of legato and slurred figures in the flute in contrast to “strange” syncopated and accented figures in the horn. This is often overtop of chordal-like textures of half notes in the ensemble with moments of dialogue. “Reality” is in an allegro moderato tempo is mostly homorhythmic in texture with brief moments of fragments that pass around the ensemble. The motifs contrast between virtuosic passages of sixteenth notes and more chorale-like quarter note triplets.

dedicated: In memory of those who died for Ukraine
premiere: never performed
key: C# minor, D minor, B♭ minor
description: Stepurko’s style is characterized by rich polyphonic texture, modern harmonies, sophisticated timbral comparisons and original reinterpretations of melodic motifs from Ukrainian folklore and religious sources. This work has a lyrical character through a cantabile bassoon line throughout overtop of accompaniment figures in the orchestra (piano) structured through short sections of varied material combined together. The opening section is marked quarter note equals 46 and features an arpeggiated triplet motif that leads to a longer note value. It begins as three triplet notes that expands as it develops to become a whole passage of triplets that transverses from the tenor to the low register. The accompaniment has a rhythmic ostinato consisting of three eighth notes leading to three tied quarter-eighth notes. Overtime, this shifts to become a dialogue texture responding to the bassoon during their longer note values. The next section “Poco piu mosso” has a more vocal-like theme in the tenor register of the bassoon with written-out ornamentation. The third section “Piu mosso” combines elements of the two earlier themes into one long cohesive theme overtop of repeated eighth note chords to create forward rhythmic momentum. Then a “Meno mosso” section featuring a two-sixteenth followed by a dotted quarter note motif occurs in a sequential motion ascending and descending across the range of the bassoon. The accompaniment alternates between being in homorhythm with the bassoon and rhythmic ostinatos of chords. In the orchestral version there is an added cadenza at the end of this section at the end of measure 57 not included in the piano version. A final section that returns to the opening material occurs. However, the theme in the bassoon is now rhythmically augmented overtop of the original rhythmic ostinato in the accompaniment. The original material is developed differently with new variations to conclude the work.

premiere: June 14th at 4pm in Indianapolis, USA at Eidson-Duckwall Recital Hall at Butler University for the 2025 International Double Reed Society Conference by dedicatee (bsn), Catherine Bringerud (pno)
key: G minor, G major, F major, E minor
description: This is a short one-movement work in ternary form that is inspired by Ukrainian folk dance and music. The A section “Allegretto” consists of an energetic dance-like melody featuring staccato eighth and sixteenth notes leading to tenuto quarter notes. Grace notes are added into the melody to imitate folk singing. The piano plays accompaniment figures such as ostinato eighth notes or syncopated chords in the left hand changing with the harmony every couple of measures combined with occasional counter melody in the right hand. In the middle of the section the music changes character with a shift from G minor to G major. The B section “Andante sostenuto” features a more lyrical folk-like melody based around scalar and arpeggiated motion consisting of eighth and quarter notes overtop of an accompaniment piano part consisting of a bass line in the left hand and figures in the right hand to support the harmonic changes.

premiere: January 2023 in Chuhuiv, Ukraine by Mykhaylo Mamin (fl), Anna Mamina (pno)
description: This is a short one-movement work in ternary form that takes inspiration from barcarolles, which are a Venetian boat song tradition sung by gondoliers. Typically, they have a gentle and rocking rhythm in 6/8 or 12/8 time signature to depict the rocking motion of a boat gliding over waves. The work begins with a short piano introduction that introduces the two rocking rhythmic motifs of 1) quarter note followed by an eighth, and 2) dotted eighth, sixteenth, and an eighth note. Often throughout the A Section “Tempo di Barcarolla” the flute and piano are utilizing these motifs either in a homorhythmic texture or in a dialogue manner such as the motif being passed back and forth while the other has a long note value. Overall, the flute part is very lyrical and vocal-like consisting of scalar and arpeggiated motion. At the end of the A section, the piano becomes more active introducing arpeggiated sixteenth notes trading between the hands to set up the new character for the next section. The B section changes character to become more anxious and tense. The thematic material consists of two main elements: 1) an offensive marcato dotted figure in the piano’s left hand and 2) a pleading descending line in the flute. It begins with a string of sixteenth notes that weave around the harmony while the flute plays a syncopated melodic line overtop. The return to the A section begins with variation as the flute plays a highly ornamented line of sixteenth notes filling in the theme with step-wise passing tones and arpeggiated intervals from earlier, while the piano brings back the ostinato accompaniment. Next, the flute returns to the original melody while the right hand of the piano takes over the sixteenth notes, which later transfer to the bass line. As it progress the flute plays a richly ornamented contrapuntal line of sixteenth notes that fill in the original theme, while the piano plays an ostinato figure underneath. Finally, the flute returns to the original melody when the piano’s right hand takes over the melody with a new syncopated motif introduced in the left hand to conclude the work.

instrumentation: cl, bsn, pno, guitar, vla, db, drums
premiere: not performed yet
description: This is a short one-movement work in a jazz style that features a head (melody) with some variations throughout to imitate the idea of improvisation in the clarinet and bassoon. This is overtop of a texture of a stereotypical jazz combo of piano, guitar, bass, and drums. However, Novokhatsky also includes a classical element of a chordal accompaniment played by a viola, which is unusual in jazz idioms. The work opens with a brief accompaniment introduction with typical jazz motifs played by the combo to set up a bossa nova feel for the piece. The bassoon then enters with the head that is based around the perfect fifth interval. Eventually, the clarinet enters as the head begins to undergo slight variations. The texture between the clarinet and bassoon is mostly homorhythmic in unison or consonant harmonies such as a perfect fifth. Next, the clarinet becomes more virtuosic playing a string of eighth notes that noodle around while the bassoon plays a more arpeggiated and bass line passage underneath, which is a variation of the double bass line. Eventually, a return to the original head in similar texture occurs to bridge into another variation. Finally, another return to the head occurs with a brief coda in the combo of jazz idioms to conclude the work occurs.

premiere: 2017 at Sumy College of Music by Viktoriia Khorolska (bsn)
description: This is a one movement work with four main sections that combines elements of folklorism in a fantasia style. The work opens with a cadenza in a very improvisatory manner featuring virtuosic passages traversing throughout the range of the instrument. The next section “Moderato” is an energetic dance featuring sequential passages of staccato sixteenth and eigth notes ornamented with grace notes and triplet sixteenth or duple thirty-second notes to create a folk-like character. As it develops a rhythmic motif of dotted eigth followed by a sixteenth note is introduced adding more momentum into the phrase. Next, a “Meno mosso” section takes the theme from the previous section and develops it into a virtuosic passage of constant thirty-second notes. This is followed by a short “A tempo” section that makes the theme disjunct by inverting it into larger intervals. The final section brings back the dotted rhythmic motif from earlier combined with elements from the cadenza-like opening, which leads into a “Largamento” providing one final improvisatory statement to conclude the work.

dedicated: Yuri Vasilevich for the international saxophone competition “Kyiv-Paris Selmer”
premiere: 2002 at the competition
performace_considerations: accelerando/ritardando beaming used
description: This is a one-movement work that explores the melodic capabilities of the bassoon in an avant-garde aesthetic. The saxophone, flute, and bassoon versions have been used as mandatory pieces for competitions in Ukraine. The beginning begins with longer note values that use dynamics and glissando to create moments of intensity. There are motifs with grace notes commonly associated with bird motifs throughout history. This leads into an eighth note melody with the bird motifs from the beginning interrupting the line. This leads to a moment of accelerando and ritardando beaming on a repeating note imitating the chirping of a bird. Afterwards the melody becomes more disjointed with larger intervals used. Eventually, this develops into virtuosic moments of thirty-second notes in different groupings such as five and seven that sequentially lead to the high register of the instrument, like a bird attempting to take flight but unable to achieve this due to their broken wing. This leads into a more aggressive syncopated section of accented eighth and sixteenth notes. Eventually, a more lyrical line and the bird motif emerge in the accented passage to conclude the piece.

premiere: November 24th, 1999 at Stanislav Lyudkevych Concert Hall at Lviv Philharmonic by Myron Bloshchychak (fl), composer (bandura)
recordings: CD: 1) Mystery Instrumental music of Oksana Herasymenko - YouTube 1) Vadym Bezanyuk (sax) (https://youtu.be/x3odudgMNCQ?si=DX8i9w08ixkl7Qeo) 2) Oleh Revutskyi (sax) (https://youtu.be/GxVTGeSQFZo?si=or7OwUruH1BPwbJp) 3) Dmytro Pylypchak (cl) , Elehiya Strun (banduras) (https://youtu.be/ACdEBpjDR0o?si=NyQL953pv4RvCsdj)
description: This is a short one-movement work that features a beautiful and moody folk-like melodic line overtop of lush harmonies with a nostalgic character. The work begins with a grandiose introduction marked “Andantino molto cantabile” comprised of an arpeggiated figure. After a fermata on the dominant chord, the flute enters with a vocal-like theme mainly in stepwise motion with dramatic larger leaps that rhythmically consists of half, quarter, eighth and dotted quarter notes. Underneath the piano plays arpeggiated motifs that are often syncopated in the right hand. As the piece progresses the B theme the flute moves to the higher register. The piano then takes over the theme in a polyphonic interlude that adds virtuosic flourishes near the end. The flute then re-enters with the B theme now a perfect fifth lower, while the piano now incorporates triplet figures into the accompaniment to conclude the work.

premiere: unknown
recordings: YouTube: 1) Composer (fl) (https://youtu.be/__uLhye5Oto?si=8IP6AkAm7ZBs_zBB) 2) Anton Churikov (fl) (https://youtu.be/UVLLZ62hylQ?si=vMeyLgK3f-0iQeJl) 3) Karina Dryshlyuk (fl) (https://youtu.be/pViiEZCs9Bk?si=8W5uRwOOI_vC8VLB) 4) Olena Serik (fl) (https://youtu.be/W_vcig5KuJk?si=Khn_Q179aAjno3yy)
description: This work is based around a folk like theme that takes inspiration from the music of Bukovyna in Lviv oblast of Ukraine. The structure of the piece presents a simple theme that utilizes folk elements such as Ukrainian scales and ornamentation such as glissandos to imitate singing, which then continually becomes more and more virtuosic as it develops. After the theme is presented a flourish of thirty-second notes cascades up and down the bottom and middle registers of the flute. This sets up the motif of thirty second notes cascading throughout the rest of the piece. Other virtuosic motifs incorporated are tremolos and the use of frullato. Also, as it develops the flourishes and technical passages become more disjunct going from scalar, to arpeggiated to large intervals. Eventually, a contrasting section occurs that consists of staccato eighth notes with mordents that begin on every beat but then shift to just the second beat creating a syncopated-like feel. It comes back a section time to conclude the work.

premiere: never performed
performace_considerations: both parts use bass and treble clef
description: This is a short one-movement work in a moderato tempo in three main sections. The A section begins with a lively melody of staccato eighth notes and sixteenths in the first bassoon combined with staccato eighth note and eighth rest accompaniment in the second bassoon, which weaves in and out of moments of homorhythm with the occasional moment of extra notes when the first bassoon has a quarter note. The B section is more of a dialogue between the two parts. The second bassoon introduces a dotted eighth note and sixteenth motif underneath a half note in the first bassoon. This alternates with a similar line of eighth notes and sixteenths in both parts. Next, this is contrasted by a more legato melodic and vocal-like line in the first bassoon overtop of a string of eighth notes that is mostly scalar with the occasional moment of large intervals. Eventually, a return to the dotted eighth and sixteenth note motif occurs with a new melody of an eighth note leading to an accented dotted quarter note in a descending sequential manner. The piece concludes with a reprise of the A section.

extended_techniques: glissando, key clicks, multiphonic, slap tonguing, sing & key click, sing & play, tongue ram
performace_considerations: There are aleatoric sections. written using some graphic notation 1) note heads with black line until changing notes 2) note beamings that follow contour of phrase extending into two staves 3) squiggles for how much vibrato to use 4) timing in seconds for how long a motif or section lasts 4) no beaming utilized 5) unspecified pitch where notes continue upwards with an x as the notehead.
description: This work is a virtuosic display that pushes the possibilities of extended techniques and tone colors available on the flute that explores unconventional ways of notating and writing music. At the beginning of the piece is marked “Rubato Allegretto” denoting an improvisatory character with forward momentum. The work opens with an unspecific length of a low “D” that then cascades to the upper register of the flute achieved by accelerando beaming. Next, the introduction of key clicks occurs to provide contrasting sound effects through the quick switching between regular playing and key clicks within a phrase, which creates a groove to the music. This is then contrasted with unspecific note values that manipulate the use of vibrato on the flute that crescendo to fragmented motifs in between each statement. Eventually, the key click motif returns that initially is dominating the texture but overtime fades into the background. The music then returns back to the vibrato exploration but not with longer more lyrical passages between slurred unspecific rhythmic values. The work continues in this manner alternating between the key click motif and other extended technique explorations: 1) glissando, 2) multiphonic 3) singing and playing. Over time these extended techniques begin to incorporate into the key click motif when the flutist performs key clicks while singing specific syllables. Finally the use of aleatoric sections appears to conclude the work.

premiere: 1973 at NMAU for a concert hosted by the Student Union of Young Composers by Roman Ivanchenko (bsn), Yulian Pechenyi (vln), composer (pno)
key: none used - folk scales and harmonies
performace_considerations: accelerando beaming (bsn)
description: This is a two-movement work taking inspiration from Western Ukrainian folk music and culture. The first movement “Evening in the Mountains” (Vechir v horakh) is a recitative marked “Parlando, rubato” and is a dialogue between the ensemble that becomes more active, virtuosic and polyphonic as it progresses. It begins with a pedal on the pitch “G” in the piano with a atheme in the violin overtop, which the bassoon responds to with a variation of. The next statement is more urgent marked “Imperativo” featuring faster rhythmic note values in the solo line in the violin with chords on sfzordano chords on the downbeats of the measures. This accelerandos into a “Piu mosso” and becomes more virtuosic with double stops and thirty second notes added into the texture of the violin part, while the bassoon plays a bass line. This then becomes a polyphonic texture of a scalar passage being offset by a beat in the bassoon and violin while the piano plays tremolo chords.  This texture continues developing until the violin and bassoon have separate and individual lines in a polyphonic texture leading to a final chord that morendos in the ensemble. The second movement “Wedding in the Field" (Vesillya na polonyni) is a rondo marked “Allegro vivacissimo.” The A section features a two-measure accented motif comprised of half, quarter, and a eighth leading to a dotted quarter note. This is overtop of various accompanimental textures such as chords and scalar eighth note passages. The B section is marked “Dolce” and has a more transparent texture with a homorhythmic line of quarter and eighth notes in the violin and bassoon with interjections of a two sixteenth and a eighth motif from the piano. The C section features a dance line melody in the violin with a bass line in the bassoon that trades off with the piano. Eventually, the three instruments come together and develop into indpedent polyphonic lines with the bassoon taking over the melody marked as a solo. Each time the A section returns it becomes more virtuosic and rambunctious like a Zabava (party) progresses during the night at a wedding.

premiere: unknown
description: This is a short one-movement work inspired by the picturesque scenery of the mountains and forest of the Carpathian region in Western Ukraine. The work opens with a flute cadenza using sixteenth notes moving in scalar motion. Next, the piano enters at the “Andantino” section playing a countermelody of sixteenth and quarter notes underneath the flute melody consisting of the same rhythmic values. The melodic content begins to shift to using more folk harmonies.Each phrase continues to build intensity through dynamic increase, added ornamentation, thicker harmonies and the tempo speeding up. This leads into an “Allegretto” section that is a passage of sixteenth notes built on a repeated note motif overtop of long note value chords in the piano. As it progresses it becomes more slurred and the tempo decreases leading into an “Andante” section. The work continues in this manner alternating between more lyrical slower section and more lively dance-like sections.

published: self-published available through Sheet Music Plus Press
premiere: January 22nd, 2022 in Chamber Hall at National Symphony Orchestra of the Polish Radio in Katowice, Poland by dedicatee (bsn)
performace_considerations: treble clef is used occasionally, low register double tonguing section
description: This work is a five-movement suite based on Western Ukrainian folklore and music. The first movement “Carpathians is calling you” opens with a drone-type section on the pitch “D” that is interrupted with grace notes that grows and then dies away into a long silence. From the silence and dance-like melody inspired by Hutsul folk music emerges the occasionally gets thrown off by meter changes. The second movement “Morning in the mountains” is a slow lyrical melody in the tenor register that gradually expands with each sequence into a quasi-cadenza-like moment before restarting again now in the upper register. The third movement “Life of a wild forest” opens with a repeated staccato and grace note motif that grows and dies away twice. The second section is an uneven dance that is metrically grouped as 3+2 that features large intervallic jumps, flourishing runs, and double tonguing. The fourth movement “Interesting Hutsulian village” has an opening lyrical melody with an aggressive low register articulated section built on a motif of two beats of looping sixteenths and accented eighth notes that expands into a quasi-cadenza-like motive to return to a variation on the opening melody. The final movement “Dance with a beautiful Mavka” is an energetic and light waltz-like motif that gets interrupted by a measure of duple to depict the danger lurking for the young man dancing with the Mavka who according to folklore is unknowing being enticed and lured to his death.

premiere: 2013 in Ukraine by Igor Iermak (fl)

key: B♭ major, C major, F major
description: This is a one-movement work with elements and motifs reminiscent of a Vivaldi bassoon concerto combined with neoclassical harmonic language and influence of liturgical music. The opening is a short twelve measure “Moderato” orchestral introduction presenting the main theme in a light and playful character through pizzicato. The bassoon then joins in over this texture with a slurred and dolce espressivo version of the theme. This leads into the next “Allegro” section that is a flurry of scalar sixteenth notes as an orchestral interlude. The third main section “Adagio religioso” the bassoon re-enters in the same legato character but much slower this time. The theme is overtop of a more chordal and legato string accompaniment that is arco. Then a return to “Moderato” occurs which mostly consists of long tones and a flourishing scale that goes into a tremolo motif in the strings, which the bassoon takes over. Then another return to the “Adagio religioso '' occurs as an orchestral interlude to return back to the opening “Moderato” legato theme with a contrapuntal string accompaniment. This leads to the next main section “Presto '' which features a fragment sixteenth melody that develops in a longer, more cohesive phrase in the bassoon overtop of the accompaniment of constant sixteenths in the strings. Eventually, once this section winds down we arrive at the final section “Lento”, which is a contrapuntal treatment of motifs from earlier in the work that elongates into long tones to conclude the piece.

description: This is a five-movement suite from earlier in Fiala’s career which his style was described by Biernel as having a “warmth, astonishing intimacy of expression with a touch of humanity.” (Biernel, 20) The work reflects the composer’s fascination with Hindemith’s writing. The first movement “Allegretto con grazia” utilizes brief motifs in changing meters to create repetitive segments in a contrapuntal texture. There are three main motifs 1) two eighth notes in a descending perfect fourth that ascends a perfect fifth to a quarter note followed by three descending eighth notes, 2) two eighth notes either ascending or descending second, and 3) eighth and two sixteenths in a scalar motion. These motifs are developed by connecting into larger phrases through the interaction of the different voices. The second movement “Chant” is in a largo tempo in an ABABA form. It opens with a Ukrainian folk melody in the horn solo that is subdued and lyrical. This melody gets passed around the ensemble in a contrapuntal texture underneath. The B section is marked “piu mosso” in a more transparent texture featuring a melody divided between two instruments overtop of accompaniment figures in the rest of the ensemble. The movement explores a variety of key centers throughout. The third movement “Fugetta” has an energetic character in an allegro vivace tempo which presents a theme consisting of eighth, tied eighth, and quarter notes in a fugal texture beginning in the bassoon followed by the oboe, clarinet, horn, and finally the flute. The following movement “Intermezzo” is in a moderato espressivo tempo that takes a theme and switches it between different textures 1) homorhythmic passages, 2) trading off, and 3) solo playing. The last movement “Finale” in an allegretto pomposo tempo. This movement also takes a couple motifs that are developed and fragmented through variations and changes to texture such as contrapuntal, trading off and cannon entry like an echo as it progresses. The main motif in this movement is two ascending eighth notes to a dotted eighth note that descends to a sixteenth and eighth note. However, as it progresses the direction and intervals change. Overall, this work demonstrates Fiala’s rejection of avant-garde idioms. It shows his preference for classical forms and influence of Ukrainian folk music with transparent textures, harmonic dissonance, and incisive rhythms.

description: This is a short one-movement work, which is a virtuosic display that would be a great encore type piece for a recital. The piece opens with a piano introduction that is “off” and not presenting a typical waltz pattern. The flute then enters with an endearing staccato eighth note melody which prompts the piano to switch to a typical waltz accompaniment. This melody in the flute quickly becomes a virtuosic display of sixteenth notes cascading up and down the registers of the flute. First it is slurred and then becomes articulated with a repeated note motif introduced. The piano switches roles and responds briefly with fragments of the motifs when the flute is resting. Eventually, a “docle” section emerges with a vocal-like slurred melody in the flute and an accompaniment ostinato in the piano. Very quickly, the character shifts back to the energetic and articulated one from previous to conclude the work.

description: This is a four-movement work that uses Kolyadky (Ukrainian Christmas Carols) ranging from very well-known and more obscure songs. The first movement “Andante” begins with a serene prelude in a call and response manner that introduces the carol Boh predvichnyi narodyvsya (Eternal God was born). The next section “Andante moderato” is followed by a contrapuntal treatment of Oy, bachyt’ Boh, bachyt’ Savaof (Oh God Sees, the Almighty Sees) featuring the melody weaving between the flute, oboe, clarinet, and horn overtop of a bass line in the bassoon. Finally, the movement closes with Vselennaya veselysya (Universe, have fun!) in two contrasting characters. First, a energetic “Moderato” featuring the melody and spirited countermelody with sixteenths and second, a “Maestoso” in a choral manner. The second movement Allegro is in an ABA form. The A section begins with Na nebi zirka (Star in the sky) is a lively dance-like character with a constant stream of sixteenth notes in the accompaniment. Next, Nova radist’ stala (A new joy became) is introduced featuring a legator four measure phrase that rotates around the ensemble in different instrument pairings overtop of a staccato ostinato. Then Vozveselimsya vsi razom nyni (Let us have fun all together now) takes over in a similar character to the opening of the piece. The contrasting B section follows that consists of short alternating “Largo” and “Allegro” sections in a manner that the faster section is chasing after the slower to depict the character of the carol Irod-tsar za Khrystom Hanyavsya (King Herod chased after Christ). This eventually returns to the A section that brings back all of the previous material in a slight variation and new tonicizations. The third movement “Largo lamentoso, poco rubato” based on Ne plach, Rakhyle (Don’t cry, Rachel) is an oboe solo with a virtuosic cadenza overtop of accompaniment figures in the rest of the ensemble. Occasionally, the other instruments take over the melody in an interlude fashion. The final movement “Allegro vivo” begins with Radist’ nam sya yavyla (Joy has been revealed to us) consisting of a melody overtop of a constant stream of repeated eighth notes. Eventually, Vo Vyfleyemi nyni novyna (There is News in Bethlehem Now) is introduced into the opening texture that continues on. Next, a fugal treatment of Rozhdestvo Khrystove (The Nativity of Christ) occurs before a final section that combines elements from earlier, which builds into a “Poco a poco stringendo” to conclude the piece.

key: I (D major), II (D minor), III (G major) IV (G major), V (E♭ major)
description: This is a five-movement suite in a neoclassical style combining polyphonic and homorhythmic textures. The first movement “Allegretto” is energetic and rhythmic with two main sections. The first section has a bass line in the bassoon and a melody of eighth notes, quarter notes and tied notes in the oboes. This progresses into becoming syncopated with the use of rests inserted. The second section consists of homorhythmic syncopated eighth notes. The next movement “Allegro” opens with a staccato quarter note with a rest on the second beat accompaniment in the oboes underneath a melody in the bassoon. This develops into a homorhythmic line of quarter notes to lead into the second section. It consists of a bass line in the bassoon with a motif consisting of quarter note and three eighth notes in the oboe that develops and variates. This is contrasted with homorhythmic moments of quarter notes or various groupings of eighth notes with an eighth rest. A return to the opening material occurs with the melody in the first oboe this time. This leads into a final homorhythmic accented quarter note section into a sforzando piano on the pitch “C” crescending into three accented eighth notes in an upper neighbour motion. The third movement “Moderato” consists of two main sections. First, long tones combined with a constant stream of eighth notes passed around the ensemble. Second, homorhythmic half notes that alternated between on the beat and time over the bar line leading to two dotted quarter notes to distort the metrical feel of 3/4. This develops back into the eighth note material from earlier. The following movement “Moderato con moto” is mostly homorhythmic, consisting of quarter and half notes with the occasional moments of melody and accompaniment texture. The final movement “Allegretto” consists of sections that begin more homorhythmic and develop into more polyphonic writing with a main motif introduced for each section such as an ascending scalar line of dotted eighth and sixteenth note.

premiere: composer does not know
description: This is a short one-movement work in ABAB with a brief coda. The A section features a lyrical slurred theme in the flute overtop of a repeated note motif that is followed by sequential eighth notes that first begin in small intervals and become more disjunct into larger intervals. The flute melody features stepwise and neighbour motion with small intervals. A sighing motif of a descending fifth is introduced at the end of the phrase that then gets incorporated throughout the following phrases. In the B section the piano continues utilizing the same material from the previous section but in new combinations, while the flute’s character switches to a more energetic and dance-like character with syncopated figures utilized. After the return of the B material is a brief coda consisting of some fragments of previous material in dialogue between the two instruments. In the return of the A material it is much more chromatic and explores many tonicizations. As well, the repeated note material sneaks into the flutes theme creating more of a dialogue between the flute and piano.

premiere: 2018 in Kyiv at the I. Karabits Competition of Young Composers by Ivan Iovenko (bsn), Khrystyna Yurko (pno)
description: This work won second prize at the I. Karabits Competition of Young Composers when it was premiered. It is an original theme with five variations showcasing the virtuosic and lyrical capabilities of the bassoon. The opening section begins with a dolce piano introduction in a moderato tempo presenting the triplet rhythmic motif that will appear in the theme. Next, the bassoon enters with a cantabile theme based on triplet eighth notes in various motions from arpeggiated, neighbour, and scalar that lead to a tied quarter-eighth note. The first variation “Allegro giocoso” has an energetic and playful character that is stereotypical of the bassoon through staccato sixteenth notes leading to an accented eighth note. This is overtop of syncopated accompaniment figures in the piano. The next variation “Moderato” turns the theme into eighth notes in an arpeggiated motion overtop of chordal writing in the piano. The third variation “Allegro” turns the theme into repeated staccato sixteenth notes with occasional slurs to bring out elements from the theme. This is combined with syncopated figures of eighth note leading to a quarter note in the piano. At the end the bassoon line becomes fragmented, while the piano takes over the constant sixteenth notes. The following variation “Allegro molto” is a more lyrical character with slurred quarter note triplets and half notes in the bassoon overtop of chordal writing with unexpected syncopations in the piano. The final variation “Vivace” is a virtuosic display of sequential sixteenth note passages and fragmented motifs that are in dialogue between the bassoon and the piano. This leads to a dramatic trill in the bassoon while the piano ritardando a motif reminiscent of the introduction material to set up one final cantabile phrase overtop of a D major7 chord in the piano.

key: D minor, A minor, B♭ major, E♭ major
description: This is a one-movement work that features lots of shifting characters and tonality often from major to minor or quickly tonicizing other key areas briefly. The opening section “Moderato” opens with a lyrical theme in the winds with interjections from the piano during their long notes or rests. After this statement a marcato espressivo section begins which combines double tongued sixteenth note passages in between statements of the theme in the winds with thick accompaniment figures in the piano. Eventually, a lyrical counter melody in the flute and other short motifs in the other winds are presented. This leads to a combination of all the short motifs occurring at once while the clarinet plays a more energetic solo. The next section “Lento” features a rhythmic dissonance by having half the ensemble in 6/8 playing a lilting quarter and eighth note melody while the other half simultaneously plays a passage of sixteenth notes leading to two eighth notes. Eventually, it becomes rhythmically consonant with the sixteenths becoming sextuplets. This returns to a reduced opening section which concludes with a virtuosic flourish of notes in rhythmic dissonance as the flute plays 14, the clarinet 11, and the piano 15 notes. The following section “Rapido” is a virtuosic piano solo with constant sixteenth notes. Eventually, the winds join in playing either sixteenth note passages or lyrical fragments. Next, a “Subito largo” section of three measures occurs in a chordal texture. The next section “Vivo” has an eighth note accompaniment in the piano underneath a leggiero melody of eighth and quarter notes first presented by the bassoon. This continues to be developed while other accompaniment and counter melody motifs are incorporated creating different contrapuntal textures throughout the section such as arpeggiated eighth note triplets and long notes with trills. Eventually the “Lento” section reappears leading into an “Andantino” section with rhythmic dissonance again consisting of scalar sixteenth note passages underneath a lilting triplet melody. Next, a “Vivace” section featuring a vocal-like melody in the horn overtop of weaving eighth note passages in the ensemble and a bass line in the left hand of the piano. Eventually, the winds come together playing the theme tutti overtop of thick accompaniment figures in the piano. This leads into a “Meno mosso” section with a similar theme in contrapuntal writing. The work ends with a “Calmo” section that is a chorale-like texture in the winds overtop of a triplet eighth note accompaniment in the piano.
It was a required chamber piece for his students

description: This is a one-movement concerto that explores a numerical system throughout the work centered around the year it was written 1991. First then is one bassoonist and nine cellists performing. The structure of the piece is based off the length it takes to pronounce the year. The work is broken down into four main sections that get shorter as it goes based off “One-Thousand”, “Nine-hundred”, “Ninety”, and “One”. Also, there are two main musical material that differ based on if the section begins with either a “1” or a “9”. The 1 sections are characterized by effective drama, sharp increases and decrease, recitative quality, dissonance, richness of tone. There is a contrast between unison and abrupt chords in a monorhythmic texture in the cellos. The bassoon participates in this by beginning and ending the work on a repetitive pitch “C#”. The nine sections are characterized by a lyrical and contemplative character with soft dynamic and timbre expressed through a flexibility of metric organization that is constantly changing. Compared to the 1 section that is mainly in 4/4. The work switches between fast and slow sections as well to create more of a contrast between the sections of the work. The writing for the bassoon is often virtuosic and in a quasi-cadenza manner. There is an exploration of the possible timbral qualities available to the bassoon. This is demonstrated through the graphic notation and directions for how much reed, how much lip pressure or amount of lip versus teeth, and different aspects of vibrato to be playing with, requiring the player to have a great control for subtle changes on the instrument. (Kovalinas, 113-121)
