description: This is a short one-movement work based on Ukrainian folk songs that undergo a variety of contrasting sections from lyrical, humoresque, and virtuosic. The opening section “Moderato piu mosso Agitato” that reoccurs throughout the piece. It consists of an energetic theme in the bassoon of staccato eight and sixteenth notes with the occasional mordent. This is overtop of accompaniment chords on the beats in the strings. The next section “Adagio Lento piu mosso features a lyrical and vocal-like theme in the bassoon in a molto legato manner mainly in step-wise of intervals of a perfect fourth and fifth overtop of a rhythmic ostinato of half note followed by a quarter note providing harmonic support. The following section “Moderato piu mosso” features another new theme in a lyrical style based around of dotted eight and sixteenth followed by two eighth notes overtop of a bass line in the lower strings and an oscillating perfect fifth ostinato in the upper strings. As it develops rhythmic diminution occurs from eight to sixteenths in the upper strings and quarter to eight in the lower strings to create more intensity. An orchestral interlude occurs where the violins take over the melody. A two-measure bassoon cadenza sets up the key change to the same name minor that combines elements from earlier in the section with material from the beginning A section. The following section “Andante” has a lyrical and vocal-like melody comprised of half, quarter, dotted quarter followed by an eighth note rhythm. The strings play accompaniment motifs underneath such as whole notes and oscillating eighth note patterns. Finally, the opening A section returns in a full restatement. This leads into a section that is a synthesize of earlier material ending with an orchestral interlude that sets up an extended bassoon cadenza in a virtuosic manner that traverses throughout the range of the bassoon in an arpeggiated and sequential manner. A final virtuosic section occurs featuring extended passages of sixteenth notes in the bassoon while the strings bring back themes and motifs from earlier underneath leading to one final statement of a variation on the A material to conclude the work.

recordings: YouTube: 1) dedicatee (bsn), Kyiv Soloists Chamber Ensemble, Volodymyr Sirenko (cond) (https://youtu.be/sCNYE1-tmUQ?si=gl_A0zmRNNYzeMaQ) 2) Zachary Senick (bsn), Wesley Shen (pno) (https://youtu.be/0sQlH44tVGM?si=Tpjn8GbGsClirS0b) 3) Taras Yarushevskyi (bsn), Olena Yakunina (pno) movement I only (https://youtu.be/ap_B5lt7-QU?si=O-xMmWivt6HvmeXY) 4) Vladislav Vitruk (bsn), Eugene Getlyuk (pno) movement I only (https://youtu.be/nLACx306nSg?si=DMRiT8FH_Mu8s7n3)
key: I (none used, A♭ Major) II (none used, E♭ Major), III (none used)
description: This is a three-movement concerto that combines a variety of influences and styles throughout. The premiere of the work received rave reviews from Ukrainian musicologists. The work was described by Mariya Zagaykevych as “discovering the enormous expressive opportunities of the bassoon by revealing moments of expressive meditations, pointed dramatic outbursts, and sincere lyricism.” Sofiya Hrytsa described it as “music that does not shock but impresses all that music can be in the highest spiritual and aesthetic level of perfection with the foremost respect to the listener.” (Bila, 231) The first movement “Sinfonia” is structured with contrasting sections connected together through cadenzas. It opens with the soloist playing a long tone on the pitch “A” that dynamically swells. This pitch is thematically important as it reoccurs throughout the Concerto. With each progressive statement the phrase expands creating a full musical line. The next section “Allegretto” has an intense and insistent character through accented eighth notes and technical articulated sixteenth passages often in a sequential or scalar motion. This section is reminiscent in style of the Jolivet Bassoon Concerto. The orchestra first responds with sequential motifs or direct quotes from the main theme. The next section “Meno mosso” features a low C drone with a quasi-improvisatory line in the bassoon that develops back into an orchestral interlude of the Allegretto material, which leads to a bassoon cadenza in a quasi-improvisatory style. This cadenza is more lyrical in nature and features large interval jumps. The next section shifts characters completely to a neoclassical line in the accompaniment involving a quarter note melody with trills overtop of chords reminiscent of the Classical Era. However, this is disturbed by the presence of polytonality with the music entering in a different key a semitone above with a melody that weaves around trying to find the tonality. This leads into another bassoon cadenza overtop of a C drone. Next, an animato section occurs that combines elements from earlier. The accompaniment has quarter notes, chords, and arpeggiated sixteenths, while the bassoon has aggressive accented fragments that develop into material similar to the allegretto. This develops into the bassoon developing the sixteenth note motif in the orchestra in a virtuosic display. Eventually, a variation of the allegretto material returns with larger intervals and longer lines of sixteenths. Another cadenza occurs to connect into the final allegretto section. The next movement “Aria” opens with an orchestral introduction of whole note chords in an impressionist color and tonality. The bassoon then presents a vocal-like theme alone in a cantabile and legato style. The orchestra plays accompaniment figures as the melody develops throughout the rest of the movement. Eventually, the movement concludes with a large virtuosic cadenza of fast arpeggios requiring double-tonguing from the bassoonist and multiphonics. The final movement “Burlesque” opens with tremolo chords in the strings to create an ominous atmosphere before presenting a theme similar to the theme in the first movement’s allegretto. It begins with three accented repeated notes and includes large intervals but outlining slightly different harmonies. The bassoon responds with this melody before presenting a completely new theme centered around two motifs: 1) eighth followed by two sixteenths and 2) three repeated eighth notes followed by a different eighth note slurred a descending semitone into three more repeated eighth notes. This develops into a fragmented section of two slurred eighth notes in a semitone motion that gets displaced by an octave later on. This leads into a more rhythmically dissonant section where the bassoon has a melody in the lowest octave that weaves around using quarter and eighth note triplets, while the accompaniment has a sixteenth note ostinato. The bassoon ends up joining in on the sixteenths before a return to the original motifs. This leads into a final cadenza combining elements from throughout the concerto such as large intervals, sequential sixteenths, and a lyrical descending eighth note line. An andante section follows utilizing the earlier motif but in a different and more cantabile character in a fugal texture with the orchestra. This leads to an accelerando that brings back the opening bassoon solo material to conclude the work.
Patsera’s musical language often utilized extended tonal areas and elements of jazz and atonality.

premiere: March 27th, 1996 in Kyiv by dedicatee (bsn)
recordings: YouTube: 1) Premiere (https://youtu.be/-WAhM6ks-48) 2) Zachary Senick (bsn) and Wesley Shen (pno) 2024 (https://youtu.be/iqaSdou_6Tw?si=vElhEdx70mDeeK7b)
description: This is a one-movement concerto that was inspired by the composer’s trip to Spain on a concert tour in 1994 written for his friend and bassoonist Taras Osadchiy. Therefore, the work features melodic and rhythmic motifs from Spanish folk music combined with elements of neoromanticism with virtuosity moments to bring a breath of fresh air to contemporary music. The work opens with a bassoon cadenza overtop of an ominous chord in the strings. The bassoon enters forte on a high C# in a declamatory manner introducing a couple of the work’s motifs such as the diminished fifth interval and three triplet eighth notes in an upper neighbour motion. This leads into an “Allegro” section where the bassoon alone presents the bass line ostinato based on a rhythmic motif of quarter note, dotted eighth rest, sixteenth note, and quarter note that provides an energetic dance-like character. The orchestra enters taking over the bass line ostinato while the bassoon introduces the fiery main theme that is centered around a string of triplets in upper neighbour motion. This section continues with the bassoon developing the theme while the orchestra plays the ostinato and other accompaniment figures. The next section consists of slurred arpeggiated eighth notes in the bassoon overtop of chords in the orchestra. This leads into a section where the bassoon plays the bass ostinato while the orchestra plays the melody before the bassoon takes over a variation of the theme overtop of accompaniment quarter notes in the orchestra. The next section continues this texture but with a lyrical melody consisting of long note values giving the bassoon the opportunity to showcase a contrasting character. This unwinds into an eighth note ostinato that morphs into the next section “Meno mosso” consisting of a vocal-like melody in the bassoon and a different eighth note ostinato overtop of chords in the orchestra. Finally, a return to an Allegro and virtuosic character occurs comprised of technical triplet passages both articulated and slurred showcasing the capabilities of the bassoon. Eventually, this connects into a rhythmically driven section where the bassoon and orchestra are in dialogue with syncopated fragments going back and forth between them. This develops in the technical climax of the concerto featuring weaving sixteenth note passages overtop of a bass line and off beats in the orchestra. Next, a return to the lyrical section occurs with a harp interlude to lead into a bassoon cadenza. This cadenza is a full display of the technical capabilities of the bassoon featuring double-tonguing and large intervals. Afterwards a return to the opening allegro section occurs. This is followed by an exciting, repeated note section in the bassoon displaying its ability for quick and crisp articulation. Afterwards, another return to the main theme occurs connecting into the final section “Vivo” as a coda featuring motifs from throughout the concerto to conclude the piece.

premiere: November 21st, 1978 by Christopher Weait (bsn), Nancy Antonacci (pno) in Toronto, Canada *The work has never been performed with orchestra
recordings: Cassette 1) Premiere - Canadian Music Centre (AR519) YouTube: Zachary Senick (bsn), Wesley Shen (pno) 2022 (https://youtu.be/Bvf92TU9q98)
description: This is a three-movement concerto that features lots of contrasting and characters throughout with inspiration from a variety of sources such as Argentinian influenced rhythm and harmonies. Zuckert has described this feature of his music by saying that “if they don’t speak for themselves, then I have nothing to say about them except that, I write the way I feel and don’t stick to any particular method or style; each composition has its own character.”102 The first movement “Allegro giocoso” is in ternary form opening with an energetic rhythmic ostinato in the orchestra to set up the character of the theme for the bassoon’s entrance. The theme features staccato eighth notes leading to accented quarter notes on beats two and four of the measure to create a dance-feel, which is contrasted by briefing moments of slurred lyricism. As the theme develops passages of weaving sixteenths notes are interspersed. The B section “Interludio español” is in a lento tempo consisting of a chordal piano introduction with Spanish harmonies that sets up a vocal-like and folk-inspired melody in the bassoon. This leads into a short and virtuosic in a sequential manner in the tenor register. The second movement “Lento meditativo” features a melodic legato line built on arpeggios and scalar motion overtop of carefully placed dissonances in a chordal style in the orchestra. Zuckert also includes optional notes to leave out to assist in facilitating breaths if needed due to the performer being unable to make the entire phrase in one breath. The final movement “Allegro molto, ben ritmico” is composed of many short sections that suddenly shift character. The opening section has a fiery character through the virtuosic articulated fragments of sixteenth notes leading to an eighth note that are in dialogue between the bassoon and orchestra. As it develops the fragments become longer into a full cohesive line. The next section “Alla musette” is a lyrical slurred melody in the upper register of the bassoon. This is overtop of an ostinato comprised of an open fifth chord preceded by a grace in the piano evoking a bagpipe character associated with the musette. A return to the opening material occurs but begins immediately with the full phrase omitting the fragmentation. This leads into a “Meno mosso” section consisting of an espressivo and vocal-like melody in the bassoon overtop of a syncopated staccato accompaniment in the piano to create a juxtaposition of characters from the earlier lyrical sections in the concerto. Another return to the opening material occurs with variations to conclude the work.

performace_considerations: very thick texture for piano reduction with three-stave writing at times
description: This is a two-movement concerto with each structured in an alternation of slow and fast sections displaying many character changes throughout. The work utilizes elements of Ukrainian folk melody, tonality, and dance combined with elements of neoromanticism such as harmonic language and structures. The concerto is dedicated to bassoonist Oleksandr Lytyvnov, who I assumed would have premiered the work in the mid-1970s. The first movement opens with an “Allegro non troppo” opens with a main theme consisting of repeated eighth notes with scalar passages to change harmonies in the bassoon overtop of rhythmically driven chords. As the section develops the melody displaces the notes into different octaves to sound more disjunct. Another variation for the second half occurs turning the rhythm into a syncopation creating more forward momentum. The slow section “Andante” features a lyrical folk-like melody in the bassoon based around eighth, quarter, and dotted quarter notes leading to longer note values overtop of accompaniment figures in the piano. There is also a third staff inserted in the piano throughout with a countermelody line while the bassoon plays longer note values. A short bassoon cadenza in a con animo character presenting scalar material connects into a meno mosso section in a funebre character that presents a eighth note melody that weaves around in the bassoon overtop of chords in an syncopated ostinato in the left hand and counter melody in the right hand. A return to the opening section occurs but starting in the second half of the opening section. This continues developing such as adding virtuosic chromatic sextuplets to connect the harmony changes. This leads into another short bassoon cadenza consisting of a descending eighth note line followed by a group of four thirty-second notes slurred into long notes. Next, an orchestral interlude in a “moderato” tempo occurs bringing back material from the slower sections. A final “Allegro” section occurs featuring a virtuosic double tonguing passage that is in dialogue with the piano. The second movement opens with an “Allegro molto” section beginning with the piano playing a fragmentation that develops adding more of the main theme until finally achieving a full presentation of it. The bassoon then enters playing the dance-like theme overtop of the original fragmentation in the piano until the bassoon arrives at an unexpected low B♭ fermata half note. This prompts a restarting of the theme with a rhythmic ostinato added to the left hand. The solo material and accompaniment continues getting more active and thicker orchestration until arriving at our perfect cadence. Next, an “Andante” section occurs featuring rolled chords in the piano with a vocal-like melody in the bassoon. Eventually, a counter melody is introduced underneath the bassoon’s long notes. A return to the “Allegro molto” material occurs. Afterwards new material is introduced such as a disjunct eighth note passage that always begins on the second eighth note of the measure in the bassoon. This leads into a “Moderato” piano interlude similar to the first movement’s interlude. Finally, the main and largest bassoon cadenza occurs. It is in a virtuosic manner featuring large articulated intervals, trills, and slurred chromatic scalar passages. A shortened reprise of the opening material occurs again leading into a short “Piu mosso” section with motifs from the opening to conclude the concerto.

premiere: 2012 in Kyiv by Serhiy Tsubko (bsn), Kyiv Camerata, Valeri Matyukhin (cond)
description: In Ishchenko’s music he continues the traditions of Lyatoshynsky and Shtoharenko incorporated in his own unique style that often intertwines elements from folklorism, avant-garde and modernism. This is a two-movement concerto. The first movement “Adagietto” opens with an orchestral introduction with long lines that develop into more melodic content overtop of lush harmonies in the strings. Each statement a solo wind emerges first beginning with a two-note fragment in the flute that gets elongated with each statement with the oboe then the clarinet. This finally passes off to the bassoon who finally presents the main theme. The orchestra slowly returns to the texture with accompaniment figures underneath the bassoon’s lyrical line. This develops into a dialogue texture with the winds in response over the bassoon longer note values. The next section “Poco piu mosso” has a slow waltz-like character with a quarter note melody mainly in arpeggiated and scalar motion overtop of chords and short accompaniment motifs in the orchestra. As the phrase develops, the bassoon melody quickens to a beats two and three eighth note motif in a two and two slurred note grouping. The texture then becomes small virtuosic passages in a quasi-cadenza style in dialogue with fragmented motifs from earlier in the orchestra. Eventually, all of these ideas combine together. The movement continues in this manner exploring these textures more while providing new variations on the material. The second movement “Allegro risoluto” has an energetic character in an unbalanced dance-like manner created through tied eighth notes throwing off the flow of passages of eighth notes. This is combined with accent eighth note to create a syncopated feel throughout creating rhythmic dissonance for the 6/8 metre. The texture often has a technical and virtuosic bassoon line featuring staccato eight notes in large intervals overtop of rhythmic accompaniment figures in the orchestra or a lyrical bassoon line overtop of disjunct staccato eighth notes in the orchestra. These soloistic moments are contrasted with short orchestral interludes or dialogue. Eventually, a large bassoon cadenza occurs consisting of technical and virtuosic passages exploring a wide variety of rhythmic groupings from triplet quarter notes to quintuplet sixteenth notes while exploring the full range of the bassoon. A return of the opening material occurs with new variations and a reworking of the material to conclude the work.

description: This is a one-movement work that explores a wide variety of textures from cadenza-like, homorhythmic, and aleatoric. The piece opens with a snare drum solo and leads into a homorhythmic section for the ensemble. Next, the opening tam-tam solo returns but with a flute melody overtop. The common concerto form structure of contrasting solo and tutti sections in either an aleatoric or homorhythmic texture continues for the rest of the piece with the following order of solos: clarinet, cello, violin, and flute.

description: This is a three-movement double concerto for a violin and bassoon soloist that received the Lysenko Award in October 2017. Stylistically this work combines aesthetics, tonal, and extended techniques from avant-garde with allusions to baroque era, Mahler, and rock music. Artistic inspiration for the work comes from two epigraphs by poets T.S. Eliot “April is the cruellest month” and B. Pasternak “The selfsame blend of fire and eeriness prevails outside and in snug dwelling,” which are depicted through the dark and ominous characters and textures used throughout the concerto. The first movement “Allegro ma non molto” opens with an orchestral introduction based on staccato eighth notes that are a perfect fourth apart that slowly get more distorted with the introduction of quarter tones in certain voices creating an eerie atmosphere. The bassoon then enters with a main theme that has some rock music influence with syncopated rhythms and aggressive character through many accented notes and large slurred intervals overtop of rhythmically driven pizzicato accompaniment in the strings. The solo violinist then enters with a disjunct sixteenth note passage providing a disruption to the musical flow that was established. This leads to the violin taking over playing a more lyrical line overtop of the orchestral introduction, which the bassoon later joins in a dialogue with the violinist both playing fragments of the melody. However, the bassoon incorporates frullato to create a harsher texture. This develops into another syncopated and rhythmically driven section with motifs from the original bassoon theme, violin counter melody combined with more syncopated accompaniment figures in the orchestra. Eventually, the perfect fourth motif returns without any distortion in the orchestra. This leads to another lyrical section where the violin and bassoon are playing in an echo-like texture that finally unifies to conclude the movement. The next movement “Adagio ma non molto” opens with the perfect fourth motif that slowly gets distorted again but this time with three different rhythmic values creating a more contrapuntal texture. The bassoon enters with an ominous and vocal-like theme contrasted with a disjunct and aggressive pizzicato and striking the instrument passages in the solo violin creating two different characters attempting to coexist. Eventually, the roles reverse between the bassoon and violin. A final section that begins with fragmentation in dialogue between the soloists gets developed, becoming more active and virtuosic to climax to conclude the movement. The final movement “Presto ma non molto” begins with the bassoonist slap tonguing their bocal to create a popping effect while the solo violin plays pizzicato chords. This texture is interrupted by ad libitum glissandos in the orchestra. This leads into motifs and fragments of previous themes being combined together in orchestral accompaniment while the bassoon and solo violin are in a disjointed dialogue jumping around and pushing the maximum range of the bassoon. This includes jumps up to high F’s in the bassoon. This develops into an aleatoric section in the orchestra leading into a duo cadenza that features a string of sixteenth notes being passed back and forth over top of eighth note fragments that evolved into a full phrase. A return to the first movement orchestral introduction occurs while the solo violin scratches their strings and the bassoon plays multiphonics. Throughout this section a return to the earlier motifs such as major third rhythmically consisting of eighth note, quarter followed by a long note value that develops into the perfect fourth occur to conclude the concerto.

description: This is a six-movement suite in a neobaroque style reminiscent of concerto grossos written by Handel utilizing baroque forms, structures and stylistic elements with some modern aesthetics. Throughout the concerto there is a minuetto movement that occurs three times but is reduced on each successive return to it. The first movement “Tempo di minuetto” sets up the work by presenting the minuetto theme in an orchestral introduction consisting of stereotypical orchestration of melody in the first and second violins and a basso continuo line in the cello and double bass. However, the minuetto is metrically thrown out of balance by constantly switching between 3/4 and 4/4 metres. The solo instruments respond with new material in a contrapuntal texture. Then the movement concludes with a two-measure dialogue between the orchestra soloists. The second movement “Alla marcia” begins with a quasi-lament bass line in the strings with a line broken into fragments between the soloists for four measures presenting a double dotted motif before the English horn taking it over with the orchestra responding with the motif during its long note values. This motif and line continue developing until a virtuosic section occurs consisting of short technical passages comprised of arpeggiated motion in the soloists overtop of accompaniment figures in the orchestra. Eventually, a return to the opening material occurs with the role of the soloist and orchestra reversed. The next movement is another “Tempo di minuetto” missing the last section from the first movement. The fourth movement “Lento lugubre” opens with the double dotted motif from the second movement. The next section presents a lyrical melody first in the English horn followed by the flute and bassoon overtop of chords and short accompaniment figures in the orchestra. A return to the double dotted motif occurs leading to a long note in the bassoon and English horn that the orchestra plays two pizzicato chords spaced out underneath to end the movement. The following movement “Vivace ma non troppo” is centered around a fiery passage of sixteenth notes overtop of downbeat and offbeats in the other voices. The texture begins with just one instrument playing the line of sixteenths shifting to it trading off between instruments and finally becoming tutti in the ensemble with septuplet flourishes overtop in the soloists. The final movement is another “Tempo di minuetto” with only the opening section with the entire ensemble playing together with the flute and English horn joining the violins and the bassoon joining the cello and double bass on the basso continuo.

description: This is a one-movement work that is based on mikromotyvy, which are rhythmic and melodic motifs that are generated by algorithms through independent combinatory systems. The material for these motifs ranges from three to seven notes in length originating from one of the 518 songs by folk singer Yavdokha Zuyikha. Her collection of songs were published in Ukraine and became a source for many of Hrabovsky’s works. These motifs are superimposed on a completely different rhythmic canvas, constructed by the composer. These quotes from the folk songs are not used in a typical fashion as expected in classical music. Hrabovsky uses the interval of the melodic movement that is inherent in Ukrainian musical folklore but transferred to a distinctive rhythmic context. Therefore, everything is dictated by controlled random processes placed in certain frames, which their combinations ensure the fluidity and variability of the musical flow. The overall structure of the piece is based on the system of mikromotyvy linking together smaller portions of the pitch and rhythmic material as the building blocks to create larger structures, which generate new pitch material and rhythmic patterns to be derived from for the next section. This also determines the timbral qualities through the interplay of foreground and background texture between the melodic lines and polyphonic harmony. Throughout the piece five different types of backgrounds are utilized that link together the various algorithms that create a total of thirty different timbral variations. Each section has its own instrumentation based on a number series that differentiates the form. Eventually, this creates a three-part canon in the foreground that changes polyphonic textures. Overall, this work creates a unique approach to form through combining algorithmic systems with folk elements and polyphony in an avant-garde musical language.

description: This concerto explores the technical and lyrical capabilities that the bassoon is able to express through fiery articulated passages contrasted with vocal-like melodies. It opens with a moderato con moto section that has the bassoon playing alone a line of repeated long tones on the low Bb that gradually develops adding in B-natural with other instruments joining in on the motif in unison beginning with the contrabassoon. The motif continues to expand chromatically upwards as the orchestration thickens until a diminished fifth motif is introduced by the English horn prompting some contrapuntal writing to occur before a melody is introduced in the bassoon. This melody continues developing until it arrives at the climax of large interval slurred eighth notes, which hands off the melody to the horns for an orchestral interlude. Eventually, the bassoon re-enters in unison with the horns on the melody before taking over a soloistic role again. This leads to a short cadenza moment of a descending scalar passage in the bassoon that is separated into two parts by a pizzicato chord in the orchestra. This leads into the next main section “Piu mosso” that features a more virtuosic weaving around staccato triplet eighth note line in the bassoon overtop of a dotted eighth and sixteenth motif introduced in the orchestra. This motif in the orchestra begins in dialogue but gradually over time dominates the soloist as their material changes to repeated note triplets. Next, a return to a more mysterious character occurs with a lyrical oboe solo setting up a slower and more lyrical line in the bassoon. This develops and intensifies until arriving at another short cadenza moment similar to earlier, which leads into a longer cadenza moment. This is then interrupted by the orchestra and another attempt occurs at the cadenza that leads us back to the low B♭ from the beginning for a section where the melody is continually searching for the B♭. This leads to another short cadenza moment. Next, a return to a more lyrical melody in the bassoon overtop of accompaniment figures in the orchestra occurs, which like early continues to develop, intensify and thicken in orchestration until arriving at the penultimate and virtuosic page-long cadenza the music has been waiting for. This leads into a final presto section with motifs from throughout the concerto to conclude the piece.

description: This concerto is infused with the spirit of neoclassicism with each movement referencing a different musical period. The work reflects neoclassicism in both the style and orchestration choices, which is combined with elements of contemporary musical language. The first movement “Con moto” is reminiscent of the Baroque era, despite the pronounced sonata form that reminds one of a Concerto Grosso with its aspiration to rhythmic unity. Therefore, the bassoon is treated as one of the solo instruments within the dense sound of the orchestra. The second movement “Largo” evokes a direct association with Bach’s arias through the bassoon’s melodic line with an almost ascetic means of presenting the thematic material. In the reprise, the French horn solo enhances the spatial effect and serves as a preparation for the bassoon's virtuoso cadenza, which acts as a bridge between the second and third movements. The final movement “Allegro” has Mozartean inspiration through the thematic idioms and cadence that evoke a kaleidoscope of "recognition” with a highly anticipated quote from Mozart’s Symphony № 40, which leads back to the recapitulation. Finally, an elated coda brings back the expected elements for the end of a concerto while evoking parallels with Shostakovich's symphony finales.

description: This is a one-movement work with four main sections. The first section is an introduction that is inspired by Krzysztof Penederecki featuring evolving patterns in the strings and a quasi-cadenza-like motif that is first in a canon but develops in an aleatoric texture. In the second section the winds join adding melodic material that is based on a variation of Messiaen’s modes of limited transposition. The bassoon is in contrary motion to the two flutes moving together in parallel motion. This is overtop of the strings that are sustaining a high pedal point, which replicates the sound of crickets. This section became the second movement of his Concertante for Piano. The third section presents an arrangement of an Andalusi Nubah song, which is a music genre from North Africa. description: This is a one-movement work based on outer space. The Corona Australis is a constellation in the southern hemisphere of the sky discovered by the Greek astronomer Claudius Ptolemy in the second century. Musically, the piece explores timbre and rhythm by flowing between slight changes occurring over time. The piece has an unusual form that has a couple main motifs and sections that return and are transformed. The piece begins with an A section consisting of multiphonic whole notes in a staggered entry not in any pattern. Then a B section comprised of dotted quarter note where different instruments drop out at random intervals revealing a wide variety of textures, colors and timbres available in a woodwind quartet through exploring as many possible instrumental combinations. Then the main motivic material is introduced in the C section which is a syncopated sixteenth note melody that develops into a thirty-second note motif in the flute over top of an accompaniment ostinato that alternates between consonance and dissonance. Then a two-measure interruption involving the bassoon knocking on the body of the instrument leading to a repetition of the thirty-second note motif beginning with the bassoon, and staggered entry by the oboe and flute overtop of a syncopated repeated note ostinato in the clarinet. Then a one-measure unison 5:4 eighth note motif is played by the entire ensemble to lead back to the A section. This then leads to a staggered entry of the syncopated clarinet motif but this time it is on the beat that develops in intensity through quicker rhythm and louder dynamics until the thirty-second motif of the C section returns. Then the B section comes back but instead starts on beat four instead of the downbeat. This grows dynamically until arriving at forte which simultaneously becomes the four measure Coda consisting of rhythmically unison chords.

description: This is a short one movement work that is based around the idea of major tonality as the composer challenged herself to write a piece only using major chords as a response to combat the intense emotions from the beginning of the full scale war in Ukraine. description: This work consists of six short movements each depicting a very different character. The title comes from Latin meaning “Against all hope, I hope” which is the title of a poem by the famous Ukrainian poet Lesya Ukrainka. The poem discusses how the speaker is maintaining a sense of optimism and hope for the future despite the hardships and grief they are enduring. The speaker of the poem provides a sense of strength that they are certain they will conquer the evil and grief consuming their life. Logistically, the work involves using a computer to produce different sound effects such as wind and water droplets. Musically, the first movement is an introduction that has wind sound effects from the computer and the flute playing jet whistle to set the atmosphere for the following movements to come. The next movement “Scene 1” has the computer producing water droplet effects. At the beginning, the flute plays a two note motif of a sixteenth tied to a half note followed by a half note in unison with the accordion. Then the flute plays key clicks alone in a dialogue with the water droplets. The second half of the movement features a contrapuntal line of sixteenths (staccato eighth in flute) note rotating around the ensemble one note at a time. The movement concludes with a return to the unison texture from the beginning. “Scene 2” features a loop effect in the computer with a repeated note motif of eighth notes in the flute and triplet sixteenth notes in the accordion. The second half of the movement brings back the rotating note texture from the previous movement. The third scene utilizes an overtone effect on the computer. At the start the flute and accordion play in unison, except the flute has their notes tied together, while the accordion articulates them. As it progresses, the flute plays a melodic line that is mainly stepwise with some small intervals that are rhythmically built around a triplet sixteenth motif leading to a longer note value. Then a return to the original texture occurs to end the movement. “Scene 4” has a resonance effect in the computer. This movement has a much more energetic character with forward momentum. The flute plays a theme overtop of a two sixteenth followed by an eighth motif in the accordion that becomes fragmented. As it develops triplet sixteenths in descending chromatic motion are introduced into the flute line. Eventually, this merges into the accordion and flute playing in unison with some bass clef notes in the accordion to interrupt the line. The final scene has a bus effect at the beginning and the end but changes to an electricity effect at the climax on the computer. The flute begins alone playing harmonics in a simple rhythm of quarter, dotted quarter followed by an eighth note leading to a half note (sometimes tied). The accordion then enters with the theme played in cannon to the flute. The flute switches to normal playing when the accordion enters. It then becomes more active turning into repeated eighth notes in groups of five separated by a beat and a half of rest. As it develops more eighth notes are added to each statement and the rest gets shorter becoming one beat. Finally, it reverses until it is a single eighth note with the rests getting longer until it is an entire measure to conclude the work.

description: This is a short one-movement work that incorporates a very typical classical like phrase but has it be in conflict or “controversy” by the introduction of extended techniques to throw off the phrase. The composer describes the work “tells about the search for harmony and peace in society. Often, competing with each other, we lose our true human qualities, which can lead to tragedy. However, this piece has a positive ending - with the belief that love of the heart and wisdom ultimately win in our world.” The work begins with the piano introducing a rhythmic motif on the highest C on the piano. The flute enters dissonantly on a D using frullato to distort the tone that is preceded by a B grace note to compete against the C the piano is playing. During the flute long notes the piano has virtuosic flourishes of notes. After this introduction, the flute presents a very consonant and classical era-like melody in F major tonality reminiscent of a gavotte. The piano begins to be in dispute with this as they do large glissandos and introduce dissonant notes outside of the flute’s F major tonality. Eventually, this becomes repeated eighth note G’s in the piano, while the flute continues their F major melody. Over time, the flute becomes more influenced to incorporate flourishes of technique, double tonguing articulation, and extended techniques such as frullato, air noise, and key clicks. As well, the flute’s original melody becomes fragmented to create more discohesion. This leads to the end of the work when all of this controversy between the two instruments climax into a large glissando in opposite directions, ascending in the flute and descending in the piano to conclude the work.

description: This is a short one-movement work marked “Allegro” with a dance-like character incorporating elements of Ukrainian Polka with the use of syncopations throughout. The work begins with an eight-measure piano introduction using a common bass line in the left hand often found in an accordion part for a polka band, while the right hand has a melody and offbeat harmonic shots. The flute enters with the theme built on a period. The antecedent consisting of a two measure unit comprised of a dotted eighth followed by a sixteenth motif leading to two staccato eighth notes in the first measure The second measure is an accented dotted quarter note slurred to an eight note. The next two measures are a string of eight slurred eighth notes. The consequent using the exact same rhythmic form, except the final two eighth notes are now a quarter note ending on the tonic. After a second statement of the theme the piano plays it while the flute rests. The flute then re-enters with a fragment that prompts the theme to become “crooked” in the piano with syncopations and sixteenth notes incorporated. The flute then enters with the secondary theme built around groups of slurred sixteenth notes weaving around leading to staccato eighth notes. The piano accompaniment is now a bass line of quarter notes in the left hand with offbeat chords in the left hand. Eventually, there is a lyrical moment of slurred quarter and half notes in the flute, while the piano plays a syncopated motif from earlier underneath. Afterwards, the flute takes over the motif. A return to the original main theme and material occurs to conclude the work.

description: The piece consists of two movements. The first movement for two clarinets is based on the technique of developed segmented aleatoric common in Boulez’s piano works of the 1950s. The two main segments are placed in the middle of the page as the starting point with the choice of direction of the sequential derivatives either clockwise or counter-clockwise executed one after another chosen by the performer at an arbitrary tempo. The various segments consolidate together until the performers arrive at the end of their segments, which they go to the finale segment in the very center of the page. The second movement for two bassoonists uses a technique of indirect and extended key area that becomes replaced by free atonality. The piece develops through two fugue episodes. The first one is in a lyrical, duet style and the second one is a virtuoso featuring fast passages starting in the bottom two octaves, which utilize double-tonguing and playing on the reed alone. The material is developed through double counterpoint by augmentation and diminution. Overall, the piece is very technically complex, utilizes the extreme registers of the instrument and long polyphonic melodic phrases.

description: This work is the first in a larger collection by the composer of short works structured in a series of improvisations for solo instruments. The inspiration behind this work is to show the full cycle of how a thought forms and then disappears in the mind. This is a short one-movement work in an improvisatory style. It opens with accented long tones that dynamically grow to a fortissimo. Afterwards, fragmented motifs lead to longer note values based around the opening pitches of “C#” and “F#”. As it progresses the fragments become more virtuosic and the longer note values expand melodically. This leads into a three triplet sixteenth motif on the repeated pitch of “F#” spaced out by rests that alternate with material from the opening.

This is a one-movement work in ternary form in a neoclassical style intended to provide more repertoire for young performers. The A section is an “allegro” in an energetic and dance-like character. The bassoon has a melodic line featuring staccato eighth notes and slurred sixteenths in the tenor register overtop of accompaniment figures of a quarter note chords and offbeat eighth note chords. The B section “moderato” features a lyrical line of slurred eighth notes that are either stepwise or arpeggiated. The orchestra has half note chords in the bass line combined with a motif of an eighth note rest followed by three staccato eighth notes. The return of the A section brings some slight variations that lead into a final “piu mosso” that is virtuosic in character consisting of long lines of slurred sixteenths in a stepwise or arpeggiated manner.

description: All of Solonskiy’s works are written with a pedagogical purpose in mind to be applied in a concert setting. Each of the pieces were written for a particular student of his to address their particular challenges in their playing. He chooses to use characters from folklore and fairytales to make them approachable and easily understood by the student allowing them to bring their own imagination, emotions and moods into the music based on characters they are familiar with. His goal is to comprehensively reveal the beauty and expressiveness of woodwind instruments through the color, technical, and artistic capabilities. This is a short one movement work in an allegretto tempo written completely in bass clef focusing on a variety of articulation switching between slurred, staccato and accented passages. It opens with the piano presenting a fragment of the main theme which the bassoon takes over playing the main theme in its entirety overtop of accompaniment figures. Another more legato and slurred main theme in the bassoon is presented as a contrast to provide character shifts throughout. These two themes are in dialogue for the rest of the work.

description: This is a short one-movement work that as described by the composer “The flute and piano join forces to conjure a shimmering nocturnal dance - an ode to the fleeting brilliance of fireflies.” (Kuzmenko, foreword). Throughout the piece Kuzmenko utilizes fast virtuosic passages of sixteenth notes, whimsical ornamentation, and crisp staccato articulation to depict the fluttering of a firefly in motion. The piano provides the foundation of the scene depicting “moonlit grasses and the hush of twilight” (Kuzmenko) through the rhythmic syncopations underneath the flute and constant streams of wandering triplet eighth notes. Overall this piece is “a musical snapshot of nature's quiet spectacle, where light flickers, vanishes, and reappears - never quite in the same place twice. Listeners are invitees to imagine themselves in a field at dusk, surrounded by tiny lanterns of life, each note a glimmer in the dark.” (Kuzmenko). Musically, the work opens with a “Spirited” section that has energetic sixteenth notes in the right hand and syncopated quarter (or two tied eighth) notes in the right hand giving dance-like character. The flute then enters with the theme built around the energetic sixteenths leading to eighth notes ornamented with grace notes. The section continues developing through changes in the interplay between the two instruments and variations to the material. The next section “Dreamy” has a contrasting character with the introduction of a constant stream of triplet eighth notes in the piano that are underneath a more lyrical and vocal-like theme in the flute. Rhythmically, throughout are brief moments of rhythmic dissonance between the flute and piano when duple and triple note groupings are occurring simultaneously creating a sense of intensity in the phrase. This section is also much more intimate from the softer dynamics utilized beginning at piano with swells to mezzo-piano and an ultimate climax to mezzo-forte. Eventually, a brief accelerando occurs to lead back into the opening material. However, this time as articulated staccato passages are introduced into the flute line to enhance the lightness in the character. As it progresses more trills are introduced until the flute holds a trill for 4 measures to unwind the section to set up a “Mysterioso” section. This section is reminiscent of the previous “Dreamy” section. Next, an “Ad libitum, tempo rubato” section occurs which is the most virtuosic moment with the use of sextuplet sixteenths creating grand flourishes. A final return to the opening material occurs now with triplet sixteenths incorporated from the previous section as ornamentation to conclude the work.

description: This is a short one-movement work that goes through a variety of characters to depict the magical world of fairy tales based after Thumbelina by Hans Christian Anderson. The composer describes the inspiration of the piece by saying that “for many years [fairytales] tried to create a better world for us. This is an attempt, although for a short time, to return to this wonderful world of the forgotten spiritual poetics that is so important for every child and adult, in a world of lost beauty, kindness and mercy, light and bright dreams of fancy.” (Stankovych, foreword) The work opens with a section marked “Rubato” where the piano plays a simple motif of quarter, eighth and dotted half note in the left hand. Then during the dotted half note the flute and right of the piano play a flourish in harmony that cascades upwards setting a magical atmosphere. The flourishes then get extended into a full passage with a bass line in the left hand underneath. Next, a similar structure is followed but now with the flute playing half of the flourish and passing it to the piano’s right hand creating more of a dialogue texture. This leads into the flute taking over the virtuosic line that weaves around the upper register, while the right hand of the piano plays a melodic line and the left hand plays a bass line. This evolves into a quasi-cadenza of the opening material in the flute overtop of a chord in the piano. The piano interrupts with a weaving triplet line prompting the flute to switch to more melodic material. The piano continues to respond with the triplets during the flute's longer note values. This leads into a calmer section based around more melodic material in a dialogue texture between the flute and right hand of the piano overtop of a bass line. Eventually, a return to the “Rubato” returns to conclude this opening section. The next main section “Moderato” begins with a sparkling arpeggiation of sixteenth notes in contrary motion between the two hands of the piano. The flute then enters with virtuosic flourishes cascading up and down the registers leading to longer note values often with ornamentation. As it progresses it becomes a motif of two thirty-second notes leading to a longer note value with frullato. Then it becomes a melodic line that alternates between frullato and ordinary texture like two characters conversing with each other. Eventually, another “Rubato” section returns bringing back the virtuosic qualities and writing with various syncopation ostinato patterns in the piano underneath. The work continues bringing back various motifs from earlier in the flute underneath until the final main section “Andante” occurs. It is reminiscent of an early section but now the flute plays the melodic material, while the right hand of the piano does the virtuosic passages overtop of whole note chords in the left hand. As it progresses, the texture between the flute and right hand becomes more dialogue transitioning into the flute taking over the virtuosic flourishes overtop of syncopated accompaniment in the piano. However, the virtuosic passages are broken down into one-measure units leading to a fermata like the opening again. Next, a “Piu mosso” has a constant line of sixteenth notes (or septuplets) passing back and forth. This leads into a return of a melodic line in the piano and sixteenth note arpeggiations in the piano again. Eventually, the flute joins in on the sixteenth notes to conclude the work.

description: This is a short one-movement work that incorporates elements of folk music within a modern compositional style. The work begins with whole notes that utilize frullato to give an unconventional timbre create an eerie and unsettled atmosphere for the opening. A quarter note melody based around semitone motion leading to fourth or fifth interval is introduced into the frullato longer tones. A measure of silence occurs to signify the end of this opening section. The next section has an energetic dance-like character featuring a constant stream of eighths in either arpeggiated or stepwise motion, which get ornamented with sixteenth notes often in semitone motion. This leads into a sequential passage of a motif consisting of two eighth notes leading to an eighth note. This sequence connects into the next section of a melodic line rhythmically comprised of quarter and eighth notes that are disjunct due to notes being displaced in different octaves. This material continues to be developed such as into syncopated motifs and also combines with elements such as the arpeggiated motifs from the earlier dance-like section. The work concludes with a complete return of the opening material with the final note being changed from the pitch “G” to the tonic of this section “A♭.

date_written: Initial undated sketch and draft of the first movement & brief sketches of other movements, March 29th 1985 (handwritten), rev. June 16 1995 (typed-up), rev. 200x (In Sydorenko’s personal electronic files there is a list of works that list a third revision as 200x. I believe this indicates he had plans or was working on revisions to extend the piece, which the 3 handwritten sketches are for.)
unpublished: handwritten manuscripts and sketches in composer’s personal archive available courtesy of Halyna Sydorenko (ISMN number M-706032-44-3) (The work was most likely planned to eventually be published through HyperText Plus, which did not occur due to Sydorenko passing away unexpectedly.)
premiere: most likely April 4th, 1985 in Toronto by Richard (cl) and Larkin Hinder (bsn) (The following names “Amanta, Richard, and Larkin Elizabeth Hinder”, their phone numbers, and the date “Apr. 4 2:30 P.M.” are handwritten on an earlier draft of the work. As part of the Walter Buczynski Fond at the University of Toronto Music Library in Buczynski’s calendar from 1985 on this date is written “230 Sydorenko.” Therefore, I hypothesize that most likely this piece was performed in a recital or an exam on this date by those musicians written on the score with Sydorenko’s composition teacher Buczynski present. Communication with Amanta Scott and Larkin Hinder was unable to verify the details due to how long ago this may have occurred resulting in them being unable to recall any details or still having any programs in their possession from this time period. I have been unable to track down a program through the University of Toronto recital archive due to the archive only holding BMus student’s programs and not BA students, which Sydorenko was.)
description: Based on my analysis of his sketches and communication with his sister Halyna, I hypothesize that this work most likely began as an assignment for a course or lessons with Buczynski during his studies at the University of Toronto and was performed for an exam or recital as part of his studies. The earliest handwritten sketches have educational notes such as a tone row and various inversions and retrogrades written out and a form chart to structure the piece. It also has the ranges of the clarinet and bassoon and adjective description of each register such as the bassoon’s middle register described as “mournful, dull” and the clarinet’s altissimo register as “piercing.” There also appears to be edits and suggestions written by another person, who I assume to be Buczynski as his phone number is written on the bottom of the page. The original title on the handwritten manuscript from 1985 is Panneaux 19 but it later was crossed off with a red pen. The typed-up manuscript from 1994 has the title listed in this annotation Piéces décoratifs: La poésie. Communication with Halyna has resulted in a hypothesis for a possible inspiration for this work based on the various titles. Wasyl had an interest in art nouveau and was particularly fond of the work of the painter Alphonse Mucha. The original title Panneaux 19 is a term used to reference this style of painting. But then Wasyl crossed it out and picked a more specific title of La poésie, once he decided to add sketches for future movements to align with a possible inspiration from the work of Mucha. Mucha has a series of four works titled The Arts, with one of the paintings titled Poetry. Therefore, it is hypothesized that the first movement is based on this painting from the series and the other three sketches were to be of the other three paintings. Additional changes are the tempo marking in the 1985 version is marked poetically, quarter note equals 66. However, the 66 has been crossed off and replaced with 56 in red pen. The 1994 version has no indication of tempo marking given. Throughout the 1985 score there are only small changes marked in red pen such as note changes in measure 34 in the clarinet. Written is the pitch “F” but it has been circled and “G” written above. This piece is a short one-movement work structured in a condensed ternary form based around an unusual ten-note tone row (G-E♭-B-F-F♯-D-D♭-C-E-B♭) instead of the expected twelve-note row. The A section is built around three main motifs: 1) a slurred ascending interval of a sixteenth note to a longer note value; 2) a grace note slurred ascending interval to a marcato eighth note; 3) dotted eighth note, sixteenth and eighth note. However, as the section develops the motifs combine together to create a longer line. These motifs mainly interact in a dialogue going back and forth between the clarinet and bassoon. Near the end of the section the triplet note motif from the B section is introduced in the clarinet overtop of the A section motifs in the bassoon. The B section features a constant line of triplet eighth notes that get passed between the clarinet and bassoon. As it develops the clarinet adds ornamentation to the figures and the A section motifs return underneath. Eventually, a brief “Piu mosso" section with the opening material leading to a unison long note occurs to conclude the piece. The differences between the 1985 and 1994 version are surface level only and engraving and have not changed any of the content. In the 1994 version the changes are as follow: 1) all of the articulation, dynamic, ritardando and accelerando markings are missing; 2) the grace note figures are rewritten sometimes as dotted eighth, sixteenth, eighth note; 3) sometimes the figure consisting of an eighth note followed by sixteenth rest is now rewritten as a dotted eighth note; 4) the note changes marked in red pen in the 1985 version have been implemented such as in measure 34; 5) different enharmonic of notes have been used such as measures 36-39 the D♭ is now a C♯ in the clarinet. There has also been edits from the initial undated first draft of the piece such as change of notes, which I hypothesize might be due to making a mistake in the utilizing the tone row which he then noticed and fixed for the final version. Additionally, there are markings and comments written in red pen in a different handwriting, which I presume is Buczynski’s handwriting and advice. The handwritten sketches for the other movements varying in their level of completion. The first sketch has two drafts of sixteen measures in 3/4. One version is titled “#1 Slow” and the other “#1 Calmato” that are quite different and there is no indication of which version was written when. However, on an earlier sketch page that belongs with La poésie there appears to be the early working of the triplet sixteenth motif from “Slow” also on the page. This leads me to believe it is the second movement and it is titled #1 as it's the first sketch of the three new movements he was working on. Due to “Calmato” and “Slow” being quite different and both sketches labeled as #1 I believe are the main material for the two main sections (A and B section) of the movement with plans to turn it into a ternary form similar to La poésie. The “Calmato” material has a much more lyrical and vocal-like line with two-measure slurred phrases which the bassoon echoes fragments of in a dialogue texture. The “Slow” material is much more with a syncopated line featuring duple and triple sixteenth notes in a quasi-cadenza like manner in the clarinet overtop of an arpeggiated bass line in the bassoon that begins as quarter notes and becomes a triplet figure comprised of eighth, two sixteenth, and an eighth. The second sketch is titled “#2 Con moto” is written in 4/4 with only four measures written. It has a dance like character with a humoresque staccato eighth note motif in the bassoon that varies by adding sixteenth notes into the line underneath a theme of mostly eighth and sixteenth notes in the clarinet. The final sketch titled “#3 Andante” only consists of a lyrical slurred melody consisting of seven-measures with a one beat pick up in 4/4. The bassoon part is blank with no rests written suggesting it was yet to be added.

piece_title: Dedication to Heroes And the dead, and the living, and the unborn defenders of Ukraine
premiere: 1) bsn verison not performed yet 2) 2) bcl version March 5th, 2025 at DAM at “Music Without Borders” by Yuriy Levytskyi (bcl), Oleksandr Shtyrbu (organ), Andriy Lyshak (snare drum)
performace_considerations: additional legno part for a third musician who keeps a metronomic pulse either by hitting the rim of the snare drum with the back of a stick backstage or tapping the body of the piano onstage; permanent use of pedal in the piano
description: The original idea of this work began in the fall of 2024 with two different versions in mind: 1) bass clarinet and organ, 2) bassoon and piano. The bassoon and piano version of this piece was written for Zachary Senick inspired by his project completed on March 9th, 2025. The composer highly recommends using the full title in programs but just the “Dedication to Heroes” portion may be used if necessary. Martynyuk’s music “is a breath of the Ukrainian melos, that comes alive in modern harmonies. It’s music, in which past and future meets in an elegant sound of the bandura, in mighty choirs, and a lace of instrumental colors.” An important element of Martynyuk’s work is the preservation and reinterpretation of folk elements combined with modern aesthetics to help convey the Ukrainian national heritage. Therefore, the works are a conversation with the past in the present to create a future. The meaning of the title is a musical requiem dedicated to those who fought, currently fight and will fight for Ukrainian independence. The work takes inspiration from the famous Cossack song “Oy Moroze Morozenku”. This song has a dichotomy celebrating both the heroic and tragic fate of Cossack leader Morozenko. Therefore, Martynyuk uses this to create a dichotomy between remembrance and grief to showcase the strength and indestructible Ukrainian spirit. At the end of the work the Ukrainian folk song “Oy u luzi chervona kalyna” (Oh in the meadow a red flower) in measures 173-176. The legno part at the beginning represents the constant movement of time to convey eternity and the dropping out of the legno part represents a minute of silence in Ukraine that occurs every morning at 9. An important musical element is the many changes in dynamics and tempo juxtaposed with cadenza-like fragments to create an improvisational character to the piece, best represented in the section from measure 155-161. Overall, the work contrasts between vocal-like lines reminiscent of a simpler time evoking the Ukrainian spirit and more virtuosic cadenza-like moments depicting the constant struggle the Ukrainian people are fighting through to protect their autonomy to keep their spirit alive.

unpublished: manuscript available courtesy of the family
description: This is a short one-movement work that often utilizes contrapuntal writing between the two instruments and contrasting sections. The work begins with an “Andante” section that the guitar begins alone establishing an ostinato pattern that is an arpeggiation leading to a chord. The flute enters overtop of this accompaniment with a vocal-like melody that incorporates glissandos. As it progresses the guitar accompaniment becomes more embellished. The next section “Ben ritmico” is comprised of a motif of two eighth notes, followed by a dotted eighth and sixteenth, followed by four more eighth notes in an arpeggiated manner. The flute presents it first over syncopated ostinato of quarter and dotted quarter notes in the guitar. Throughout the section the two motifs alternate between the two instruments imitating a dialogue. The section ends with a unison fragment played by the two instruments that leads to a “Cantando” section. It features a vocal-like melody in the middle register of the flute while the guitar plays chords and sixteenth note fragments in response to the flute during long note values. Eventually, the fragments expand and are played in unison by the two instruments, like two people agreeing on things throughout a conversation. It also becomes much more contrapuntal near the end of the section and introduces a motif comprised of two thirty-second and a sixteenth notes. The following “Molto espressivo” section features a string of sixteenth notes that is structured on arpeggiations and repeated notes, while the flute plays syncopated fragments of sixteenth notes and the thirty-second note motif. Eventually, the flute becomes expanded to a full phrase to lead to a return of the first two opening sections of the piece to conclude it.

premiere: November 24th, 2023 at “Young Composers Concert” at NUCU in Kyiv by Dmytro Malin (bsn), composer (pno)
description: This is a two-movement work utilizing neoclassical forms with jazz harmonic language. Each movement is structured in two main sections. First, an “Arioso” section that features the bassoon playing solo that is attacca into a “Piece” section which has the bassoon and piano both playing where the main theme is presented and developed. The first movement’s arioso is rubato and quasi-improvised based around arpeggiations in a variety of rhythms with some influence from jazz harmony. The “Piece” is marked “Animato” beginning with the bassoon presenting a melody overtop of a driving eighth note ostinato in the left hand and interjections in the right hand when the bassoon is resting. The melody switches between moments of lyricism through slurred legato lines and humoresque through staccato eighth notes. Eventually, the roles reverse with the piano taking over the melody and the bassoon playing the ostinato eighth notes. This leads to a final two measures where the two instruments align on an eighth note arpeggiated line into a chord to conclude the movement. The second movement’s arioso is marked “Andante mosso” in a more virtuosic character featuring technical passages in scalar and arpeggiated motion combined with large intervals. The “Piece” is marked “Animato assai” and features the same texture as the previous movement. However, the melody this time is more cantabile with it being comprised of whole notes in the bassoon. This leads into a virtuosic section of sixteenth note arpeggios in dialogue between the bassoon and the right hand of the piano combined with chords in the left hand. Next, a “Moderato” section consisting of a cantabile melody in the bassoon with accompaniment figures centered around two stepwise sixteenth notes followed by a large interval eighth note in the piano. Eventually, the sixteenths and eighth note ostinato creep back in. The ostinato motif develops into sixteenths as the piece climaxes while all of the motifs interact leading to a final tonic chord.

premiere: December 12th, 2024 at the Lviv Organ Hall for concert series “Music of Iron and Concrete” by Halyna Tsybulnyk (fl), Ustym Khavunka (ob), Oleksandr Nesterov (cl), Denys Levytsky (bsn), Taras Stasyshyn (hn)
description: This is a two-movement work in contrasting characters that uses elements of traditional classical form combined with a modernistic choice in harmony, often juxtaposing different tonal areas simultaneously. The first movement “Andante” has a lyrical character that opens with a short melodic fragment in a dialogue between the instruments in conflicting tonal worlds. The flute begins with a one-measure motif based around arpeggiation in D major, which the oboe responds with a variation of this motif that starts in the middle of the initial motif on the dotted quarter (or quarter tied) in a conflicting B♭ major. The other instruments play in a contrapuntal texture that utilizes fragments of the flute motif such as the perfect fifth and major third interval in the bassoon and the semitone motion in the horn. The section progresses by developing the material into a longer phrase and exploring more tonal areas, such as the next iteration of the motif in the flute is now a whole tone higher in E major and expanded longer. The other voices continue in the contrapuntal texture while presenting new material such as an arpeggiated eighth note line that weave around the harmony in the clarinet. Eventually, this develops into a section with new material consisting of a cascading line of arpeggiated quarter notes that are offset throughout the ensemble, beginning with thirds in the flute that become more disjunct through certain notes in the line being expands the interval such as a perfect fourth and by other notes being displaced from the expected octave such as instead of descending a third the note ascends a sixth creating a sense of instability until the music returns to material based off the opening section with some new variations to conclude the movement. The second movement “Allegretto” has an energetic character that opens with a melody borrowing motifs from Hutsul folk music is split between the oboe and flute consisting of eighth and sixteenth notes overtop of a syncopated accompaniment line of eighth notes in the clarinet, bassoon, and horn. The section develops by new material being introduced overtop of this texture, such as the flute playing a fragment and syncopated version of this melody that is offset by an eighth note from the melody. The next section presents a new melodic line in the flute comprised of four sixteenth notes leading to eighth notes. This is overtop of short fragments such as two slurred eight notes, four slurred sixteenth notes, or a variation of these two combined, which pass around the ensemble to create a larger and cohesive line. Eventually, the texture in the ensemble changes to syncopated quarter notes in the oboe, bassoon, and horn combined with a new countermelody in the clarinet mainly consisting of eighth notes that harmonically weave around. A return to the opening material occurs, but quickly variates to become similar to the secondary melody. The movement continues to alternate between material from the two themes until the work concludes.

This is a three-movement work in a neoclassical style using typical forms. The first movement “Allegro ma non troppo” is in ternary form and begins with a dialogue between two groups in the ensemble. The flute and bassoon have a lyrical and slurred line while the oboe, clarinet, and horn have a staccato eighth note line. As it develops the staccato line becomes syncopated. This material develops into a contrapuntal texture with some of the lines utilizing fragmentation from the earlier material and others presenting new material. The fragmentation is often passing around in a dialogue. The movement continues bringing back the themes in different textures and combinations. The next section “Lento assai” is a lyrical flute solo consisting of eighth notes leading to longer note values overtop of accompaniment figures. The return to the A section features new fragmentation and combination of the material. It also presents the Lento assai theme and fragments now in this more energetic character. The following movement “Adagio” has an espressivo line in a semplice character first in unison in unison in the clarinet and bassoon that continues in a canon-like texture as it develops to be more active with eighth notes incorporated in. The final movement “Rondino” has a form of ABACADA. The A section begins with a three eighth note motif in the bassoon consisting of the pitch “C” going up an octave than back down an octave to a “Bb” unexpectedly. The flute and clarinet start with fragments that get expanded into a playful theme of eighth notes with various syncopations from rests. As the movement progresses the bassoon line becomes virtuosic passages of sixteenth notes outlining the harmonic progressions. The B section “Andante” is an espressivo and lyrical solo in the oboe with no accompaniment. The return of the A begins with the bassoon ostinato but with a variation to the theme in the horn and a new line added in the upper winds. The C section “Subito meno mosso, cantabile” presents material reminiscent of the second movement. The next return of the A section is all variated material. The D section “Andante” is an espressivo and lyrical line that passes around the ensemble with short virtuosic fragments, which develop into contrapuntal lines. The final return to the A section features the bassoon ostinato in a different tonal area with a a couple co lines of earlier material combined together.

description: This is a one-movement work that is based around the text from the title that slowly develops and expands until it climaxes producing the whole phrase. The piece opens with a bassoon cadenza that is unmetered utilizing graphic notation for the performer to establish the exact character. The flute and oboe enter with isolated fragments before the bassoon takes over with another cadenza-like graphic notated phrase. Another fragment of the upper winds occurs but this time the two instruments trade off without any silence in between their statements. This leads into the two isolated sections of bassoon cadenza and the fragments being combined at the same time developing into a section where the whole ensemble is performing the cadenza-like motif. The next section begins as a calmer character featuring long trills with glissandos that break down back into the fragments, which allows for the4 flute to introduce a fragment of the text as their response. These fragments continue developing while the cadenza-like becomes re-introduced until the whole phrase is spoken achieving its goal.

description: This is a short one-movement work centered around creating a dramatic interplay between the flute and piano. The main theme of the work comes from the composer’s second symphony, which he decided to use as inspiration to write a new work utilizing it for flute and piano. The flute often has a vocal line to be a voice in memory of the victims of war. The composer takes inspiration from the monologue style used by Shostakovich in his post war symphonies. It begins with a “Moderato” in a legato character where the piano introduces the main theme. The flute then enters with a counter melody that includes rhythmic elements from the main theme the piano is playing. As the section progresses the flute takes over the melody, while the piano takes over the counter melody the flute was playing but then fragments it between the hands. This leads into a unison statement of theme between the flute and the two voices of the piano. The next section “Andante” presents fragments of the main theme in the piano while the flute plays a passage of eighth notes ascending and descending across the range of the flute. A return to the opening tempo and material in the piano occurs, while the flute responds with eighth note fragments. The following section “Allegro ma non troppo” presents a new theme in the flute that is more disjunct mainly consisting of eighth notes in large intervals overtop of quarter notes in the piano. As it progresses elements from the main theme sneak into this theme. The piano takes over playing the second theme that turns into a sequential passage of ascending eighth notes while the flute plays a lyrical syncopated melody overtop that develops into the main theme. It then undergoes variation while the eighth note sequential passage returns in the piano. The work continues in a dialogue texture between the flute and piano utilizing fragments from the various themes to conclude the work. The ending of the piece quotes the coda from Arthur Honegger’s Third Symphony “Anti-War”.

description: This is a three-movement concerto in a neoclassical style that borrows some elements from modernist aesthetics. The first movement “Allegretto giocoso” begins with an orchestral introduction that becomes more active and intense as the voices build on top of one another to become more contrapuntal. Eventually, the flute and bassoon enter with the theme in a dialogue passing off to each other in two measure sections that then become more fragmented as it develops. The material features syncopated and technical material presented earlier in the introduction. As this section continues it is contrasted with more lyrical and legato lines based off arpeggiation but displaced into larger intervals. The orchestra provides rhythmic support underneath creating more energy with syncopated motifs. Later, the flute and bassoon become more contrapuntal allowing both the staccato and lyrical motifs to coexist simultaneously which leads into homorhythmic passages. Eventually, a large bassoon cadenza occurs in a virtuosic manner using large interval staccato notes and grace notes typical in bassoon writing. Next, a virtuosic flute cadenza occurs featuring fiery and flourishing technical sextuplet passages. The movement then ends with a return to earlier material in contrapuntal texture that becomes homorhythmic to conclude the movement. The second movement “Andante sostenuto” features lyrical melodies that the soloists take turns performing overtop of accompaniment figures in the orchestra. As the movement develops the lyrical lines become more virtuosic and disjunct leading into a dialogue of fragments between the soloists to create one large line. The orchestra becomes more active with triplet eighth notes underneath. The rest of the moment combines the different motifs together to occur simultaneously contrasted with homorhythmic sections. The final movement “Allegro distinto” features lots of the same textures and elements from throughout the concerto with new material that is in a similar character and manner.
