description: In Levitin’s chamber and instrumental music there is often inspiration from his teacher, Shostakovich’s music demonstrated through the “dramatic opposition of aggressive motor rhythms, contemplative writing and dance rhythms, as well as by the overall finesse and economy of means.”59 This is a three-movement concerto. The first movement “Allegro ma non troppo” begins with a lyrical theme in the clarinet based on scalar and arpeggiated motion overtop of constant eighth notes in the orchestra. Eventually, the bassoon enters with the theme in canon to the clarinet. As it develops it becomes a more contrapuntal texture with the orchestral accompaniment becoming more active adding in scalar passages of sixteenth notes overtop of the eighth notes. An orchestral interlude leads into the second theme presented in the bassoon consisting of repeated sixteenth notes leading to scalar eighth notes overtop of eighth note chords on beat one and three in the orchestra. This develops in a very similar manner to earlier leading back to the main theme, which becomes fragments that pass between the soloists. This then comes together to create a homorhythmic section between the soloists with the orchestra playing a countermelody and eighth notes. The rest of the movement continues in this manner of presenting new themes or motifs that get developed using similar techniques with returns to the main theme until an “Andantino” return in the soloists with trills in the orchestra. This prompts a final virtuosic “Presto” section to conclude the movement. The second movement “Andantino” features a lyrical melody first presented in the clarinet with the bassoon joining in a canon overtop of quarter note chords on beat two and three and a dotted half note bass line in the orchestra. The final movement “Vivace” begins with an orchestral introduction that presents a playful eighth and sixteenth note theme. The movement shifts between this theme and a more lyrical theme throughout using similar textures and techniques of development. The majority of the movement is the soloists with prominent lines while the orchestra plays accompaniment figures.

description: This work is a grand virtuosic and musical display of a flutist through a theme and six variations exploring a wide range of characters. The theme marked “Moderato grazioso” has a semplice quality depicting a pleasant picture of folk like in the countryside. Musically, it consists of an arpeggiated major chord played as staccato eighth notes. It expands into a larger melodic line with quarter and dotted quarter notes utilizing Ukrainian folk harmony. The first variation marked “Andante cantabile” has a lilting and care-free character from a constant string of eighth notes in a 6/8 meter. Motifically, it brings out the title through constant switches between a loud and soft dynamic creating echo effects. Melodically, it uses lots of scalar, arpeggiated, and neighbour motion, but as it progresses the intervals widen leading attacca into the next variation “Vivace” is centered around a constant string of staccato sixteenths that undergo various slight changes to articulation, accents and dynamics creating an echo effect. The following variation “Parlando rubato” is built around six eighth notes with embellishments of mordents leading to a longer note value such as dotted half or half note. The character of this one is improvisatory and mysterious. As it progresses frullato is incorporated to create a new texture, while also making the line more active with other rhythmic values such as triplet eighths, sixteenths, and thirty-seconds acting as embellishments. The fourth variation “Andantino” is very virtuosic with passages of articulated thirty-second notes cascading across the registers of the flute in scalar motion. The next variation “Allegretto scherzando” has a dance-like quality that is centered around an eighth, two sixteenth, and an eighth rhythmic motif that gets expanded upon and melodically explores around. The final movement “Presto” is one last virtuosic display of triplet sixteenths built on the opening major arpeggio presented in the theme, which harmonically explores the range of the flute.

description: This is a one-movement work that contrasts between moments of sublime lyricism in the style of an elegy and virtuosic displays of technique that have an improvisatory character that undergo a variety of character shifts. The work opens with a “Lento meditativo” section beginning with the flute alone playing a vocal-like line marked espressivo. The piano then responds with an arpeggiated figure. The flute then re-enters to take over the arpeggiated motif overtop of chords in the piano. While the flutist plays longer note values such as half notes the piano plays a weaving line consisting of quintuplet or sextuplet sixteenths leading to two eighth notes. The section continues developing upon the material becoming more active and contrapuntal with a sense of dialogue between the two instruments. Eventually, the next section “Pochissimo mosso” features an espressivo and vocal-like melody in the flute overtop of a bass line in the left hand and arpeggiated sixteenth notes in the right hand of the piano. As it progresses the flute melody becomes embellished leading into a brief virtuosic cadenza comprised of disjunct triplet sixteenths. Afterwards, the piano plays a passionate interlude consisting of a melodic line in the right hand built on primarily eighth and sixteenth notes and a bass line in the left hand. This leads into an unexpected “Allegro agitato” section built around a simple melodic line in the flute overtop of an accented and syncopated ostinato in the piano. Next, a “Moderato e dramatico” section returns to a virtuosic display in a contrapuntal texture. This is followed by an extended cadenza with both of the two main characters in the flute. The first part utilizes arpeggios cascading to the upper register and then a stepwise motion downwards to a fermata. The final statement of the cadenza breaks from the pattern brining in the virtuosity of flourishes of technique climbing to the High “C”. Afterwards a return to the “Allegro agitato” occurs before the final section of the piece “Lento de a lontano”, which brings back motifs from earlier to conclude the work.

description: This is a short one-movement work in a lyrical character structured in an introduction and three main sections connected with short transitions. The piece opens with a eight measure introduction in the piano that is chordal. The bassoon enters as a pickup to the ninth measure to begin the A section, which has a melancholic character. The bassoon plays a lyrical melody consisting of eighth, quarter, and dotted quarter notes in a minor with chromaticism on the second eighths of the beat, often as a lower neighbour motion. The B section removes the chromaticism and sticks strictly to a minor. The C section is more energetic and active, featuring longer lines of eighth notes compared to earlier. The piece concludes with a reprise of the A material.

description: Vyshynskyi’s music often balances the aesthetics of late romantic and minimalism that is characterized by its intellectualism and intertextuality. This work consists of three short movements exploring how ostinatos with slight variations can create different textures and timbres in an ensemble. The first movement “Sostenuto” is marked quarter note equals 45 and consists of long note values, which the entire ensemble begins on the pitch “Ab” that change independently by a quarter note leading to another longer note value creating moments of dissonance as the ensemble weaves around the pitch “Ab”. As the movement develops the pitches expand outward creating lusher harmonies. The next movement “Moderato” opens with a piano solo in a disjunct manner through large intervals and accented syncopations. As it develops grace notes are introduced into the line as it becomes a contrapuntal texture between the two hands. Eventually, as the line begins to climax the winds enter with a homorhythmic syncopated line on a repeated note creating a cluster chord. Both the piano and winds undergo a gradual rhythmic diminution and dynamic increase until the end of the movement. The final movement “Andante” features a poco dolce chorale in the winds that explores dissonances and cluster chords rhythmically comprised of quarter and half notes. The piano enters on the last note of their first phrase creating a canon-like texture between the winds and the piano for the duration of the movement.

description: This work has symbolic meaning for the composer as he finished writing it the day before the full-scale Russian invasion began, which he then went to fight for Ukraine in the 48th separate assault battalion. This is a short three movement work consisting of a standard fast-slow-fast structure presenting a variety of musical characters through changes in the flute’s part, while maintaining a similar accompaniment in the piano. The first movement “Allegretto grazioso e lusingando” has a graceful and tender character. The piano opens the piece with a bass line on the downbeats in the left hand and combined with an ostinato arpeggiated sixteenth note motif in the right hand. The flute then enters with slurred arpeggio sixteenth notes leading to staccato eighth notes in stepwise motion leading to the next harmonic change. As it progresses the melody in the flute becomes ornamented with grace notes and trills. After three statements of the main melody with progressive ornamentation the music undergoes a diminution to become eighth, quarter and half notes now creating a much more lyrical character before returning to the original main theme material. The second movement “Andantino cantabile” has a similar piano accompaniment to the prior movement. However, now the flute has a slurred vocal-like theme that becomes virtuosic flourishes of thirty second note passages in a similar fashion to a singer adding melismas as the theme develops in an aria. The final movement “Allegretto con grazia” has the same similar accompaniment, while the flute plays a dance-like theme of sixteenth notes leading to staccato eighth notes or a slurred dotted quarter note followed by an eighth in a descending minor sixth motif.

description: This is a one-movement work depicting the village Eschelbronn in Germany. The bassoon soloist represents Paul and the flute soloist Manuela, who were the owners of the home that the composer and his wife stayed at. The music is non-programmatic and attempts to convey the warmth the composer felt in the village as a means to express his deep gratitude to the residents' hospitality. The work is in a through-composed style with a melody that continues to develop and grow in the bassoon as the work progresses. The bassoon is the prominent voice the entire time with the flute joining in contrapuntal texture with a counter-melody. Very rarely does the play as the primary soloist, only on occasion on a short rest in the bassoon. The string orchestra and piano play accompaniment figures the entire time, often chords or short fragments in response to the soloists. The orchestra provides lush and thick harmonies for the soloist to play overtop of. Overall, the work portrays a nostalgic character.

description: This is a four-movement suite in a style very typical of early twentieth-century French wind writing reminiscent of Paul Taffanel’s wind quintet and Darius Milhaud’s wind pieces. The first movement “Sous la feuillée” is in ternary form in an Andantino tempo marked “tres tranquillo” opens with an espressivo theme in the oboe that the flute joins in on for fragments to highlight key cadential moments, which comes back throughout the movement in new key areas and harmonies. This is overtop of accompaniment lines such as ostinato sixteenth note arpeggiation in the first bassoon and first clarinet, a bass line in the second bassoon, and drones and counter-melody in the horns. The second section “toujours tres tranquille” begins with sixteenths leading to eighth notes motif in the horns in parallel third motion, which gets passed around the ensemble. This is combined with longer note values in the rest of the ensemble providing harmonic support. This continues developing until we climax back into the original theme again. Eventually, the motif returns into the texture to help tie everything together to conclude the movement. The second movement “Radieuse matinée” marked Allegretto con grazia opening with an energetic and cantabile theme in the flute consisting of a measure of eighth and sixteenth notes leading to a longer note value combined with accompaniment figures in the ensemble. Eventually, the oboe enters with the second theme built around an arpeggiated triplet eighth note figure that rises and then meanders downwards in duple eighth notes. The texture then becomes a dialogue passing this theme around while the texture develops into more contrapuntal writing, such as having the main theme woven in. The rest of the movement continues developing and reworking this material in different textures and characters becoming more agitated as it climaxes before returning to the original dolce character. The third movement “Promenade sentimentale” is marked Allegretto non troppo utilizing a similar approach of writing taking elements of structure and styles from the previous movements such as opening with the clarinet playing the main theme with the flute joining on fragments for emphasis and typical accompaniment figures.  However, the character of the main theme is more pedantic and heavier. This is contrasted with a lively middle section “Piu vivo” with a dance-like character. The upper winds play a detached eighth note followed by two sixteenth motif overtop of rhythmic accompaniment figures such as an offbeat motif in the horn and a bass line in the bassoon. A “Lento” section in a chorale style briefly interrupts this allowing for a return to the opening character and reworking of the original material before the Piu Vivo returns. This interruption occurs again leading to a final return of the opening material to conclude the movement. The final movement “Ronde villageoise” is marked Allegro giocoso in a lively dance-like character. It consists of an energetic theme of eighth and sixteenth notes organized in a period initially played in unison by the clarinets overtop of rhythmic accompaniment figures. As it develops a more vocal-like theme is introduced in the flute, while the accompaniment becomes more virtuosic.

description: Tarnopolski’s music combines two distinct aesthetics in paradox: 1) a search for a dissonant euphony that is developed from a foundation of carefully arranged sound material with a focus on timbre and texture, and 2) theatrical musical imagery that ranges in emotion. He achieves this through the use of structure to convey the musical idea, which provides the foundation for the stylistic and concrete substance of the musical material. This is a short one movement work that takes a chorale melody by Johann Rudolf Ahle and reconceptualizes it in a contemporary context. It begins with the melody being performed as originally written in a lyrical style in the tenor register of the bassoon. The rest of the work explores performing this melody utilizing multiphonics

description: This is a short one-movement work in ternary form that constantly shifts meter every measure or two creating an element of instability in the phrasing through it being shortened or extended unexpectedly. The A section “Allegretto” features a motif of three sixteenths leading to a tied quarter note weaving around the home pitch of the piece “F♯.” As the phrase progresses the character switches from a slurred lyrical line to humoresque staccato eighth notes. Eventually, the sixteenths climax to eigth in a row, while dynamically growing to fortissimo at the apex in the range on the pitch “C♯.” The B section “Adagio” resembles a vocal line with embellishments mainly travelling in step-wise or small intervallic motion with moments of quick flourishes for excitement.

description: This is a short one-movement work that depicts an evening outside with friends through the dialogue between the instruments and the use of air noises in the flute to imitate the wind. The work opens with the flute playing the main motif consisting of six repeated note triplet eighth notes with the first one being tenuto, the next five staccato and the last one tied over to a dotted half note. On the dotted half note the flutist adds air noises. The guitar then responds to the motif with chords. The motif is then repeated in the flute and the guitar’s response is expanded upon with a simple melody in the top voice overtop of the chords. The next motif undergoes variation with the last note melodically changing to a major 9th interval. This time the guitar enters during the motif creating an overlap like a person chiming in on a conversation. The work continues developing the motif and the guitar playing a contrapuntal line at the same time of the flute. The flute during the climax briefly deviates from the main motif. Afterwards, it returns to the motif and continues to simplify until it returns to its original state to conclude the work.

description: This is a one-movement work that utilizes a variety of contemporary techniques to reinterpret the traditional structures of classical music through aleatoric sections and unconventional notation. The piece opens with an unmetered section where the left hand of the piano has a semitone aleatoric motif and sporadic right-hand fragments. This is combined with an improvised-like quasi cadenza line first in the flute, then the bassoon. As the section progresses the flute and bassoon lines become shorter and closer together to create a dialogue. The next section is metered consisting of one measure motif that is repeated with small changes over time in a sequence-like manner. This leads into a homorhythmic legato melody in the flute and bassoon overtop of a disjunct passage of sixteenth notes built on large intervals such as minor ninth. Eventually, this develops back into the opening quasi-cadenza material. However, this time the flute and bassoon are overlapping and interrupting each other.

description: This is a four-movement work that combines elements of chant and renaissance music with avant-garde aesthetics. The first movement “Tranquillo” begins with long notes with varied entrances throughout the ensemble. Eventually, this leads to a homorhythmic section of long notes where the note values get shorter as it progresses until it arrives at quarter notes. This climaxes into a virtuosic trumpet cadenza. The movement ends with another homorhythmic section in the brass overtop of an eighth note accompaniment in the piano. The second movement “Allegro sostenuto” features technical and disjunct lines weaving between the instruments until a solo piano ostinato emerges to end the movement. The third movement “Andante” opens with a solo clarinet long-tones that evolves into a dialogue with the flute overtop of repeated long-tone on the pitch “E” in the piano’s right-hand. This leads into a repeating septuplet and sextuplet sixteenth note section amongst the ensemble. The final movement “Largo” begins with a bassoon solo with other instruments joining in on long tones as it progresses. Eventually, the oboe takes over with a repeated note motif over the long tones to end the piece.

description: This is a virtuosic one-movement work in a similar style to the popular Paris concours pieces written for bassoon. This work was conceived as a contest piece for the All-Ukraine Competition and has been reused for various competitions in Ukraine over the last forty years. The work has three main sections following the typical slow-fast-slow structure of a contest piece. It opens with a mysterious “Lento cantabile” section that has a calm character with moments of unexpected harmonies. It begins with a four-measure piano introduction in homophony consisting of eighth and quarter notes. The bassoon enters overtop of this with a vocal-like melody. The largest section “Allegro” features a lively articulated repeated sixteenth note motif and energetic melody with the roles traded between the instruments. Over time this motif develops into a syncopated rhythmic ostinato on a repeated chord based on Eb. This leads into a 7/8 section with a dance-like character based on repeated sixteenth note chords with an alternating accent pattern of 2+3+2 and 2+2+3. The bassoon follows this pattern with a disjunct staccato eighth note line. Eventually, this evolves into sixteenth notes in the bassoon climaxing into a high D with a descending glissando to bring back the motif and melody at the beginning of the allegro. This leads into a homophonic scalar line that develops into a dialogue of ascending sixteenth triplets between the bassoon and piano climaxing to a high D# half note in the bassoon, where the repeated sixteenth note motif returns in the piano to a fake ending with the bassoon playing a long low Bb alone. However, the piano enters on the last eighth note of this Bb with a sforzando low A to bring a return to the Lento cantabile section. This final section has some variations in harmony and rhythm from the opening.

description: This is a five-movement suite that utilizes a wide array of contemporary extended techniques on the flute to depict different characters and stories from Ukrainian folk fairy tales. The first movement “Koza dereza”or “Bully Goat” depicts the story of a goat that is bought by a family. The goat continues to lie to the family causing the father to sharpen his knife to butcher the goat, but he escapes and hides in a rabbits home and continues to lie to various other animals getting into various situations. The moral of the story is the dangers of being deceptive. Musically, the movement is marked “Andante capriccioso” and opens with a theme in the flute with foot stomping on the rests. Then, virtuosic articulated nontuplet runs are introduced. This leads into a repeated sixteenth note motif marked as “like the bleating of the goat” to represent the goat character. Next, tremolo multiphonics are added into the texture creating an goat noise like effect. The next section is percussive and energetic through beat boxing and a line of eighth notes that alternates between regular notes and key clicks. The movement continues in this character with motifs from earlier being incorporated. The second movement “Kolobok” or “The Runaway Bun” depicts the story of a little round bun (bread) that suddenly comes to life and escapes the home of a poor elderly couple. The couple chases Kolobok who runs into various animals that try to eat him but continues to escape each encounter by singing a song. Eventually, a fox catches Kolobok by complimenting his singing and eats him. Musically, it is marked “Adagio sempre accelerando” that presents a continuous stream of sixteenth notes that begin in the low register that climb to the upper register. As it progresses, singing and playing to represent Kolobok’s song is introduced. Near the end the motif begins more disjunct and articulated to display the danger Kolobok is in. The movement ends with a motif that becomes more and more fragmented and shortened until it is a whole note depicting Kolobok’s death. The following movement “About the seven Gaivron (Rook) brothers and their sister” is about seven brothers who are under a curse and are turned into birds and their sister sets out on a journey to break the curse to save them getting help from the sun, moon, and the stars. The story has a happy ending with the sister saving the brothers and the family lives happily ever after. Musically, the movement opens with an “Adagio” section that has a declamatory theme using arpeggiation that becomes more disjunct and virtuosic with sextuplets introduced. The next section “Moderato” begins with a line of frullato half notes that is followed by a sixteenth note motif built on a two slurred, two slurred articulation with intervals that expand as it progresses then compacts to close the section. The next section “Andante legato” is built around sixteenths (or triplet sixteenth) notes leading to a tied quarter note, which has singing and playing on the quarter note. This is followed by another “Moderato” section that brings back to the two motifs, which variates and expands upon the material such as making the frullato half notes syncopated beginning on beat four of the measure. A final “Largo” section is centered around a motif of a quarter note followed by a dotted eighth and sixteenth note. After two measures of silence a disjunct sixteenth note line is played cascading from the low to the high register of the flute to conclude the movement. The fourth movement “Mr. Kotskyi” is about an old abandoned cat .A fox finds the cat and decides instead of eating the cat they can get married instead. They then convince the other animals that he is a fearsome beast, which prompts the animals to provide him with a feast making them masters of the forest. The story teaches the morals of using one’s wit and resourcefulness. Musically, it begins with a “Lento” section that has quarter notes with glissandos to imitate a cat meowing. A melodic line is then played that has the flutist say the word “Meow” throughout. The final movement “Sirko” is about an old, loyal sheepdog abandoned by his owner due to his age. Sirko meets a kind wolf and they plan for the wolf to kidnap the baby from the family so Sirko can jump in to rescue the baby resulting in him saving the day and winning his family back. To repay the wolf for his help Sirko sneaks the wolf into a family wedding to enjoy the feast of food. The story teaches the morals of friendship and gratitude. Musically, it begins with an “Allegro section” that has an energetic dance-like character consisting of sixteenth notes often in scalar or arpeggiated motion leading to an eighth or quarter note. The next section “Andante” uses glissandos and frullatos on quarter and half notes to imitate a wolf howling. Finally, an “Allegretto” section alternates and incorporates material from the previous two sections to conclude the work.

description: This is an one-movement work that takes Ukrainian folk songs as the basis for a virtuosic display in a romantic style. The work opens with an introduction that begins with fortissimo declamatory chords in the piano that the flute responds to. It continues with virtuosic quasi-cadenza-like statements from the flute in between these chords. Next, a vocal-like melody is presented in the flute overtop of quarter note chords in the left hand and the melody or brief echoes in the right hand of the piano. As it develops quick embellishments such as septuplets and thirty-second note triplets are inserted into the theme, which leads to a cadenza movement marked “staccato vivamente” consisting of a double-tongue descending scalar passage in the flute. The next section “Andante” presents a lyrical theme in the flute overtop of a bass line in the left hand on beats 1 and 3 combined with chords on beats 2 and 4 in the right hand of the piano. As it develops it becomes embellished as a string of wandering triplets into the upper register of the flute, while the right hand of the piano plays the melody. It then progresses into passages of sixteenth notes featuring scalar and larger intervals highlighting the harmonic progressions. Throughout this section two voice writing is used to show the important melodic notes to bring out. The following section "Più mosso scherzando” marked “ben leggiero” consists of a motif of an eight note with a preceding grace note that is followed by two slurred sixteenth notes in scalar motion that leads to passages of sixteenth notes. The piano mostly plays an accompanimental texture that occasionally joins in on the passages of sixteenths. It is briefly interrupted by a three-measure “Adagio” in a lyrical style as a contrast. Next, an “Allegro energico” section presents the theme in the piano, which the flute later joins in to add a virtuosic passages of sixteenth (quadruplet and quintuplet) notes. Afterwards, a “Vivo giocoso” with a lively dance-like character mainly built around sixteenth and eighth notes in the flute with eighth note chords and bass line in the piano. Eventually, another two-measure “Adagio” returns as contrast before a final brief “Presto” with material from earlier to conclude the work.
Kovaleva’s music is inspired by a turn to realism by reflecting on life through the traditions of classicism and romanticism. There is often use of folklore primary sources.

description: Malyi’s compositions are structured and inspired by utilizing a different method or technique for each specific work to shape the musical material. This work takes inspiration from Pre-Christian aesthetics and songs through the use of polymodality, texture such as heterophonic passages, and timbre. However, it uses newly composed motifs and materials. This is combined with an alternative approach to development by using motif variation, which a similar approach can be seen in works by composers such as Stravinsky, Bartok, and Ligeti. The alternative development is combined with a combination method utilizing elements of polyphony techniques and minimalism. Specifically, almost all of the time throughout the work there is the dichotomy between stable and unstable that is often expressed through a main stable voice in an ostinato texture interacting with secondary unstable voices in a changing counterpoint texture. The first movement “Allegro vivace” opens with the main motif in the flute consisting of four notes in descending stepwise motion with the last note changing interval such as a major third and augmented fourth. This motif is consistent throughout the movement with small variations as it gets passed around the ensemble for each section. The rest of the ensemble’s accompaniment figures become more contrapuntal and rhythmically active as the movement develops. The next movement “Andante con moto” is based around a motif that is built by each note being played by a different voice to create a larger line. The opening section is built on longer note values that pass around the ensemble, which sound closer together as it progresses until the first note of one voice lines up with the last one of the preceding voice and eventually overlapping creating a thicker texture. At the end of the section frullato is introduced to create more variety in the timbre and texture. The next section begins with staccato eighth notes in a consistent chain of one after another. Eventually, the eighths develop into two sixteenth notes and develops into a larger main motif played in one voice consisting of eighth, two sixteenth, eigth, and quarter note. As it reaches the climax the voices overlap like the previous section to conclude the work. The third movement “Moderato” begins with the main motif played by the oboe comprised rhythmically of eighth and quarter notes that is a continual ascend to the peak of the motif. The clarinet provides accompaniment figures of a longer note leading to a staccato eighth note. Next, the bassoon takes over the main motif with the clarinet dropping out of the texture while the flute joins in with a new accompaniment figure creating a contrapuntal texture in the ensemble. Afterwards, the clarinet re-enters with a variation of the main motif with a homorhythmic texture in the rest of the ensemble of accented eighth notes to create a syncopation and to destabilize the metres. The motif gradually is expanded into a passage of ascending stepwise sixteenth notes, while the texture becomes more contrapuntal as it continues until returning to a more transparent texture of material passing around the ensemble to conclude the movement. The fourth movement “Andante moderato” is built around three main motifs 1) thirty-second note followed by a dotted eigth, 2) a whole tone scalar motif, and 3) a chromatic sixteenth note passage introduced in measure 161 by the clarinet. These motifs interact and develop independently of one another. They also get recombined and fragmented throughout creating a variety of different textures. Eventually, this climaxes into a virtuosic flute passage of sextuplets that becomes fragmented to conclude the movement. The final movement “Veloce” is comprised of two main motifs that are alternated between. The first motif is a whole tone scale that is in a texture of a scale of sixteenths that rotate around the ensemble in different note groupings such as the flute plays six sixteenth notes before passing to the clarinet that plays four sixteenth notes. The other motif has a more dance-like quality as it consists of staccato eighths leading to an offbeat accent that is tied creating a syncopated quality. This motif is also more vocal-like adding to the dance-like character. The rest of the movement continues developing these motifs such as the sixteenth notes becoming sextuplet sixteenths notes in a neighbour tone motion. Over time, the various developments from throughout are combined to conclude the work.

premiere: October 10th, 2011 in Lviv, Ukraine at “Contrasts” festival by Dmytro Medolyz (fl)
description: This work consists of five short movements each in a contrasting character highlighting a different aspect of flute playing. The first movement “Lento” has a pastorale and poco recitando character featuring a repeated note motif throughout. It opens with the repeated note motif that has short fragments that interrupt this motif. Each interruption is more expanded until a full passage occurs that develops to become more virtuosic. However, the repeated note motif works its way back in briefly throughout to connect the different elements and ideas to create a fully realized phrase. It resembles how a musician improvises by taking a brief fragment or idea and continually expands upon it to create something new but continues to utilize elements of it throughout to create a cohesive idea. The next movement “Allegretto” is a virtuosic stream of quintuplets that wander around the different registers of the flute. Throughout the movement various rests are inserted to slightly throw off the momentum being created. The third movement “Allegretto” is centered on a rhythmic motif of two sixteenths and triplet sixteenth. Throughout it develops by undergoing slight variations and recombination of the fragments before returning to the initial material. The following movement “Adagio” has a cantabile espressivo character featuring slurred, legato phrases that are highly ornamented resembling a singer performing an aria. Often throughout a phrase will begin in the upper register to then jump to the lower register at a softer dynamic to create a dramatic contrast. The final movement “Allegro” consists of a string of staccato eighth notes in a disjunct manner that are constantly being reinterpreted into new groupings and undergoing slight variations as it develops. Eventually, at the end it becomes a phrase of two slurred sixteenth notes ascending across the registers of the flute before one last fragment of staccato eighth notes to a trill in the upper register of the flute that then descends staccato eighth notes to the low register to conclude the work.

description: This is a five-movement suite taking inspiration from folklorism through the depiction of the average village life combined with romantic structures and harmonies. The first movement “Morning in the Garden” is marked in an Allegro vivace tempo in an ABA Coda form. It features two motifs that quickly pass around the ensemble. In the A section a motif of four sixteenth notes and an eighth note - ascending perfect fourth followed by descending stepwise motion. In the B section a motif of two sixteenths and two eighths - ascending stepwise motion ending with a descending minor third. The next movement “Melody” marked Andante cantabile is in a polyphonic texture presenting a melody in the oboe, countermelody in the clarinet, and a bass line ostinato in the bassoon. The flute switches around their role throughout between melody and bass line. The following movement “Pastoral” marked Andantino that consists of a melody that passes around the ensemble overtop of long tones. The fourth movement “Humoresque” marked Allegro non troppo is an AABA Coda form. The A section has a joking character through the use of staccato eighths and accented quarter notes. The B section marked Un poco piu mosso has two main sections: 1) virtuosic passage of sixteenth notes overtop of a countermelody and a bass line and 2) an eighth note bass line in the bassoon underneath a syncopated eighth note motif in the flute and oboe. Eventually, the B section unwinds becoming a fragmented one beat motif that leads into a fermata chord to set up a reprise of the A material. The final movement “Raining” is in ternary form. The A section marked Allegro scherzando (quasi presto) has a frantic character features a quarter note section where the ensemble is chasing the flute. The ensemble plays on the downbeat while the flute plays on beats two and three. The flute line develops into eighth notes as the phrase progresses. The B section marked Un poco meno mosso is in a cantabile and lyrical style presenting a folk-like melody in the oboe over a dotted half note accompaniment. Then a leggiero melody is presented in the clarinet overtop of a quarter rest followed by two quarter notes accompaniment. A return to the first melody occurs this time in the flute and bassoon.

description: This is a collection of five short pieces that are from the composer’s middle period of works and are each free in form and tonality that can stand alone or be performed in a full cycle. The first movement “Recitative and Dance” is in ternary form with a typical contrasting middle section. The A section is marked “molto tranquillo” consisting of a vocal-like line that is highly embellished in the lower octave of the flute, emulating traditional Jewish singing. The B section marked “Allegretto” has an energetic and quirky dance-like character due to the alternating triple and duple feel from the alternating 3/8 versus 4/8 metres. Rhythmically it consists of slurred sixteenths leading to staccato eighth notes in a step-wise or arpeggiated manner. The second movement “Improvisation” marked “tranquillo” has a similar character to the first movement of a highly embellished vocal-like melody, but this time written above the staff. The next movement “Scherzetto” marked “allegro” is constructed on a unity of structure that includes lively rhythms and a bird-song quotation. Musically, the movement is built around meandering strings of eighth notes that progress sequentially up and down the range of the flute. In between this material are sections of contrasting materials. A contrasting “cantabile” section occurs that features a folk-like melody in the lowest register of the flute mainly consisting of quarter notes with grace notes throughout. The fourth movement “Romance” marked “Andante” features a highly embellished melody where tempo changes and rubato throughout in the style of a bel canto aria by a powerful opera diva. The final movement “Cadenza & Finale” opens with a “Tranquillo” section that is a virtuosic display of technique that bears a relationship to the recitative motifs of the first movement. The next section marked “Vivace assai” is reminiscent of a hora, a traditional celebratory Jewish dance often done at weddings and Bar Mitzvahs to honor the guests of honor. It often features lifting the couple in chairs. Musically, the main characteristics are the fast-pace and high energy typically in 2/4 or 3/8 often beginning slow and speeding up as it progresses. Often, it uses types of Freygish scales. It begins with a virtuosic display of long passages of slurred sixteenth, which eighth notes and sixteenth rests are introduced as it progresses. This leads into the “Tempo di danza” which features a typical Klezmer-like melody with syncopation and embellishments. A return to the “Vivace assai” occurs to conclude the work.

description: This is a five-movement suite that explores five different characters utilizing elements such as form from neoclassical with language and idioms of avant-garde. The piece utilizes the full range of expressions that the bassoon is capable of producing from lyrical and cantabile playing to short and articulated. Movements one through three are based on Emily Dickinson quotes. The first movement “Love can do all but raise the Dead” creates a sense of longing and anticipation through an unsettled and wandering ostinato pattern in the piano underneath an espressivo and legato melody in the bassoon that avoids resolution by constantly extending the phrase. The second movement “Oh, honey of an hour” is a quasi-samba using a rhythmic and dance-like left hand ostinato combined with right hand syncopated figures in the piano. The bassoon plays technical passages often consisting of arpeggiated sequences or fragmented parts of scales combined together with rests creating an energetic and light character combined with atonal harmonic language to produce a quirky dance. The third movement “There is a solitude of space” creates a simple and melancholic character through an accompaniment piano and vocal-like melody in the bassoon. The movement takes inspiration from tintinnabuli, which is a compositional style by Arvo Pärt that is inspired by chant music by combining two voices of one arpeggiating the tonic triad with another diatonic mostly stepwise motion in a minimalist nature. The fourth movement “L’Allegro” is based on a quote by John Milton “Hence, loathed Melancholy… Mirth with thee, I mean to live.” The movement opens with a quarter and eighth note motif in the bassoon and piano that intensify and grow in flourishing passages of sixteenth notes. The final movement “Der Abschied” is dedicated to Valentin Bibik and is based on a quote by Taras Shevchenko “Proshchai, svite! Proshchai zemle.. (Farwell world! Farewell earth…).” The first section is a quarter note arpeggiated melody in the bassoon in dialogue with a quick articulated tremolo-like motif in the piano creating an ominous character. This leads the next section consisting of a more vocal-like bassoon line overtop of an accompaniment piano part featuring a sequential two sixteenth and an eighth note motif that becomes a simple eighth note accompaniment before joining in contrapuntal dialogue with the bassoon. This evolves into the next section that features a syncopated ostinato E in the left hand of the piano underneath dialogue between the right hand and the bassoon that intensifies through shorter note values and accented articulation. This section continues growing and variating while the ostinato changes pitches every so often eventually becoming an aleatoric section where the two hands of the piano slows down tempo independently from one another while the bassoon remains constant to end the piece.

description: The first movement “Allegro” opens with multiphonics passing between each of the soloists, while the orchestra interweaves sixteenth note triplets in a chromatic motion creating a chaotic and unsettled atmosphere. Eventually, the texture settles into a syncopated homorhythmic passage of short fragments by the soloists, while the orchestra creates a dialogue of the chromatic motif creating a pattern and order from the initial chaos. As it develops the orchestra becomes part of the dialogue with the soloists, which allows for the fragmented statements to become a longer phrase creating cohesion in the whole ensemble. This gets interrupted by a return of the triplet motif but with more repeated and scalar motion inserted creating a sense of momentum to the phrase. This is in a dialogue texture as it rotates around the soloists. As it develops the texture becomes more contrapuntal allowing it to dive back into chaos. Eventually, the soloists introduced a new motif played in homorhythm based around the augmented fourth interval almost imitating a siren as an attempt to regain control. The movement continues in this manner between passages organized together and more disjunct and chaotic passages. This goes attacca into the second movement marked quarter note equals 45 beginning with a dissonant chorale-like passage in the soloists in dialogue with a bell in the percussion section. However, this soon breaks apart as each of the soloists plays different fragments of the opening in a contrapuntal texture as the orchestra slowly joins in and eventually taking over. Afterwards, the opening dissonant chorale returns but this time in a canon with the soloists being one group and the orchestra responding as another group two beats later. The movement continues alternating between the chorale and fragmented sections with a flute cadenza before the final section of the movement, which reverses the order with the soloists responding to the orchestra. The final movement marked quarter note equals 100 begins with material reminiscient of the first movement. This time we have ostinato sixteenth notes, which the pattern changes with each successive passage combined with a syncopated rhythmic melodic line. However, this time the rhythmic line continues developing and growing rather than small repetitive motifs. As it progresses motifs from earlier in the work such as the weaving chromatic triplet sixteenth and augmented fourth (now written as diminished fifth) are snuck into the texture creating a cohesive synthesis of the work. The movement continues playing with the already established motifs while presenting new materials and textures that often get reworked into material that is familiar, such as the opening sixteenths becoming more chromatic, which creates a merging of the old and new. Eventually, the soloists vocally sing “jazz licks” which essentially are the various rhythmic motifs from earlier being combined to create a rhythmic interplay imitating improvised jazz scatting. This results in only the soloists singing and the orchestra snapping their fingers on the final beat to conclude the work.

description: This is a short one-movement work in a folk style utilizing two Ukrainian folk songs “Krutyi bereh krutyi” (Steep shore) and “Podolyanochka” (Little girl) in ternary form in an allegro moderato tempo. It opens with a stately two-measure introduction with a chain of accented notes throughout the ensemble. Then the first folk song is introduced in the clarinet in a lively and accented character. The other winds provide harmonic and countermelodic support. Throughout the section the theme goes under variation developing through pitch, polyphony and texture. The middle section “Meno mosso” introduces the second folk song in the bassoon in a sharp contrast of character now using legato articulation. This section uses various polyphony development techniques such as a canon of the theme in reverse at rehearsal 9. The reprise incorporates some key differences from the opening such as a switch from the original minor to major, and later having fragments of the theme passed around the ensemble compared to one instrument playing it.

description: This work comes from a collection of short pieces he wrote for woodwinds and piano including a Gavotte for flute, a Waltz for clarinet, a Menuet for oboe, and an Andante for English horn. It is a short one movement work that utilizes a Ukrainian folk song. The piece opens with a two-measure fragment from later in the melody in the piano. The bassoon enters with a full statement of the melody in a cantabile character using a slurred and legato style overtop of an accompaniment piano part. The rest of the work continues presenting the melody in the bassoon with moments of dialogue in the piano. The opening two measure fragment is used as a brief piano interlude throughout.

description: This is a three-movement suite that uses folklore inspiration and elements of folk song and dance. The title takes inspiration from Trypillia, which was a culture from the neolithic and chalcolithic time period (5500-2750 BC) from the Carpathian Mountains, Dniester, and Dnipro regions of Ukraine discovered by archaeologist Vikenty Khvoyka in 1896.79 They are known for their pottery, agriculture, and their “burned house horizon.” This concept states that they burnt down their homes when an inhabitant passed away turning them from “dwellings of the living” into “homes of the dead” to make space for new ones.80 Therefore, the history of these people have been lost and forgotten as history has progressed.  The first movement “Morning in Trypillia” is an Andante moderato that alternates between two main sections. The first section features a folk-like melody of eighth and quarter notes that wanders around C mixolydian mainly in step-wise motion, perfect fifth and minor third interval. It is presented first by the flute alone followed by the whole ensemble playing it in unison. The occasional accompaniment figure occurs. The second section is a chorale texture comprised of half, quarter and eighth notes. As the section develops it switches tonality from C major to C minor and other various tonicizations in between. The next movement ”Light Over the Dnipro” is an Andante misterioso also has two main sections. It opens with the flute playing a solo one-measure ostinato in the lowest register. The clarinet then enters with a melody overtop that becomes a syncopated and rhythmic ostinato of tied eighth notes. Then bassoon and clarinet play a one-measure countermelody that becomes the rhythmic ostinato. Eventually, the oboe enters with a melody of half and dotted half notes overtop of the two ostinatos that are intertwined. The second section ”Piu mosso” is livelier with a dance-like character in a triplet meter that has a homorhythmic texture of eighth and quarter notes. As it develops it becomes fragmented and passes around the ensemble, which then gets interrupted with two-measures of the opening flute ostinato before returning to the homorhythmic texture. The movement concludes in a similar manner with the flute ostinato dying away. The final movement ”Dance of Ancestors” is an energetic dance that opens with a rhythmic ostinato of eighth followed by a quarter note in an perfect fifth interval in the clarinet and bassoon. The flute plays a virtuosic sixteenth and eighth note melody with grace notes. Next, the oboe enters with a dotted quarter note counter-melody. Eventually, the oboe, clarinet, and bassoon play a passage of sixteenth notes underneath the flute melody. The section continues with the melody passing around the ensemble while switching accompaniment textures underneath. The second section presents new melodic material that rotates around the ensemble. The movement continues to alternate between the material to conclude the work.

key: I (G major, C major), II-IV (none used)
description: This is a four movement suite inspired by Henri Rousseau who was a 19th century French post-impressionist painter known for his exotic depictions of jungles. Each movement is a musical depiction of a different Rousseau painting. The first movement “The Dream” depicts the scene of a woman lying and dreaming amongst various plants and flowers within a jungle. Musically, Povolotsky has a floating legato melody overtop of chordal and accompanimental lines in the piano. The movement develops becoming more virtuosic until a soaring flute cadenza into the upper octave of the flute occurs. A return of the A material occurs leading into one final virtuosic cadenza to conclude the movement. The next movement “Merry Quartet” depicts a family playing music in a natural scenery. The piano plays an ostinato jumping eighth note line underneath a dance-like theme in the flute consisting of groups of slurred sixteenth notes weaving in a scalar motion leading to staccato eighth notes. Eventually, the sixteenth notes sneak their way into the right hand of the piano creating a dialogue with the flute like a family communicating with one another. As it continues the rhythmic feel gets interrupted through changing metre changes to conclude the movement. The third movement “Snake-Charmer” depicts a woman in the shadows of a jungle playing a flute to charm a snake spiraling around her feet. Musically, the flute represents the woman and the piano the snake. It opens with the flute playing an unaccompanied solo contrasting lyrical and virtuosic moments to charm the snake or piano into joining into the texture, which begins hesitant with longer note values that develops more virtuosic and dialogue-like over time. Eventually, the piano takes over with their own cadenza moment before a final brief return to the A material to conclude the movement. The final movement “Farandole” depicts a joyous celebration of people dancing the French farandole in an outdoor scene. The farandole is a folk dance in 6/8 where dancers link hands following a leader in a winding path with music played by pipes and drums. Povolotsky features a weaving melody in the flute traversing from the low to high octaves that alternates between scalar and arpeggiated motion that leads into a rhythmic motive of three thirty-second notes scaling to a staccato quarter note. Throughout, a pattern of three is used to structure material. The piano plays an accompanimental role mainly with chords on the big beats in the left hand and eighth note arpeggiations of the harmony in the right hand.

premiere: August 15th, 2023 in Saskatoon, Canada by Glenda Lindgren (ob), Zachary Senick (bsn)
key: I (G major), II (C minor), III (A minor), IV (A minor)
description: This is a four-movement suite inspired by the animated film The Tale of Despeareaux, that follows the adventures of a mouse named Despeareaux in France who is sent to the dungeons for violating their laws by talking to humans. The first movement “Allegro” is an energetic and bright character. The opening begins with a lyrical melody in rhythmic unison that becomes more contrapuntal and staccato as the phrase progresses until the instruments have independent lines, like the beginning of a story slowly unfolding and sharing more details. The movement ends by the melody being interrupted with unexpected half note trills leading to a “mysteriously” section that ambiguous weaves around harmonically and ends without a cadence creating anticipation for the next movement. The second movement “Allegretto” is a humoresque and ironic eighth note accompaniment in the bassoon with an oboe melody that has an unsettled and unstable character due to the unexpected rests and accents thrown in. As the movement progresses the bassoon joins in as a countermelody with sixteenth notes. The third movement “Largo” has an ominous character through the use of dissonance added into the harmonic progressions. The form is ABA with the A section being a slow contrapuntal dialogue that leads to a rhythmic unison string of eight notes that create unexpected intervals and dissonances often on the offbeats. The B section is singing oboe melody overtop of an arpeggiated bass line in the bassoon. The final movement “Allegro” is an energetic dance-like character that often has an air of mysterioso to it due to the unexpected harmonies that appear. Often the bassoon has a bass line or a countermelody underneath a melody in the oboe. The movement features lots of sudden character achieved through the contrasting staccato and legato markings throughout.

This work consists of four short movements each in a contrasting character to compile a suite utilizing a neoclassical approach to form and phrase structure combined with contemporary harmonic language. The first movement “Melody” is in a moderato tempo. It opens with a slow melody consisting of dotted half and quarter notes in the bassoon overtop of a tremolo in the piano, which evolves in fragmented interjections. The flute initially enters as a countermelody that has moments of unison with the bassoon. This leads to a piu mosso section where the flute and bassoon are trading off, first eighths and then groups of two sixteenths overtop of arpeggiated quintuplets in the piano. The movement continues with the alternating between sections of melody and trading off texture developing into quicker note values and thicker textures. The next movement “Waltz” has a sort of unsettled character as it the stereotypical roles of the waltz are manipulated. The flute plays a melodic line, but it is syncopated with ties combined with flourishes of weaving sixteenths disrupting the natural flow expected. The bassoon provides stability by playing an accompaniment role of dotted quarter notes on the second beat. However, this is thrown off by the piano accompaniment, which starts on the second eighth note of the bar each time. This creates a metrical ambiguity allowing for an unbalanced waltz character to occur. The third movement “Sketch” is in a moderato tempo featuring slow arpeggios and long notes in the piano underneath a quarter note melody in the bassoon. Eventually, the flute enters with glissandos before presenting a more active second melody that develops into a unison motif of arpeggiated quarter notes in the ensemble. The “Final” movement is in allegro molto tempo in ternary form. It opens with a cluster chord motif of two quarter notes that jumps over three octaves between the hands in the piano. This motif creates instability in the 3/4 metre for the winds trading eighth note passages. The B section is a meno mosso with similar lines in the winds but the piano now is in dialogue with the winds eventually becoming unison.

description: In Stutschewsky’s music he had a preference for smaller forms from classical music with inspiration from idioms of Jewish music and serialism of Schoenberg, in which he became a member of his circle. This work is four short movements in contrasting characters. The first movement “Allegro moderato” is in ternary form. It begins with an energetic homorhythmic section mainly consisting of eighth and sixteenth notes leading to quarter notes (sometimes tied eighths). As it develops brief moments of contrapuntal writing interrupt this texture for a measure or two. The B section “Sostenuto” uses similar writing but now a more legato character with triplet eighth notes. The next movement “Allegro molto capriccioso” is in ternary form. The A section is built around a three-quarter note motif that gets passed around changing intervals and articulations creating different characters. As it develops it becomes more contrapuntal with other short motifs being added into the texture such as two eighth notes. The B section “Molto tranquillo” presents a cantando theme in the flute, a countermelody in the oboe and accompaniment figures in homorhythmic that are often syncopated in the clarinet, bassoon, and horn. A short stringendo leading to a “Vivace” section consisting of fragmentation concludes the movement. The following movement “Lento” features a molto cantando theme that is lyrical with brief moments of virtuosic flourishes first played by the flute overtop of countermelodies and accompaniment figures. Eventually, it becomes fragmented and passed around the ensemble in a dialogue texture. The movement continues in this manner with returns to the theme in a new instrument with different accompaniment figures alternating with dialogue of fragments passages. The final movement “Grotesque” is in ternary form in a “Allegro vivace” tempo. The A section is a chain of different short staccato motifs in each instrument that connect together to form a longer line. These motifs develop to become a homorhythmic line. Throughout other short motifs are introduced into the homorhythmic textures creating brief moments of contrapuntal writing. The B section “Piu lento” is a four-measure section that begins contrapuntal and develops into a homorhythmic chorale.

description: This is a four-movement work the explores avant-garde techniques, aesthetics and styles of writing. The first movement “Adagio” is in a rubato tempo in an unmetered and improvisatory manner. It begins in a dialogue-like texture with the bassoon playing fragments leading to a long note in which the piano responds to. As it develops the two instruments intertwine more. The second movement “Tempo libro” is a bassoon cadenza also in an unmetered and improvisatory manner. It consists of virtuosic flourishes of notes combined with extended technique sections such as frullato, multiphonics and quarter tones. The following movement “Marcatissimo” is a quirky dance-like character that is unbalanced due to the 5/8 metre and syncopation throughout. It also features large intervals both slurred and articulated in the bassoon. The two instruments are in a contrapuntal texture the entire time. The final movement “Adagio” is in a dialogue-like texture with a melodic line that is infused with extended techniques in the bassoon. The has short fragments leading to a long note during the longer note values in the bassoon line.

description: This is a one-movement work inspired by surconventionalism utilizing one convention or algorhythm throughout. Surconventionalism is centered around the idea of polystylistic music by composing music based on existing musical structures placed in a different context in order to create a new reality. Therefore, conventional language is used by the composer while also consciously breaking the rules governing its syntax by the unexpected and untypical juxtaposition of traditional elements to distort the listener’s expectations. This results in the transformation of the basic structure of music to achieve a deep structure through distortion techniques. Fox opens with a quarter note melody in the lowest register of the piano that is based on a two-note chromatic sequence. This line continues for the entire piece with small transformations over time. This is combined with a long tone motif in the winds where each voice enters in a cannon. This motif evolves over time becoming more active until it becomes a fragmentation of the piano line. Later the horn contrasts this with a different fragmentation briefly. Eventually, the long note motif becomes its own melodic line through all of the staggered entries in close succession of each phrase. At the end of the piece the winds join into a transformed version of the melody for three measures leading to a whole note in the clarinet overtop of the quarter notes in the piano. This texture dies away into silence to conclude the piece.

description: This is a suite in three-movements that depicts three baroque-era dances that are re-inspired with a neoclassical lens of modern rhythms, elements of jazz harmony, and unexpected dynamic effects. The inspiration for the work came from harpsichord works of French Baroque composers Francois Couperin and Jean-Philippe Rameau (N. Jacobchuk 161-163).The first movement “Gavotte” has a light and elegant character in ternary form. The movement opens with a theme of four eighth notes slurred 2+2 leading to bouncy quartet notes that are overtop of a quarter note bass line in the piano. As the music develops both parts become more complex and embellished with ornamentation creating a more intricate dialogue. The B section is more lyrical with a syncopated chordal line and a theme in the upper voice in the piano with a scalar motif with vocal-like melismas in the upper register of the flute. The return of the A section comes back immediately ornamented, however with new choices this time such as a reference to the grupetto popular in the classical era. The next movement “Pavana” features inspiration from jazz harmonies combined with the dance-like baroque character. It opens with accompanimental figures of an oscillating eighth note line in the right hand and bass line in the left hand, while the flute plays long note values that develop into a melody in the low register that is reminiscent of “a lyrical confession revealing the inner world of a person.” (N. Jacobchuk 161 Translated Z. Senick). As it progresses the piano becomes more active with moments of response. The section climaxes with a virtuosic thirty-second note scale that takes the melody above the staff. A piano interlude consisting of triplet eighth note arpeggiation takes over. This leads into a contrasting “Piu mosso” section that consists of a more lively character with a motif of leaping sixteenth notes from the upper register to the middle register of the flute. The texture is more polyphonic with a dialogue between the flute and the piano, which leads into a virtuosic cadenza by the flute consisting of various sixteenth note motifs. A return to the opening material occurs to conclude the movement. The final movement “Jig” has a very joyful and fun character. The flute melody consists of a sequence of staccato eighth notes that lead to a longer note with a mordent, while the piano plays chords on each beat. However, the theme and accompaniment constantly undergoes variations such as next the rhythmic pattern becomes playing just on the first and third eighth of each beat. The work continues in this manner with each alteration of the material becoming more virtuosic with the introduction of sixteenth notes and frullato. After it has reached its full virtuosity it switches to a contrasting character that brings a more calm lyrical atmosphere with a vocal-like melody in the flute and chords and downward arpeggiations in the piano. The work shifts back to the original character to conclude the work.

description: The composer describes that the work “evokes Beethoven’s Für Elise, continuing the line of lyrical musical reflections. At the same time, it establishes a structural and expressive link to Wagner’s Tristan und Isolde. Within a contemporary sonic field defined by extended techniques, the piece recontextualizes specific intonational cells and motivic units from Wagner’s opera, illuminating them in a new light.” (Tarnopolski via email 2026). The work opens with a “Liberamento” section that is very delicate with the flutist performing breath noises that slowly develop into full tone, which the vibrato creeps in becoming more noticeable. Next, a “Rubato” section introduces a motif that then has a variety of extended techniques and textures incorporated to reimagine it in different contexts and characters such as using vibrato manipulation, multiphonics, and quarter tones. Then, a “Piu mosso” section has a virtuosic flourish of thirty-second notes based on quarter tone scales that are rhythmically grouped in alternating different subdivisions of quintuplet and sextuplet. This is followed by a “Rigorosso” section that brings back techniques from earlier in the piece but completely reworking the motif to be quite different. As it progresses it becomes more active and intense through the quicker rhythms and simultaneous incorporation of extended techniques into the phrase. This climaxes into an accelerando in a sequential pattern of nontuplets that are oscillating. The final section of the piece returns back to the opening texture with the focus being on the breath and air effects creating an overall synthesis to the work.

description: This piece originally comes from a larger work the composer wrote inspired by Molière’s “Le Bourgeois Gentilhomme”, which he then took this portion and rewrote it into a piece for flute and piano. This is a short one-movement work structured with a short introduction followed by ternary form in a neoclassical style incorporating elements of a gavotte such as a graceful and dance-like character, a clear melody, and homophonic textures. The introduction marked “Quarter note equals 120” presents a dance-like melody of eighth and sixteenth notes leading to quarter notes over top of chordal accompaniment in the piano. The main body of the work is marked “Vivo” and consists of two main sections. The A section presents another dance-like melody of eighth and sixteenth notes that are mostly articulated and staccato creating an energetic character. At the beginning the flute and right hand of piano are in homorhythm while the left hand plays a leaping bass line. As it progresses offbeats are introduced into the texture. The B section is much more disjunct featuring a fragmented motif of three sixteenths in the flute, while the piano plays eighth notes jumping between the two hands creating a disjointed melody. The return of the A material features alternation between homorhythm and syncopated polyphonic writing in the right hand of the piano now. This creates a dialogue of two different characters coming together.

description: This a short one movement work that utilizes a mixture of traditional notation, graphic notation, and extended techniques. The work begins with a long note value that undergoes a series of transformations to explore various texture. It uses three different textures: 1) singing while playing, 2) vibrato manipulation, and 3) glissando. After silence another long note occurs that begins without vibratot and explores the use of glissando before adding vibrato back into the sound. Eventually, frullato is introduced into the texture. Next, the work becomes more virtuosic with articulated flourishes that cascade to the higher register. Afterwards, key clicks and multiphonics are utilized until it is interrupted by the performer yelling “Ah!” to surprise the audience. The work continues in this manner getting more virtuosic while reincoporating different combinations of extended techniques to create a range of textures. A final whole note with singing provides a return to the opening character that is contrasted with key clicks to conclude the work.

description: All of Solonskiy’s works are written with a pedagogical purpose in mind to be applied in a concert setting. Each of the pieces were written for a particular student of his to address their particular challenges in their playing. He chooses to use characters from folklore and fairytales to make them approachable and easily understood by the student allowing them to bring their own imagination, emotions and moods into the music based on characters they are familiar with. His goal is to comprehensively reveal the beauty and expressiveness of woodwind instruments through the color, technical, and artistic capabilities. This is a short one-movement work that focuses on articulation and slurring of large intervals. It opens with a brief piano introduction marked “Risoluto” consisting of accompaniment figures. The bassoon enters with the main theme in an “Allegro” tempo. The main theme is an eight-measure period that consists of four articulated sixteenth notes leading to an eighth note comprised of an upper and lower neighbour motion followed by arpeggiation of five articulated eighth notes. This then immediately goes into a descending scalar motion of four eighth notes in a two slurred-two tongued figure followed by a lower neighbour leading to a quarter note. The second half of the period has the same figure but different notes in the final measure. This is overtop of a bass line in the left-hand and offbeat chords in the right hand to create a folk dance-like character. This theme continues to develop with slight variations such as grace notes added. The next section “Magnifico” presents a new theme comprised of syncopated quarter note motif in a slurred and legato character. As this develops the melody becomes eighth notes and more fragmented featuring larger intervals. Eventually, a reprise of the opening material returns to conclude the piece.

description: This is a one-movement work in a neoclassical style using typical forms, structures, and compositional techniques combined with aesthetics and extended techniques from the avant-garde movement such as frullato and glissando. The work opens with a “Moderato Sostenuto” section that begins with the flute playing the main theme alone in the middle register. As the theme develops the other instruments enter one at a time playing a drone, starting with the clarinet. This is taken over by the oboe, allowing the clarinet to present a triplet eighth note motif. This continues with the bassoon followed by the horn taking over the drone eventually leading into the triplet motif. The next section “Moderato meno mosso” is a homorhythmic texture composed of eighth and sixteenth notes in the oboe, clarinet, and bassoon. Eventually, the flute enters overtop of this texture with a virtuosic passage. Afterwards motifs from the opening of the section are traded around the ensemble. The following section “Agitato” features aggressive and articulated sixteenths notes in a texture of the flute solo in dialogue with the rest of the ensemble. This leads into a cut time section with a tutti syncopated ostinato leading into another homorhythmic section featuring tremolos. However, these tremolos are arpeggios that the musician quickly repeats similar to the effect aleatoric writing achieves in the avant-garde movement. Eventually, a clarinet solo emerges playing the main theme from the opening. This develops into a dialogue texture between the clarinet and the ensemble. Eventually, the clarinet drops out and this leads into a “Staccato sempre” section that features a bell-like line of long note values with a sforzando articulation in the horn overtop of staccato eighth and sixteenth fragments in homorhythm in the ensemble. Overtime the ensemble becomes contrapuntal. This leads into an espressivo and vocal-like melody in the flute and bassoon overtop of accompaniment figures in the oboe and clarinet. A return to an “Agitato” section occurs featuring a virtuosic quasi-cadenza solo first in the oboe that is followed by the bassoon and flute. This leads to a contrapuntal section feature motifs from earlier in the work. A return to the “Moderato” character occurs with a motif based off two eighth notes in an ascending third interval that alternates between minor and major is passed around the ensemble. A solo line emerges overtop of this texture that also passes around the ensemble. Eventually, this becomes an unison quarter note line in the ensemble with repeated triplets in the flute. This leads into a short quasi-cadenza moment in the flute interrupted by the staccato sixteenth motif from earlier. The work ends with a “Sostenuto” section that brings back the main theme in the flute overtop of drones passed between the bassoon and horn.

description: This is a short work that explores the comic side of bassoon writing through short staccato sections that jump around the ranges of the bassoon. description: This is a short one-movement work with a blissful character marked “Animato” with the flute performing a vocal and folk-like melody overtop of accompanimental figures in the piano. The theme in the flute is built on long notes that grow to triplet quarter notes and quarters leading into the next long note mainly in stepwise motion combined with the occasional small interval. The piano has syncopated rhythmic figures creating forward momentum and energy in the music. Occasionally, the syncopated figures sneak into the melodic line in homorhythm with the piano. As the piece develops the melody climbs upwards through the register and becomes more active with longer passages of smaller note values between the long note values. The work concludes with the piano playing an arpeggiated sequential figure leading to a whole note chord, which the flute then plays a quasi-rubato fragment of four eighth notes with ornamentation leading to a final whole note fermata.

description: This is a one-movement work for piano quartet with electronics that are depicted through graphic notation of bubbles of different sizes in the score to communicate the different sounds and events occurring. The work is inspired by the story of Hero and Leander from Milorad Pavić’s novel The Inner Side of the Wind. Throughout the work the quartet is playing for a mysterious young girl Heroneya who is both at times like day and at other times like night that allows the listener to pass through ancient times, destinies, and lives. This is juxtaposed with the Hero's life that transudes the life of Leandre. This is represented through the violin that embodies the main elements of the world: water, air, and fire combined with the mystery surrounding them. Musically, the piece begins with short, fragmented motifs that are in dialogue across the ensemble. As it develops into longer lines that are interweaving and competing amongst each other in the ensemble the electronics begin to be introduced. The electronics evolve into elemental noises such as water and wind. Creating an ominous and mysterious atmosphere. This texture morphs into a cohesive line where the ensemble plays harmoniously together creating a cohesive line that interacts and builds off one another. Slowly, the lines become more contrapuntal creating more dissonance across the ensemble as it morphs into fragmented material reminiscent of the opening. This prompts the electronics to become more industrial, robotic, and man-made to contrast the earlier importance of the elements. Eventually, the ensemble comes together in a homorhythmic texture that leads into an electronic solo returning more to the elements to conclude the work.

description: This is a short one-movement work that briefly explores a variety of different characters by constantly changing tempo and style. This work highlights the range of character and musicality a flutist can achieve. Pedagogically, this could be a good piece for a young student to perform in a contest to demonstrate a wide range of their playing abilities. The work begins with a “Lento” section that is a vocal-like melody mainly consisting of quarter, eighth and half notes in the lower register of the flute overtop of rolled chords in the piano. This develops into a “Piu mosso” that becomes more active introducing sixteenth notes and dotted quarter notes to set up the next section “Allegretto”. This features a dance-like melody of eighth and sixteenth notes with grace notes inserted to create a quirky character. The piano plays an oscillating eighth note bass line and countermelody underneath before switching to simply playing a quarter note bass line in the left hand and off beat chords in the right hand. The flute melody progresses to become more virtuosic to become a full passage of sixteenth notes. This is immediately contrasted by an “Andantino” section that has a flowing theme of eighth and sixteenth notes mainly in scalar and arpeggiated motion traversing across the range of the flute. This is overtop of similar accompaniment motifs from the last section. Next, an “Andante” section features elements from the previous section’s theme but with more ornamentation, while the piano responds with counter melody material. A final “Allegro” section that is reminiscent of the ending of the “Allegretto” concludes the work.
