description: This is a three-movement work that “displays a chain of emotional states from the lyrical and romantic mood at the beginning through restlessness and rhythmic instability in its middle movement to the concluding mediation and apprehension of the past developments.”73 The formula for this piece is “epitomizing the objective principle and entering into a dialogue by playing its weighty phrases in counterpoint with the solo part.”74 The first movement “Lento” opens with a lyrical bassoon solo that weaves around the pitch “D” with some incorporation of quarter tones. The strings enter with longer note value dissonant chords, while the bassoon them continues to expand and develop. Eventually, when the bassoon switches to a smorzato section the strings become contrapuntal, which leads into a short virtuosic bassoon cadenza. The strings re-enter playing fragments of the quintuplet sixteenth notes from the cadenza in a canon-like texture. This continues developing until a climax of a rhythmic dissonant accented repeated note that ends abruptly as the bassoon holds over into a fermata note. The movement continues revisiting the earlier material and textures presented. The second movement “Tempo libro” is unmetered using note heads with a black line leading to the next event to connect together fragments of quicker note value or accelerando beamed groups. These fragments rapidly pass around the ensemble creating a larger cohesive line. Eventually, “Allegro agitato” section in 3/4 metre occurs consisting of fragmented motifs leading to a long note that is often trilled in a contrapuntal texture. This leads into a bassoon cadenza featuring virtuosic passages leading to an extended technique such as frullato or multiphonic. The final movement “Lento” is reminiscent of the first movement bringing back the themes, motifs and textures.

description: This work is the first in a collection of unaccompanied works for various instruments written by the composer. It has been selected as a mandatory piece for the International Flute Festival 2026 in Essen, Germany. This work is a virtuosic display of everything the flute is capable of by pushing the technical boundaries and use of extended techniques. The work undergoes a series of short sections each highlighting a different character and aspect of flute playing. The piece opens with an “Andante mosso, semplice” that introduces a simple and lilting melody that progresses to introduce frullato and singing while playing. The next section “Presto” explores what is possible for a flutist in terms of singing and playing. The third section “Allegro assai” is a syncopated ostinato pattern that rotates an accent to different subdivisions within the phrase while shifting meters to create a forward momentum. This leads into a virtuosic sequence of quintuplets to be contrasted by a return to the opening material of the piece. This time the concepts are expanded on much more before turning into a “Largo e tragico” which is a beautiful melody in the lower register of the flute that gradually the voice responds to during the longer note values. The following section “Andante con moto” is an undulating string of eighth notes in changing meters and dynamic changes to create a wave-like effect. The next section “Allegro assai” explores multiphonics. This is followed by an “Appassionate, prestissimo, senza misura” which is a virtuosic display of technique. Afterwards alternating sections of fast articulated and slurred technical passages occur for the climax of the piece. Finally, a return to the “Largo e tragico” occurs to ground the listener again and provide a contrast to conclude the work.

description: This is a one movement work based on stylistic and musical elements from folk Ukrainian dance. The hopak originates from the Zaproozhian Cossacks and comes from the Ukrainian word “to hop”. The dance is known for its energetic and lively character and consists of men performing high leaps, squatting kicks, rapid turns resulting in an impressive display of strength and agility. Musically, hopaks are usually in 2/4 time with an improvisatory character as the tempo and pacing from section to section often changes. This piece is a short-one movement work in an Allegretto tempo with the form ABBCBBA. The A section has a virtuosic motif of sixteenth notes in a sequential manner with two thirty-second notes on the syncopation at the beginning of the bar. The B section uses the same rhythmic materials but the thirty-second notes have been shifted to a different position. The sixteenth notes have become more disjunct. The C section drastically changes character to much more lyrical and calmer character reflecting a break in the dance where it begins again to rebuild energy. Musically, it features a motif of triplet quarter and eighth note leading to a beat of thirty second note flourishes. The return of the B material is harmonically different.

description: This is a two-movement work that explores many extended techniques and timbral possibilities available to the bassoon to depict a person who is wandering through life preoccupied by their thoughts that constantly get interrupted by their surroundings. This is demonstrated through the constant character characters and surprise introduction of extended effects that is contrasted with material that develops becoming more virtuosic like a person’s anxiety that begins to race when they are overthinking. The first movement begins with fortissimo multiphonics that are immediately contrasted with a more humoresque line stereotypical of the bassoon. This phrase develops and climaxes into a multiphonic. As the section continues developing it becomes more disjunct as it extends into the high register of the bassoon. The next section “Eighth note equals 60” begins more lyrical but gets thrown off with the introduction of quarter tones and becomes more frantic with the use of accelerando beaming. These accelerando motifs often lead to a multiphonic or a longer note value to stabilize the music briefly. As it continues more extended techniques are introduced to explore the different timbres possible on the bassoon similar to a person being zoned out and exploring all of the possibilities for a situation. This eventually climaxes into accelerando beamed multiphonics into a virtuosic display of septuplets to allow the work to begin to unwind. The work concludes by becoming less virtuosic and returning to a simpler more vocal-like line that is disjunct climbing to a high D. After holding this high D for a long period bisbigliando are introduced to distort the timbre and introduce some uncertainty into the music allowing a final multiphonic to emerge to return where we began the work.

description: This is a one-movement work in a rondo form that uses a folk-like melody, tonality such as the Ukrainian minor scale, and dance elements. The A section begins with a six-measure piano introduction consisting of an ostinato bass line in the left hand and fragments of the theme in the right hand. The bassoon enters with the main theme in a bounce and ironic character comprised of staccato eighth notes with syncopated and accented quarter notes overtop of accompaniment figures consisting of chords, scales, or fragments echoing the bassoon with the bass line ostinato in the left hand. A four-measure piano interlude ritenuendos into a “Cantabile meno mosso” B section that is a lyrical and slurred vocal-like line in the bassoon overtop of unwinding eighth note accompaniment that slowly changes harmony over time in the piano. The reprise of the A section ends in a one measure fragmentation of the theme that is passed back and forth between the two instruments, which leads in the C section. This section is a bassoon cadenza consisting of a descending eighth note passing in an ad libitum manner. The final A section ends with a three measure poco a stringendo al fine leading to a final fermata whole note chord.

The A section “Allegretto” opens with solo bassoon playing energetic and virtuosic sounding theme of eighth notes and staccatos that weave around in a scalar pattern. description: These are two short pieces in a late romantic style for a larger collection of eleven pieces for various instruments with piano: 1-2 for flute, 3-4 for oboe, 5 for cello, 6-7 for clarinet, and 10-11 for horn. The first piece “Humoresque” is in ternary form with a joking and ironic character. The A section marked Scherzando features an articulated melody that includes grace notes and downward intervals in a sequential motion followed by an arpeggio overtop of accompaniment figures in the piano. The piano takes over a melodic role when the bassoon has rests. The B section marked cantabile features a vocal-like melody in the bassoon combined with lush chords in the piano underneath. The piano takes over the melody in little interludes between phrases in the bassoon. The second piece “Impromptu” consists of a vocal-like melody overtop of arpeggiated sixteenth notes. As the piece progresses the melody becomes more active with the introduction of sixteenth notes in the bassoon, while a repeated sixteenth note motif is introduced in the piano to create an insistent character. The piece then continues on with the original texture to conclude.

description: This is a short one-movement work in an allegro scherzando tempo. It has a joking and ironic character that features a couple of energetic motifs that recur throughout. The piece opens with a quirky four measure piano introduction that leads into the first main theme presented by the bassoon consisting of mostly eighth notes with the occasional sixteenth. The oboe then enters with a syncopated counter-melody that has similar characteristics and elements to the bassoon line occurring. Next, a dialogue between the winds and piano occurs setting up a one measure motif that is passed around the winds overtop of a chromatic eighth note line in the piano that evolves into fragments of the canon material before dropping out of the texture. Finally, it re-enters participating with a full statement of the canon. Then a return to a dialogue section between the winds and piano occurs again. This leads into a new quarter note scalar theme in the flute and oboe overtop of rapid sixteenths in the piano’s right hand. This section develops and eventually returns back to the opening piano introduction and bassoon theme in a different tonal center. This time the counter-melody is in the clarinet instead of the oboe. The movement continues with a reprise of earlier material until a two measure homorhythmic ending consisting of syncopated eighth notes leading to a half note that concludes with a group of three grace notes to a final accented eighth note.

description: Silvestrov was a prominent member of the Kyiv Avant-Garde in the 1960s. However, in the 1970s he turned to a post-modernist style described as metaphorical music. It consists of a polystylistic method that combines elements of tonality, atonality, modality, and texture all together. It is dominated by characters of meditation, contemplation, and uncertainty. This is a short one-movement work in an Andante tempo. It is structured around a two-measure motif in the lower register of the piano consisting of a three triplet eighth notes on the pitches “D” and “G” with the second measure introducing an “Ab” that lead to octave quarter notes on “D”. However, often the motif is fragmented with only the first measure being played. Throughout the work this motif is used to ground and structured the piece as a means of a short interlude between each phrase of the lyrical solo passages in the bassoon that tonally shift around. The bassoon part is marked quasi recitativo with lyrical and vocal-like lines written that used quarter, dotted quarter and eighth notes in both duple and triple subdivisions. Underneath the bassoon line is the text of the hymn in Ukrainian that is used as inspiration for the piece.

description: This is a work comprised of three short contrasting character movements showcasing a different aspect of music and playing the flute. The movements do not have descriptive titles and just a tempo marking. The first movement “Quarter note equals 136” begins with a whole note that starts pianissimo that crescendos to forte, which gets passed around the ensemble. Eventually, the come together playing in homorhythm followed by a staggered entrance to lead into the second section consisting of disjunct triplet sixteenth notes with rests inserted that pass around the ensemble. description: The work depicts a wintery scene based on a stanza from a poem by famous Ukrainian poet Lesya Ukrainka: “Then the wind sometimes abandons; Through the window snow - grits; And in the door abandoned lines,Evil cold carrying with it” (Translated Z. Senick). It is structured in five main sections that unravel a story by presenting a different character. The opening “Vivace schercoso” opens with a four note motif of staccato sixteenths beginning on the second of the beat. It begins as step wise with a major third to the last note, but the intervallic relationship alters throughout. As the phrase progresses it gets manipulated such as being reversed and slurred or augmented into eighth notes. This is overtop of chordal quarter note chords (sometimes trilled) and countermelody sixteenth notes in dialogue to the flute. The “Moderato” section presents an espressivo and lyrical theme of repeated eighth notes that then meander beginning in the low register of the flute and expanding upwards. The piano follows in a canon texture. This section develops and concludes with a lyrical melody consisting of quarter note and longer note values in the flute and a rhythmic ostinato in the piano. Afterwards, the “Allegretto con moto” section is a virtuosic flute cadenza representing the cold wind taking over. The music sequentially in different patterns mainly centered around sextuplet sixteenth notes traverses the full range of the flute like a cold wind sweeping across the landscape to get to a person’s window and door. The final “Vivace” brings back material from the opening to conclude the work.

description: This is a short one-movement work in which the composer describes his Ukrainian identity as an important inspiration of the piece, saying “that a composer cannot create music in isolation from his cultural lifeline, and tries to maintain that lifeline with his audience.” (Stankovych, foreword) This work is in a dialogue texture between the two instruments. It opens with short melodic fragments with inspiration from folk music in a rubato and improvisatory character that lead to a longer note value that the piano responds with one note. As it progresses, the two voices between to overlap in a contrapuntal texture where the piano gets extended into a triplet meter grouping, while the flute remains in duple creating a dissonance between the two voices and worlds that beautifully weave together, like a person trying to find a way to represent the different parts of their identity together harmoniously. Eventually, the piano gives in and joins the flute’s duple meter in their motifs. This leads into a solo in the piano where the various motifs from throughout are incorporated into one cohesive voice. Afterwards, a return to the original dialogue texture occurs to conclude the piece.

description: Akimenko wrote in a romantic style that incorporated the impressionist techniques around him. He typically had a tendency toward miniature forms with the use of programmatic titles with a strong interest in Ukrainian themes and subjects that is demonstrated in this piece. This is a short one-movement work that explores both the lyrical and virtuosic capabilities of the flute. The work opens with a Pastorale marked “Moderato” that consists of a flute cadenza that sequentially works upwards the range of the flute. A short piano interlude presenting a fragment of the next section’s theme sets it up. The “Andante sostenuto” marked “dolce” features a lyrical, slurred, and vocal-like melody in the flute combined with chords in each measure and occasional quarter notes in the piano. Next, a “con gracia” featuring a syncopated ostinato in the piano with a arpeggiated triplet sixteenth leading to an eighth note in the flute. Eventually, it molds into scalar passages before returning to the original “Andante sostenuto” theme in the flute with a more active accompaniment part in the piano. However, this time the theme becomes more active and virtuosic with embellishments occurring to conclude the work.

This work has four short movements using traditional structures from classical music combined with serialism aesthetics. The first movement “Prelude” is in an allegro molto tempo in ternary form. The A section begins in a contrapuntal texture with frequent short rests creating a dialogue between the two instruments. It develops into a line of sixteenth notes leading to a passage of trilled quarter notes. The B section “Meno mosso” has a theme presented in the clarinet that the bassoon responds in canon but often using opposite intervals such as descending instead of ascending in the original. The return of the A section expands the passage of sixteenth notes longer this time. The second movement “Scherzando” is also in ternary form in an allegretto tempo. In the A section presenting a quirky theme consisting of syncopated eighth notes and two sixteenth notes leading to a staccato eighth note motif. This little motif is often trading off in a dialogue manner. The B section “Meno mosso” has two espressivo lines weaving around one another. As it develops the bassoon shifts to more accompaniment figures. The next movement “Lamento” begins with a lyrical theme in unison consisting mainly of eighth notes leading to a longer note value. Brief moments of contrapuntal or dialogue texture occur between unison or homorhythmic passages. As it develops the music becomes more active progressing to duple and triplet sixteenth notes. An abridged reprise of the A section occurs but with the bassoon entering in canon on a variation of it. The final movement opens with a lively three measure “Presto” that consists of two slurred eighth note starting on the offbeat. The two instruments are in contrary motion homorhythmic until the last statement, which is in dialogue. The main section of the movement “Allegro moderato” opens with a dance-like theme of eighth and sixteenth notes leading to an accented quarter note in the bassoon, which the clarinet enters in canon. Eventually, the opening motif returns with different intervals in a dialogue texture that begins homorhythmic. Overtime this motif develops into four sixteenths leading to an eighth note that connects into a final “Presto” section with the original motif to conclude the work.

description: This is a short one-movement work in ternary form using elements of form, harmony and motifs from neoromanticism. The reprise of the A section features some slight variations such as the large interval jump is now ascending rather than descending in the opening.

description: This is a one-movement work in memory of Denisov, who was Pavlenko’s teacher at the Moscow Conservatory. The work explores avant-garde style and techniques associated with Denisov. The work opens with a “Poco adagio” section that features a dialogue-like texture with a lyrical line in the bassoon with fragmented responses in the piano during the bassoon’s longer note values. As it develops the texture becomes contrapuntal with three-stave writing in the piano occurring. The next section “Poco agitato” returns to a dialogue-like texture with virtuosic thirty-second note fragments passed back and forth between the bassoon and piano, which develops into a canon-like texture with rhythmic dissonance of different note groupings of the technical passages occurring simultaneously such as quintuplet, sextuplet and septuplet. Eventually, a more melodic line emerges from the chaos in the bassoon part, which the piano begins to echo. A return to the previous texture takes over again. Later, new material emerges consisting of a disjunct large interval nonuplet with rests inserted into the phrase that occurs in the piano underneath glissandos that becomes a melodic line in the bassoon. The piano switches between textures of the disjunct line and echo the bassoon creating quick character changes. Eventually, this is interrupted by the technical canon-like chaotic section returning again. It develops into new material of thirty second notes overtop of accompaniment figures, whose roles alternate between the bassoon and piano each phrase. This leads into a large and virtuosic bassoon cadenza featuring technical flourishes, large intervals, and extended techniques. A return to the opening material occurs to conclude the work.

key: I (E minor), II (A minor), III (C major), IV (E minor), V (C major), VI (C major, E minor)
description: This is a six-movement suite that has alternating movements between a prelude and a fugue resulting in three sets of preludes and fugues. This work is in a neoclassical style following the rules and principles of prelude and fugues established in the Classical Era. A performer could easily perform a selection of either 2 or 4 movements rather than the whole suite, if desired. The first movement “Prelude I” is marked “Andante” and is polyphonic with a melody in the flute, countermelody in the oboe and a bass line in the bassoon for the first section. Then the bassoon presents a new melody while the flute has an ostinato slurred sixteenth note line. Eventually, the flute takes over the melody which is embellished arriving at three measures of homorhythmic chords. The next movement “Fugue I” has a theme of quarter and eighth notes that begins in the bassoon followed by the oboe and flute. “Prelude II” consists of a beat of slurred sixteenths that trade between the flute and oboe over top of long tones and bass line figures in the bassoon. Eventually, the sixteenths align together moving in parallel sixths. Afterwards, the sixteenths trade between the oboe and bassoon, while the flute has a melody that leads back to the opening material to conclude the movement. “Fugue II” has a five-measure introduction of tied whole notes that enter independently throughout the ensemble with four quarter notes in the bassoon leading into the first statement of the theme by the oboe. This theme consists of eighth, quarter and half notes tied to a quarter. The final “Prelude III” opens with a homorhythmic section in a chorale style. The rest of the movement mainly consists of long tones in two of the voices and a melody that leads into a final homorhythmic section. The final “Fugue III” opens with a fourteen measure homorhythm introduction before beginning the theme in the oboe overtop of a bass line in the bassoon. This theme consists of eighth notes with eighth rest inserted throughout.

description: This is a short one-movement work in a neoclassical style. It is based around a motif in the oboe consisting of three slurred triplet sixteenth notes in an upper neighbour motion followed by two staccato eighth notes leading to either two more eighth notes or a half note. Occasionally, the bassoon echoes this motif when the oboe has half notes. Otherwise, the bassoon provides harmonic support through bass line figures that become more contrapuntal as the piece progresses. This piece rhythmically mainly features eighth, quarter and half notes besides the triplet sixteenth motif combined with the occasional eighth or quarter note rest.

description: This is a three-movement work with no title indications given using aesthetics and techniques from the avant-garde movement. The first movement is marked “quarter equals 60” written in an unmetered form. It starts with the same theme presented in each of the voices that becomes different as it progresses. However, each part is written with a different amount of spacing between each note. For example, the first couple notes which are homorhythmic do not line up but rather appear like one of the parts is syncopated. Often throughout the movement the beats do not line up, for example one part will have two eighth notes and their next note of the following beat written before another voice has all three of their triplet eighth notes written. I believe this could be to indicate the players each playing the theme at their own will independently of one another creating a contrapuntal and improvisatory-like texture. The second movement has no marking or tempo indication given. It features the same elements as the previous movement except the theme begins alone in the flute with the oboe joining the second phrase and the bassoon finally on the third phrase. The movement ends with an aleatoric section with only note heads given with different amounts of spacing between the notes for each part. The final movement is marked “half note equals 54” metered in 2/2. It features a note that gets passed around the ensemble beginning as a long note value becoming shorter as the movement progresses until it becomes a sixteenth note. The movement concludes with a passage of eighth notes in large intervals.

description: This is a short one-movement work in ternary form that uses elements of neoclassical structure combined with stylistic influences from jazz. The A section is divided into an ABA form. The first part is a homorhythmic line of straight-feeling eighth notes leading to a syncopated quarter note in clarinets 1-5 overtop of a quarter note bass line in the bassoon. This section is structured with a first and second ending. The next section are eight measure phrases in a homorhythmic texture built on a syncopated ostinato. The first phrase ends with a solo bass line in the bassoon to connect to the next phrase. A one beat sixteenth note lick in the bassoon leads into a reprise of the opening section. The B section comprises three short sections and switches to a quasi-swing feel through dotted eighth and sixteenth note rhythms and slur markings of the off-beat eighth slurred to the main beat eighth note. The first section has a thicker texture often with a solo line in clarinet 1, homorhythmic accompaniment figures often as little fragments in clarinets 2-5, and a bass line in the bassoon. The second section modulates to the dominant key, A major back to the original homorhythmic texture. However, these phrases are more lyrical and use longer note values such as dotted quarter notes for a contrasting character. This leads into a fermata to set up the final section “meno mosso” which is a solo line in clarinet 1 overtop homorhythmic long tones in the rest of the ensemble. A Da capo al fine provides a return to the A section.

description: This is a short one-movement work in a folklore style that takes inspiration from folk music. The work opens with the flute playing alone a simple melody comprised of sixteenth, eighth, quarter, and half notes. The piano then enters during a rest with an arpeggiated figure joining in with accompanimental figures during the second half of the phrase. The theme is then embellishment throughout the rest of the work as it explores different tonalities and harmonies.

Vereshchagin’s style has been described as a “combinatorial game” (VUE) as he combines elements of avant-garde with traditionalism. The main features of his music are a complex harmonious language displaying various polyphonic and avant-garde techniques together to create a perfect sense of shape and proportions in building compositional structures through his accuracy of musical details and choice of artistic expressions. This is a one-movement work in ternary form. The A section “calmato semplice” features a lyrical melody overtop of accompaniment figures. As it progresses the figures become more active leading into an “animato” with a two sixteenth and eighth note ostinato bassoon and horn creating a constant line of sixteenths to lead into an accented syncopated homorhythmic passage setting up a quasi-cadenza moment in the flute. The B section “Adagio soave” features fragments and short motifs that are variated and combined in different ways utilizing various polyphonic techniques to explore a variety of characters. Vereshchagin also introduces extended techniques of frullato and glissando to create more variety in the ensemble texture. The return of the A section only utilizes material from before the animado section.

description: This is a short one-movement work in a rondo form with a brief introduction and coda. The piece is characterized by insistent rhythmic patterns and abrupt contrasts that are developed through small rhythmic variations of looping motifs. The A section features homophonic writing in the oboe and bassoon that is in homorhythm with the piano. This is combined with a low E quarter note in the piano’s left hand solidifying the meter changes. The use of rests in between the short homophonic fragments creates a sense of the line being interrupted constantly. The B section is contrasted presenting a lyrical quality through a continuous stream of sixteenth notes trading off between the oboe and bassoon. The coda presents a reiteration of the musical textures established throughout the piece that progressively dissolves into the material from the introduction.

description: The original title of the piece was “Three Slow Pieces” that was later renamed to Introspection in 1996.The work consists of three untitled movements that are only denoted with a tempo marking. The first movement “Quarter note equals 44” begins with the flute playing a more lyrical line consisting mainly of longer note values in a slurred articulation, while the harpsichord has more virtuosic flourishes underneath. As it develops the flute begins to introduce extended techniques such as frullato and smorazto to distort the sound before becoming more virtuosic creating a dialogue of the two instruments responding to one another with similar statements. Eventually, it progresses to these statements dove-tailing and becoming an unified phrase together. A return to the original texture occurs but now with more virtuosity and extended techniques incorporated to conclude the movement. The next movement “Quarter note equals 34” is structured in a back and forth dialogue where the two instruments alternate playing solo passages that are in a quasi-recitativo style. One of the main rhythmic motifs throughout is the use of quintuplets in various forms. The final movement “Quarter note equals 40” features a repeated note motif in the flute overtop of syncopated long note values that weave between consonant and dissonant moments creating an unstable foundation. As the flute part develops it incorporates extended techniques to alter the tone and color. Eventually, the harpsichord emerges to play one soloistic passages before leading to the final long note value in the two instruments to conclude the work.

This is a short one-movement work in a neoclassical style that takes inspiration from neoclassicism by utilizing the form of an invention and combining it with more modern motifs, aesthetics and tonal language. The work has a fugal-like texture but plays with the rules and expectations of how the voices should interact. It opens in the left hand of the piano with a semitone eighth note motif between D and Eb that is displaced by an octave on the last eighth. However, the flute enters with a different descending four quarter note motif with the intervals of perfect fourth, semitone, and perfect fourth. This leads into the second half of the motif consisting of an eighth rest followed by seven eighth notes. The bassoon enters during the second measure of the flute’s motif with the same motif, except it is rhythmically displaced with an added quarter note rest between each note in the motif. This allows the ending of the flute’s second statement to line up with the end of the bassoon’s first statement. This section continues to develop in this manner with unexpected treatments of the motifs and breaking of the rules in the flute and bassoon. This is combined with the piano individually developing their motif from measures 1-2. This leads into a short development section where the ensemble is together. The winds weave the second half of the motif between one another overtop of a descending line of accented quarter notes in the piano This leads to a meno mosso section expected to lead back to a recapitulation. Instead, the music winds down to conclude the piece without a recapitulation.

description: This is a short one-movement work that follows the stylistic and structural elements of the classical style through an invention. It features three-part counterpoint with a short exposition, slightly longer development and a short recapitulation in a fugal texture. The exposition presents a theme first by the bassoon mainly in the tonic key with a brief moment of chromaticism. The clarinet then enters with the theme, while the bassoon switches to counterpoint. This is then followed by the flute’s entrance of the theme with counterpoint in the other voices often utilizing fragmented motifs from the theme in the dominant key (B♭ major). The development section expands and provides variations upon the theme and motifs often changing and recombining the instrumentation such as switching between only two members of the ensemble playing in pairs of counterpoint such as clarinet and bassoon, then flute and bassoon. Eventually, a brief recapitulation returns beginning with the three-part counterpoint texture with the theme in the flute and accompaniment in the clarinet and bassoon to conclude the work.
This work is polyphonic using the form of an invention in an extended tonal language.

description: This is a short one-movement work in a humoresque character. The work is structured around two main sections with a form of ABCBA’A. The A section consists of mostly staccato eighth notes in an arpeggiated manner that are contrasted by slurred motifs such as dotted quarter slurred to an eighth note and eighth followed by two sixteenth notes all slurred together. The B section is lyrical featuring slurred one or two-measures motifs that are combined in a sequential manner to create a larger phrase. Rhythmically, it consists of quarter and half notes. A brief connecting section of a passage of sequential staccato eighth notes starting on a high “A” back down to the low “G” to set up a return of the A material. The brief C section is comprised of accented disjunct eighth notes. However, the final return of the A material has the material in a different order and some slight variations before a full original statement of the A material. The end of the A material undergoes a ritenuto that leads to a three-measure closing material of sixteenth notes leading to a long note to conclude the work.

description: The inspiration of the piece comes from a bible verse (Genesis 1:6) that describes the second day of creation where God establishes an expanse to separate the waters to create the sky. The work opens with a lyrical melody in the flute using step-wise motion and small intervals based around a rhythmic motif of an eighth followed by three descending triplet sixteenth notes. The accordion plays chords underneath with rhythmic fragments in response when the flute has longer note values such as a half note. As it develops the accordion responses to the flute becomes elongated and more contrapuntal. The flute theme also becomes more active with the introduction of quintuplet thirty-seconds, grace notes, and syncopations. Next, the accordion plays an interlude that incorporates the motif played by the flute previously. Then, the flute interrupts with material similar to earlier playing in one measure fragments alone, which the accordion responds to alone to lead into the next section. It begins with staccato slap tongued notes in the flute that are fairly chromatic leading to a longer frullato note. The intervals of the sixteenths become more disjunct as it progresses. The accordion plays an independent line underneath comprised of syncopations and short sixteenth note motifs to provide forward momentum. As it develops the flute sixteenth notes go from duple to triple note groupings that prompts a return to the original motif coming back in a more lyrical style. The next section consists of pulsating rhythmic line in the accordion with sporadic single staccato eighth notes in the flute that overtime expand into a full phrase. Eventually, the roles reverse and the flute takes over the pulsating rhythmic line and the accordion plays the eighth note line. This is followed by a section of multiphonics in the flute while the accordion plays sixteenth notes in the upper voice and chords in the lower voices. Afterwards, a synthesis of previous material occurs for the final section of the piece to conclude the work.

description: This is a short one-movement work in three main sections based on popular Italian songs of the 1930s and 1960s. The work is based on the principle of citation from the postmodernist movement characterized by its inherent stylistic beats, the play of images, contrasts, and re-interpretation of meanings throughout. The opening “Tempo improvizato” is structured as a one measure piano introduction that leads into a homorhythmic flute and bassoon melody. The piano responds with fragments to this melody during their longer note values. As the piece progresses the flute and bassoon begin to deviate into a more contrapuntal texture, while the piano becomes more active with larger phrases until it becomes a full accompaniment. The next section “Molto piu mosso” continues this accompaniment texture in the piano with the flute and bassoon returning to a homorhythmic line that turns into a call and response. The final section “Lento” consists of two independent lines in the flute and bassoon overtop of a simple eighth note accompaniment in the piano that slows down into chords, which the flute and bassoon trill dotted half notes over top of to conclude the piece.

description: This is a short one-movement work that is jazz-inspired utilizing rhythmic, harmonic and stylistic elements typical of jazz music to emulate an improvised jazz-solo. The piece is structured through motifs that develop into a virtuosic passage containing a flourish of notes often in thirty-second notes or quintuplet and sextuplet sixteenth notes that travel across the range of the bassoon. There are two main motifs that are used throughout: 1) through are triplet eighth notes with a rest on the second one of each beat to imitate a swung style, and 2) repeated articulated notes leading to a long note with frullato that crescendos to imitate how a jazz musician will use growling as an expressive tool.

description: This is a four-movement suite in a neoclassical style that utilizes typical form and conventions while exploring elements of consonance and atonality within the ensemble. The first movement “Prelude” opens with a declamatory motif of dotted eighth note followed by a sixteenth note leading to a longer note in a canon entrance in a cluster chord. This prompts a virtuosic staccato sextuplet response in the flute. After a grand pause the next section features a semplice theme in the flute overtop of accompaniment figures in the ensemble. A return of the opening material occurs an octave higher moprhing into triplet motifs from the semplice theme throughout the ensemble. The next movement “Fugue” presents a slurred theme that weaves around the tonic pitch “F” played first by the oboe. A modulation to F♯ occurs to transition into a contrasting playful section that consists of staccato arpeggiated motion that leads to a perfect fourth non-staccato motif. Eventually the opening theme returns in a staccato articulation and rests inserted for the second half of longer note values, such as quarter note becoming eighth note followed by an eighth rest played by the clarinet. This is followed by a return to the original theme played in homorhythm and contrary motion. It is then fragmented and passed around the ensemble. Another contrasting section occurs with a vocal-like melody in the flute, arpeggiated eighth notes in the oboe and clarinet, and a bass line in the bassoon. A final fugal section occurs to conclude the movement. The third movement “Canon” presents eighth notes leading to a longer note value that oscillates a ascending minor third interval first played by the flute alone. This is followed by entrances in the oboe and then clarinet, which each entrance is accompanied by an increase in the tempo. This material continues to be developed leading into a slower contrasting section that is a variation on the motif. It is repeated quarter notes leading to a descending minor third. The movement continues to develop the material as it speeds back up. The final movement “Cadenza and Chorale” features a chorale consisting of eighth, quarter, and half notes in a mostly step-wise motion in the oboe, clarinet, and bassoon, which is mostly in homorhythm with occasional moments of counterpoint. This is combined with a virtuosic staccato sextuplet alternating octaves on the pitch “E” in the flute. The ensemble gradually accelerando throughout the movement before abruptly returning to the opening tempo. A final section that brings back material from the opening of the first movement concludes the work.

key: I (G major), II (G major, G minor), III (C major)
description: This is a four-movement work in a neoclassical style utilizing compositional techniques and harmony from earlier periods. The first movement “Andantino '' is polyphonic featuring an arpeggiated eighth note motif that has an eighth rest inserted often on the downbeat to disrupt the flow. In the recapitulation this returns as articulated sixteenths on each eighth note. This is combined with a melody and countermelody. The second movement “Allegro” opens with a quarter note line beginning in the bassoon with each oboe added successively to each phrase. This leads into the quarter notes being traded amongst the ensemble. This is alternated with “Andantino” sections that take the melodic content from the first section but changes the rhythm to include a combination of eighth and quarter notes in the bassoon with counter melodies in the oboes in a polyphonic texture. Then a return of the trading eighths occurs that develops into a unison ostinato on the pitch “D”. The next section features a bass line ostinato in the bassoon, an arpeggiated accompaniment in the second oboe and a lyrical melody in the first oboe. This section develops to become more polyphonic and equally independent lines as it modulates to g minor. A return to the opening allegro occurs but in reverse entrance order and long tones until a voice joins the motif. Then the andantino section occurs with some small variations leading to a silent bar. Then one last statement of the trading eighths occurs leading into a forte-piano chord under a fermata to conclude the movement. The third movement “Andante” consists of a polyphonic texture with a couple motifs that repeat throughout. There is an eighth note melody line, staccato sixteenth with rests inserted on either repeated notes or arpeggios, and a sixteenth followed by a dotted eighth note in a descending motion. These motifs develop and are combined in different textures throughout. This leads to a homorhythmic sixteenth note passage repeating two notes in a row in an arpeggiated manner to conclude the movement. The final movement “Allegro scherzando” opens with two accented eighth notes followed by an eighth rest motif that the voices weave in and out of the texture. Eventually, this develops into different motifs that relate, for example flipping it to be eighth note rest followed by four sixteenths in a repeated descending third interval. A new motif is introduced around a neighbour tone motion in two variations: 1) two sixteenths and an eighth under a slur 2) three eighth notes in a neighbour motion. This movement alternates between polyphonic and homorhythmic textures.

description: Bruk’s style once immigrating to Finland has been described as “embracing native Finnish material in a way that nourishes his own distinctive brand of early twentieth-century free-tonal music.”16 The work is a five-movement suite that goes through a variety of styles and characters. The first movement “Mirage” opens with a cantus-firmus like line that gradually becomes more active and intricate as it develops going through various forms and textures such as trading eighth notes and trilled quarter notes. The next movement “The Old Dance” is in ternary form and features an eighth note waltz-like bass line in the bassoon that develops in sixteenth notes. Throughout the movement it alternates between the eighth and various sixteenth note variations. The theme is mostly a virtuosic display of sixteenth notes. The “Meno mosso” features a theme composed of quarter and eighth notes in the clarinet overtop of a bass line that combines arpeggiated and scalar motion in the bassoon. The following movement “Invention à la Shostakovich” is centered around a rhythmic motif of a dotted eighth followed by a sixteenth (and its reverse) that briefly becomes three triplet eighth notes. It is mainly in a dialogue texture. The fourth movement “March à la Prokofiev” has triplet and dotted eighth followed by sixteenth motifs that pass back and forth that develop into brief homorhythmic statements. The final movement “The Autumnal Shadows” consists of a lyrical and vocal-like theme in the clarinet and three arpeggiated staccato eighth note accompaniment in the bassoon. Halfway through the roles switch with the clarinet now playing five eighth notes starting on the second eighth of the bar while the bassoon plays a waltz-like theme. Eventually, the two instruments play the accompaniment line together in harmony. The work concludes with the bassoon returning to the theme with a fragmented accompaniment from the clarinet.

extended_techniques: artificial harmonic (db), double-trill harmonic (cl, bsn), frullato (cl, bsn), multiphonic (cl, bsn), quarter tones (bsn cl, db – no fingerings given) rebondi continu (db), vibrato (cl)

description: This work is based on the last two lines of a poem by Ukrainian poet Oleh Lychecha poems La Carpe. The two lines are: “Et dans un long tournoiement/J’entrarais alors dedans l’étang céleste” that form a silence before the work. As it begins a feeling of the slow and imperious movement towards the surface appears creating a metaphorical musical gesture created through the inversion of resonance. This approach creates a reverberation on the surface creating an alternative environment. The exploration of resonance is assisted by using 14 pre-recorded stereo sounds that start and then spatialize the notes in the score. Therefore, it is recommended to use six speakers to spatialize the sound and to amplify the instruments to obtain a correct balance of timbres. Musically, the work opens with the ensemble playing rhythmically consonant motifs on different repeated notes in each instrument that become more and more syncopated from one another until they become their own independent lines. The use of quartertones are employed into the lines to create dissonance and an unsettled quality. Various extended techniques are also implemented to explore a variety of textures, resonances, and timbres as they are combined in different combinations to create different characters. Eventually, the lines become homorhythmic briefly but using a different technique in each instrument simultaneously, which leads to a dramatic silence to conclude the section. The next section consists fragmented motifs in a contrapuntal texture that become more rhythmically active as it develops. Eventually, material from the opening is introduced into the parts creating a juxtaposition of the two worlds and types of resonance. The work continues to alternate between these textures as they compete for dominance as they develop and introduce new variations to employ more textures.

description: The title of the work Kotygoroshko is a character from Ukrainian folklore. The story is about a boy with great strength born out of a pea who saves his siblings from an evil serpent in a battle with an iron mace. Afterwards, Kotygoroshko embarks on a journey where he meets three magical men and a grandfather. The grandfather attempts to kill Kotygoroshko. However, Kotygoroshko conquers by killing grandfather, taking his treasures, and saving a princess. This leads to Kotygorohsko to explore a deep pit where he discovers some baby birds that he protects from vultures. He eventually gets out of the pit and marries the princess. This is a programmatic three-movement suite depicting this fairy tale using elements of Ukrainian folk music. The first movement “Bulava” (Mace) in a moderato comodo tempo depicts the first part of the story. Musically, it is written in a sonata form with the first section begins with an unbalanced dotted eighth and sixteenth followed by eighth notes motif in a 3+2 note grouping. This progresses into a section that consists of a string of sixteenth notes trading amongst the ensemble depicting a struggle or battle occurring. Next, it returns to the opening motif except it is more active with more sixteenths added in to depict the excitement from the success of defeating the serpent. Then, we get a slower more lyrical contrasting section that has fragmented from other motifs in the accompaniment. Eventually, we return to the opening motif with fragments of the sixteenth note passage becoming incorporated in. Next, variation of the opening material occurs through fragmentation and long tones supplemented in. The rest of the movement continues in this manner. The second movement “Didok” (Grandfather) in a molto grave tempo depicts the second part of the story. Musically, this movement opens with a major sixth interval motif in contrary motion in the clarinet and bassoon underneath a slower, lyrical melody in a chordal texture in the piano. Next, the roles of motif and melody flip. The movement continues developing these motifs with slight variations. The final movement “Gryff” (Vulture) in a presto feroce tempo depicts the final part of the story. Musically, it is written in a rondo form. The A section presents a motif of mostly eighth notes that end with a quarter note slurred to an octave above eighth note in a 3+2+2 note grouping. This motif combined with sforzando and accents provide an energetic and ferocious character. There is a contrasting lyrical and slurred melody consisting of mostly eighth notes and dotted quarter notes. The rest of the movement continues providing variations and different intertwining of these two main motifs in different textures. Overall, this work combines elements of folk music through melody, rhythm and tonality with elements of neoclassicism such as form and variation principles with contemporary harmonic language to depict a beloved Ukrainian fairy tale.

instrumentation: fl, ob, cl, bsn, vln, vlc, harpsichord, tam-tam
premiere: October 6th, 1997 in Chisinau, Moldova by Ars Poetica Ensemble, Oleg Palymsky (cond) at “The Days of New Music International Festival”

description: This is a one-movement work that combines elements of early music and chant with aesthetics of avant-garde. The first section “Mesto” opens with slow and dissonant double stops in the cello that become consonant in a chant-like manner. This then repeats with the violin. This motif then is repeated by the winds with a disjunct melody in the violin with the cello joining in countermelody eventually. The next section “Senza metro” features a repeated note motif that is contrasted by members of the ensemble singing “kyrie elision” on mono-pitch chant. At the end of the section a harpsichord cadenza appears out of the silence. As it progresses the flute emerges with a stepwise melody that leads to another repeated note motif that is dissonant traded around the ensemble until a flute melody emerges. This is the echoed in the winds until they come together in a tutti scalar motif overtop of arpeggiated sixteenths in the strings leading into the final section “Largo ed un poco piano.” This is a neobaroque character with a clear melody and countermelody overtop of a figured bass accompaniment in the harpsichord and bassoon which is interrupted by a single hit of the tam-tam that slowly fades away. This is the only note the tam-tam plays in the entire piece.

premiere: unknown
description: Akimenko wrote in a romantic style that incorporated the impressionist techniques around him. He typically had a tendency toward miniature forms with the use of programmatic titles with a strong interest in Ukrainian themes and subjects that is demonstrated in this piece. The work opens in an Andante with a haunting melodic slurred line in the flute alone. The piano then joins as it picks up with a “Con moto (Moderato)” at a piano dynamic with a melodic line as a whisper while the flute plays a repeated “A” of different rhythmic values. This proceeds into a sequential pattern of sixteenth notes in descending intervals that get larger, while the piano plays eighth notes meandering upwards. The roles than reverse with embellishments added to the flute part. Next, a virtuosic display occurs with the flute playing a string of triplet sixteenths in the upper register that meander around that is overtop of chords in the piano. This continues developing with other material inserted, while the piano becomes more active playing a rhythmically dissonant triplet eighth s underneath. A return to the opening “Andante” material occurs that leads into an “Andantino” that features an eighth note motif of large intervals that become more compact. This becomes more embellished and eventually leads into an “Allegretto” consisting of a motif of duple eights meander to a group of three triplet eighth notes. This is initially in the flute overtop of chords in the piano, which then becomes contrapuntal with the piano participating to conclude the work.

premiere: Isidro Santos (bcl) and Inna Poroshina (pno) in Spain
recordings: CD “Pages of Life: Nadiya Poklad Clarinet Music” in 2015 at the Organ Hall Conservatory of Music in Brugge Belgium by Isidro Santos (bcl), Inna Poroshina (pno)
description: This is a one-movement work with three main sections that explore a variety of tonalities throughout. The opening section “Andante” depicts the moon featuring a calm and legato melody mostly consisting of eighth notes and quarter notes leading to longer half and whole notes. The second section “con moto” has more motion and lilt to with a dance-like melody utilizing a quarter note followed by a eighth note motif contrasted with active runs of sixteenths in the bassoon over an accompaniment piano part. This section depicts the shimmer of the stars in the sky. The final section is an “A tempo” back in the original, calm character that develops to be more active with triplets incorporated into the melody before returning to a motif similar to the opening.

premiere: never performed
key: C minor, C major, B♭  major
description: This is a one-movement work that demonstrates the lyrical quality of the flute that takes inspiration from Lacrimosa, which means “tearful” or “weeping” and is associated as part of a requiem. It is typically involved with the Dies Irae of a mass for the dead and has a solemn and mournful character achieved through slow, melancholic melody. The flute often has a vocal-like melody that features large interval jumps of sevenths and octaves or even larger to depict this struggle. The harp often has an accompanimental role with very idiomatic passages of chords in the left hand and arpeggiated motion in the right hand. As the work progresses elements of the accompaniment such as the arpeggiated thirty-seconds notes intertwine themselves into the ornamentation of the melody in the flute. The music climaxes into a brief moment of virtuosity for a cadenza of sextuplet sixteenth note in a sequential manner in the flute before returning to a restatement of the theme in its original texture. Next, a contrasting “Tranquillo” section occurs composed of the main thematic material being in the right hand of the harp with eighth note chords in the left hand, while the flute plays fragmented countermelody of triplet sixteenths often syncopated beginning of the second of the beat in response. Eventually, this is interrupted by an “Agitato” section that is a dialogue of triplet sixteenths passing back and forth between the two instruments. Another attempt at the “Tranquillo” then occurs leading into a return of the opening material to conclude the work.

premiere: never performed
description: This work is built around a falling gesture with a melodic line that often rises and then falls in the flute overtop of accompaniment figures in the piano to depict the cyclic quality of nature that one would observe staring off into the distance of a landscape. The work opens with an arpeggiated eighth note line in the piano going across the hands, which moments of melodic content as it unravels. The flute enters with a triplet motif that chromatically weaves around the middle register. As it expands it becomes more melodic and expands the register. Eventually, in the piano the accompaniment briefly morphs into triplet quarter notes to give more space for the flute to climax to their highest point in the piece both register wise to a High E and rhythmically with a string of sixteenth notes. The piano then introduces a grace note motif as an echo that is very reminiscent of a bird off in the distance, which overtime sneaks into the flute line. The flute line continues to become more virtuosic with longer lines of sixteenth notes and more disjunct and larger intervals.

premiere: never performed
description: The title of this work Lemon was chosen by Fedko as a cheeky play on words as the work itself sounds “sour” due to the harmonic choices utilized. This is a short one-movement work that explores different tone colors such as having the flute playing in their lower register instead of always being the highest voice in the texture. The opening section “Andante assai” begins with a dialogue between the flute in their lowest register and the oboe in their middle to higher register. Next, the clarinet enters with a countermelodic line and the bassoon with an arpeggiated bassline creating a four-voice contrapuntal texture, which continues developing until it arrives at a fermata to conclude the section. The next section “Andante mosso” consists of an interlocking accompaniment in the flute and oboe that is trading off sixteenth notes in an ostinato pattern, while the bassoon plays a lyrical melody overtop of a countermelody in the clarinet. A return to the “Andante assai” occurs but not in the original texture. The bassoon brings back its arpeggiated bassline, but the oboe emerges into a soloistic role with new melodic content while the flute in the low register and clarinet in the middle and upper register play an accompaniment in homorhythm. However, new material that is more aggressive syncopated motif being presented in homorhythm amongst the ensemble interrupts briefly for four measures. The original material returns but more active with passages of sixteenth notes in dialogue now. The following section “Andante con moto” changes character to a playful character through staccato passages of eighth and sixteenth notes that rotate around the ensemble overtop of accompaniment figures. This continues developing until its arrival a dissonant chord that intensifies and crescendos through a fermata to set up the brief coda section “Andante maestoso.” This is a five-measure chorale that explores dissonances in order to arrive at a final consonant G minor chord to conclude the work.

description: This piece is inspired by the idea of an actor reciting a monologue on stage. The structure of the piece resembles a speech going through a variety of characters creating a wide range of moods from mediation to agitation. The first section is centered around the pitch E-natural and utilizes inspiration from sonorism. The piece opens with a long note that in a free and calm character explores the various manipulation of timbre possible on the bassoon through, vibrato, quartertones, different timbral fingerings, glissando and smorzato to create slight variations like an actor beginning a start of a speech with a small idea that is growing and developing. The piece slowly opens up pitch wise leading into the next section that is a coherent melodic idea, like an actor expanding the speech into a main idea through the formulation of complete sentences. As this section develops the music becomes much more rhythmic, the character of the piece becomes more frantic and passionate, almost creating a dialogue amongst oneself how an actor would defend their points and position in the middle of a monologue. The piece eventually slows down reverting back to the opening character but with a full musical language incorporated, as if an actor coming to a conclusion. Stylistically, the piece combines elements of modality with free atonal techniques. An example of this is the use of the chromatic scale commonly used in classical music, but extending its tonality to include quarter tone pitches not common in classical playing and bassoon technique.

dedicated: Ukrainian musicians resisting the annihilation of our culture during Russia’s invasion commissioned by the Artemis Musicians’ Society
premiere: March 30th, 2024 in Vancouver by Renz Eulric Adame (enghn), Katelin Coleman (bsn)

description: This work takes inspiration from Ukrainian folk music in a style that borrows melodic, ornamental, rhythmic, timbral and poetic elements fused with contemporary musical language and techniques. Pidgorna developed this style through her field work as a folklorist recording folk songs in Ukraine during 2012-2013. Lesya’s Song is based on an earlier work she wrote for two folk voices and layered double bass that features her own invented folk songs, which is set to poetry by nationalistic Ukrainian poet Lesya Ukrainka. The work takes inspiration from the Russian invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Musically, the invasion is represented by aggressive interruptions reminiscent of fanfares, which are going against the lyrical folk lines evoking imagery of singing amidst a war. An important motif throughout the piece is the frequent minor ninth leaps which encapsulate an attempt to capture voices breaking in lamentation. The piece contains three main sections. The opening “cantabile, with voice cracking” presents the repeated note motif in the English horn that depicts a singer’s voice softly cracking as they intensify a line. The bassoon immediately responds with a slurred minor ninth interval repeated twice to help establish a character of lament in the music. The English horn responds with a lyrical melody that begins with the minor ninth interval. These motifs continue to be developed and interact with one another throughout this section until we arrive at the second section “aggressive, bird-like, squawky.” In this section we begin a character change through the introduction of successive accented triplets that are reminiscent of a fanfare that destabilize the music creating the dichotomy of legato vocal-like melody and articulated disjunct characters. This depicts the juxtaposition of the imagery of singing amidst a war happening around them to the audience. The final section “rubato” returns back to the opening material and character. However, this time the score instructs to hold the rests a little longer creating a sense of longing for earlier times before the war began evoking the concepts of nostalgia and tradition. Overall, this piece takes elements of folk music and structures it in a contemporary manner to depict intense emotions.

description: The inspiration of the work comes from spending time with his son as the composer describes that “Once, in the earliest days of my son Leo, at his cradle on the watch of his sleep I fell into a dream of being a lion who was having a dream too.” The opening section of this piece begins with a mysterious character created by the flute utilizing extended techniques of air noises and harmonics. The pianist then begins to add delicate arpeggiated sextuplets to create a dream-like effect. The flutist then develops into a full tone lullaby-like melody overtop of the piano’s texture before returning to air noises leading to a whistle tone this time. Afterwards, the character immediately shifts to darker and more sinister with disjunct and fragmented motifs in the flute and aggressive clusters in the left hand of the piano. This is briefly interrupted with elements from the earlier lullaby and delicate nature of the opening elements. A return to this new disjunct and aggressive character occurs and begins undergoing development such as as an aggressive repeated triplet sixteenth note motif that is introduced. Once again this is interrupted being the more lullaby-like elements. Next, the work begins to develop the sinister side again with the introduction of tongue rams and virtuosic flourishes ascending across the registers of the flute. The work continues in this manner of alternating between the two characters and developing the motifs previously introduced. Eventually, the opening lullaby character is victorious by concluding the work in an espressivo manner with a vocal-like line and a long note value leading to harmonics before finally ending with air noises just like how the dream began.

description: This is a six-movement programmatic work depicting the adventures of a boy named the “Little Prince” in Montréal. The story begins in a hotel dining room where he trips on the carpet. This is followed by a stroll through Expo 67, where his feet get tired prompting him to ask his father to stop walking for a while. Then, the boy becomes homesick missing his kitten, which the parents instruct him to have fun and he won't be lonesome. Finally, the trip concludes as Little Prince falls asleep and relives the experience in his dreams. The first movement “Hotel dining-room” is a tempo di minuetto in Da capo form. It consists of a melody overtop of accompaniment with flourishes of sixteenth note passages. This develops into a homorhtymic passage. The following movement “A stroll through Expo 67” is in an andante leggiero tempo is mostly contrapuntal with various motifs being introduced as it develops. This is abruptly interrupted by a two measure subito lento e pesante mainly consisting of accented quarter notes. The return of the material mainly features lines of sixteenth notes that pass around the ensemble that is interrupted by a four measure vivo section. This manner continues for the rest of the movement where the material is interrupted by a contrasting character such as moderato and lento sections. The third movement “Nostalgia I: Serious One” has a chorale-like texture using carefully placed dissonance to create moments of tension. The next movement “Nostalgia II: Serial One” is a parody of the previous movement in an avant-garde style using elements of serialism and only presenting fragmentation of the material with rests inserted. There are also acting throughout such as the ensemble all sighing deeply together. The fifth movement “Sunrise at Dorval Airport” is in a lento tempo consists of a short theme that is passed around the ensemble with different accompaniments throughout, which is attacca into the final movement “Dream on flight home” which is in ABACDEA. The A section “Allegro” opens with a syncopated homorhythmic passage creating an energetic dance-like character. This leads into constant sixteenth notes that are passing around the ensemble with accented eighth note motifs underneath. As it develops different motifs are introduced underneath the sixteenths. The B section “Lento” is based around half note and quarter notes that are doing dynamic swells. Next, the A section returns in a more contrapuntal texture combining all of the motifs from the earlier A section. The C section “Poco meno mosso” is marked “marcato” consisting of eighth notes that are unbalanced by accenting either only the third or fifth note of each measure. The D section “Lento meditativo” begins with half notes that dynamically swell that gradually become more active into eighth notes then sixteenth notes. This develops into homorthymic misterioso tremolos in the ensemble. This leads into the E section “cantabile” which is a lyrical theme in a canon before a return to material from the A section but with variations and not presented in the same order as previous. This is interrupted by a two measure Lento to prompt a full return of the original material at the beginning of the movement to conclude the work.

description: This is a short one movement work with Spanish folk dance inspiration that comes from Zuckert’s past when he lived in Argentina (1923-1929) after he left Ukraine. This is a lively and syncopated dance that creates forward momentum. The piece opens with piano accompaniment of eighth notes, often with the root on the downbeat and then a chord on either beats 2 or 3 with a sole arpeggiated note on the other beat of the measure providing the syncopated feel. The flute plays an ornamented and virtuosic line that often begins either on the second sixteenth or second eighth note of the bar providing momentum to the next measure. The melodic content often utilizes step-wise or neighbour motion in the flute. As it progresses sixteenth note triplets are introduced to provide ornamentation and contrast. Next, the second melody features a rhythmic motif of an eighth note, two sixteenths and an eighth note tied over the barline to another eighth note, which concludes with two more eighth notes. Eventually, a melodic motif of the octave is incorporated into the melodic content, while the two themes are combined and reworked together. There are brief moments where the piano joins in on the melodic content playing in unison with the flute or in response. The piece continues reworking or revisiting earlier material until it concludes.

premiere: 1982 at LNMA by student quintet

description: This is a short three-movement suite in a neoromantic style with contemporary influence in terms of harmonic language and idioms in a similar style to Hindemith’s kleine kammermusik for wind quintet. The first movement “Marcia” has a quirky character in an ABAB form. The A section is a dotted eighth and sixteenth melody in the upper winds and an accompaniment that alternates between staccato quarter notes and a slurred quarter to an eighth note and eighth rest in the bassoon and horn. This leads into the B section that features a chromatic triplet sequential line that constantly drops and builds. The second movement “Andante” opens with a lyrical and legato horn solo consisting of eighth and quarter notes. Eventually, the oboe joins in with a countermelody before the rest of the ensemble enters with long tone chords. This leads into an oboe melody that has a quasi-improvisatory character. The next section features contrapuntal chromatic lines weaving around each other through the oboe, clarinet, bassoon, and horn. Finally, the movement ends with a flourishing sextuplet run in the flute and clarinet that sets ups the final “Piu mosso” triplet section comprised of a homorhythmic line in the flute, oboe, clarinet and bassoon that the horn responds to before returning to the earlier oboe melody. The final movement “Allegro non troppo” is a fiery character that features ascending triplets that constantly swell to sforzandos overtop of accompaniment figures such as quarter notes. The harmonic language in the piece often includes chromaticism and sometimes non-western scales such as the Ukrainian minor scale.

published: Muzychna Ukraina (Kyiv 1968) in “Ensembles of Woodwind Instruments, Volume 6: Quartets”
range: fl I (C4-C7), fl II (D4-F6), cl (G3-E6), bsn (B♭1-A♭4)
key: I (A♭ major), II (D♭ major), III (E♭ major), IV (A♭ major)
description: This work is a four-movement suite in a neoclassical style with some elements of folklorism incorporated. The first movement “Humoresque” is in an ABA form in a vivace tempo with elements of folk music and dances. The A section has a light and playful character through a staccato eighth note melody with occasional slurred sixteenths in the first flute. This is overtop of accompaniment figures or homorhythmic passages. The B section is a legato character with a quarter note melody with an accompaniment consisting of a four-note ascending motif leading into a scale that gets traded around the ensemble. The second movement “Joke” is a quirky allegretto that alternates between articulated and slurred motifs to have constant character changes throughout. It features large, slurred intervals in the melody combined with a sigh-like motif consisting of a pickup into a quarter note slurred upward to an eighth note. The accompaniment often includes articulated large intervals in the bassoon and off beats or short syncopated motifs in the other instruments. The next movement “Waltz” incorporates stereotypical elements of Viennese waltzes in an andantino tempo. The accompaniment often has a downbeat quarter note or dotted half note to give the pulse and beats two and three in another voice underneath a legato and singing melody. The piece concludes with “A Fun Moment” which is an allegretto with folk elements that features a staccato bass line in the bassoon, accompaniment figures and a lively melody consisting of eighth and sixteenth notes.

premiere: composer does not know
description: This work consists of four virtuosic movements that display the technical side of flute built on different motifs that are expanded upon in a sequential manner. The first movement “Andantino” has a tied eighth note that is followed by descending arpeggiated thirty-second notes that lead to three eighth notes each time in a different articulation and motion. Next, this motif gets variated to become a sequence of four sixteenth descending arpeggiated notes leading to a staccato sixteenth note. A final variation that is more disjunct occurs putting a major sixth interval into the middle of the arpeggiation. The second movement “Allegretto” is in ternary form using a Da Capo al Fine. It begins with an arpeggiated descending motion of six slurred sixteenth notes that lead to a trilled quarter note followed by two sixteenth notes like a quasi nachschlag. This gets variated to become three disjunct large interval eighth notes. Next, it progresses into a whole passage of sixteenth notes to conclude the section. The B section consists of three slurred eighth notes fragments that extend into a longer phrase. The fragments are concentrated by staccato sixteenth notes in sequential thirds motif. The following movement “Andantino” features a repeated note motif that begins with a semitone fragment inserted in between. As it develops the fragment it becomes longer and more virtuosic flourishes. The final movement “Andantino” is built in a similar fashion where a fragment is expanded upon becoming longer and more virtuosic as the movement progresses. This movement features the most amount of manipulations of the motifs and most use of many large intervals.

published: self-published through Sprint-Service (Kyiv 2021) “Music for Wind Instruments”
premiere: 1980 at Concert Hall of NUCU in Kyiv by Oleskiy Boyko (cl), Yuri Konrad (bsn), Nadia Jacobchuk (pno)
recordings: 2009 at NRCU by Oleskiy Boyko (cl), Yuri Konrad (bsn), Nadia Jacobchuk (pno)
description: This is a three-movement work in a neoclassical style combining traditional structures with a more modern harmonic language. The first movement “Allegretto giocoso” is in sonata form opening with a playful theme presented in the clarinet overtop of accompaniment figures. The bassoon outlines the melodic contour with staccato notes, while the piano provides harmonic support through chords. This develops into a connecting section leading into a more lyrical and legato secondary theme in the clarinet combined with an ostinato line that unfolds in the piano. Next, a contrasting section occurs featuring a rapid dialogue between the clarinet and bassoon built on G and F major scales ascending in the clarinet and descending in the bassoon. This develops into the climax with homorhythmic arpeggios in all three instruments. This is interrupted by a subito piano interlude in the piano that leads into the development section. The development begins with an arpeggiated line in the bassoon, which the clarinet responds with a countermelody that the piano imitates. The character changes from playful to more triumphant with the introduction of large intervals in the winds and piano chords. Then the “piu mosso” begins with three fragments of the main theme in the clarinet and bassoon that develops fully before a connecting section. Finally, the movement concludes with material taken from the earlier piano interlude. The second movement “Moderato non troppo” is in ternary form. The movement opens with a bassoon solo monologue in the low register. Next, the A section begins with the clarinet entering in their lowest register in a contrapuntal texture that eventually weaves together into a homorhythmic texture in dialogue with F major, F♯ minor and E major arpeggios in the piano. These thematic lines imitate one another in a sequential manner throughout the B section. The final movement “Allegro scherzando” is a dance in a humorous character with inspiration from folk music. It utilizes rhythmic and tonal elements from the Hopak. The movement features rhythmic ostinato lines in the piano, polytonality between the winds and contrasts between articulated and legato characters. The movement consists of four short sections in the form of ABCBDACB.

description: This piece is centered around the idea of sounds arising from silence inspired by minimalism. Overall, it explores this relationship and importance of silence in music through the predominance of soft dynamics and changes to small details. This is manifested through the interaction of the performers deciding how to convey these elements through their choice of how their individual segments contribute to the whole piece through their choices of how long to play each segment, how much silence to take before beginning a new segment and which segment to respond with next as they can be played in any desired order.
