description: This is a virtuosic six-movement suite as a homage for Francisco Goya, who was a Spanish romantic painter that reflected the historical upheavals and influenced generations of composers. The title refers to his collection of 80 prints using the technique of aquatint published in 1799. Goya described that the themes of the works come from the “extravagances and follies common to all society”69 depicting well-known persons of the time. The work is structured on a variety of different sections in each movement that is inspired by a certain picture from the collection combined together to create a cohesive piece. The first movement is slow marked eighth note equals 68 and begins with a section titled “Francisco Goya y Lucientes Paintor” which is the first of the 80 in the collection and it is a self-portrait of Goya. Musically, it features a half note tied to a dotted eighth note followed by a sixteenth leading to a dotted half note played on the contrabassoon, which is echoed in the piano. As it develops the piano responses become thicker and more active. The next section “The say “I will” and give their hand to the first coming” consists of an oscillating sixteenth note cluster chord motif in the piano. This becomes fragmented and the bassoon interjects in the rests often with one to three sixteenth notes. The following section “Here comes the bogey-man” consists of short sixteenth note fragments of either two sixteenths or three triplet sixteenth notes separated by rests in a homorhythmic texture. Afterwards “Nanny’s boy” section is rhythmically dissonant with repeated duple eighth notes in the left hand of the piano competing with arpeggiated triplet eighth notes in the bassoon. Eventually, the roles reverse. The final section “Tantalus” consists of arpeggiated sextuplets with two notes in a row before changing in the bassoon overtop of a disjunct and rhythmically dissonant piano accompaniment. The second movement is also slow marked quarter note equal 63. The first section “That dust” and second section “There was no help” consists of multiphonic long notes in the bassoon marked pianissimo underneath a rhythmically complex piano line marked fortissimo that continually ascends and descends. The next section “He broke the pitcher” brings back the two sixteenth notes motif leading to scalar runs with eighth note interjections in the piano in between the bassoon’s fragments. The final section “They already go plucked” expands the scalar runs into a full phrase with contrapuntal lines in the piano. The third movement is marked dotted half note equals 40 and begins with the section “Fine advice” consisting of an oscillating major second in eighth and quarter note triplets with a contrapuntal line in the piano that switches between triplets and dotted eighth followed by a sixteenth note motifs throughout. The next section “Should God forgive her. She was her mother…” takes the motifs that were expanded and puts them homorhythmic in the bassoon and right hand of the piano overtop of a syncopated bass line in the left hand. The final section “Hush” brings back the original piano line combined with a weaving sixteenth note line in the bassoon that ends with the bassoonist saying “Shhh” to conclude the movement. The fourth movement is marked quarter equals 60 and opens with the “They spruce themselves up” section that has sixteenth note motifs in dialogue between the bassoon and piano. The next section “They are warm” is based around a slurred descending interval that becomes larger overtime in the contrabassoon that the piano responds with four cluster chord eighth notes. The final section “The chichillas” features repeated articulated sixteenth notes in the contrabassoon with eighth note chords in the piano. The fifth movement is marked quarter note equals 60 opening with the section “Will the disciple be wiser?” is a dialogue of quarter and half notes between the contrabassoon and piano alternating when they change notes. The final two sections “Bravissimo” and “Thou who canst not” are marked quarter equals 126 and it is an energetic dance-like character with an energetic bass line ostinato and offbeat chords in the piano and melody in the contrabassoon that switches between beginning on the beat and syncopated. The final movement is marked eighth equals 63 and begins with the “And they still won’t go” section brings back material from the very opening of the piece. The following section “Squealers” continues the same piano accompaniment while the contrabassoon plays a melody while crowing a pitch on the reed in their mouth simultaneously. The next section “It is time up” is an aggressive and rhythmic character in a contrapuntal texture. The final section “The dream of reason brings forth monsters” consists of a long tone on the low Bb in the contrabassoon while the piano plays a disjunct accompaniment to conclude the work.

premiere: 2022 CD recording “Modern Lullabies”
recordings: CD: 1) Modern Lullabies: Track 04 (Dux 2022) by dedicatee (fl), Carlos Peña Montoya (harp) YouTube: 1) by dedicatee (fl), Carlos Peña Montoya (harp) (https://youtu.be/Y65hnOtZQNA?si=AuBd5mmsUNRy4Cr8)
description: This is a short one movement work with folklorism inspiration depicting a scene from the poem “Rzeczka” written by Polish poet Julian Tuwim. The poem describes a small river flowing and winding like a glittering ribbon that sparkles disappearing into the landscape. The work opens with a vocal-like melody in the flute based around repeated triplet eighth notes leading to a longer note value with quarter or eighth notes in between to motif into a longer phrase. Underneath is an oscillating piano accompaniment emulating the river flowing. At the beginning the piano has eighth notes in the inner voices and half notes in the outer voices with quick grace notes at the start of the measure in the right hand. This accompaniment develops into a disjunct line of thirty-second notes that become more compact intervals, like the river hitting an area of rough water briefly before returning to the calm. Eventually, the accompaniment becomes arpeggiations to reach the climax through a dramatic crescendo to a large rolled chord spanning across the piano followed by a silent fermata. A return to the opening texture occurs but now with brief moments of virtuosic thirty-second notes alternating between the flute and piano. The flute then takes over with a virtuosic display like a sparkling light dancing around on the water. A final section with the return of the triplet motif concludes the work.

premiere: Fall 2020 in Kharkiv by Anastasia Golovko (fl), Yaroslava Serdyuk (pno)
key: I (A# minor, none used), II (C♯ minor), III (D major), IV (A♯ minor)
description: This work is in a sonata cycle of four movements with a monothematic principal applied. For example, the main theme appears throughout such as in the middle section of the second movement in a transformed manner, and then later becomes the basis for the finale. Each movement in ternary form that highlights the lyrical and vocal qualities of the flute in different musical contexts. The first movement “Allegretto cantabile” is in sonata form with an abbreviated reprise functioning as a coda. The A section features a motif of a tied quarter that is followed by sixteenth notes in a neighbour motion leading to a quarter or two eighth notes all under a slur in the flute to demonstrate how it can sing through a melodic line. The piano accompaniment features a bass note in the left hand on the downbeats and an arpeggiated sixteenth note ostinato in the right hand highlighting the harmonies. The B section displays a lyrical theme consisting of slurred quarter, eighth and dotted eighth note in stepwise or small intervals. The return to the A section features sequences of fragments from the theme such as using the neighbour motion in a syncopated manner. Then a diminution of the B theme occurs now in half and quarter notes. The piano accompaniment is more transparent now with chords in both hands. A return to the original A material occurs to conclude the movement. The next movement “Adagio con duolo” is a form and variations with a solemn character. The piano accompaniment is chordal while the flute plays a vocal-like theme of slurred quarter, half and whole notes to highlight the flute’s tone colours and vibrato. A “Piu mosso” section contrats by creating a more active texture with quarter notes in the piano and long note trills in the flute. The following movement “Allegretto amabile e semplice” is comprised of an arpeggiated bass line in the left hand and melody when the flute is not playing in the right hand. The flute has another slurred and vocal-like melody of eighth, quarter and dotted quarter notes mainly stepwise and small intervals. The B section has a dialogue texture to it where a short motif of a grace note followed by four eighth notes passes between the flute and both hands of the piano in unison. The final movement “Allegretto narrante” has a declamatory character with a theme built on a half note followed by quarter note to highlight the meter. The piano accompaniment is primarily quarter notes when the flute is playing and thematic material when the flute is not playing.The accompaniment becomes more active as it progresses to become eighth notes in the right hand.

premiere: 1997 in Kyiv by dedicatee (bsn) with Ukrainian Radio Symphony Orchestra, Volodymyr Sirenko (cond)
recordings: YouTube: 1) Premiere (https://youtu.be/n5zKAOhYKqw) 2) Zachary Senick (bsn) and Wesley Shen (pno) 2023 (https://youtu.be/Yuxvw0kvIYc?si=pWNvPeRgVcGGfSjA)
description: This is a one-movement concerto-like work that alternates between sections of monologue in the bassoon with orchestral accompaniment that bridges different sections together. Hubarenko’s musical process for this work can be perceived as a free improvisation unfolding toward the final figurative synthesis through powerful dynamic waves to form linear momentum. He combines this with an excellent knowledge of orchestral colors to enhance his lyrical dramatic style similar to Samuel Barber and Vaughn Williams. The work opens with a “Sostenuto” section that features a lyrical line that becomes more disjunct with larger intervals as it becomes more rhythmical active from duple to triplet eighth notes. After it unwinds to a whole note on the pitch “Bb” the orchestra enters in unison on this pitch as it weaves around becoming more tonally ambiguous leading to a cluster chord, which another monologue in the bassoon emerges from. This pattern continues of the orchestra entering in unison at the end of the phrase and becoming more ambiguous. Eventually, a rhythmic ostinato on the pitch “B♭” of dotted eighth note and sixteenth note leading to a quarter note that is tied the first time and untied the second time. As it progresses it builds to become a cluster chord as the bassoon plays a melodic line overtop. This leads into the second section “Andante cantabile” with a vocal-like line in the bassoon overtop of a drone, running line of eighth notes, and countermelody. This eventually develops into another short monologue leading back to the opening orchestral interlude. The next main section “Allegro non troppo” has a waltz-like character with a slurred melodic line in the bassoon overtop of a syncopated bass line. As it develops a countermelody is introduced in the upper strings that merges into a character shift in the accompaniment with a weaving eighth note line that creates a more rigid character. The melody continues expanding climaxing to a high E in the bassoon held for three measures. Afterwards, the bassoon joins this new character with a melody based off the motifs introduced by the orchestra earlier in the section. This winds down material from earlier that finds its way back to the home pitch of “B♭” to conclude the movement on a low B♭ in the bassoon that is held for four measures as the orchestra sets up a final cadence consisting of the lower strings playing B♭ that is unsettled with a B-natural in the first violin to conclude the work.

premiere: October 5th, 2024 in Lviv, Ukraine by dedicatee for Contrasts Festival of Contemporary Music for the “Spirit and Breath” project
extended_techniques: air noises, inhaling/exhaling, multiphonic (fingering given), overblowing, whistle tones
performace_considerations: section of music are boxed with the amount of seconds the performer should take to perform them, notation for inhaling and exhaling used
description: The work is centered around two main ideas that are in juxtaposition that occasionally have other material interspersed. The two main ideas alternate while undergoing slight variations as they get more intense and aggressive until the climax. The first main idea is the use of air noises and inhaling/exhaling by the performer that begins ethereal but uses dynamic swells to intensify and change character in order to transition into the other material. The second main idea consists of a string of disjunct short note values in a staccato articulation preceded by a grace note in a large interval. During the phrase are drastic dynamic changes from pianissimo to fortissimo that are constantly switching. Eventually, the two ideas are developed: the first incorporating longer note values, full tone and trills; and the second becomes more virtuosic with arpeggiated motion written in accelerando beaming. This leads into a final lyrical phrase that becomes whistle tones to conclude the work in suspense with the audience expecting more or a return to the original material.

dedicated: written for project “Music of Young Lviv Composers 2023” by Ukrainian Classic Live
premiere: April 4th, 2023 in Lviv, Ukraine at Lviv Organ Hall by Marina Spirina (fl)
description: Hurina describes that the inspiration of the work is “based on the alliterative poem 'Sir Gawain and the Green Knight' of unknown authorship from the 14th century, which is dedicated to the adventures of Sir Gawain and King Arthur. It reflects the spirit of chivalry and faithfulness to one's word, overcoming trials that stand in your way. To be honest, these ideas strongly resonate with today's realities, where our heroes on the battlefield exhibit this spirit of chivalry, loyalty to the country, and the struggle for freedom. I hope that listeners will feel everything I wanted to convey with this composition and discover new meanings in my work.” Musically, the work has a dotted rhythm that comes back throughout the piece to tie together different interludes like a recitative wandering around but always returning to its main point. In the opening the work begins with a dotted quarter note followed by an eighth note in descending minor third interval followed by rests. Like one word that sings into silence creating anticipation. This gets transformed into a dotted eighth followed by two thirty-second notes as the phrase elongates into a full statement. This opening section continues becoming more virtuosic and insistent through the incorporation of arpeggiation and accents into the phrase. Eventually the opening motif returns now with a trill on the first statement and the second statement being intervallically expanded. The piece climaxes into a fortissimo frullato long note through a sequential passage of the dotted motif now transformed into a dotted eighth followed by a sixteenth note. The work closes with an incorporation of the various ideas from earlier now recombined that is interrupted with one final attempt of the opening motif that is now successful in creating a two measure unit of them utilizing the intervals emphasized earlier in the work. The final phrase returns to a wandering arpeggiation that leads into the second variation of the motif to conclude the work.

description: This is a one-movement work in a lento tempo that presents a melodic and vocal-like theme in the bassoon that explores a variety of tonalities throughout. This is overtop of various accompaniment textures and figures such as an arpeggiated eighth note bass line in the left hand with chordal eighth notes in the right hand. As the movement progresses the accompaniment becomes more active becoming sixteenth note arpeggiation and syncopated chords in the right hand. The bassoon melody also becomes more active developing into passages of sixteenth notes that are in a sequential manner.

description: This is a short one-movement work that is not typical of her style. Typically, Besedina’s style is very emotional with great contrasts and varied textures. However, this piece utilizes elements of avant-garde through the use of some extended techniques with unconventional textures, forms, and structures. Throughout the work the concept of psychedelic is an inspiration achieved through the use of ostinato and monothematism to mesmerize the listener. The work begins with an ad libitum clarinet solo that presents the main theme in an improvisatory manner. This leads into a virtuosic cadenza-like arpeggiated passage in the flute overtop of a rolled piano chord. Next, an arpeggiated ostinato motif begins in the right hand of the piano, which the flute joins in on. The bassoon then enters with a legato secondary theme. Eventually, the flute develops into a virtuosic passage with a large glissando. This prompts the arrival of a contrapuntal texture based around short, fragmented motifs overtop of the ostinato still occurring in the piano. Eventually, the texture evolves to virtuosic ad libitum passages in an aleatoric texture. Different short fragments such as tremolos and quintuplet sixteenth notes are inserted into the texture to create a much more active quality to the music now. The music continues developing with different variations and new material being recombined until it climaxes to a dissonant frullato chord competing with an aleatoric piano line. A return to material from earlier in the work leading to a final chord that dies away to conclude the work.

premiere: Original Premiere: It was scheduled for the beginning of 2022 but was unexpectedly cancelled due to the start of the full-scale Ukrainian-Russian war; New Premiere: December 10th, 2024 in Toronto by Zachary Senick (bsn)
description: This is a short one movement work in ternary form that explores the expressive and technical aspects of the bassoon. The A section “Adagio sostenuto” features a lyrical and vocal line mainly in scalar and arpeggiated motion that weaves around harmonically between key areas. As it progresses a string of articulated eighth notes accelerando with an abrupt return to the original tempo with fragmented material from earlier in a more aggressive character due to the introduction of accents. This then rallentando through a motif of eighth notes outlining harmony belonging to F♯ major with some chromaticism climaxes to a fermata whole note on the pitch “F♯”. ‘The B section “Piu mosso” has an improvisatory character consisting of disjunct line imitating two-voice writing. The poco rubato slurred sixteenth notes weave around in the lower register of the bassoon that lead tenuto-staccato eighth notes two and a half octaves higher in the tenor register. As it progresses the sixteenth passages become shorter and fragmented, and while the eighth note line is extended with sixteenth notes added beforehand. Eventually, this combined into one virtuosic line of sixteenths traversing the range of the bassoon arriving at a high C♯ fermata whole note. The return of the A section opens identical to the beginning of the piece but instead of developing and climaxing it fades away with a half note followed by a quarter note rest motif, which leads to a final dotted half note on the pitch “G” to conclude the work.

description: This is a short work with two contrasting characters between the movements and is perfect for a student to develop their lyrical and technical playing. The first movement Melodie has a very melancholic and nostalgic character that flows effortlessly around the range of the flute in an Andante tempo. The movement opens with a simple and vocal-like melody in the middle register of the flute built upon arpeggiation and neighbouring motion utilizing quarter notes leading to a dotted quarter followed by an eighth rhythmic motif. This is overtop of chords in the piano that blossoms into taking over the melody, while the flute plays strings of arpeggiated eighth notes leading to a longer note value. The melody returns in the flute with some variations and a more intense character as the chords in the piano become repeated eighth notes now. This leads into a virtuosic flute cadenza before a return to the melody now with a triplet eighth arpeggiation accompaniment in the piano creating a nostalgic character to the previous material. Eventually, the instruments trade roles before one final statement of the theme in a texture similar to the opening. The second movement Valse opens with a virtuosic display of arpeggios in the flute. The piano then joins in setting up a waltz accompaniment for the theme to be presented in the flute consisting of eighth notes leading to a tied quarter note. The second presentation of the theme adds ornamentation such as mordents to create more musical interest. There is a brief “Poco meno mosso” section that features a more lyrical flute melody introducing longer note values and dotted rhythms. The piano shifts into play a counterpoint role taking over moments of melody and moments of countermelody to create a contrast in texture from the waltz character.

description: This is a short one-movement work in an “Andante” tempo. As it develops, it becomes a line of weaving eighth notes that goes above the staff, which begins on the syncopation of the first beat. The piano takes over the melody in the right hand with an arpeggiation in the left hand. A return to the original texture and roles occurs to conclude the work.

description: This is a short one-movement work in a neo-romantic style with the form featuring an lyrical flute line and accompaniment figures in the piano. The piece begins with a motif of a tied half note to an eighth note followed by three eighth notes leading to the next figure. The three eighth notes are in smaller intervals producing a vocal-like line. As it progress, chromaticism is introduced into the line. The piano accompaniment is flowing arpeggiated eighth notes. This leads into a contrasting “Piu mosso” section that is more passionate and virtuosic in 12/8. The melodic line in the flute becomes more active with the introduction of longer strings of eighth notes and sixteenth notes in a scalar motion. The piano playings dotted quarter note chords underneath. This climaxes into a trill for an entire measure on a “D” above the staff while the piano plays an augmented fragment of the opening motif none as a dotted eighth followed by three sixteenths leading into a return of the opening material now an octave higher in the flute above the staff. The piano texture now has the melody added into the right hand. Eventually, the accompaniment becomes triplet eighth notes instead of duple before returning the opening texture to conclude the piece.

description: This is a short one-movement work that comes from a larger work “Suite of Dances” that features a variety of instrumentations: cello & piano, flute & piano, piano trio, and solo piano. Program notes of the work describe it as “a cool, languid glide through a summer’s night. We are drawn in by the soaring lines of the solo flute, filled with nostalgia; the piano responds, colouring the theme with soft, impressionistic harmonies.” (Furiant Records, linear notes). This work reimagines a waltz in a more nostalgic and melancholic character providing more complexity to it. The work opens with a flute cadenza with an improvisatory and enchanting character through the use of a repeated note motif that grows into more melodic material, technical flourishes cascading to the high register of the flute, and pitch bending. Next, a piano introduction occurs setting up the waltz character with a typical accompaniment in the left hand of the tonic on the downbeat and chords responding on beats two and three. This is underneath a melodic theme in the right hand. However, this waltz as the title suggests has a melancholic feel through the lush and minor harmonies utilized creating a darker character as opposed to a typical major chord progressions used in a waltz to create a bright character. Afterwards, the flute enters with the theme that has some slight melodic and rhythmic variations but has kept the overall structure. The piano then plays a two-measure segue into the B theme played by the flute, which begins less rhythmically active. As it progresses sixteenth notes are reintroduced to give it more forward momentum. The piano accompaniment for the B theme has changed to an oscillating eighth note line utilizing thirds in the left hand and chords primarily quarter notes that have a countermelody to them in the right hand. Another four measure segue occurs in the piano to conclude the section and prepare a return to the A theme. A final flute cadenza that brings back elements from the opening occurs to conclude the work.

description: This is the first movement “Slowly, sad” of a larger suite “Meridian” that combines a melodic line with rhythmic ostinatos to create an interwoven texture throughout. It has folk music inspiration but uses own original themes. The work begins with a melodic line based around the pitch “A” that expands outwards as it progresses. This overtop of longer note value chords in the rest of the winds that explore dissonance through open voicing. Eventually, fragments of the melodic line appear in the other instruments in a polyphonic texture. The next section “Lively” features a livelier variation of the theme in a contrapuntal and canon-like texture overtop of an oscillating sixteenth note ostinato. This ostinato gradually develops from a semitone motion to an arpeggiated figure as the section develops in some of the instruments allowing a more interwoven texture of four main parts occurring simultaneously1) main theme 2) fragmentation of the theme 3) semitone ostinato 4) arpeggiated ostinato, that imitate the flow-like state of a meridian. Eventually, a return to the opening material occurs that quickly adds in a fragmentation that rhythmic diminution from quarter triplets to sixteenth notes to create a final climax to a final fermata chord to conclude the work.

premiere: October 3rd 2018 in Kyiv by Vladimir Antoshin (bsn), Ukrainian Radio Symphony Orchestra, Volodymyr Sheiko (cond)
style: neoclassical, neoimpressionism, jazz influence, avant-garde: sonorism
description: This is a one-movement work in two main sections. It opens with a “Largo” that begins with the strings presenting a syncopated rhythmic ostinato providing an accompaniment foundation for the bassoon to enter with a disjunct theme in a lyrical quality. As the material develops the phrase becomes longer connecting the shorter opening statements, dynamically increasing, and more rhythmically active progressing to a moment of sextuplet sixteenth notes. This climaxes into a brief bassoon cadenza in a virtuosic manner consisting of arpeggiated passages traversing from the bottom to tenor register. Afterwards, a return to the opening material occurs but now highly ornamented with the orchestra in a more dialogue texture to the soloist. This leads into the second main section “Allegro moderato” consisting of a disjunct articulated passage of sixteenth notes in the bassoon. The orchestra plays accompaniment figures underneath and then responses with passages of sixteenth notes during the soloist's rests. This develops into a more contrapuntal texture with both playing passages of sixteenth notes simultaneously. Eventually, it becomes fragmented to set up a “Meno mosso” orchestral interlude featuring a similar texture. Next, a brief transition section occurs that gradually decreases tempo, rhythmically diminution, and texturally thinning to set up the return of the “Largo”. The listener expects this to be a full return as in a typical ternary form. However, it is only a brief introduction before returning to the opening “Allegro moderato” material but this time with rests inserted in the lines creating a more dialogue texture between the soloist and orchestra. As it develops the line becomes whole again returning briefly to a full passage of sixteenth notes with no rests. Finally, material that is reminiscent of the largo in its structure and lyrical character is presented in the bassoon overtop of figures typical of the allegro moderato creating a final synthesis of the different elements of the concerto being combined to conclude the work.

description: This is a short one-movement work marked “Allegro” that is based around the concept of syncopations through the use of rests and accents to create a groove from it. The work begins with an eight-measure piano introduction of an open fifth drone in the left hand, while the right hand plays a syncopated scalar motif leading to rhythmic and syncopated chords. The flute then enters with a melodic line built around dotted rhythms while the piano piano plays syncopated chords in the right hand and an eighth note bass line in the left hand. When the flute is resting the right hand takes over the thematic material. The flute then plays a new theme consisting of sixteenth notes leading to tied notes creating syncopations. As it develops it becomes more virtuosic with strings of sextuplet sixteenth note flourishes from the low to the high register. Eventually, the dotted rhythm motif returns now with the flourishes incorporated into the line. A “Meno mosso” section occurs that combines the two themes into one cohesive theme where they are equal overtop of accompanimental figures in the piano. As it progresses the theme gets fragmented and syncopated with the insertion of rests. A return of the “Allegro” section occurs to conclude the work that is more virtuosic featuring elements from earlier with more extended passages of sixteenth notes with accents on the first and fourth of each beat.

description: This is a one-movement work with three main sections that takes inspiration from Ukrainian folklore and music and combines it with avant-garde language and idioms. The title Molfar comes from Hutsul culture and refers to men with supernatural abilities living in the forests of the Carpathian Mountains. Their abilities combine different elements of magic, fortune-telling, and healing. However, in oral stories throughout history, molfars have often been depicted as channeling their powers through black magic for evil purposes, which is demonstrated through the mysterious and aggressive characters that emerge from what begins as light and pure characters. Musically the piece takes inspiration from traditional Hutsul folk music utilizing the Ukrainian minor scale, which raises the 4th and 6th scale degrees on a natural minor scale, which is combined with contemporary rhythms, harmonies, and extended techniques such as multiphonic. The first section is a lyrical and mysterious melody in the bassoon that starts soft and grows over an erratic piano accompaniment depicting the beginning of a journey into the forests. This evolves getting more intense through increased motion in the piano accompaniment that leads into the next theme, which is a more aggressive staccato motif being traded between the bassoon and piano. Eventually, a variation of the opening melody returns in the bassoon that leads into a bassoon cadenza section with interruptions from the piano. During this cadenza section there are prepared piano interruptions to depict the evil character of the molfars attempting to take over. The final section of the piece is a fast and energetic dance-like motif that is taken from the fifth movement “Mavka” in Carpathian Sketches in triplet meter that gets interrupted by duple meter to depict a battle against the evil molfars.

description: This piece is a paraphrase of the well-known theme Czardas. Overall, this is a virtuosic show piece demonstrating the technical capabilities of the violin and bassoon. The piece opens with a short virtuosic piano introduction leading into the violin that presents the theme with the bassoon taking over before beginning variations on the theme. The violin and bassoon go through a couple variations before arriving at an Allegro section. Next, a meno mosso section occurs where the piano performs solo eventually leading into a capriccioso section. Afterwards the music goes through multiple accelerando, ritardando and tempo changes before returning back to the Allegro section that ends with a virtuosic sixteenth passage in the violin and bassoon to become a short coda.

premiere: May 25th, 2025 in Italy at Festival Maggio Sermonetano by dedicatee (fl), composer (pno)
description: This is a short one-movement work with the subtitle “L’eterno fanciullo” evoking a simple and elegant style. Pedagogically, this would be a great first solo for a young performer because it stays in the middle register of the flute, rhythmically mainly comprised of quarter, half and whole notes with the occasional eighth note pickup. As well, it would be a good introduction to accidentals as the melody harmonically weaves around. The work features a vocal-like melody mainly consisting of step-wise motion and intervals of a third in a slurred articulation. The piano provides a quarter note countermelody in the right hand and a bass line with offbeats in the left hand creating a steady rhythmic ostinato. Eventually, the melody becomes fragmented to an eighth note pickup to a quarter note followed by rest in the flute for the climax of the piece before returning to the theme in a new tonal center. The piano accompaniment becomes a constant stream of arpeggiated eighth notes to provide a change in texture. Afterwards, a return to the original opening material returns to conclude the work.

premiere: April 9th, 2025 in Toronto by Zachary Senick (bsn)
description: In general, Lys’ style is characterized by an interest in lyrical and expressive writing through a melodic and polyphonic focus that unfolds in layers of texture. Often, features of Ukrainian folk melos are combined with an increased role of phonism harmonies that synthesize the achievements of modern compositional techniques. The work Monologue takes inspiration from the literary technique in which speech is broadcasted in first person address to both themself and others to depict the inner world of themselves creating a psychological portrait. Therefore, this work sets up a psychological, confessional, frank nature of a statement broadcasted in first person as an internal monologue that is full of self-reflection of their experiences and comprehension. As a result, it is a representation of a collision of the inner personal thoughts of the composer with the outside world through their experiences of the tragic events of the Russian invasion of Ukraine. Musically, the work is written using ideas of Lado in a freely interpreted technique of modality combined with authentic folk sources of Ukrainian music particularly in the level of rhythmic organization. Therefore, it is a synthesis of these two worlds, the inner Ukrainian personal thoughts and the outside world being aggressively forced upon them. This juxtaposition is musically represented through uneven accented rhythms, the presence of short phrases that dynamically swell encompassing a small range in the lower register of the bassoon that is interrupted by pauses. This represents a recitative character “as if a story-teller wanting to navigate their inner monologue, but something restrains him, he searches for suitable phrases, that reveals his internal condition.” (Olena Lys, Translated Zachary Senick) Gradually, the asymmetrical melodic motifs are transformed into symmetrical phrases in a longer lyrical line in a section marked “Cantabile.” This creates a dramatic nature to the music to express the painful emotions from their experiences. This connects into the second section that consists of lyric-dramatic statements that are interrupted by repetitive triplet eighth note motif featuring insistent repeated pitches that are marked “Agitato and Marcato” demonstrating the collision of the unprotected inner world with the external threats of the outside world, particularly of one living through war. The phrase continues to undergo development through mechanistic genre melodic principles leading to an expressive climax in the high register of the bassoon. Afterwards, a return to the recitative character occurs “as an endeavor to understand and accept the events, that are happening, but given all of this is fairly difficult to do.” (Olena Lys, Translated Zachary Senick) The work concludes with a brief coda closes the work with material from the opening but with a more melodic and requiem-like returning to the lowest register of the bassoon that represents “painful numbness in the common collective grief of the Ukrainian people, as they search for support, or a particular accumulation of energy before the next phase of the fight.” (Olena Lys, Translated Zachary Senick) The final phase suddenly jumps to the high register of the bassoon “like a ray of hope, full of concentrated expression.” (Olena Lys, Translated Zachary Senick). However, the original motifs still persist in the background “as a sign of all those painful losses from the war that will take a very long time to make sense of and mourn by the Ukrainian people, that this monologue every Ukrainian and every conscious caring person will endure.” (Olena Lys, Translated Zachary Senick)

description: This is a short one-movement work centered around a dotted quarter, eighth, and dotted quarter note rhythmic motif in a semitone upper neighbour motion The work is in an Andantino tempo with rubato throughout. It opens with the main motif at a mezzo forte dynamic and sequentially ascends through the range of the bassoon, while becoming more rhythmically active with short passages of eighth notes until a climax at a high D half note under a fermata at a fortissimo dynamic. Afterwards, it returns to the opening motif a perfect fifth higher than the opening. It undergoes a similar development to an arrival at a high D♭. The work ends with a one-measure fragment of the motif at a mezzo piano dynamic.

This is a short one-movement work that is a virtuosic display for the flute that incorporates elements of folk music with a few extended techniques. The work opens with a “Moderato” section where the flute (or pan flute) plays a lively motif first alone built on a thirty-second note to a dotted sixteenth note that leads to triplet (either eighth or sixteenth) notes. The cimbalom enters with accompaniment figures that alternate between being on the beat and syncopated. Next, is a pastorale with an improvisatory character as it consists of a melody that is a highly embellished overtop of quarter notes in the cimbalom. This is followed by a “Giocoso” section that has energetic flourishes of notes in the flute with accompaniment figures in the cimbalom beginning on the beat that shift to syncopated. Afterwards, a “Lento” section features a vocal-like melody in the flute that includes singing oscillating pitches “E” to “D” at the same time. The cimbalom plays a passage that is primarily a passage of sixteenth notes with the occasional moment of other rhythms. A final “Allegretto” section brings back the opening material in the flute with a more active accompaniment part in the cimbalom to conclude the work.

description: This is a theme and variations on the classic and well known “Happy Birthday”Theme that utilizes a contrast of characters and musical styles throughout. The theme is marked “Cherffully” presents the melody in the right hand of the piano and chordal accompaniment in the left hand in a rhythmic pattern of half, quarter and dotted half note. Variation I “Lovely” presents the theme in the lowest register of the flute overtop of arpeggiated eighth notes in the left hand and counter melody in the right hand of the piano. Variation II “Secretly” opens with a rhythmic ostinato in the piano consisting of two staccato eighth notes on the same repeated note followed by slurred two sixteenth and eighth leading to an accented quarter note. This is overtop of a bass line in the left hand. The flute embellishes the melody with a line of eighth notes filing it in harmonically. Variation III “Jazzy” brings back the melody closer to as written in the middle register of the flute with some “jazzy” inflections added such as glissandos and trills, while the piano is in dialogue with echoes in the right hand and a waltz-like pattern in the left hand of the piano. Variation IV “Mystically” has an ostinato of constant sixteenth notes in the piano while the flute sings a pedal on the pitch “C” and plays the melodic content as half notes overtop. The final variation “Happily” turns the melodic content into a triplet rhythmic subdivision often using repeated notes in the flute, while the piano has an ostinato bass line and chordal figures. This leads into a final arpeggiated sixteenth note texture in the piano while the flute trills on the tonic (F) in the upper register climaxing into a frullato whole note and final sfozando tonic chord across the ensemble.

description: This is a one-movement work in an avant-garde style. Hodziatsky was a prominent member of the Kyiv Avant-Garde, and this work follows in his style from that period. His music often takes inspiration from both the neoclassical style of Stravinsky combined with Western Second Viennese and avant-garde composers. Hodziatsky declared against the use of dodecaphony within his work, which was common in the serial music of the time. The work begins with a sixteenth note fragment in the flute overtop of staccato quarter note at the start of each fragment in the oboe and clarinet. This develops into a longer and cohesive line in the flute overtop of long notes that change and weave in and out of one another in the ensemble. Slowly, the accompaniment becomes more active and independent creating a contrapuntal texture eventually, becoming a canon-like texture of the line in the flute. This material winds down into a rhythmic and contrapuntal duet between the horn and the bassoon. Gradually, the ensemble joins back one at the time beginning with the clarinet followed by the oboe. The introduction of the flute denotes a new section “Meno mosso” featuring a theme in the flute overtop of trilled long notes changing at different times throughout the ensemble, which were set up at the end of the previous section to create a seamless transition between the sections. Motifs from earlier in the piece are brought back into the flute overtop of this texture before returning to the original meno mosso material. Eventually, the accompaniment texture changes to tutti chords with the occasional dialogue during the flute’s longer note values. As this progresses the oboe as juxtaposition to this legato and calm texture with material from the beginning section as interruptions that develop into a full line. This leads into a contrapuntal duet of the flute and oboe playing this earlier material, which the clarinet joins in for a while before returning to a duet. Later on the clarinet, bassoon, and horn re-enter with the chorale-like accompaniment again underneath the flute and oboe’s contrapuntal staccato sixteenth lines. A final return to the duet texture returns this time winding down into motifs from the calmer sections in dialogue to conclude the work.

description: This is a one-movement work with many contrasting characters and sections often switching between elaborate polyphonic textures and meditative lyricism creating intense moments of drama. It is written in an avant-garde style and aesthetic that explores different textures available to a wind quintet while utilizing extended techniques such as frullato, multiphonic, and quarter tone glissandos done by the lip for the bassoonist. The first main section is untitled and marked quarter note equals 60. It features a motif of three triplet sixteenths tied to a long note in the clarinet that the oboe echoes. As the section develops a disjunct sextuplet sixteenth motif is introduced in the flute overtop of a melodic fragment in the bassoon that expands into a full line. This leads into a thick contrapuntal section with virtuosic fragments passed around the ensemble that emerge from the texture. Eventually, the virtuosic fragments become elongated and overlap to climax into a return to the opening triplet sixteenth motif in canon in the woodwinds with interjections from the horn on their long notes. The next section “molto cantabile” features a solo line first in the flute, followed by the clarinet overtop of a cluster chord. As this section develops the solo entrances enter in a fugal-like texture. This leads into a “Piu mosso” that is rhythmically driven with different syncopated motifs occurring throughout the ensemble that slowly build together. The following section “Allegretto” is a homorhythmic passage where the entire ensemble plays frullato creating an aggressive and intense character. Afterwards an “Andante” section occurs featuring a canon entry of a virtuosic arpeggiated passage that is rhythmically dissonant as the oboe plays a nine-note grouping while the other members play ten note groupings. This passage leads into trills in a contrapuntal texture, which continues to alternate between the two textures. Eventually, the two textures become combined with a solo instrument playing the virtuosic passage while the rest of the ensemble have the trilled texture. The next main section “Piu mosso” brings back the different syncopated lines from the earlier Piu mosso section now in homorhythm underneath a solo line that is passed around. This develops into another contrapuntal section of various virtuosic lines amongst the ensemble. Following this is a “Meno mosso” section in a chorale-like style. This leads into a “Presto” section which brings back the triplet motif from the beginning in the upper winds but rewritten in different time signatures and in more of a dialogue texture. A rhythmic ostinato with new material is introduced in the bassoon and horn underneath. This develops into trading sixteenths amongst the ensemble while the horn continues the ostinato. Eventually, the ensemble comes together and plays the ostinato tutti while the horn plays a solo line composed of long note values. However, overtime this is interrupted to the trading sixteenth texture amongst the ensemble. During the return to the ostinato the horn now plays a triplet eighth note solo line before returning to the original long note solo. The final section of the piece “Molto andante” begins with a solo clarinet line in a legato and calm character. The ensemble enters in a contrapuntal texture in which an oboe solo with a lyrical and folk-like melody emerges to conclude the work.

description: This work consists of five short movements in contrasting characters with neoromantic stylistic tendencies structure utilizing elements of classical structure. Each of the movements does not have a descriptive title or character indication. The first movement marked quarter note equals 90 opens with short declamatory-like statements mainly comprised of triplets leading to longer note values that are in dialogue moving around the ensemble. Next, a melodic line in the flute consisting of arpeggiated sixteenth notes leading to a dotted quarter note that is followed by staccato eighth notes. This is overtop of accompaniment figures in the rest of the ensemble. The rest of the movement develops these motifs with brief moments of homorhythm or an echo-like texture. The next movement marked half note equals 60 has a chorale character, which gets more rhythmically active as it progresses and plays with dissonances throughout. The third movement marked quarter note equals 110 is built around an eighth note, sixteenth rest, and sixteenth note ostinato on a repeated note. Throughout the movement a triplet motif is in struggle for dominance creating rhythmic dissonance, with moments it prevails with the ostinato dropping out. However, at times it switches to dotted eighth and sixteenth note allowing the ostinato to be prevailing. The following movement marked quarter note equals presents a lyrical theme first in the flute that the oboe joins in on. As it progresses and develops the texture becomes more contrapuntal until there are four completely independent lines occurring simultaneously. This leads to a four repeated sixteenth note motif that gets passed around the ensemble to conclude the movement. The final movement marked quarter note equals 120 switches between various eighth note passages such as arpeggiated, repeated, and weaving motion. Eventually, a more melodic motif comprised of dotted quarter and dotted half notes is introduced into the texture. This leads to all of the passages being combined together to conclude the work.

description: Na Tr’okh (For Three) is a post-Soviet phrase for when men get together to drink horilka (vodka). The work is structured to imitate a casual conversation that ebbs and flows like men chatting at a bar together. The piece opens with three distinct characters between the three parts, which could represent different roles within the conversation. The oboe has a longer, lyrical line reminiscent of one man telling a story while the bassoon has a short staccato line that interjects similar to a man interrupting and responding throughout the story. Finally, the clarinet produces air noises representing a role of a man actively listening along to the exchange. The piece develops into a fiery, technical section where each instrument passes the line around, like when a conversation gets heated with different opinions. This also includes the introduction of extended techniques such as frullato and multiphonics to help convey a more agitated character. Finally, after the piece climaxes the three instruments play a short unison passage to signify that they found a common ground and agreement leading into a slower more dialogue-like section that utilizes quarter-tones to create an expressive quality imitating the inflections fluctuations that naturally occur in speech. Finally, the piece ends with a slap tongue and playing with no reed section to create a whimsical, drunk character leading to the three musicians slumping over asleep in their chairs.

description: This is a short two-movement work consisting of a prelude and a fugue utilizing elements of structure and form from neoclassicism combined with chromatin harmonies. The first movement “Prelude” consists of an oboe melody that weaves in and out of traditional harmony with chromaticism to create moments of suspense. This is overtop of a bass line in the bassoon featuring lots of chromaticism and accompaniment figures in the clarinet that develops into a countermelody. The second movement “Fugue "presents a humoresque melody of articulated sixteenth notes based around a neighbour tone motion that expands outwards. There is three main developments of the theme which are carried out. The theme is first presented in the clarinet, followed by the oboe, and then the bassoon. When the bassoon enters a countermelody occurs in the clarinet to provide more melodic interest. Throughout the movement this fugal texture is contrasted with motifs from the theme utilized in either a homorhythmic or contrapuntal texture. For example, an one-measure motif from the theme is passed around the ensemble that leads back into another fugal section. Finally, a section of new material occurs to connect into a homorhythmic passage of weaving sixteenth notes that leads into a statement of the second half of the theme again. This prompts a final return to the original fugal texture with some slight variations from earlier to conclude the work.

description: This is a one-movement work inspired by outer space. Naiad is a satellite of Neptune with an irregular and nonspherical shape that was discovered by the Voyager-2 spacecraft in 1989. The word Naiad originates from mythology, which are female spirits or nymphs that gather around springs, streams and brooks. Overall, the composition is based upon free atonality with elements of serial music and micro-series. It utilizes cluster consonances from the series and micro-series throughout the piece to harmonically tie the work together. Polyrhythms are used to create different rhythmic frameworks within the piece. The work explores different register contrasts and timbral contrasts through his own symbols and unconventional directions to achieve a new quality of sound for the listener’s perceptual analysis of the score. The form of the piece is Intro, ABCBDBA, Coda. The piece opens with a short introduction of the piano plucking the strings. This leads into the A section of aggressive long notes in the bassoon in unison with cluster chords in the piano. This leads to the B section which consists of multiphonic notes that utilize goat-vibrato (vibrato produced with the lips like a saxophonist) and pitch bending over top of a 7:4 quarter note motif in the piano. This develops by the bassoon joining into the motif on the eighth note level and eventually progressing to the sixteenth note level. This leads to the C section consisting of a passage that is a string of thirty-second note that the bassoonist and piano weave around one another. The piece then goes back to the B section. Then a new D section is presented using elements of aleatorism and improvising. Then the piece returns to the B section, except the second motif is presented first this time. Then the A section returns leading into a coda that incorporates the string plucking from the introduction with the bassoon playing whole notes in the low register.

description: This is a four-movement suite that depicts various scenes of a city at night viewed by a lyric hero. The music is written in a sensitive and highly emotional manner. The first movement “Shadows on the Wall” is a misterioso character that has constant eighths or sixteenths going spread throughout bassoons I-III with a syncopated bass line in bsn IV. The second movement “Crazy Party” is upbeat and rock n roll inspired. It consists of syncopated motifs and accented figures in bassoon I-III overtop of a running bass line in bassoon IV. The third movement “Feelings” is an intimate and lyrical andante that mostly features a melody in bassoon I and accompaniment roles in bassoon II-IV. The final movement “Insomnia” is an anxious and uneasy character that lilts through the night featuring a sixteenth and eighth motif throughout.

description: This is a short one-movement work that takes typical elements of a nocturne but incorporates virtuosity and elements of 21st century music such as switching meters. The work opens with a “Tempo rubato” section that is a quasi-cadenza in a virtuosic descending arpeggiated figure in the flute overtop of a chord in the piano. This leads into an introduction in the piano to set up the main section of the piece “Andante” in a cantabile character. The flute enters overtop with a vocal-like line in long slurred passages. As it progresses the character becomes more agitated as the piano becomes fragmented and the flute becomes more disjunct with larger intervals and articulation added into the melody. Eventually, an “Agitato” section takes over that begins with a piano introduction with a flute melody entering in overtop. The same development occurs until it becomes a short flute cadenza this time leading into a brief “Moderato” section that is a dialogue of a motif between the flute and piano before a final return to the opening “Andante” section to conclude the work.

description: This is a short one-movement work that takes elements of structure and stylistic elements of a Classical Era Waltz but reimagines it with Ukrainian folk inspiration. This waltz brings Ukrainian inspiration through it being very melancholic and sorrowful and using a melodic line that weaves between the traditional minor scale and Ukrainian scales, while incorporating harmonic moments from folk music as was typical of Ukrainian Romantic era composers such as Lysenko. It begins with the piano setting up the character through a typical waltz pattern of a bass note on the downbeat and harmony on the offbeat. The flute then enters with a melancholic melody of quarter and half notes that weave around. As it develops it becomes more active with strings of eighth notes introduced in the flute melody and a dialogue created by the piano responding with countermelodies. Eventually, this progresses into a quasi-rubato and cadenza-like passage in the flute consisting of eighth notes. The piano then takes this over returning to the opening material with added ornamentation.
Kouzan’s music is influenced by Ukrainian folk music and the composers Bartók, Schoenberg, and Varèse.

description: This is a four-movement suite in a neoromantic style with elements and inspiration from folklorism. Overall, the work can be characterized by its logical structure with melodic lines that are lyrical and expressive combined with moments of dissonance to create tension. The instrumentation choices throughout provide colorful and rich contrasts. The first movement “Moderato marciale” in the form of ABACABC presents an opening theme in a march style featuring dotted eighth and sixteenth rhythms split between the first clarinet and oboe overtop of ostinato chords in the horns. As it develops the whole ensemble becomes involved becoming more contrapuntal such as a line of triplets trading between the bassoons and fragmentation echoing the theme. This leads into a secondary section marked “cantando” that is more lyrical overtop of chordal writing in the accompaniment. As the section develops the triplet fragment from the first section is introduced into the texture setting up a return to the A section. Next, another contrasting section occurs in a legato character and more transparent texture consisting of a melody, downbeat chords, and a bass line. The following movement “Berceuse” in an Andante quasi adagio tempo presents a folk-like melody beginning in the first clarinet solo. Slowly the other instruments enter with each successive part being more active allowing the texture to become thicker. For example, the horns enter first with a half note slurred to a quarter note motif and eventually ending with an eighth note ostinato in the first bassoon. Throughout the movement different accompaniment figures are presented to change the character and texture. The third movement “Scherzino” is in an Allegretto con grazia tempo and has an energetic dance-like character presenting a theme based around sixteenth notes overtop of accompaniment and ostinato figures and motifs. The final movement “Finale” has three main sections 1) Maestoso, 2) Andantino con moto, and 3) Allegro. The first section is an introduction setting up the main theme to come with fragments from it in a regal character. The next section begins with a full presentation of the main theme first in the oboe in a giocoso character with accompaniment figures rotating around the ensemble. Eventually, a secondary theme and countermelody are presented in a cannon texture. This leads to a reprise of the introduction section that gets expanded and switches between moments of contrapuntal and homorhythmic writing until the earlier material emerges. The final section is a short coda presenting the opening material in a faster tempo.
Kyva’s musical language combines elements of folklore, impressionistic colors and features from neoromanticism

description: This is a one-movement work in an ABA form. The first section “Largo” opens with a slow harp introduction in an arpeggiated texture that begins slow and speeds up as it progresses. Then the oboe enters with a repeated note motif on the pitch “E”, which the bassoon echoes on the pitch “D” while the oboe changes to the pitch “F”. This section continues changing pitches going between consonant and dissonant intervals until arriving at chords in the piano to initiate a new rhythmic motif based on sextuplet sixteenth notes. This leads into a more melodic triplet melody in the bassoon with accompaniment figures in the oboe and piano as an interlude before returning to the harp introduction again. This leads into the repeated note motif with the roles flipped in the oboe and bassoon. The second section “Allegro” is a trading sixteenth note texture between the oboe and bassoon over top of a rhythmic piano accompaniment. This eventually aligns and becomes a full melody with the harp providing countermelody and accompaniment role. This leads into the final section “Andantino” bringing back the opening harp introduction and repeated note motif again.

description: This is a suite in three movements that utilizes elements of neo baroque dance forms and motifs to depict the composer’s creative interest in English baroque music and Shakespeare. This work was after his vocal cycle on 12 sonnets of Shakespeare for bass and piano. The first movement “Gavotte” is in a moderato con moto tempo in ternary form. This movement features a stately theme played by the bassoon that is light and staccato in nature comprised mainly of quarter and eighth notes. Combined with accompaniment figures in the piano. Throughout the movement there are subtle shifts from major to minor briefly. The movement incorporates more modern harmonic choices by exploring a range of keys through such as C major, A major and F# major. The next movement “Rigadon” is in an allegro tempo resembling the English folk dance contra dance in three main sections. This movement has a simple and lively character through a melody of arpeggiated staccato eighth notes aiming towards quarter notes combined with two sixteenth note pickups to lead into the next phrase. The piano accompaniment mainly utilizes rhythmic chords often in an ostinato pattern. The first section is in a two part form of two periods with a repetition of the second one. The theme is presented in a homophonic texture in a tonic-dominant harmonic relationship. The next section “Meno mosso” contrasts the major theme with a new theme in minor through three phases that are developed. First, the new theme is presented in two sentences. This is followed by the fragmentation of the material. Finally, material from the first theme appears in four measure phrases. Then an abbreviated reprise of the A section occurs. The final movement “Gigue” is also in an allegro tempo in ternary form. This movement is inspired and depicts the popular character Robin Hood. This movement has a fun and playful character through the dotted eighth and sixteenth note motif in an ascending sequential motion creates an energetic momentum to the music. The piano provides accompaniment chords often in an ostinato that has little interludes of triplets when the bassoon is not playing. The theme is a typical classical period that receives a variation treatment as the music develops with an increase of ornamentation as well.

description: This is a short one-movement work depicting a scene from Ukrainian folklore about the mysterious Rusalka. She is a beautiful maiden of the water who represents the soul of a drowned girl. They are often depicted as having long beautiful hair and wearing a wreath made of sedge that utilized their appearance for evil purposes to lure men to their death. They live in groups in crystal palaces at the bottom of rivers and emerge in the springtime on Green Thursday or also known as Rusalka’s Easter. This work depicts this imagery of a Rusalka using her charm, dancing, and singing to trick a single man into his death. Musically, the work utilizes elements from Ukrainian folk music such as melody construction, harmonic progressions, and rhythmic motifs. The opening section “Andante, Sostenuto” has a lyrical slurred melody of eighth and quarter notes in the flute, while the piano plays accompanimental figures underneath. As it progresses the piano accompaniment becomes more active adding an oscillating major second eighth note ostinato. Next, a “Piu mosso” occurs which allows the flute part to become more virtuosic adding ornamentation, sixteenths, and a sextuplet flourish into the melody. This leads into a quasi-cadenza passage that has a sequential eighth note phrase that begins as eighths, which turn into sixteenth notes. This is overtop of whole note chords in the piano. Afterwards, a “Lento piu mosso” presents a weaving eighth note line in the flute that exploits chromaticism while the piano plays chords on every beat. This is then contrasted with a lively “Allegro” section imitating a dance. The flute plays a string of articulated sixteenth notes in a scalar motion while the piano plays a bass line with offbeat chords. This gets interrupted by a return to the opening “Andante, Sostenuto”. However, this time the melody is highly ornamented with many sixteenth note passing and neighbour tone motion while the piano plays long note value chords. Finally, a Da Capo takes place to return the listener to the mysterious character representing the death of the man, while Rusalka attempts to begin luring in her next victim to conclude the piece.

description: This is a seven-movement suite in a folklorism style utilizing elements of folk melody and dance depicting the life in the past of an average village person. The first movement “Departure of a country carriage” is in ternary form using a Da capo al fine. The A section “Allegretto” is in a homorhythmic texture featuring a syncopated melody through the use of ties comprised of quarter and eighth notes. The B section “meno mosso” features an arpeggiated motif in the horn and clarinet that leads to a drone, which the flute and oboe play a short melody overtop of. The next movement “The beauty of road landscapes” is in an an “Allegro ma non troppo” tempo and has two main sections that alternate: 1) a sixteenth note line in the flute overtop of syncopated eighth note accompaniment figures and 2) a homorhythmic section comprised of a two-measure motif made up of eighth, sixteenth, and a dotted eighth notes. As the first section returns the accompaniment undergoes slight variations. The third movement “Breakfast on the grass under a canopy of trees” is in an “Andante” tempo and has a ternary form fully written out. The A section consists of a melody in thirds in the oboe and bassoon combined with an accompaniment line in the clarinet and horn. The B section marked “Trio” is a contrapuntal texture between the flute, oboe, and clarinet. The following movement “The playful games of children around a hazel bush” is in an “Allegretto” tempo consists of a melody and an accompaniment line that passes around the ensemble in different groupings that eventually results in the ensemble playing all together. The fifth movement “A conversation of shepherds’ pipes” is marked “Rubato” consisting of short virtuosic fragments passing between the flute, oboe and clarinet overtop of long tones. The bassoon and horn are tacet this movement. The subsequent movement “Meeting with an old barrel organist” is in an “Andantino” tempo that opens with an arpeggiated eighth note ostinato motif in the horn. The oboe enters with a melody and the flute, clarinet, and bassoon play chords. The final movement “Dances at sunset and walking by the lake” is very similar to the first movement. It has the same A section, but has a new B section in a moderato tempo. It features chords in the oboe, horn and bassoon underneath a melody in the flute and clarinet.

description: This is a one movement work that explores all of the timbral possibilities that the flute can achieve through various manipulation of tone and extended techniques. The title is a structural element of the work due to the whole piece being built around sounds associated with the name with the performer trying to depict the title throughout the piece. Musically, the work is centered around the pitch “E” and only utilizes variations of tone colors and contrast in sound to achieve musical contrast throughout depicting nature. It begins with using only air noises to create a mysterious character. It slowly intensifies as the inhaling and exhaling gets closer together while undergoing dynamic swells like a storm brewing. Eventually vibrato is incorporated into this technique to change the color of the sound. This then develops into whistle tones to create a bird-like effect. Next, the use of actual tone and overblowing is added into the texture to create a switch between a settled and unsettled atmosphere. Eventually, key clicks create a raindrop-like effect. Finally, double-tonguing and glissandos are introduced to widen the musical picture to combine all of the nature-like effects together to create a unified musical image.

description: The inspiration of the title “Pagoda,” which are multi-tiered towers with an upward-curving roof that served as religious buildings to house relics and honor important spiritual concepts such as the five levels in Japan representing the elements of earth, water, fire, wind, and air. Musically, the work takes inspiration from traditional Japanese flute playing traditions. The work can musically be divided into five sections to represent the different elements. The opening encapsulates the air through the use of air effects of the flute and the sound of the performer’s breath giving life to the beginning of the work. Musically, it uses short and frenetic motifs that elongate as it evolves into a wind section, where rustling wind noises begin in the electronic track. As it progresses the material becomes more lyrical and calm while the electronics take over with a more mystical character transforming into a section to depict the water and then fire elements. The work continues to switch between the different sizes of flute bringing back different motifs and textures creating different earthly and supernatural textures to depict the world around the listener creating a new ecosystem of sounds for the listener to explore.

piece_title: Paraphase on a Ukrainian Folk Song
premiere: 2016 at NMAU by Pavlo Shevchuk (fl), Nina Bahrina (cl), Dmytro Drach (bsn)
description: This is a short one movement work that is based on the Ukrainian folk song “Oy khodyt’ son” (Oh the dream goes by) in a calm character reflecting the lullaby nature of the folk song. The piece develops the theme while reworking material to create a variety of textures throughout. The piece opens with an introduction that utilizes fragments of the melody in each of the parts that interweave together that lead into a rhythmic motif of dotted eighth followed by a sixteenth note. Next, the clarinet takes over the melody while the bassoon echoes a different part of the melody during its longer note values. The two parts weave between each other creating a constant cyclic feel of the melody. Eventually, the flute enters taking over the melodic role overtop of contrapuntal accompaniment parts in the clarinet and bassoon, which become more active as the section develops becoming a string of eighth notes. Next, the music begins to become a more agitated character with the introduction of accents and syncopation into the texture when the bassoon takes over the melody representing the intensifying of the dream. This becomes a fully contrapuntal texture, which climaxes to a fermata chord on B major allowing a reset to the original calm lullaby texture of the opening. This closing section begins with a four-note fragment of the melody in a canon around the ensemble leading to the dotted eighth and sixteenth rhythmic motif that then unwinds to the final chord that is then repeated after two beats of silence. This leads to another two beats of silence before the bassoon playing the tonic alone to conclude the work.

description: This is a seven-movement suite in a neorenaissance style featuring elements typical of this style such as steady beat, balanced phrases, and polyphony. The first movement “Corale” is in a slow tempo featuring four-voice polyphony in an imitative style. The voices weave in and out of one another with a few moments of clarity when the voices are moving in similar rhythmic motion. For example, at rehearsal 2, two of the voices have two quarter notes followed by a tied half note while the other two voices have a dotted half note followed by two eighth notes. The second movement “Ricercare” is imitative and contrapuntal in a medium tempo. Each of the voices enter separately beginning with the second bassoon, followed by the first, then the third, and finally ending with the fourth. The third movement “Contrappunto” is a slow contrapuntal movement when each of the parts enter separately with a slight variation of the melody in order to follow practices of renaissance polyphony. The fourth movement “Caccia” features the voices in canon in a strict melodic imitation at the perfect fifth beginning with the second bassoon starting on Bb, followed by the third on F, the fourth on C, and finally the first on G. The fifth movement “Contrappunto” is reminiscent of the earlier one utilizing motifs from it in a different order and combination of polyphony. The sixth movement “Canzone” is a very slow, legato song-like character. It features a lyrical melody in the first bassoon, an accompaniment ostinato two slurred eighth note motif in the second and third bassoon, and a bass line in the fourth. The final movement “Motetto” is a polyphonic texture. The opening has each of the voices entering separately on an independent line each moving on their own while the other voices have a note of a longer value. Throughout there are brief moments where certain voices will align in homophonic polyphony, for example two measures before rehearsal 2 in second and third bassoon. Eventually, the movement ends with a section of imitative polyphony where triplet sixteenths are echoed throughout the ensemble.

description: This is a six-movement suite that explores the different colors the bassoon can achieve through many lyrical sections contrast with articulated playing. The first movement “Intrada: Stamping Dance” is a virtuosic bassoon cadenza that utilizes two voice part writing that evolve overtime into one voice before going attacca into the second movement “Scherzo I: Kozak Mamai.” The title references Ukrainian folk paintings of the seventeenth to twentieth centuries that portrays a Cossack hero often smoking a pipe while playing the bandura outside, usually with his horse nearby. These paintings have become a national symbol of Ukrainian culture. This movement is a fast scherzo featuring technical sixteenth passages and triplets with large articulated intervals overtop of a mostly accompaniment piano part with occasional moments of response and dialogue. The third movement “Aria: Tears” is a slow and pensive line in the lower range of the bassoon that grows into the tenor register overtop of a syncopated chordal accompaniment in the piano. The next movement “Scherzo II: West Wind” that features a sixteenth note motif in the piano that slowly changes overtime. The bassoon begins with a lyrical melody that later becomes sixteenth notes that join into a dialogue with the piano before returning back to the lyrical quality that dies away leaving the piano motif to finish alone. The fifth movement “Duma: Variations” uses prepared piano to imitate Ukrainian folk instruments. This is combined with a folk inspired melody in the bassoon that undergoes variations throughout the movement. The final movement “Tango” features a tango-like melody in the bassoon with a syncopated accompaniment in the piano that constantly gets interrupted by short virtuosic cadenza-like fragments.

description: “Subtitled "Triana," is a five-movement virtuoso work for flutes (C flute, piccolo and alto-flute, one performer) and piano that is finally rooted in the rich flamenco tradition of the Iberian Peninsula. At the same time, it is not a traditional work that attempts to mimic the flamenco style, but rather uses the internal structures of the alegrias,farrucas, siguiriyas, cante hondas, sabicas and other flamenco f01ms as melodic, harmonic and rhythmic progressions that weave in and out throughout the movements of the piece freely. The flutist is an active physical presence not in only purely musical matters, but in certain gestures that closely resemble a dancer. The work's other characteristic is that it will exist in being able to have other elements added to it ad libitum: (a) percussion (performing Iberian percussion instruments), (b) flamenco dancers, (c) flamenco guitarist. The two movements being performed tonight are the opening, Cante Hondo, which reflects the style of cafe cantante (tavern performances in urban settings) and Persona III, a musical portrait of the great classical flamenco dancer and choreographer, Luisa Triana.” (Program note from partial premiere written by composer)
