description: This is a four-movement work in a neoclassic form of a partita incorporating traditional structures and dances that incorporates elements of folklorism. He was one of the leading composers in the new folkloric wave that begun in the 1960s. He often combines traditional elements of classical music with Ukrainian folk music, particularly Hutsul folk music and dance. In this style he builds the work around short melismas derived from idiomatic folk rhythms and melody often creating asymmetrical phrases expanded through troping. The first movement “Prelude” is in a moderato tempo has a stately character that is centered around a dotted eighth and sixteenth note motif. The opening is homorhythmic in texture with two beats of this motif leading to a half note. This section alternates with more active sections consisting of technical passages of sixteenth notes often in scalar, arpeggiated or neighbour motion in various textures such as a solo line over long tones or a trading off around the ensemble. The second movement “Dance” is marked in a con moto tempo in ternary form. It consists of a bass line, syncopated accompaniment figures and fragmented melodic ideas that develop into a full line, often in a sequential manner. The B section takes motifs and utilizes them in a trading off texture. The third movement “Elegy” is in an andante tempo consisting of a folk-like melody overtop of whole note chords, and an ostinato accompaniment motif comprised rhythmically of eighth, dotted quarter, eighth note. As the movement progresses the texture becomes more contrapuntal with a counter melody being added into the texture. Eventually, a second folk-like theme is introduced, overtop of quarter note chords with a countermelody added later on. This develops into a march-like section with a repeated triplet note leading to a quarter note ostinato. The movement concludes with a final section that incorporates the themes and motifs from throughout the movement combined together. The “Finale” movement is in a vivo tempo opens with a quirky syncopated bass line inspired by syncopated folk rhythms played solo in the bassoon. An ostinato line of quarter note followed by a dotted eighth and sixteenth note motif in the horn is added. The flute and oboe interrupt this with oscillating whole tone eighth notes, which an energetic solo of eighth and two sixteenth notes in a scalar motion emerges from. A return to the opening section occurs with the horn playing an echo of the bass line while the earlier horn motif is passed around the ensemble. This continues developing with new motifs introduced eventually leading into a tutti statement of the bass line that climaxes to a Db minor with a raised fifth chord. Afterwards the bass line is in the oboe, which gets fragmented while the ensemble plays staccato quarter notes. This develops into a syncopated homorhytmic passage. Next, the bass line returns with each voice adding in one at a time. A final tutti section of the eighth and two sixteenth motif from the clarinet solo earlier is played to conclude the work.

description: This is a five-movement suite exploring a wide range of characters, tone colors and textures, and styles in a virtuosic and lyrical display of the flute’s capabilities. The first movement “Intrada” marked “moderato” that is built around a motif of an eighth followed by two sixteenths in scalar motion leading to a quarter note in various intervals. In between these statements are virtuosic passages of slurred sixteenth and thirty-second notes. This leads to an “Andante (legato)” section of arpeggios that alternate between small closed intervals and disjunct. As it progresses, some sixteenth notes are introduced. The following section “Animato” brings back similar material to the opening leading into a virtuosic display of articulated thirty-second notes leading back to the opening material to conclude the movement. The second movement “Rondo” marked “Allegro” begins with a longer note value with frullato leading to triplet eighth notes. Next an “Allegretto” section presents an energetic dance-like character consisting of sixteenth, eighth, and quarters (with grace notes) in changing mixed metres playing with the changing 2+3 patterns. A return to the opening material in a different tonality occurs. Another “Allegretto” follows this time with just eighth and quarter notes but with the same concept regarding metre. The movement continues in this manner with the original material alternating with “Allegretto" sections with different variations. The third movement “Dialogue” marked “Adagio” opens with eighth notes in dynamic swells leading to a longer note value with a fermata. The texture then becomes a two voice texture with a dialogue that is written using two staves. The following movement “Variation” marked “Vivace” opens with a declamatory statement of an accented dotted quarter note followed by staccato eighth notes leading to a flourish of sixty-forth notes. This is then contrasted with material built around longer note values with frullato leading to triplet eighth notes in a 2 slurred, 1 tongued articulation. A contrasting “Animato” section is built around a rhythmic motif of three eights followed by a quarter followed by an eighth note to create a theme with a lilt and forward momentum. The final movement “Monologue” opens with an “Andante” section that has little fragments leading to a longer note value with a fermata that has pitch bends and glissandos to create a sighing effect. As it develops the fragments become elaborated into full phrases that then become more virtuosic with the introduction of sixteenth notes. Next, a “Tragico” section built similar to the opening occurs but is more virtuosic in the fragments this time. Afterwards, an “Andante dolcissimo” section also has fragments leading to fermatas but this time incorporates harmonics and quarter tones to create a new texture to conclude the work.

description: This is a three-movement work that explores the idea of one pitch benign expanded upon slowly to evolve into a new section. The first movement “Parlando rubato” begins with a flute solo on a repeated note motif on the pitch “D” that slowly expands lower and returns back to the pitch “D”. The clarinet then joins in rhythmic unison a fifth lower that quickly develops into its own independent line. This continues expanding in both parts until they arrive together again, which the horn enters with their own independent line. This process continues leading to the bassoon entering with an independent line and the oboe entering in unison with all of the instruments interacting together now. The second movement “Scherzando” is a quirky rhythmic and dance-like character with the emphasis changing between beat 3 and 1 based on the placement of accents in the parts. The final movement “Lento” opens with long tones in the clarinet, bassoon and horn with a melody in the flute and countermelody in the oboe. This leads to a repeated note motif that is traded around the ensemble overtop of long tones.

The section undergoes a constant shift between accelerando and ritardando to create an ebb and flow effect akin to a stream of water in nature. Next, a return to the opening material in a “dolce, cantabile” character occurs. description: This is a short one-movement work in a neoclassical style. The opening section “Andante grazioso” presents a theme in the flute with a trill ostinato in the oboe, an arpeggio ostinato in the clarinet, and a bass line in the bassoon. The oboe ostinato develops into an eighth note countermelody. This develops into an oboe solo melody combined with a polyphonic texture of countermelodies in the other voices. This leads in a more homorhythmic section to lead to the next “Poco a poco piu agitato” section, which consists of a line of sixteenths with a sixteenth rest at the start of each beat overtop of an arpeggio figure in the bassoon. This continues developing into a flourishing scalar passage of thirty-second notes in the flute and character to lead into a “Largo” section, which is homorhythmic and chorale-like. A return of the opening section occurs with variations such as the melody in the oboe and different ostinatos. A final virtuosic cadenza section occurs featuring first the clarinet, then the oboe, and finally flute overtop of fermata chords by the rest of the ensemble to conclude the work.

description: This is a three-movement work in a neoclassical style utilizing conventional forms and phrase structures combined with more modern harmonic language with moments of dissonance creating neo impressionist aesthetics at times. The first movement “Semplice” begins with a regal homorhythmic theme. As it develops the flute introduces interjections overtop of the longer note values in the ensemble. This leads into a two-measure fragment that gets passed around, which is overtop of chords with the entrances becoming closer together as it progresses becoming a canon-like texture. This morphs into a return of the opening theme. Next, a “Pastorale” section that is half the tempo and consists of a one measure fragment of eighth notes leading to a trill that is in a canon-like texture. Another return to the opening theme occurs but this time in smaller pairs overtop of drone-like chords to conclude the movement. The second movement “Contemplativo” is in ternary form. The A section features a vocal-like melody overtop of accompaniment figures. As it progresses it develops into the B section “Con moto” which consists of a virtuosic sixteenth note passage in the flute overtop of sequential and ostinato patterns of eighth notes and triplets in the other voices. This leads into a rhythmic dissonance of triplet sixteenths in the flute and clarinet competing against duple sixteenths in the oboe and bassoon that completes to an abrupt stop through a caesura before a return to the A section. The final movement “Burlesco” has a lively character with an energetic theme consisting of sixteenths, eighths and syncopation through an accented offbeat. The texture switches between moments of melody over accompaniment chords or figures contrasted with homorhythmic moments. The middle section features a syncopated sixteenth motif that provides more forward momentum and energy to the movement.

description: This is a five-movement work that combines elements of postmodernism and neoimpressionism to explore a wide variety of characters and textures in quintet playing. The first movement “Shlyakh kohannya” (Via d’amore) is in a slower tempo with the direction “Langrilur ma nobile” that opens with a homorhythmic line in a descending motion in the flute, oboe, and clarinet that the horn and bassoon respond with accented long notes. This texture develops in a quasi-cadenza moment in the flute that the oboe joins midway. This leads into a leggiero section that is a descending chain passing throughout the ensemble, which returns to a homorhythmic line in the ensemble for a measure before a fragmented sixteenth note motif passing around the ensemble. The movement ends with a repeated note motif with interjections in between the statements. The next movement “Vse vpered” (Ça ira) is in a lively tempo centered around a disjunct quintuplet motif. Eventually, a liscio melody sings out overtop of this texture that constantly trades off mid phrase between the clarinet, flute, and oboe. The third movement “Hazavzhdy” (Forever) is structured on alternating adagio and allegretto sections. The adagios feature lush homorhythmic chords with accelerando and ritardando beamed sixteenth notes coming in and out of the texture. The allegrettos consist of chains of small fragments that are connected through each instrument of the ensemble to create a larger phrase. Finally, the movement ends with a quirky three note motif and rests in the bassoon that the clarinet plays grace notes into the downbeats. The fourth movement “Sklyane sertse” (Glass heart) is a harpsichord variation consisting of a sequence of eighth notes that gets developed and transformed throughout, which are interrupted by subito flourishes of notes in a quasi-cadenza manner. Eventually, a more melodic line built on a sequence in an articulated and lively character is introduced. This leads to an aleatoric measure in the clarinet and bassoon to end the movement. The final movement “Zapoviyi” (Overtaken will) is a tranquillo character with lyrical contrapuntal lines that use different instrumentation pairings to express different colors in the ensemble.

description: This is a three movement work with contrasting characters showcasing the virtuosic, playful and energetic, and the lyrical sides of the flute. The first movement “Moderato” begins with a technical display of slurred sixteenth notes leading to an eighth note in the flute, while the piano has an oscillating ostinato pattern of eighth and quarter notes. As it develops the ostinato pattern becomes syncopated providing a rhythmical feeling shift to the music. Eventually, a new theme is presented first in the flute followed by the piano consisting of a couple staccato eighth notes leading to a small segment of slurred sixteenth notes. The piano accompaniment then becomes more contrapuntal playing sequential fragments. A return to the original material occurs briefly. The piano then changes to a more contrapuntal accompaniment with some variations in the flute to conclude the movement. The next movement “Adagietto” presents a lyrical melody that is constantly grouped 3+2 for the 5/4 subdivisions of the meter. Rhythmically, the theme marked “Cantando” consists of sixteenth, eighth, quarter and half notes. The movement opens with the flute playing the theme alone. The piano eventually enters with a countermelody in the right hand and a long note value root in the left hand with quarter note arpeggiations above. As it progresses variations to the theme and accompaniment occurs such as syncopation added into the left hand of the piano. The movement closes in the same fashion as it opened with the flute playing the theme alone. The final movement “Vivo” has an energetic quality with a flurry of sixteenth and eighth notes with accented syncopations throughout in a quasi-rondo form. The movement opens with the piano with accompanimental figures setting up the character of the movement. The flute then enters marked “Giocoso” with the theme of passages of sixteenth notes leading to eighth notes, often with an accented syncopation. This is contrasted with sections with a more semplice character presenting a dance-like quality with the theme presenting a dotted eighth followed by a sixteenth motif with a more vocal-like quality with simple accompanimental figures in the piano.

description: This is a one-movement work in a quick and lively tempo that utilizes the technique of double phasing. The opening of the piece features the flute and oboe phasing a cell together that consists of an eighth note motif that alternates between the pitches “G” and “B♭” with rest inserted. Simultaneously, the clarinet and bassoon are phasing another cell that is an eighth note on the pitch “G” followed by a rest. As the section progresses the two instruments in each of the cells become phased apart from one another at one rate, while simultaneously the whole ensemble becomes unphased at another rate. In measure 25, a new cell is started in the clarinet and bassoon based on a motif that includes ascending eighth notes followed by multiple repetitive eighth notes and eighth rests in a row. The clarinet begins this cell alone with the bassoon entering in the eleventh measure. All of this happens while the flute and oboe continue to phase apart in their original cell. In measure 59, the clarinet and bassoon present a lyrical melody that begins in long note values and gradually increases to quarter notes overtop of the flute and oboe until they finally come together. This leads to an unison statement of the flute and oboe cell by the whole ensemble that becomes unphased and eventually comes together for a final tutti statement of the motif leading to the final unison long note “G” to complete the piece.

description: This is a through-composed fantasy based on six songs by French singer Edith Piaf who sang in the cabaret and chanson genres. The six songs referenced are La vie en rose, Milord, Hymne a l’amour, La foule, Padam padam, and Non je ne regrette rien. The piece presents a variety of melodies and motifs from her songs that are developed in a variety of characters. The opening section “Calmo” begins with a chordal piano introduction leading into the violin presenting the first melody, which the bassoon joins with counterpoint during the violinist’s long notes. The next section “Scherzando” presents a staccato sixteenth note motif that develops over time until moving onto the third section “Piu tranquillo” that has a lazy quasi-jazz feel melody in the violin and bassoon overtop of piano accompaniment. Next, the piece goes into a stricter “Poco meno mosso” with a dialogue back and forth between the violin and bassoon over the piano’s waltz-like accompaniment. This is followed by two cadenzas, first in the violin and then the bassoon before returning to a tempo. Eventually, this ritardandos into a “Sostenuto” section that features an ostinato pattern in the piano, arpeggiation in the violin and a lyrical melody in the bassoon. Finally, the piece closes with a “Piu maestoso” that consists of a melody in the violin, counter-melody in the bassoon and arpeggiation accompaniment in the piano.

description: This is a short one movement work in ternary form that highlights the lightness and flexibility the flute has in its articulation. The A section “Allegro vivo” has a dance-like character featuring two main rhythmic motifs: 1) eighth, two sixteenths, and eighth; and 2) an eighth followed by four sixteenth notes. These motifs with sixteenth notes create forward movement towards the proceeding eighth notes or quarter note that follows. The flute mainly plays sequential passages centered around the rhythmic motifs that are in scalar and arpeggiated motion, while the piano plays a syncopated fragmented version of the motif consisting of sixteenth rest, eighth note, and three sixteenths. This interplay creates a constant cyclic feel to the music as it provides a constant string of motifs and sixteenths that dovetail off one another. The B section consists of a motif of repeated articulated triplet sixteenths that trade between the flute and piano measure by measure. This develops into the piano playing chords on each beat underneath the flute until it interrupts with a virtuosic flourish of a G major scale to lead back to a simplified return of the A section composed of just one phrase to conclude the work.

description: Lesia Dychko is known for being one of the leading composers of the New Folklore Wave. This work takes inspiration from folk melody and dance playing around with turning motifs and characters from it into a virtuosic display. The piece opens with an “Andante” section that is comprised of a vocal -like slurred melody with grace notes in the lowest register of the flute. Rhythmically, it is changing meter every measure like a person unevenly singing a folk tune. This develops into an “Agitato” section that is much more active as the rhythm introduces duple and triple sixteenths and an accelerando. This section continues climaxing by showcasing virtuosic flourishes eventually resulting in the final 17-tuplet to an eighth note with a glissando to a fermata high “G♯”. Next, a “Tragico” section is a demanding display of double tonguing through a constant stream of staccato thirty-second notes. Afterwards, a “Vivace” section has a more dance-like quality with a staccato quarter note with a preceding grace note motif throughout that is contrasted by sequential scalar triplet eighth note passages slurred by each beat. As it progresses the triplets become larger intervals and frullato is introduced. Then an “Andante dolce” section brings back the opening melody back now an octave higher. It then switches back and forth between it being played regularly and played using harmonics to create a new texture and color to conclude the work.

description: This is a one-movement work that incorporates elements of folklorism and neoromantic following in the footsteps of nationalist composers of the end of the nineteenth century such as Lysenko. It was originally part of a collection of pieces for various wind instruments and piano. Musically, it utilizes a vocal-like melody in a folk style combined with lush harmonies and accompaniment motifs from the romantic era such as a weaving eighth note line. The work is in ternary form. The A section “Andante poco sostenuto” is a cantabile melody in the bassoon with accompaniment figures in the piano. The B section “Allegretto mosso” presents a second theme first in a lyrical character then repeated in a marcato character. The return of the A section leads to a short Coda where the bassoon holds a long tone while the piano unwinds eighth notes into a final chord.

description: This is a short one-movement work with a playful character exploring different major tonicizations and tonalities throughout. The first section features a dialogue between the ensemble. The horn and bassoon play a staccato eighth and slurred sixteenth note motif while the flute and oboe play a line of sixteenth notes that switches between slurred and staccato overtop of slurred quarter notes in the clarinet. Eventually, the ideas get combined such as the horn and bassoon motif overtop of the clarinet motif. This leads into the next section consisting of a lyrical melody in octaves in the flute and oboe overtop of chords in the rest of the ensemble. Later, the melody gets passed to the horn and bassoon with repeated quarter note chords in the rest of the ensemble. A return to the original texture occurs. This leads into the third section that takes the opening horn and bassoon motif combined with a march-like ostinato of repeated eighth and sixteenths in the upper winds. Eventually, the other opening motifs are reintroduced into the texture with variations such as the slurred quarter note motif now in a chordal texture in parallel motion. The work continues developing this material with the occasional introduction of new triplet eighth note material worked in to conclude the work.

description: This is a one-movement work in an avant-garde style written in an unmetered and improvisatory character. It opens with half and quarter notes with slurred grace notes before each note. This develops into the theme being played without the grace notes as one uninterrupted line. Next, a passage of notes first in an unspecified rhythm that becomes accelerando and ritardando beaming occurs climaxing into a long note with graphic notation for the vibrato. The following section features a contrapuntal texture with two staff writing for the solo bassoon to differentiate the different voices. Eventually, a hymn-like melody interrupts this texture, prompting a second attempt at the contrapuntal section. After this section climaxes a final return to the hymn-like material with multiphonics to imitate and resemble a choir now singing the hymn. Therefore, the sound is not distorted by the lower overtones but more of a focus on the higher overtones of the bassoon.

description: Stronko’s music combines a wide array of influences combining classical and romantic traditions, Eastern modality and sense of meditation, the theory of four-dimensional time by Heidegger, and avant-garde experimentation with timbre and texture. This is a short two-movement work mainly influenced by classical and romantic traditions with a contemporary harmonic language. The first movement “Preludio” is in sonata form and features an arpeggiated sixteenth figure that is in a contrary-motion texture between the two instruments. It creates a constant chain of sixteenths with the occasional sixteenth rest to allow the player a moment to breathe in their repetitive line. There are moments of a dotted eighth and sixteenth motif that interrupts the flow throughout. The two voices eventually come together for a final statement to conclude the movement. The second movement “Fuga” is a double fugue on two themes. The second bassoon begins the movement with a theme that is echoed in the first bassoon a perfect fourth higher, which undergoes typical fugual functions until it arrives at the introduction of a second theme in the second bassoon that occurs while the first bassoon is finishing their first theme statement. The work continues in a fugal texture of the second theme to conclude the work.

description: The title of the work takes inspiration of the mathematical concept of prime numbers, which is a whole number greater than 1 that cannot be exactly divided by any whole number other than itself and 1. This is a one-movement work in a virtuosic manner that takes a theme and progressively gets more virtuosic as it progresses. The opening theme consists of disjunct arpeggiated eighth notes leading to a dotted quarter note in a changing meter that throws off any pattern from being established. The melodic content meanders up and down the registers of the flute. Each section features a different rhythmic element such as sixteenths, dotted sixteenth followed by a thirty-second, and thirty-seconds. This work requires and showcases the contemporary possibilities that the flute is capable of through each progressive statement incorporates a different extended technique to explore a wide array of tonal colors and textures that the flute is able to create. Eventually, the piece ends with a “Tranquillo” section that delivers the most lyrical and vocal-like character to conclude the work.

description: This is a one-movement work that is centered around the idea of taking a fragment in a calmer character in a transparent texture that develops becoming more agitated and thicker texture. The work opens with short slurred virtuosic fragments leading to a longer note value played by the flute, which are responded to by large interval staccato passages that go from duple to triple note groupings in the winds. As the passage develops the parts slowly merge together creating a new and more chaotic texture. Eventually, this section winds down ending with a texture of a repeated note changing rhythmic patterns from duple, sextuplet, and nonuplet in the harp combined with inhaling and exhaling noises in the flute. The next main section “Lento” combines the virtuosic fragments from the opening now in homorhythm creating a calmer character overtop of prepared effects in the harp and piano. As it develops the winds become more contrapuntal and add extended techniques such as glissando to explore a variety of textures and timbres in the ensemble. Next, an A tempo occurs that consists of a constant line of thirty-second notes passed around the ensemble overtop of multiphonic notes creating a thick and busy texture. Eventually, the ensemble switches to the large interval motif from the opening, while the piano continues the thirty-second note texture combining elements from earlier into this continual texture. The final section “Rubato poco rallentando” combines all of the elements and motifs throughout to create one final climax of the parts all intertwining before rhythmically and motifically aligning together cohesively to unwind resulting in the harp and piano playing a final long note that the players wait for the sound to fully disappear to conclude the work.

description: This is a three-movement work in a neoclassical style using typical forms and structures combined with lots of exploration of key areas through tonicizations. The next section presents a lyrical theme in the first clarinet that becomes more contrapuntal in the accompaniment as it develops. This gets transformed into an eighth, quarter, two eighth note motif that continues to pass around. This leads into an oscillating triplet quarter note ostinato in the second clarinet overtop of whole notes that connects into the opening material. description: This is a three-movement work. The first movement “Run-Away Rhythms” opens with a clear melodic line and unison rhythmic accompaniment figure with lots of syncopations. description: A common aesthetic in Verykivsky’s music is his varying of folk song material over ostinato melodic patterns. This is a four-movement work in a neoclassical style using common structures, forms, and harmonic language. The first movement “Theme with Variations” is in a moderato tempo with five variations and a coda. The theme is presented in harmony in the oboe and clarinet overtop of a bass line in the bassoon. The first variation presents the theme identical in the flute overtop of a scalar passage mostly consisting of eighth notes in the oboe and clarinet. The second variation makes the theme in the oboe more active inserting faster note values in a scalar motion into the theme overtop of a countermelody in the clarinet and a bass line in the bassoon. The next variation is marked “Piu mosso” adds triplet sixteenth notes in the theme in the oboe, with offbeat eighth notes in the clarinet and flute, and a bass line that begins arpeggiated then becomes scalar in the bassoon. The following variation turns the theme into repeated sixteenth notes in the flute, in which the oboe and clarinet participate in this texture overtop of a bass line in the bassoon. The final variation brings back the theme in its original form played in octaves in the flute and oboe overtop of a countermelody in the clarinet and a bass line in the bassoon. The second movement “Scherzo” is in an allegro tempo in ternary form. The A section presents an energetic theme consisting of staccato eighth and slurred sixteenth notes combined with an eighth note followed by an accented, syncopated quarter note. It is often played in harmony at the same time in the flute, oboe, and clarinet overtop of a bass line in the bassoon. As the section progresses the oboe and clarinet switch to accompaniment figures. The B section marked “Poco meno mosso” changes keys and presents an espressivo and cantabile melody in the clarinet overtop of offbeat accompaniment motifs in the flute and oboe combined with a bass line in the bassoon. The following movement “Song” is in a larghetto tempo in ternary form, which opens with a folk-like melody in the bassoon solo. The other voices play accompaniment figures when they enter. The melody gets passed around the ensemble with a countermelody introduced. The B section changes meter to 6/8 presenting a new theme first in the oboe that has a lilting feel from the quarter followed by an eighth note rhythmic motif used. This section is more active with a staccato sixteenth note bass line in arpeggiated and scalar motion in the bassoon. The final movement “Rondo” is in an allegro tempo in Rondo form. The A sections are in a very similar style and texture to the opening of the second movement, which is then contrasted with various lyrical sections written in a texture of melody, countermelody, and bass line.

description: Avidom’s music often can be characterized as a synthesis of stylistic elements of Jewish music and folklore, especially dance rhythms and East Asian music. This is a four-movement work combining these elements in a neoclassical style. The first movement “Allegro non troppo” is in ternary form that combines different energetic contrapuntal lines together in a march-like character that lead to brief passages of homorhythm for a couple measures. It features a rhythmic motif of dotted sixteenth rest (or tied) followed by thirty-second, dotted sixteenth and thirty-second. The B section “Meno mosso” occurs with the same motifs and similar material. The next movement “Allegro capriccioso” is also in ternary form and begins with a low drone on the pitch “D” in the horn with a dance-like theme in canon starting with the flute, then clarinet. The bassoon interrupts with a countermelody that becomes fragmented in the upper winds prompting a homorhythmic passage. The B section “Meno mosso” consists of a bass line in the bassoon and a syncopated eighth and sixteenth note accompaniment ostinato, and a scherzando theme in the oboe built around a dotted eighth and sixteenth rhythmic motif, large intervals, and brief flourishes of sixteenths or triplets. The return of the A section immediately combines the theme, drone and countermelody. It develops in a similar manner to earlier. The third movement “Andante sostenuto” features a legato and slurred theme built on large intervals and arpeggiations overtop of chordal accompaniment with various moments of counter melody inserted. As it develops the theme becomes more scalar in motion. The “Finale” movement has a ABABA. The A section “Allegro giocoso” features disjunct eighth notes in a two slurred, one tongued articulation. This gets passed around and built up as different instruments join in with various variations being combined in a contrapuntal texture. The B section “Moderato” features a rhythmic syncopated ostinato underneath an arpeggiated theme traversing up and down the range of the instrument in an arpeggiated manner of eighths and sixteenths leading to a longer note value. The return of the A material features different instrumentation of the parts. The return of the B section is greatly reduced. The next return of the A material immediately combines two voices together in contrary motion. This leads to a final homorhythmic scalar passage of eighths that becomes sixteenths from the bottom to the top of the instrument’s ranges resulting in a final Bb major chord missing the fifth of the chord to conclude the work.

This proceeds to the second section which continues the weaving line but now it is an eighth against six texture with a different melody that begins in the flute until the oboe takes over and breaks the weaving texture shifting to a contrapuntal texture briefly. description: This work features components of minimalism throughout to explore a variety of textures within an ensemble. Over time the ensemble is influenced by the piano expanding their line to imitate the piano’s rapid motifs and eventually replacing the piano. This section climaxes and then enters in a piano solo, which then has the ensemble slowly joining in creating a coherent phrase and texture amongst the ensemble. The second movement “Lento” explores the softer and delicate playing possible opening with an expressive and melodic line in the piano. The other instruments eventually participate in an accompaniment role playing soft long tones creating a texture like a haunting echo to the piano line. The final movement “Vivo” is a grotesque scherzo with short fragments of fast notes rotating around the ensemble to create one longer cohesive line. description: This is a three-movement work in similar style of his other works. The first movement “Con moto, rustico” opens with a theme in the flute, which each voice enters gradually in a contrapuntal texture beginning with the clarinet, followed by the oboe, bassoon, and horn. Gradually, the texture merges to become a texture of a solo line with accompaniment figures underneath morphing into a homorhythmic passage to conclude the section. The next section “Larghetto” begins with a slurred cantabile theme in the bassoon with the voices entering gradually in a contrapuntal texture that develops into a short quasi-cadenza moment in the clarinet that instructs the use of vibrato. This leads into fragmentation that becomes an intertwining line of sixteenth notes that weave around in the flute and clarinet to allow the other instruments to return in a contrapuntal texture that creates rhythmic dissonance. This texture unwinds into a measure of silence before a final homorhythmic passage to conclude the movement. The next movement “Andante rigoroso” begins with an espressivo horn solo. Once again the other voices enter gradually in a contrapuntal texture, while the oboe takes over a variation of the theme from the horn. This leads into a homorhythmic passage to a long note with a fortepiano crescending to a dramatic caesura to create suspense for the next section. The bassoon presents a new espressivo theme, which continues to be developed and reworked throughout the section until a return of the horn solo to conclude the movement. The final movement “Rapido preciso” features a leggerio theme consisting of eighth and sixteenth notes overtop of accompaniment figures. This gets developed until a virtuosic quasi-cadenza passage of thirty-second notes occur in the clarinet. A two measure “Sostenuto molto e maestoso” consisting of lyrical melody in the horn overtop of chord in the ensemble bridges into the next section “Lento e soave.” This section has a semplice melody in the flute overtop of a lilting quarter note followed by an eighth note accompaniment figure. As it progresses different textures and variations occur such as trilled eight note accompaniment motif with the melody becoming more flushed out with quicker note values. This leads into a quasi-cadenza section in the flute that utilizes frullato. A return to the opening material returns but reworked differently than the opening. A final “Largo maestoso” section occurs to conclude the movement that begins homorhythm in a chorale style. The final phrase has the melodic content in the flute overtop of a chord in the ensemble leading to a final chord on a fermata whole note.

description: This work consists of nine short movements written in a style that combines elements of serialism and twelve-tone in a highly systemized way regarding pitch, rhythm, and tempo relations with melodic and rhythmic motifs from Ukrainian folk music. All of the movements, except five have just a metronome marking and no descriptive title. The first movement “quarter note equals 132” has two main motifs: 1) quarter note tied to an eighth with a sixteenth note rest followed by a slurred sixteenth to an eighth repeated twice 2) three beats of disjunct triplet eighth notes. The motifs are variated and fragmented throughout such as the first motif is played in reverse. Initially, the motifs are in dialogue that develop into a contrapuntal texture occurring together. The next movement “eighth note equals 132” presents a folk-like theme solo in the bassoon that utilizes a tone row. The horn enters with its own independent line related to the theme while the other woodwinds enter with the theme in a fugal texture in the order of clarinet, oboe, then flute. The following movement “quarter note equals 84” alternates between three different materials: 1) a lyrical theme in a homorhythmic texture, 2) a energetic staccato repeated sixteenth note theme, and 3) a theme that combines elements of both. The fourth movement “eighth note equals 144” is a duet between the flute and horn that features two independent lines that weave in and out of one another mainly consisting of quarter, eighth, and sixteenth notes. The next movement “Largo, quarter equals 40” is chorale-like mostly in a homorhythmic texture. The following movement “quarter equals 126” is a quirky dance-like character with a theme based around perfect fourth interval that alternates between duple and triple feel achieved through 2/4 and 3/8 metre changes. As the movement develops it becomes more contrapuntal with different accompaniment lines added underneath. The seventh movement “dotted quarter equals 72” combines staccato large interval eight note motifs with legato sixteenth in either ostinato or scalar motion together in different textures throughout. The eighth movement “quarter equals 58” takes two lines that are in dialogue with one another that join together after a quasi-cadenza flute moment into a homorhythmic passage to conclude the movement. The final movement “quarter note equals 144” is another quirky and energetic dance-like character that combines weaving around eighth notes with syncopated accompaniment figures in changing metres to destabilize the groove.

description: This is a three-movement work that includes idioms from avant-garde and neoclassical that are in opposition. Overall, Pavensky’s music is characterized by diversity through the inclusion of polystylistic elements using a neoclassical musical language and folk inspiration while experimenting with elements of avant-garde aesthetics, twelve-tone, and sonorism. The first movement “Prologue” is in an allegro ma non troppo tempo opens in a neoclassical style presenting a theme in dialogue between two groups. First the flute and oboe at a mezzoforte dynamic that is echoed by the clarinet, bassoon, and horn at mezzopiano. Eventually, the two groups come together playing in unison which is contrast with short sections of contrapuntal writing. This leads into a “Meno mosso Scherzando” section consisting of a bassoon solo with short fragment interjections from the upper winds. This develops into an avant-garde section in a thick contrapuntal texture with short solos that emerge overtop of this texture. The theme and motifs presented continue developing and slowly increasing in tempo until returning to a reprise of the opening material. The second movement “Minuet” opens with chorale-style quarter notes in the ensemble that are in an atonal harmony which are interrupted with brief moments that are tonal in a Viennese Waltz style. This leads into a polytonality section where each instrument plays an independent line each in a different key signature (flute C major, oboe A major, clarinet Gb major, bassoon G major, and horn F major) that is weaving in and out of one another. Next, a theme is played in cannon around the ensemble that leads into a development of the Viennese Waltz material presented earlier that climaxes in a a chain of chromatic sixteenth notes building in score order to a trilled fermata note. This is immediately contrasted by unconventional air noises. A reprise of the opening section occurs that leads into a flute cadenza to end the movement. The final movement “Epilogue” is in an allegretto con moto tempo opening with a homorhythmic forte passage. This leads into a section where eighth notes trade around the ensemble to create a larger, more cohesive line. This is interrupted by moments of homorhythmic fragments. Next, a clarinet solo is presented overtop of a contrapuntal texture. Eventually, a return to the minuet material from the previous movement occurs to set up an aleatoric section. This is contrasted by a neoclassical section before more second movement material returns. Finally, the neoclassical dominates and a full minuet section with all of the stereotypical and required elements is presented to conclude the piece.

description: This is a four-movement work in a neoromantic style. The first movement “Allegro moderato” is in an unusual form. The A section begins with a four-measure introduction, which material is later used to bridge phrases and sections together. The main material features an eighth note arpeggiated ostinato bass line first played by the bassoon with a playful theme of a slurred triplet sixteenth to a passage of staccato eighth notes beginning on a repeated note before descending in arpeggiated manner first played by the flute. This is followed by a stormy “Piu mosso” section featuring an ascending accented quarter note line that gets passed around and becomes more active and contrapuntal leading into a “Piu tranquillo” section. It features an arpeggiated melody of sixteenths and eighth notes in the flute with accompaniment figures in the rest of the ensemble. Next, a short section of the opening material is used to bridge into a “Appasionato e cantabile” section that is centered around an improvisatory-like descending melody first played by the bassoon in its upper register that gets passed around overtop of accompaniment figures. Finally, a full return to the A section with both themes occurs. This is followed by a return to the “Appasionate e cantabile” material except the theme has some variations and develops into a chorale texture. An ending coda section occurs that takes a fragment of the opening theme played half tempo written as eighth note triplets and quarter notes in a lyrical style as solos that pass around the ensemble to conclude the movement. The second movement “Adagio doloroso” features a folk-like melody overtop of an eighth note accompaniment. It is first played by the oboe that is passed to the bassoon, which then becomes fragmented passing quickly around the ensemble. Then the flute plays the full melody and then clarinet before arriving at a short coda centered around an arpeggio to conclude the movement. The third movement “Sostenuto ma scherzando” opens with a syncopated ostinato in the clarinet and bass line in the bassoon. A theme based on quarter notes and an eighth and two sixteenth and note motif is introduced that is passed around until it develops into a virtuosic passage of staccato sixteenths in the oboe, clarinet, and bassoon. A return to the opening theme occurs with different accompaniment figures in the ensemble and develops differently. This leads into a B section consisting of a lyrical melody overtop of a syncopated sixteenth ostinato. Eventually, the melody becomes fragmented leading into a passage of sixteenth notes for a return to the main theme. A brief “Allegro risoluto” section occurs as a bridge to go attacca into the final movement “Allegro giocoso” which has a fiery dance-like character consisting of an exciting and virtuosic theme based on a sequential motion of a motif using eighths and sixteenth notes with flashy scalar passages to connect phrases in ternary form. Throughout the section the motif is developed and fragmented until arriving at a second theme based on four arpeggiated sixteenth notes leading to two descending eighth notes, which then is developed and interacts with the opening theme. A contrasting B section “Poco meno mosso” section occurs with a folk-like melody in the horn overtop a driving ostinato of repeated eighth notes and other accompaniment figures. Eventually, an accelerando of the ostinato alone occurs to return to the A section.

key: I (G major), II (D major), III (D major)
description: This is a three-movement work in a neoclassical style using typical structure, phrasing, motifs, and idiomatic writing characteristic of wind quintet writing combined with elements of Ukrainian folk song and dance. The first movement has a ternary form. The A section “Allegro” opens with two repeated sixteenth notes leading to a long note in a canon texture in score order beginning with the horn and ending with the flute. This leads into a contrapuntal texture with each of the parts playing a variation of one another built around staccato eighth and sixteenth notes. This develops until a homorhtyhmic texture emerges in a chorale-like texture of quarter and half notes. This texture is then alternated with the contrapuntal texture. This sets up the B section “Meno mosso” that consists of a slurred and lyrical melody in the flute and oboe overtop of accompaniment figures in the rest of the ensemble. The melody then gets passed to the horn and bassoon before developing into a contrapuntal texture that prompts the return of the A material. A short coda “Vivace” section that is the opening material concludes the movement. The next movement “Andante cantabile” starts off with a folk-like vocal melody played by the horn alone. For the second phrase the clarinet enters in canon to the horn, while the bassoon enters with a countermelody. For the following the oboe and flute enter in canon briefly before switching to accompaniment figures. The movement continues developing the material getting more virtuosic until it climaxes. Then the instruments begin to drop out of the texture until the horn is left alone to finish playing the theme with grace note ornamentation now added. The final movement is built around a variety of short sections that are combined together. The first section “Allegro” has a dance-like character of syncopated melody of eighth and sixteenth notes leading to a quarter or dotted quarter note. As it develops the texture becomes more contrapuntal with virtuosic passages of sixteenth notes passing around. The next section “Meno mosso” returns the theme back to the original sparse texture, which develops in a similar fashion. The following “Moderato” is a short four-measure transition with a motif that gets passed around in score order beginning with the flute and ending with the horn. The next section “Andante” consists of a lyrical theme and accompaniment figures. The following “Allegretto” brings back the original theme in a canon-like texture that leads into an “Allegro vivo” presenting the theme in the original texture, which develops in the same fashion as before. This leads to the final “Presto” consisting of articulated sixteenth notes in the flute and oboe over top of accompaniment figures. This becomes the final phrase consisting of homorhythmic eighth notes leading to a rest. After the rest, a final motif on the tonic “D” of two sixteenths, dotted quarter tied to eighth followed by three eighth notes is played to conclude the work.

description: This is a five-movement work exploring many different textures and aesthetics of the avant-garde movement. Bibik was one of the first Ukrainian composers who turned to avant-garde musical language in the 1960s seeking to combine with traditional elements. Overall, his music is characterized by open emotionality, improvisation and spontaneity of development utilizing techniques of continuing variation of troping, massive canon, tone clusters, and simultaneous tempi. This creates a style that is based upon contrasts such as active sections with calmer contemplative sections. The first movement “Larghetto” is in ternary form. It features a vocal-like theme first in the oboe taken over by the bassoon then the horn in one tempo that is overtop of aleatoric weaving eighth note passages in another tempo in the flute and clarinet. A middle section with a duet between the horn with a melody and bassoon with an accompaniment. The return to A section has accompaniment long tones added to the texture. For the next movement “Comodo dolce” the whole ensemble is in the same tempo. It features an eighth note arpeggiated-like motif that is in a canon-like texture that gets developed into a larger line. This is overtop of long notes that turn into either frullato or multiphonics. The third movement “Allegro” is a quirky gigue like character with a theme of eighth and sixteenth note over larger intervals overtop of longer note values that incorporates glissandos and frullato to create unusual textures. There are moments of virtuosic repeated or scalar note passages throughout. Often, key clicks are used to contrast the louder sections to get a wide range of dynamic possibilities. The following movement “Larghetto” consists of two sections once again featuring multiple tempi simultaneously occurring. The first has a melodic line overtop of accompaniment texture, often half notes and occasional moments of echoing the solo line. The second is homorhythmic section in a cluster chord harmony. The final movement “Larghetto” has two main sections. The first section has the same material as the A section in the first movement but different instrumentation. The theme is in the flute with aleatoric material in the clarinet and bassoon and the B theme in the horn. There is new material added in the oboe as interjections. The second section consists of air noises using graphic notation leading to a final tutti multiphonic to conclude the piece.

premiere: 1974 in Minsk, Belarus at the Forum of Young Composers by Grigory Moseyko (fl)

description: This is a short one movement work in an improvisatory and virtuosic manner featuring many scalar flourishes contrasted by calmer lyrical eighth note passages. The work begins with a lyrical and wandering phrase in an Andante con moto tempo consisting of quasi-arpeggiated triplets leading to longer note value. This becomes a sighing two quarter note motif. It immediately becomes virtuosic with the introduction of septuplet and decuplet leading to more disjointed triplet passages. Eventually, this calms into a more lyrical passage mainly comprised of quarter and half notes with some embellished eighth notes in the lower register of the flute. As it progresses it develops into a string of eighth notes that become more disjunct. The work continues in this manner of virtuosic and calmer sections. However, each virtuosic section gets more expanded in length and more technical becoming full sequential phrases to conclude the work.

description: This is a two movement work that explores the full virtuosic capabilities of the flute through many flashy technical runs traversing across the registers of the flute. The first movement “Recitative” marked “Andante rapsodico, affannato” features a lyrical and vocal-like melody in the lowest register of the flute using quarter notes and some small glissandos. As it progresses more rhythmic variety and embellishments are introduced with each progressive statement until it becomes a virtuosic display of sixteenth and thirty-second notes up into the top register of the flute. The movement concludes with a return to the opening material and texture. The second movement “Rondo” is a rhythmic dance that alternates between 4/8 and ⅝ to create an unbalanced feel and swing to the character. It utilizes fun things for the performer to do alongside playing like stomping their foot in a rhythmic pattern and yelling “Ha!”. This movement begins as just eighth notes in the lowest register but becomes more virtuosic and expands the range with each passing statement like in the previous movement. Eventually, the work climaxes into a final flourish to a High D followed by a brief “Adagio, molto rubato” section reminiscent of the first movement before a short and fiery “Presto” takes over. This leads into a final whole note on a Low C with a glissando leading to a sung whole note to conclude the work.

As it progresses it becomes more virtuosic as it develops into full passages of scalar sixteenth and triplet sixteenths traversing the registers of the flute. The piano mainly plays an accompaniment role with bass line figures in the left hand and countermelody in the right hand.

description: This is a three-movement concerto that explores the main concepts of postmodernism through an exploration of timbralism. Denysenko experiments with uncommon and unusual textures of phonic and sonorous qualities of timbre through timbre modality. This concept reveals an artistic metaphor that clarifies the semantics of the work. The first movement “Erro - Blukaty Pomylyatyi’ (Wandering mistakenly)” is an energetic vivo that features an arpeggiated motif that gets developed and reinterpreted in different textures throughout, which leads into a virtuosic bassoon cadenza. Next, a moderato section imitating earlier material progresses back into a vivo. The movement ends with an aleatoric senza misura accompaniment in the orchestra while the bassoon finishes the theme ending on intense fermata multiphonic notes. The next movement “Esvilibrium geminorum - Rivnovaha blyznyukiv (Equilibrium of twins)” is a tranquillo that explores different extended techniques to manipulate timbre. It opens with a rhythmic accompaniment in the percussion while the bassoon plays long tones while singing and playing. Later glissandos are introduced into the bassoon line to expand the coloristic options, while the accompaniment gets thicker and busier. This climaxes into a senza misura section structure by second timings consisting of two technical aleatoric passages in the bassoon leading to a low E long note with frullato to conclude the piece. The final movement “Salve Rex - Tryvit tsaryu (Long live the King) is an allegretto that explores unspecified pitch beaming in the bassoon part to get a wide variety of articulations to expand the timbral possibilities. This is combined with short fragments that develop and connect as the movement progresses. This leads into another senza misura section in the orchestral accompaniment, while the bassoon plays long tones to conclude the piece

description: This is a four-movement work in an avant-garde style that explores a variety of textures that a wind quintet can achieve through unconventional notation and extended techniques using graphic notation. The first movement “Lento, legato '' consists of a chain of changing notes with no specified rhythm that each instrument plays one note of the phrase. This note is either straight tone or with a semitone glissando creating a variety of timbral colors as the pitches, registers, and dynamics change throughout the ensemble. The next movement “Agitato molto” utilizes similar graphic notation but introduces three motifs: 1) a chromatic upper neighbour motion, 2) descending chromatic scalar motion, and 3) a minor third either ascending or descending. As the movement progresses these motifs expand into larger phrases of flourishing notes that weave in and out of each other. As this texture develops trills begin to emerge from the texture create more variety in the timbral colors within the ensemble. Eventually, the trills dominate the texture where each part plays them tutti. However, they each change notes at a different rate weaving in and out of dissonance. Eventually, this melts into a frullato section that becomes key and valve clicks, which leads attacca into the third movement “Determinato.” After a horn glissando, a homorhythmic section on the pitch “C” in different octaves occurs in the flute, oboe, clarinet, and bassoon. A tremolo motif is introduced that contrasts the homorhythmic texture. The horn plays a short solo in a scalar motion overtop of before joining into the texture. The final movement “Risonanza” continues the tremolo texture combined with an arpeggiated melody in the bassoon and horn which they also sing a low F drone while doing so. Initially, the bassoon plays the motifs first while the horn echoes and eventually they play the motifs together at the same time. A variation of this movement is also given without the extended technique of singing and playing.

premiere: Winter 2010 at KhNUA on composer’s composition exam by Vasyl Ivanov (fl), Vladyslav Shevchenko (ob), Ihor Vasyuk (cl), Oleksandr Pastukhov (bsn)
description: This is a one-movement work in a ternary form that uses elements of structure, form, and motifs of neoclassicism combined with a modern approach to harmony and folk-like melodies. The opening section “Andante mesto” begins with solo bassoon playing an espressivo melody based on a diminished fifth or augmented fourth interval in the lowest register, which one at a time the other instruments join. The clarinet enters with a variation of it followed by the oboe and then flute which introduces a different melody based around the minor sixth interval which creates an ominous character. The section continues developing these two themes with slight changes to texture such as an introduction of a syncopated quarter note ostinato, a descending bass line, and long note trills. The next section “Allegro molto e inquieto” has a quirky waltz-like character with a melody in the flute, a bass line in the clarinet that starts on beat two, and accompaniment figures in the oboe and bassoon. Eventually, the accompaniment becomes homorhythmic quarter notes. This develops into a second more lyrical theme that gets passed around in different pairings overtop of the bass line motif. This leads into an aggressive chorale-like section utilizing accents and dissonance to unsettle it. Then, a fragment of four chromatic quarter notes from the first theme of the waltz is passed around the ensemble to set up the unwinding of material to conclude the B section. The return to the A section features variations such as the bassoon’s melody becoming fragmented and rhythmically augmented and the chromatic fragment from the B section is interwoven into the texture.

description: This is a four-movement work that is inspired by Jewish folk music and aesthetics from the culture. This piece is rooted in the traditional music of the Ashkenazic Jewish communities. The Hebrew title has a religious significance as zichronot, meaning “memories”  is a theme from Rosh Hashanah and “often carries the sense of activating memories to influence the present, such as asking God to remember past righteousness on behalf of the present generation.” (Barth, Jewish Theological Seminary, 2013). Each work is a short lyrical poem without words and thus reflecting and bringing back memories and nostalgia of Jewish culture and people. The composer notes that each piece can be played as a stand alone or played as a complete suite. The first movement “Nigun (Tune)” is an “expression of the soul and was cultivated by the Hassidim in the 18th and 19th centuries in the Jewish communities of Eastern Europe.” (foreword). It is typically a lyrical instrumental melody and is a special blend between secular and liturgical music. Musically, the movement is marked “Larghetto e mesto” and opens with a lyrical melody that incorporates glissandos and quarter tones to emulate the aesthetics of Klezmer. As it progresses it becomes more rhythmically and harmonically complex. The next movement “Mis’chak (Game)” is based on the idea of "kaleidoscopic effects of the multi-faceted and joyful Klezmorim.” (foreword) Musically, it is marked “con moto” and is a lively display of thirty-second notes and syncopated rhythms, which are interrupted by key clicks, very much like a percussive instrument taking over the spotlight. The movement ends with a senza misura quasi-candenza passage before one final return of the opening motif and key clicks. The third movement “Rikud (Dance)” is another nigun but this type of the dance variety with a fiery character from the syncopation and changing accents. The dance has an unpredictable character from the constantly changing meters. Rhythmically, it is built around eighth and sixteenth notes and melodically using step-wise and smaller intervals. The final movement “Shofar” has a “growing rhythmic, harmonic and timbre processes” that are “a succession of spirals and enveloping curves. The spiritual serenity and mystical vibration of the Shofar, which is an announcer of freedom, solemn blessing and salvation.” Musically, it opens with a virtuosic cadenza. Next, a “Vivace” consisting of thirty-second notes that are syncopated through a rest being inserted sporadically. Afterwards, is an “Adagio” section featuring a “calmo misterioso” melody utilizing harmonics, frullato, and slap tonguing to create unusual textures to conclude the work.

description: This is a three-movement programmatic work depicting different picturesque scenes of the Pampa grasslands in Argentina. Zuckert notes that the movements may be performed separately and can stand alone. In the work Zuckert utilizes aspects from vidalita, which are sad Argentinian love songs. The first movement “In the Pampa: Evening Dusk” is in a lento e triste tempo depicting as the light vanishes over the prairies in the evening. Musically, it features a melody in homorhythm in the oboe and clarinet overtop of a bassoon part that alternates between bass line and countermelody role. This develops into a texture that features sixteenth notes that pass around the ensemble in a quasi-rubato character. The following movement “The Pampa: Nocturnal Evocation” depicts the darkness embracing the Pampa and the mysterious lights that are appearing while the music of guitar is heard in the distance to break the silence. Musically, it is im a Da Capo form contrasting between lyrical lento measures consisting of a clear melody and accompaniment figures that are interrupted by a presto for one measure at a time consisting of large interval staccato sixteenth notes. This leads into a “Pochito mosso ad agitato” section that has a theme based on a quintuplet sixteenth followed by accented eighth notes in a canon-like texture. The work continues developing these contrasting characters in various textures such as a homorhythmic statement. Eventually, they are combined together by introducing some of the agitato motifs into the opening lento material. The final movement “Gaucho Caprice” depicts the cowboy’s boot heels hitting the dry soil and the silver of the buckles spinning and sparkling in the sun. Musically, the A section allegro giocoso features a texture of a theme overtop of accompaniment figures often through a staccato eighth note line in the flute overtop of a dotted quarter note bass line in the bassoon. Variations occur such as trading the eighth note line every measure between the flute and the clarinet. This is briefly abruptly interrupted by a four measure “Adagio” section.

premiere: 2004 at “Kyiv Music Festival” by Roman Vovk (bcl), Oleg Zaremsky (tsax), ? (cl/bsn)
description: This is a three-movement work based after Homer’s Odyssey. The first movement “Andante con moto” begins with longer note values in a staggered entrance texture that leads into a quasi-improvisando passage in the bassoon consisting of fragmented sixteenth notes motifs in a descending motion with rests. Oscillating slurred sixteenth notes are introduced with motifs similar to the opening being incorporated. This develops with the introduction of eight note motifs to create a contrapuntal texture with constant sixteenth notes occurring. As it progresses the sixteenths become more disjunct through larger intervals and staccato articulation. Eventually, a “Meno mosso” section occurs with material similar to the opening in a more transparent texture consisting of a melodic line and longer note values underneath. The following movement “Allegro moderato” is homorhythmic in texture featuring offbeat accents and syncopated rhythms mainly consisting of eighth, quarter, and half notes with various tied combinations that create an energetic character. The final movement “Moderato tranquillo” begins with a bass clarinet cadenza in an improvisatory character through small fragments separated by rests. This leads into an “Allegro” that has an dance-like gigue character through a quarter note followed by an eighth or reversed motif that gets unbalanced due to material being interrupted and restarted. It is in a contrapuntal texture beginning with the bass clarinet and the tenor sax with the the clarinet added later, followed by the bassoon. Eventually, it develops into longer lines of eighth notes that pass around the ensemble. A final “Meno mosso” section reminiscent of earlier in the work with some motifs from this movement introduced but in a different character to conclude the work.

description: The work is structured on two main concepts: 1) Rhapsody - virtuosic and improvisatory moments and 2) dialogue - interaction and a sense of communication between the two instruments. The work opens with a double tongued motif leading to a fermata, which is followed by a sixteenth pickup into a whole note that begins as a trill then climaxes into frullato and dies away on a trill. The piano enters during the climax of each whole note. During the third statement the motif expands into a full phrase, while the piano plays an aleatoric motif. Next, a string of articulated sixteenth notes with a molto accelerando occurs in the flute overtop of chords. As it progresses the piano switches roles joining in on the sixteenths. This becomes a contrapuntal texture with the two instruments trading playing sixteenths and eighth notes back and forth. Eventually, the original motif returns but in a contrapuntal texture with the piano echoing the flute. The next section has a more dance-like quality as the flute plays groups of sixteenths that alternate between being grouped 2 then 3. The three grouping is scalar motion, while the two grouping is a large interval. The piano plays accented and syncopated shots underneath. This develops into an aleatoric passage of sixteenth notes simultaneously occurring in the two instruments. The next main section consists of a more lyrical and slurred melody in the flute leading to fermatas overtop of chords in the piano. Eventually, the double tonguing sneaks back into the theme. This prompts the final section that is based around strings of double tongued notes being alternated with aleatoric sections in the flute, while the piano takes over the melodic role. Finally, a dialogue between the two instruments of extended techniques occurs to conclude the work.
It is nine pieces.

This is a short one-movement work utilizing elements of ricercare. It begins with the flute playing a lyrical, espressivo with accompaniment figures for two measures in the clarinet. Then, the clarinet begins the theme creating the start of the canon. This is followed by the bassoon entrance on the theme two measures later. It continues in a canon-like texture for the rest of the work with cadential moments that allow for a restart of the material.

description: This is a short one movement work that features a lyrical and slurred melody in the oboe. The melody consists of an eighth descending to two sixteenths in step-wise motion leading to two eighth notes in a third interval. This leads to a series of quarter notes. This is overtop of a legato accompaniment consisting of tenuto quarter notes and slurred eighth notes often outlining a bassline in arpeggiated motion often with large intervals in the bassoon. Often, syncopation through eighth note rests is added into the bassoon line. Throughout the rhythmic motif is utilized in the bassline but in an arpeggiated motion to echoe the oboe during their quarter notes. Overall, this piece has a cantabile character through the fluid motion and interweaving of the two voices.
Andrieva’s music often utilizes elements of folklorism.

The work is built of genre combination of romance and medieval music characteristics from the hocket while utilizing timbral contrasts. It expands the coloristic capabilities of the bassoon through different elements of genre.

key: D major, G minor, C major
description: This is a one-movement work that utilizes long melodic lines and lush harmonics from romanticism with a virtuosic cadenza. It opens with an “Allegro” section that has a repeated triplet eighth note accompaniment in the orchestra while the bassoon presents a dolce melody. This continues to develop until a small bassoon cadenza that consists of eighth notes leading to a high B and then descends to a low D. The next section begins with fragmented staccato eighth notes that become a full melody in a similar character to the opening. Next, a large and virtuosic bassoon cadenza occurs featuring large intervals and a sequence of arpeggiated sextuplets. The cadenza concludes with a trill on a long tone leading to the opening section returning. However, this time it flirts with tonality going between C major and C minor before returning to the original D major to conclude the work.

premiere: not performed yet
description: This is a short one-movement work that shifts between a lyrical and sentimental character with a humoresque character. The opening section consists of arpeggiated sixteenth notes that lead to a long note. This is then contrasted with sequential staccato triplet eigth notes, which are interrupted by slurred and lyrical eigth notes leading to a long note. The opening material then returns. This is then contrasted with another humoresque section with new material based on two slurred descending eighth notes, sixteenth rest, staccato sixteenth in stepwise motion to a tenuto eighth note, sixteenth rest, followed by a final sixteenth note to start the motif again. It develops into a continual line of ascending arpeggiated sixteenth notes. It is then interrupted by descending triplet eighth note passage from earlier to set up another sequential passage of sixteenth notes. Afterwards, the opening material returns in a different tonal area. Some slight variations occur such as a trill on the long note for the third statement to increase intensity. One final time this is interrupted by a triplet passage that leads to one final trill and concluding motif to end the work.

premiere: December 10th, 2024 in Toronto, Canada by dedicatee
description: This is a short one-movement work in a neoclassical style in a Rondo form of ABACA. The opening A section is a lively section marked quarter note equals 120 beginning in the lower register transversing to the tenor register and back down. It is comprised of syncopated motifs built around staccato eighth note and longer quarter notes with no articulation marking. This leads into short moments of four sixteenth notes. The B section is an Andante in a lyrical character that utilizes triplet eighth notes that weave in a quasi-arpeggiated motion. As it progresses grace notes are introduced to set up an accelerando that returns to A material. However, it is not a direct repetition of the A material but instead utilizing the rhythmic motifs with different harmonic implications. The C section is marked quarter note equals 70 also has a lyrical quality but features an eighth note followed by two sixteenth note motifs. The triplets in this section are now in scalar motion instead. It also utilizes the introduction of grace notes as the theme develops. This leads to the rhythmic motif from the A section that accelerando into the final A section. This time there are slight variations such as the eighth note motif becoming two sixteenth notes and the group of four sixteenth notes now being expanded to either six or eighth notes to elongate the phrase.

premiere: 1987 at LNMA by Andriy Hurnyak (bsn), Lyudmyla Duma (pno)
description: This is a one-movement work in an allegretto con moto tempo that utilizes classical forms such as rondo and a theme with various episodes in the form of ABACAD. It opens with a two-measure motif that consists of staccato eighth notes with slurred grace notes before the second and third beats in the lowest register of the bassoon. Then, in the third measure the piano enters with a counter melody that leads to development of the motif into a full phrase with an increase in range and rhythmically adding quarter and sixteenth notes. The texture of the piano switches to accompaniment providing chordal support with short interjections in the right hand. Next, a contrasting B section in the same tempo occurs where two different time signatures occur simultaneously, 3/4 in the bassoon and 6/8 in the piano. This section is a playful melody in the bassoon overtop of a chordal piano accompaniment that sounds syncopated due to the conflict of time signatures creating moments of rhythmic dissonance that resolve. Then a return to the A section occurs but develops differently to climax into a virtuosic quality with constant scalar sixteenths in unison in the bassoon and piano. Next, another contrasting C section occurs in an Andante con anima tempo, which has a legato, more vocal-like melody that occurs in a cannon starting with the bassoon followed by the right-hand, and then left-hand of the piano. Another return to the A material occurs. This is followed by another contrasting D section in an allegro tempo. This is a virtuosic section that showcases the bassoon’s technical capabilities through a string of sequencing sixteenth notes overtop of an accompaniment piano part that occasionally interjects with sixteenths. Finally, one last statement of the A material occurs to conclude the piece.

premiere: 2012 in Kyiv at the Small Hall at NMAU by Myroslava Sirenko (fl), Anna Tomchuk (pno)
description: This is a short one movement-work structured into two main sections in a rondo form. The A section features a cheeky theme comprised of staccato eighth notes and sixteenth or grace notes leading into them, which is first presented in a piano introduction. The flute then enters with the theme which develops into passages of sixteenth notes in a sequential manner. The piano often has syncopated accompaniment motifs to give a dance-like character and energy. The B theme “Allegro ma non troppo” is built on repeated staccato sixteenth notes. The contrasting B section “Andante” marked poco rubato has a quasi-improvisatory character consisting of quintuplets leading to a dotted eighth note that are in dialogue with chords in the piano during the flute’s rests. This leads into a virtuosic flute cadenza that is technical display across the registers of the flute. The initial return to the opening A material is now very disjunct with each note in the theme being displaced octaves apart. Eventually, a “meno mosso” in a lyrical character of slurred eighth notes in the flute interrupts this before a more true return to the material to conclude the work.

description: This is a short one movement work that takes inspiration from Ukrainian folk song and dance that has an energetic character. The work is structured on a main motif and contrasting sections. The work is marked “Vivo” and begins with the flute (recorder) alone playing a syncopated rhythmic motif consisting of tied eighth to a sixteenth, followed by an eighth, another tied eighth to a sixteenth, then three slurred eighth notes. The guitar then enters in homorhythm with the flute playing chords. Then, a contrasting section with a motif of two eighths and to sixteenths with the second one tied to a half note. After this brief introduction of the second motif a return to the original motif occurs with a different guitar accompaniment playing an ostinato pattern of chords underneath. Then, another contrasting section with a more vocal-like melody in the flute with small fragments responding underneath in the guitar that overtime overlaps and becomes more contrapuntal as it develops. The work continues in this manner with various contrasting sections of more vocal-like material or various sixteenth passages often in sequential or scalar motion.

description: This is a one-movement work that utilizes a few motifs that explore a variety of key centers in a neoclassical style. The title Rozdum is a Ukrainian word meaning meditation. The writing is contrapuntal, often featuring a melodic line consisting of eighth note, quarter notes, and dotted quarters combined with accompaniment figures that are either chordal through quarter and half notes or arpeggiated eighth notes, and counter melody lines of weaving eighth notes. The texture of the piece includes a line of constant eighth notes that often get traded throughout the ensemble.
