description: This is a one-movement work that explores concepts of sonorism and minimalism through the small development of textures and motifs. The piece begins with long notes alternating through the winds with the entrance marked by an accented sixteenth note in the piano that climaxes to a tutti accented sixteenth note. The next section features one measure phrase of technical quintuplet figures throughout the ensemble arriving at a tutti sixteenth note. Then elements of the two previous sections are combined by having a sixteenth note quintuplets and septuplets in the piano with longer notes in the winds in a scalar motion. This develops in the winds overtime with the note values getting shorter and the line becoming more disjunct leading to a climax of a tutti quarter note in the winds. This then winds down by lengthening the note values and becoming more scalar to end the piece.

description: This work is structured around fifteen repeated sections that the performers progress through. The work opens with a cadenza in the first bassoon in a virtuosic manner with large intervals and sudden dynamic shifts from forte to piano. The first two sections feature a texture of drones underneath and an aleatoric motif in the first bassoon and a melodic line with written out ornamentation in the second bassoon. The next two sections combine four different short motifs that interact around the ensemble. The fifth and sixth sections are mainly homorhythmic statements. The fifth is more rhythmic, comprised of thirty second notes leading to an eighth note while the sixth is more lyrical with longer notes in a syncopated manner. The following two sections alternate between homorhythm and brief canonic entrances. The ninth section is a rhythmic dialogue between the voices. The tenth section features drones in the third and fourth bassoon while the second bassoon has a string of sextuplet sixteenth notes with the sixth of each grouped accented and tied to the next beat overtop of an ostinato triplet quarter followed by a eighth on the pitch “C”. The next section takes the sextuplet and disjuncts it and creates rhythmic dissonance by introducing competing oscillating thirty-second notes in the third bassoon. The twelfth section consists of quarter notes that are disjunct and switch between fortissimo and mezzo-piano dynamics in the first and section bassoon, while the other bassoons hlonger note values. The following section combines two rhythmic ostinatos in the third and fourth bassoon, while the first bassoon has a melodic line, and the second bassoon has aleatoric material. This climaxes to an improvised section in the for the second, third, and fourth bassoon overtop of a whole note on the pitch “G” in the first bassoon. The fourteenth section consists of drones in the ensemble with a disjunct line of thirty seconds in the second bassoon. The final section has different rhythmic ostinato patterns that are rhythmically dissonant to one another as there are triplet sixteenths, dotted eighth notes, and quadruple eighth notes in a 6/8-time signature.

This is a short work in ternary form that features both the technical and lyrical capabilities of the bassoon. The A section opens with an eight-measure piano introduction in e minor that introduces the first theme consisting of four slurred sixteenths in an upper and lower neighbour motion followed by four arpeggiated staccato eighth notes. The bassoon then enters playing the theme while the piano provides an accompaniment texture with staccato eighth note chords. This theme continues developing, becoming longer with more eighth notes and sixteenths added in a row in an arpeggiated manner highlighting the harmonies. Next, a seven-measure piano interlude on the first theme, which continues underneath the bassoon’s next entrance of the second theme. The second theme is more lyrical, featuring mostly dotted quarter notes with an occasional measure of an eighth and quarter note. This is contrasted phrase by phrase with material similar to the first theme. This continues to develop until a five-measure interlude in the piano that ritardandos into the B section “Poco piu sostenuto” in C major in a cantabile espressivo character. This section has similar material presented in the short second theme phrases that appeared in the previous section. The piano has an accompaniment texture with dotted quarter note chords in the right hand and an arpeggiated quarter followed by an eighth bass line in the left hand. This is followed by a return to the A section which develops the material slightly differently than in the opening.

description: This is a short one-movement work in expanded ternary form that explores both the fiery technique and delicate cantabile playing capable on the flute. This work follows his characteristic approach of combining folk-like melodic content with complex rhythmic structures and innovative harmonies. The work begins in a “Vivo giocoso” tempo with a seven measure piano introduction broken into four measures of frantic ascending motif and two measure eighth note ostinato pattern to set up the flute’s entrance. The flute has a virtuosic theme built on three triplet sixteenths leading to either two or three eighth notes. The end of each phrase finishes with a flourish of sixteenth notes downwards. In between the phrases are brief moments of interjection from the piano creating a moment of dialogue through its response. The B section “Andante cantabile” features a lush arpeggiated accompaniment exploring different harmonic possibilities while the flute plays a vocal-like melody overtop. As it progresses, this melody becomes more disjunct through syncopation, larger intervals, and rhythmic dissonance of triplet quarter notes and quintuplet eighth notes over the piano’s duple figures. Next, the return to the A material occurs keeping the material very similar to the opening. Finally, a brief coda “Presto” occurs giving the flutist a virtuosic display of staccato eighth notes and slurred sixteenth passages to conclude the work.

This is a short one-movement work in an energetic character. It opens with a repeated note motif consisting of a pattern of eighth and sixteenth notes. This rhythmic motif expands to become a more melodic line. Eventually, 7/8 measures are thrown in to throw off the patterns and rhythmic feel that had been established. This leads into a virtuosic passage of sixteenths in various articulations in a sequential motion that climaxes to the opening motif on the bassoon’s high C. This winds down into a “moderato” section that utilizes material from the alternating 6/8 and 7/8 material. The piece concludes with a tempo primo that includes an arpeggiated sixteenth note passage to a high E followed by a two-measure reprise of the rhythmic motif descending to a low Bb.

description: This is a short one-movement work in ternary form that highlights the technical and articulation capabilities of the bassoon. It opens with an “allegro molto” section with a two measures piano introduction that introduces a two-measure motif based on a dotted eighth, sixteenth, eighth in an upper neighbour motion that comes back throughout. The bassoon enters with a pickup to the third measure with the first theme that is eighth notes in a staccato arpeggiated manner outlining e minor that ends in scalar sixteenths. The piano plays a countermelody in the right hand and chords in the left-hand underneath. This continues developing with slight texture changes in the piano until a “meno mosso” section, where the opening piano motif returns combined with a more lyrical and slurred melody in the lower register of the bassoon. This is interrupted by a short “Poco piu mosso” section that is similar to the opening but introduces articulated sixteenths in the bassoon line. Next, a return to the meno mosso occurs. This develops with the opening piano motif occurring in the bassoon, which leads into an accelerando taking the music back to the original tempo and opening material. This continues with some slight variations until a final and short five measure “Vivo” section to conclude the piece in a fiery and energetic character.

description: This quintet is unfinished as it was written at the end of Shamo’s life and only the first movement was completed when he passed away from cancer. Therefore, this is a short one movement work in a presto tempo. The work opens with a theme in the solo horn that the ensemble interrupts with a virtuosic scalar motif. This leads into a contrapuntal section where each voice enters independently with a variation of the opening horn theme. This develops to become more active with the introduction of sixteenth notes as the texture gets thicker. Eventually, a homorhythmic texture emerges consisting of eighth and quarter notes that develops first into an echo texture then into independent lines. Over time it becomes a constant line of sixteenth notes leading to an eighth note in a canon texture amongst the ensemble. The movement concludes with a passage of accented eighth notes that pass around the ensemble.

description: This is a one-movement work that goes through a variety of characters through the use of changing meters, articulations and themes. It begins in a Vivace tempo with an energetic theme in the oboe that consists of staccato eighth notes that expand downwards with occasional flourishes of sixteenth and thirty second notes. The theme passes around the ensemble with each new entry while the previous voices switch to an accompaniment role with different figures such as a syncopated ostinato. This develops into a repeated eighth note motif underneath a B theme consisting of a slurred arpeggiated quarter note melody leading to a whole note. This develops into eighth notes allowing a return to the theme with different accompaniment figures introduced. As it progresses a return of the B theme occurs. The next section involves a line of weaving sixteenth notes underneath fragmented motifs moving in a sequential manner such as an eighth note tied to a thirty second note followed by another three thirty second notes. This is followed by a section of staccato sixteenth notes in a motion of each first of the beat changing notes followed by three repeated notes with a lyrical theme that is a variation of earlier material presented. This continues developing as motifs from throughout the piece are reworked and recombined until the arrival of a 3/8 section. This features a more gigue like character with a theme centered around a quarter note followed by four eighth notes overtop of sixteenths oscillating minor thirds. Eventually, a return to the opening material with some slight variations occurs to conclude the work.

description: This is a short one-movement work in ternary form. Zubitsky’s writing is characterized by the fusing of styles together, most commonly neoclassical or neoromatic with folkorism. The A section “Allegro giocoso” itself is also in a short ternary form. It has the character of an energetic folk dance utilizing a constant switch between duple and triple note groupings achieved through metre changes between 3/8 and 4/8. The melodic line in the bassoon begins mainly stepwise but develops to become large intervals turning the major seconds into major ninths. This is overtop of a piano part that switches between accompaniment figures and echoes of the bassoon line. There is a virtuosic trading sixteenth middle section between the bassoon and piano. The B section “Andante lirico” has a sostenuto and vocal line inspired by folk melodies in the bassoon overtop of chords and arpeggiations in the piano. The return of the A section features many variations such as the bassoon opening with a new countermelody, which is brought back later when the piano plays the theme.
Patsera’s musical language often utilized extended tonal areas and elements of jazz and atonality.

description: This is a one-movement work that takes a Ukrainian folk song and combines it with elements of neoclassicism such as form and harmonic progressions. The opening section “Allegro vivo” features staccato eighth notes leading to either tenuto or accented quarter notes overtop of an accompaniment piano providing chordal support. The next section, “Poco meno mosso” is a lyrical variation of the theme. Then a return to the opening section with some variations such as sixteenths added into the theme and moments of dialogue from the piano accompaniment. This is followed by an “Andante maestoso” variation that is lyrical with a bass line in the left hand and chords on the second beat in the right hand of the piano. This is interrupted by a four measure “Poco a poco piu mosso” leading to a four measure “Allegro” before returning to the “Andante maestoso” for three measures ending in a fermata with a small cadenza moment of a scale to lead back to the “Allegro.” This is later interrupted by a short “Andante maestoso” again with a small cadenza moment leading back to a final statement of the “Allegro vivo” to conclude the piece.

description: This is a one-movement work in a neoclassical structure that presents a couple main themes presented in different characters while utilizing the freedom of an unmetered bassoon solo. It opens with a piano introduction marked “Sostenuto” that consists of arpeggiated eighth notes which leads into an unmetered bassoon solo. The solo is lyrical in nature featuring eighth notes leading to a longer note value in a slurred articulation. Next, a reduced version of this section occurs again. Next, the two instruments combine their parts together leading into the next main section “Marcato.” It consists of a bassoon line of staccato eighth notes with rests inserted in no particular pattern with interjections in the piano. This develops through sixteenth and other longer note values added creating a longer line in the bassoon and the piano part becoming a texture that is more in dialogue. Eventually, this section winds down into a “meno mosso” bringing back material from earlier that has undergone slight variations.

description: This is a one-movement work composed around the concept of abrupt silences interrupting a variety of characters. The piece opens with a “rubato molto” section with a lyrical type of melody in the lower range of the bassoon that explores the idea of tonality weaving in and out of Bb minor with the use of quarter tones to play with the listener’s expectations. The piece begins to develop getting faster and more intense character as the “poco agitato” sections begin through increase in tempo and blurring the tonality more by straying further from Western scales until the music climaxes at at forte, which is abruptly cut off with a subito four seconds of silence. This brings us to a Tempo primo that rebuilds utilizing previously presented material until another abrupt but longer silence of 7.5 seconds. Afterwards the second half of the piece begins with new material of an energetic, staccato character is presented in a “chioso, leggiero” section that presents a variety of extended techniques possible on the bassoon such as multiphonics and singing & playing. A very similar structure to the first where a section builds and is abruptly interrupted by silence until arriving at the final motif that uses a glissando motif to morendo into the silence.

description: This is a one-movement work in ternary form in a modernist style and aesthetic. The A section “Andante” opens with a fugal texture with a lyrical theme using a twelve-tone row presented first in the clarinet followed by the bassoon and violin. Eventually, a new theme using a different twelve-tone row is presented in the bassoon while the other voices continue in a fugal texture playing the original theme. The other voices over time depart from the main theme into new material in a more contrapuntal texture. This leads into a bassoon solo consisting of a descending slurred and lyrical line followed by tenuto quarter notes with rests in the bottom octave. The B section “Allegro vivace” is in a rondo form with a quirky and energetic character from the staccato and pizzicato eighth notes, repeated articulated sixteenth notes, and virtuosic slurred scalar motion sixteenths. This section is in a contrapuntal texture developing the theme and motifs presented at the beginning of the section. This leads into a bassoon solo introducing a new theme consisting of a scalar sextuplet, large intervals first articulated and then slurred interrupted by a eighth and two sixteenth motif. The clarinet and then violin enter in cannon with this theme with slight variations such as the clarinet playing the parts of theme in a different order. This develops into an ostinato consisting of different slurred large intervals in the clarinet and weaving quarter notes in the bassoon. Once the violin finished their phrase this prompts the clarinet and bassoon to play a fragment of the first three beats of theme in unison overtop of the ostinato in the violin. Eventually, the texture changes with the clarinet continuing the fragment with accompaniment figures in the violin and bassoon leading back to the material from the beginning of the allegro vivo returning. Afterwards the weaving quarter note line takes over combined with a new virtuosic arpeggiated motif in the violin eventually becoming scalar into another return of the opening allegro vivo material. This leads into a “Ritmico” section featuring a vocal-like line in the clarinet, rhythmic ostinato in the violin and a syncopated motif in the bassoon. The final section consists of solo scalar passages interrupted by dissonant tutti chords leading into an ominous bassoon solo reminiscent of earlier linking into the return of the A section.

description: This is a three-movement work written during his involvement with the Kyiv Avant-Garde during the 1960s exploring non-traditional techniques and aesthetics. During this period Zahortsev’s music explores structural and emotional extremes. Structure is explored through the organization pitch, rhythm, dynamics, and timbre according to the principles of total serialism, while emotional often through aleatoric devices being employed to create an transcendental effect allowing for a tension between still and active texture. However, this work is more conservative as it does not feature any extended techniques or aleatoric sections. It explores the concepts of total serialism the entire time. The first movement “Allegro” is an energetic character that is rhythmically driven with alternating metre changes in a variety of textures. One interesting deviation to note is that the 6/8 measures are group in 4+2. It begins in a contrapuntal texture leading to a line of sixteenths passing around the ensemble. Eventually, this becomes a solo ostinato in the bassoon overtop of pizzicato eighths passing around the strings ending in a homorhythmic passage to lead into the next section. The next section features a new repeated note motif that combines with the previous textures such as passing around sixteenth lines. This movement continues developing all of the material and recombining them into different textures. The next movement “Andante” is centered around a theme written using twelve tone. The theme opens solo in the bassoon with short fragments from the rest of the ensemble during its longer note values. As the movement progresses it becomes more active and thicker texture as it progresses, such as a sixteenth note passage in a sequential and weaving manner overtop of syncopated accompaniment. Eventually, a return to the more still character of the opening returns with the theme in the clarinet this time. However, the accompaniment figures change to be different from the opening to conclude the movement. The final movement “Allegro” features a contrapuntal texture of virtuosic lines of technical atonal sixteenth notes and eighth notes in large intervals combined with sections that are rhythmically driven by syncopated figures. A contrasting “Moderato” section occurs in a more dialogue texture with a different motif in each voice responding to one another. This leads into an active section of thirty second and sixteenth notes weaving around in different patterns. Eventually, a return to material similar to the opening occurs. However, it starts with the theme beginning in the tenth measure instead of the beginning of the section overtop of a different accompaniment that is much more syncopated and disjunct. This leads into a silent fermata bar before a return to the from the first measure to conclude the work.

description: The title “Shumka” is a Ukrainian word meaning “whirlwind” which is represented through the spinning sixteenth note motifs that constantly get passed around the ensemble at a fast and virtuosic pace combined with unexpected dissonances. The work is in a ternary form. It opens with the flute presenting the main theme that whirls around the middle register of the instrument in a scalar and sequential manner. This theme then gets fragmented as the other instruments enter in a polyphonic texture playing fragments from the theme. This leads to a long note in the flute overtop of an oscillating passage of minor second sixteenths in the oboe. As the section develops the fragments become longer and more intricate creating full independent lines. Throughout the A section the oscillating minor second motif is used for structural purposes to separate the smaller sections within the A section and has more instruments joining in with each successive reiteration. The B section features longer note values that weave between consonant and dissonant harmonies combined with dynamic hairpins emulating wind or a storm whirling around. The section develops by undergoing rhythmic diminution that allows for shorter note values to be introduced into the texture. This texture morphs the material into the return of the A material. In the return new tonal areas are tonicized throughout before returning to the home area of “G” allowing the work to end with a G major chord.

description: This is a short one-movement work in a lyrical and tranquil character that evokes an image of the beautiful landscapes of Ukraine. Musically, the work features many elements characteristic of a siciliana such as a slow Andantino tempo with a 6/8 lilting rhythmic feel from dotted rhythms in a minor key with a transparent texture between the two instruments. The harp plays an accompanimental line of flowing sixteenths to give a sense of forward motion to the music. The work opens with a lyrical melody built on an eighth note pickup to a dotted eight sixteenth rhythm leading to more eighth notes. As the piece develops embellishments such as triplet sixteenths at the start of the beat in a scalar motion are added into the flute theme. Also, small groups of two thirty-second notes at a time are added in the harp’s flowing sixteenth line as the music becomes more active. A contrasting section then occurs that turns the lyrical line into a more fragmented version of it by turning the rhythms into a sixteenth note followed by rests in both instruments to create a more dance-like character. As it develops, the rests disappear and the phrases turn into longer slurred passages to lead back into the opening material. The flute now incorporates frullato into the melody to provide a new texture to the ensemble and more virtuosic flourishes to conclude the work.

description: This is an one-movement work in ternary form with a melancholic character from the lush harmonies and mournful melody. In the A section marked “Andante molto cantabile” the flute plays a slurred legato melody built that often has intervals of a perfect fourth or fifth that create a sense of longing as the performer stretches out those intervals that is then followed by stepwise and thirds to create a singing quality. The piano has a bass line in the left hand of dotted half notes that grow into a string of sequential eighth notes, while the right hand has arpeggiated eighth notes that often begin on the second eighth subdivision of the 12/8 meter creating a push forward in the musical. The B section marked “con anima” is a contrast in character to more waltz-like. It is in the same name major with more energy from the increase in tempo, an active transformation of the piano’s right hand into a sixteenth note motif and much longer strings of eighth notes in the piano’s left hand. The flute has a similar melody to the previous section but with larger intervals introduced. There is also some rhythmic dissonance with duple eighths introduced throughout the flute and piano’s right hand to create moments of tension and release.

description: Original title is “From Japanese Haiku” [З японських гоку] but the title was changed due to confusion between the similarity of the number 3 with the word «з». This is a six-movement suite based on Japanese haikus using a variety of avant-garde elements to structure the piece to create new and unexpected textures. This work was written during the period of Hrabovsky’s career when he was involved as a member of the Kyiv avant-garde. Joel Spiegelman received a copy of the score to bring back to the United States when he met Hrabovsky on a visit to Kyiv in 1965. The work is structured using free notation without any meter but rather events or short motifs that the players respond to combined with aleatoric moments in order to create a larger form. Harmonically, this work achieves to create its own language through contrasting and combining different elements of atonal and modal pitch sequences throughout. This is also combined with different approaches to timbre through the manipulation of extended techniques and non-pitched noises with irregular moments of clusters and extremely rapid passages emerging from the texture to create a different sonic world for each movement. The first movement “The Butterfly’s Wings” is an alternating phrase by phrase duet between the piccolo and the tenor exploring different timbres with frullato in the piccolo and Flatterzunge in the tenor. The second movement “In the Dead of the Night '' has a motif that jumps back and forth between the xylophone and tenor that develops into one line in the tenor overtop of a double tongued aleatoric texture in the piccolo. The next movement “And fields and Mountains” features a staccato eighth note melody overtop of long tones in the piccolo and muted bassoon that unexpectedly leads into a rapid passage of notes in the piccolo. The fourth movement “On the tooth of the mountain” is the only time in the piece that the entire ensemble is playing and interacting together with weaving aleatoric passages combining to create a thick and active texture. The next movement “How Still is the Garden” features short phrases in the tenor overtop of long tones in the bassoon and xylophone that briefly become active to assist with the phrase through fragmentation. The final movement “Shudder Distant Hills” is a duet between the tenor and bassoon. It opens with a dialogue of a three accented eighth note motif leading to a long note symbolized through unconventional notation of a black line until the next event, which is utilized throughout the entire piece for long tones. However, the exploration occurs through the use of a multiphonic in the bassoon. After the opening section, a legato melody is presented through alternating each note between the tenor and bassoon. This climaxes into the opening motif returning in unison to conclude the work.

description: This is a five-movement suite that utilizes neoclassical elements of structure, form and compositional techniques combined with an avant-garde harmonic language and extended techniques. The main compositional techniques used throughout are ostinato, canon, and a line played by trading notes between instruments. The first movement “Andante ma non troppo” opens with a quarter and half note ostinato on E in the left hand of the piano. The bassoon and flute enter in canon on a four eighth note tied to a long note motif. The right hand of the piano joins in and turns it into six notes in a row. Next, a new motif consisting of a dotted eighth, sixteenth followed by two eighths and a quarter note tied to a long note is presented in a canon. Eventually, a return of the original material occurs with an arpeggiated ostinato in the piano instead. The next movement “Adagio” features a tremolo in the piano, a disjunct half note line in the bassoon and a melody in the flute consisting of staccato sixteenth followed by a rest on each beat. Next, a contrasting allegro section with an eighth note motif occurs in a canon in the winds overtop of an E♭ major arpeggio ostinato in the piano. Halfway through the section the arpeggio becomes polytonal with D major in the right hand and F# major in the left hand. A return to the opening section occurs with slight variations such as the bassoon line is descending now and the flute has quarter notes. This is followed by another allegro section with similar material but in different polytonalities such as C major and D major simultaneously. The next movement has no title or tempo description besides half note equals 100. It consists of either ostinato passages or chords in the piano underneath alternating sections of polyphony and trading notes in the winds consisting of quarter, eighth and sixteenth notes. The movement concludes with a long note that becomes air noises in the winds. The fourth movement “Andante” mainly consists of a cluster chord in the piano which the flute plays a solo overtop of. Eventually, the bassoon enters in dialogue playing a variation of the line. The final movement “Allegro” consists of alternating sections of polyphony often in a trading texture between the winds and homorhythmic overtop of accompaniment figures in the piano. This climaxes into a four measure multiphonic in the winds overtop of sixteenth note ostinato in the piano to conclude the piece.

description: This is a one-movement work that combines elements of folk song, dance and virtuosity together into one dynamic work. The first section is an “Andante” open with solo bassoon presenting a lyrical melody of eighth, quarter and tied half notes. As the orchestra enters with long tone chords the bassoon melody develops to become more active with more eighth notes filling in the long notes. description: This is a suite of ten short movements in a variety of characters each with a descriptive title related to the winter season, fairy tales or folklore. The main title of the piece is in Finnish “Kulkuset” as it was written after he moved to Finland with the English translation of “Sleigh Bells”. The composer wrote this work with the young flutist in mind. Pedagogically, a selection of a couple slow and fast movements would work well for a flutist for one of their first solos. The first movement “Merry-go-round” is in a moderato tempo in binary form in a whimsical character. It opens with a four-measure introduction from the piano presenting the theme. The A section the flute takes over the melody while the piano plays a quarter note accompaniment. The B section keeps the same material but tonicisizes the relative minor with some chromatic embellishment before returning to the theme in the home key. The next movement “A Merry March” is in ternary form using a D.S. al fine with a regal character. The flute plays a theme based on a rhythmic motif of a dotted eighth followed by a sixteenth that leads to quarter notes or a trilled half note, while the piano quarter note chords underneath. The third movement “Polka”is in a vivo tempo with a dance-like character. The flute has an energetic theme of staccato eighth and slurred sixteenth notes overtop of a bass line in the left hand and offbeat chords in the right hand of the piano. The following movement “Minuet” is in an andantino tempo with a calm character. The flute begins alone playing a slurred vocal-like melody in stepwise motion mainly with a few small intervals. As it progresses the melody becomes more chromatic and toncisizes a few key areas. The piano alternates between playing quarter notes underneath and responding with little fragments. The fifth movement “The Old Hedgehog” is in a moderato tempo and is in a quasi-ternary form using a D.S. al fine. The opening section has a serious character with the flute playing an insistent descending theme of quarter and eighth notes leading to a half note. The piano has accompanimental figures of eighth and quarter notes. The middle section “Cantabile” is a lyrical slurred melody of eighth and quarter notes in the flute overtop of half notes in the piano. The next movement “Droplets” is in an “Allegretto” with a cute character. It features a melody of staccato quarter note to emulate rain, which gets contrasted with moments of lyricism in short slurred fragments overtop of mainly staccato quarter notes in the piano. The seventh movement “Romance” marked sostenuto consists of a cantabile slurred melody in the flute that is later contrasted by a sequential figure of descending second motif. The piano plays arpeggiated eighth notes highlighting the harmony underneath. The penultimate movement “Little Red Riding Hood and the Big Bad Wolf” marked moderato has two characters in dialogue representing the story, ominous and playful.The ominous character features the use of dissonance and the playful uses light staccato articulation on eighth and sixteenth notes. Often fragments pass between the two instruments in a dialogue, very much so like two characters interacting. The following movement “Sketch” marked andantino features a weaving and wandering melody built around chromaticism and neighbour tone motion is first presented by the piano alone, which the flute then takes over. This prompts the piano to switch to a chromatic accompaniment line. The movement climaxes into a quasi-cadenza of two measures in the flute featuring an ascending and descending scalar passage. The movement ends by the flute playing the melody alone with the piano ending at the very end to provide a final cadence. The final movement “Sleigh Bells” marked allegro moderato has a joyful character featuring a melody built on staccato eighth and sixteenth notes with syncopations and grace notes thrown in to provide forward momentum and energy. The piano mainly has an accompaniment role playing a bass line in the left hand and syncopated chords in the right hand.

This is a four-movement suite utilizing structures and phrasing from neoclassical with contemporary harmonic language. The first movement “Minuetto” is in a moderato tempo is an unbalanced minuet in 7/8 that switches note groupings each bar throwing off the natural flow expected. For example, the opening measures are 3+2+2 followed by 2+2+3. It is in a contrapuntal texture without a clear theme being repeated. Instead, different short motifs are linked together. The next movement “Intermedio” is in an allegro tempo that features a couple motifs utilized throughout. There are disjointed eighth notes jumping around, accented quarter notes in a scalar and sequential motion, and a dotted quarter note followed by an eighth note in an arpeggiated motion. Texturally, the flute and oboe are homorhythmic the entire movement in contrast to the bassoon. The third movement “Adagio” is contrapuntal presenting a melody in the flute, accompaniment figures in the oboe and a bass line in the bassoon. At the reprise of the theme at the end the oboe takes over for the first half of the phrase before handing it back off to the flute. The final movement “Gigue” is in a vivo tempo and is an energetic dance in ternary form using a Da Capo al Coda. The A section has a theme based on dotted eighth notes overtop of a sequential triplet sixteenth motif involving large intervals. The B section combines the melody and triplet sixteenth motif into one line into three different variations for each voice creating a contrapuntal texture.

description: This is a one movement work that utilizes a mixture of traditional form and phrase structure with post-tonal harmonies and aesthetics. The work is built on the dichotomy of two characters that are in contrast 1) frenetic and energetic versus 2) tranquil and calm. The work opens with an “Allegretto” section that presents a fragment of two sixteenths followed by two eighths notes slurred together that expands into the larger theme. The piano is in an echo texture responding to the flute’s fragments. The theme contains lots of technical flourishes and disjunct writing that requires a level of virtuosity, which produces a frenetic and energetic character. This is then contrasted with a more tranquil character in the “Andante semplice” section, which is set up by a piano interlude marked “Moderato”. This new section features a more vocal-like theme that features step-wise and small intervals in a slurred and legato articulation consisting mainly of eighth and quarter notes in an alternating meter to give it a sense of unease. The piano plays a string of weaving eighth notes underneath. As it develops sixteenth notes are introduced into the texture bridging the gap back to the original frenetic character, which now has the use of frullato in the flute to create even more intensity. Eventually, it is interrupted by another “Tranquil” section with similar qualities. Next, an “Allegro” section returns to the original character but now introduces a new motif of dotted eighth followed by a sixteenth note. This climaxes into an extensive flute cadenza marked “Adagio ad libitum” that traverses from the low to the high register of the flute in a technical display of virtuosity incorporating elements from both sections/characters of the work. Afterwards, a final tranquil section with an quasi-improvisatory character due to the accelerando beaming utilized in the flute line occurs to conclude the work.

description: This is a one movement work that displays the virtuosity of the flute in a dialogue texture with the piano that is immersed in atonal language. It takes inspiration from the twelve-tone work of Silvestrov and Berg. The work opens with a twelve-measure introduction that presents all of the material of the piece that will be worked upon throughout, presented in short fragments going back and forth between the two instruments. It is structured in three main sections. The first section begins with a dialogue of the piano with a fortissimo fragment that is rhythmically dissonant with accented sixteenth notes in the right hand overtop of triplet eighth notes in the left. The flute immediately responds over the piano’s longer note values with frullato syncopated notes. The flute’s next entrance continues the rhythmic dissonance of a quintuplet overtop of a triplet. These elements of rhythmic dissonance, syncopation, and frullato give a sense of intensity for this opening section. As this section develops it becomes more contrapuntal with the two instruments overlapping in their fragments, which become expanded into a larger phrase. To conclude the section a repeated note motif is introduced combined with a ritardando to release the energy in order to set up new material, consisting of short rhythmic motifs leading to a longer note value. The two instruments are in a dialogue texture that creates a web of intricate rhythms passing around. As it develops the rhythmic values become quicker such as quintuplets, sextuplets and septuplets, while the melodic motifs become more disjunct and expanded creating a higher level of virtuosity. This climaxes into a 12-tuplet using accelerando beaming in the flute leading back to the shorter fragmentation from earlier. The work continues in this manner until a quasi-cadenza in the flute that is structured as a fugato in a single voice. It features syncopation fragments that alternate between the high and low register, which become more virtuosic with double tonguing passages. Afterwards, a return to the intricate rhythmic texture returns now with three-stave writing in the piano creating a very dense texture of voices passing around the ensemble. The tone rows are being manipulated with different inversions simultaneously occurring across the ensemble creating a web of pitches creating an echo-like texture. Rhythmically, this section is fighting between the duple and triple groupings as there are tied syncopations of sixteenth and triplets occurring simultaneously allowing a constant dissonance and a syncopation throughout. Eventually, a Tempo Primo occurs bringing back a thinner texture of two voices that is a dialogue of fragments of the tone row between the flute and piano. Motifs from earlier such as the repeated note one is brought back into a new context as this time it has dynamic swells leading into other material. As it develops a third bass voice is introduced in the left hand of the piano creating a more contrapuntal texture. The work continues reworking and bringing in variations of the motifs and materials within new variations of the tone rows to create new sonorities. The work reaches its final climax when the fourth voice is introduced and the piano returns to its three stave writing. Finally, the texture thins and a constant stream of quintuplet and sextuplet sixteenths pass around the ensemble. The work ends with graphic notation in the piano for the final measure as the flute finishes the passage. Essentially, the work is an interesting display of contrapuntal writing using an avant-garde and twelve-tone language.

description: This is a three-movement work structured in a neoclassical fashion with influence and aesthetics borrowed from modernist such as its approaches to atonality, dissonance, and textures. The first two movements of the work are in typical sonata-allegro form consisting of all of the regular elements of two themes, development, and recapitulation. The final movement is structured as a cadenza with an epilogue to conclude the work. The character of the music contrasts between two main characters: 1) restrained and lyrical and 2) agitated and rhythmically driven. The ostinato plays an important role throughout to musically bridge elements together. The harmonic language combines a wide array of influences from diatonic, chromatic, and atonal moments. The bassoon and piano play an equal role throughout the work with critical solo moments that emerge from the texture in the bassoon. The first movement “Pensive” often features flourishing arpeggiation or chordal passages in the piano while the bassoon plays a more vocal-like line. As it develops the bassoon line becomes more active becoming sixteenth duple and triplet notes. Throughout there are changing metres creating a rhythmic instability. The second movement “Agitated” contains a more dialogue-like texture with sixteenth note motifs passing between the bassoon and the right hand of the piano overtop of a sixteenth note oscillating ostinato motif. Often the passing dialogue will begin on a syncopation on the second sixteenth in the bassoon rather than perfectly lining up on the beat to take over. Eventually, the ostinato unwinds to an eighth note motif to allow a change to the more restrained and lyrical character. However, the intervals are displaced by an octave rather than creating a compact and smooth line in the bassoon. The right and left of the piano take on different variations of this bassoon line creating a contrapuntal texture that leads into a bassoon solo still utilizing large intervals. This leads into a section in a more dialogue-like texture through fragmentation that develops into a longer line. It unwinds into material similar to the opening to conclude the movement. The final movement “Slow” begins in a molto rubato style with a lyrical line that becomes more disjunct with larger intervals as it progresses and eventually jumping two octaves between figures. This leads to the final epilogue marked “steady” consisting of quarter note chords in the piano, which grace notes are added to later on. Briefly, some arpeggiation motifs from the first movement return. The bassoon plays a more restrained and lyrical line that begins with triplet eighth notes that unwinds to longer note values creating an introspective character to conclude the work.

description: This is a one movement work with six main sections that feature a high level of virtuosity in extended technical passages and intricate rhythmic interplay between the flute and piano. It also utilizes unconventional notation such as time signatures like 2 over dotted eighth and 3 over dotted eighth and unusual beaming that appears to be some type of free rhythm or accelerando. The work opens with an “Adagio sostenuto” section that has a constantly shifting metre every measure or two. This section is the piano alone playing disjunct and accented figures jumping around the registers. The next section “Allegro” is a string of articulated sixteenth notes that are weaving with the occasional large interval inserted to throw off the pattern. The flute begins alone and then passes it off to the piano to play alone. The flute then re-enters with a drone (with rests inserted) on the pitch “D♭” before playing syncopated fragments that are in dialogue with the piano. The next section “Meno mosso” opens with a syncopated bass line and syncopated theme with flourishes of notes embellishing it. The flute then takes over the theme and expands upon it while the piano changes accompaniment textures and motifs every phrase. Afterwards, an “Allegro” section has a string of triplet sixteenth notes passing around the ensemble with various syncopated figures accompanying it. As it develops the string of sixteenth notes becomes fragmented with rests inserted The penultimate section “Adagio sostenuto” brings back motifs from earlier in a dialogue texture between the instruments with the flute and piano never playing at the same time. The final “Piu mosso” section brings back a constant stream of thirty-second notes passed around the ensemble leading to some final accented chords in the piano alone to conclude the work.

description: This is a one-movement work that explores different textures that can be produced by extended techniques on the flute through frullato, glissando, and harmonics combined with unconventional ways of notation through graphic notation and different note beamings. The work opens with the flute playing long note values with dynamic swells on the pitch “B♭”. After a fermata measure of silence, the flute introduces the first motif of a sixteenth note followed by a dotted eighth note, which is often tied to a longer note value. The piano responds in dialogue with the motif and chords. The theme gets developed while the piano presents new syncopated material during the flute’s rests. Next, the flute’s line becomes more virtuosic with cascading quintuplet and septuplets from the upper to lower register. This section continues developing virtuosic lines that alternate with more lyrical passages with the piano in a dialogue texture. Eventually, extended trills or passages of trills are introduced in the flute line and virtuosically climaxing to 14-tuplet sixteenth notes. The piano part becomes more contrapuntal and disjunct with large intervals jumping between hands and independent writing separate and oftentimes in rhythmic dissonance from the flute, such as quintuplet eighths or 10-tuplets against sixteenths or eighths. Eventually, a flurry of sixteenth notes cascading across the piano transitions to the next section that has chordal writing in the piano with unconventional beamed passages of sixteenth notes in the flute. As it develops the music stabilizes again with the flute returning to regular sixteenth notes. This is followed by a “Meno mosso” section that is featured around a constant stream of sextuplet eighth notes with a bass line underneath and moments of lyrical writing in the flute that becomes fragmented. The introduction of frullato on longer note values is introduced. The music becomes more intensity as the eighth note sextuplets become sixteenth notes with moments in rhythmic unison and moments where the piano switches to rhythmic chords. It then calms down returning to the eighth note subdivision leading into a section of graphic notation. Afterwards, a “Moderato” section presents a simple eighth and sixteenth note motif in the flute, which the piano responds with syncopated chords during the rests, which then overlap. Next, a quasi-cadenza of virtuosic technique occurs in the flute. The piano then sets up a rhythmic groove with chords leading into an aleatoric section in the ensemble. Afterwards, a “Andante cantabile” section presents an ostianto of triplet eighth notes over a drone in the piano occurs. Then virtuosic technical passages occur in the flute while the piano plays intricate rhythmic accompaniments underneath. A final “Maestoso” section bringing back material from earlier to conclude the work in which a direction at the end of the score is written for the final section, which is repeated to gradually reduce the dynamic from forte to niente. The piece can be finished on any note or chord when the niente is achieved.

description: This work pushed the capabilities of the flute to “explore the wide possibilities of the flute using many extended techniques [through 4 techniques]: 1) The slow fluctuation of pitch, achieved either by a change in air or lip pressure 2) A microtonal lip glissando 3) Strike or slap the keys of the instrument and 4) Bisbigliando - rapid alteration between fingerings of the same note.” (Lozben, foreword) This work is a virtuosic display of technique, artistry and control for a flutist to convey contemporary language and techniques into a cohesive phrase that highlights the details and contrasts. The opening section “Lento rubato” is a lyrical, slurred, vocal-like line. As it progresses, extended techniques are slowly introduced into the phrase to create new textures. Next, the rhythm becomes more complex and accelerando beaming is introduced to create moments of higher intensity through a swell inserted into the line. This is followed by the line becoming more disjunct through larger intervals and syncopation created through sixteenth rests. The “Poco tranquillo” section continues in the same manner by systematically introducing more complex extended techniques, rhythms and elements of disjunct to keep intensifying. Eventually, a climax is reached. This is followed by a “come primo” section that unwinds returning to the opening texture to conclude the work.

description: This is a three movement work that combines structures and forms from classical music with some aesthetics and textures of avant-garde music to explore a wide range of expressions possible by the flute. The first movement is built around a dichotomy of changing characters. It begins with an “Andantino” section that opens with a piano introduction that presents the theme consisting of a falling triplet eighth note motif in the right hand that leads to chords in the left hand. This sets up a quasi-improvisatory cadenza in the flute in a virtuosic manner that leads into the theme and an accompanimental role of arpeggiation in the piano underneath in a neo-impressionist harmony and style. As it develops it undergoes variation and fragmentation to lead to an “Allegretto” section that takes fragmentation of the melody and presents it in a more virtuosic manner of sequential sixteenth note passages overtop of intense and heavy chords in the piano. Next, a “Meno mosso” returns to a calmer presentation of the theme in the flute, which becomes virtuosic overtop of chords changing every couple of measures. Then, a “Piu mosso” occurs where the pianist plucks the strings of the piano while the flutist plays fragmentation of the theme material now in triplet sixteenth leading to an eighth note rhythm to create a more mysterious and frantic character before a return to the more lyrical character and virtuosic cadenza. The rest of the movement continues in the same manner contrasting the two lyrical and frantic characters. The second movement “Adagio” opens with a half note bass line in the piano that the flute enters overtop of to play a meandering theme of a quarter note tied to sextuplet sixteenth notes that move around the register of the flute in a sequential manner. This is then contrasted with a mainly step-wise and lyrical theme built around eighth notes leading to a longer note value in the flute overtop of an oscillating ostinato pattern in the right hand of the piano being introduced. The flute part continues to become more virtuosic as it develops until it climaxes into a passage of sweeping thirty-second notes weaving around the high register. The final movement “Allegretto” is built on a constant repetitive sixteenth note motif. The piano introduction introduces it as a fragment which builds into a constant line that never stops for the rest of the movement, usually acting as a motor in the piano part. The flute enters with two repeated sixteenth notes changing around in a sequential manner. Eventually, this is contrasted by a more lyrical theme in the flute while the sixteenth motor continues in the piano. Finally, the flute plays alone taking over the sixteenth repetitive motif to end the work.

description: This is a three-movement work that demonstrates the full technical and espressivo capabilities of the bassoon while introducing the use of extended techniques to explore the timbre and textural qualities available on the instrument. The first movement “Allegro rubato” searches for diagonal thinking by embedding harmonic motifs into a melodic line such as combining sweeping arpeggios intertwined into a lyrical melody. Often at the end of phrases an extended technique is incorporated such as a multiphonic to alter the sound and texture creating more variety and expression. The first section has a quasi-improvised character utilizing shorter fragments. The next section “Allegro” features disjunct larger intervals exploring the range of the bassoon. This is followed by an “Andante” section consisting of sequential sixteenth note arpeggios that develop to become more weaving around. This material undergoes development before arriving at the opening material. The second movement “Theme and Variations” presents a lyrical melody with arpeggiations incorporated in the middle and tenor registers in an “Andantino con moto” tempo, which is followed by four variations before returning to the theme. The first variation mainly has parts of the theme being displaced in different registers such as the first five notes now an octave lower and the next fragment of the phrase an octave higher than originally written. The next variation becomes more active, filling in the theme with quicker note values such as duple eighth, triplet eighth, and sixteenth quintuplets utilizing motions such as passing, neighbour and arpeggiated tones. The third variation features tempo changes switching between “Allegro” and “Meno mosso” that features sequential sixteenth and triplet figures that climaxes into a high C that glissandos downwards. The final variation “Moderato” incorporates extended techniques into the theme with every note being either a multiphonic, harmonic, or pizzicato sound. The final movement “Pathetic monologue” is in an “Adagio appassionato” tempo. It presents a theme reminiscent of the romantic era that becomes gradually more active and virtuosic as it develops becoming thirty-second note quintuplet, sextuplet, and septuplet passages, which leads to one final multiphonic fermata note to conclude the work.

description: This is a three-movement work that combines elements of traditional structure and form with aesthetics and techniques of avant-garde. The first movement “Andantino” presents a lyrical theme in the flute that is built around a three note motif “E-F-D” that meanders around expanding outwards as it develops. The piano plays an independent role providing contrapuntal textures with its own three note motif “F♯-G-D” acting as a variation alongside the flute. The movement progresses through different textures and methods of combining and interacting the motifs. An “Andantino” section presents a secondary theme built around a lower neighbour motion and a minor third interval that is expanded out to be more disjunct, creating a quirky character. Eventually, a return or recapitulation of the main theme in its original state from the opening measures occurs to lead into a short flute cadenza followed by a short postlude to conclude the movement. The second movement “Allegro moderato” has a contrapuntal texture and fully independent lines between the flute and both hands of the piano. The flute has an energetic melody comprised of sixteenth notes leading to a longer note value that begins on the downbeat than becomes syncopated over time. Throughout a 3/4 measure is thrown in to break the rhythmic patterns being established to create a moment of instability. The final movement “Andantino” begins with a piano introduction setting the character and presenting the triplet sixteenth motif used throughout. Once again the texture is very contrapuntal with an independence of parts throughout. Throughout the material undergoes slight variations to display a wide range of characters from tranquil and vocal-like to more energetic and dance-like. The work concludes with a syncopated technical passage climbing to a held high B♭ in the flute while the piano plays rapid thirty-second aleatoric figures in both hands to end with uncertainty and chaos.

description: This is a one-movement work that combines elements of classical form and structure with avant-garde aesthetics, techniques and textures. This is a unique work in the collection as it is the only work specifically written for piccolo and piano by a Ukrainian composer. The Sonata begins with a theme being presented in the piccolo that utilizes repeated notes for emphasis, technical flourishes and pitch bends. The piano responds with staccato chords. This leads into a brief quasi-improvised cadenza moment in the piano before a full statement of the theme in the piccolo with accompaniment figures in the piano, typically eighth note chords underneath the piccolo’s more active moments and then technical flourishes during the piccolo’s longer note values. The material in the piccolo is usually lyrical in nature with technical flourishes and embellishments added as the phrase develops. The next main section marked “Giocoso” has a more dance-like character featuring a lilting line consisting of three eighth notes leading to a group of sixteenth notes in a sequential manner. The piano plays chords on the main beats with the occasional pickup to create forward momentum. As it progresses, the piano becomes a more equal and active voice in the texture creating a dialogue between the two instruments.. Eventually, a new texture takes over consisting of the pianist knocking on the wood of the instrument as interjections in between a fragmented line in the piccolo. As with previous sections, it develops into a full fledged dialogue of independent parts between the two instruments that interweave together. Eventually, this gets interrupted by a more lyrical “Adagio” section in which the piccolo plays a string of slurred eighth notes overtop of chordal accompanimental in the piano. As it develops, it becomes more virtuosic and complex leading back to the opening material to conclude the work.

description: This is a three-movement work that explores both the delicate and technical aspects of the flute through intricate rhythmic and metrical changes constantly throughout. The first movement contrasts back and forth between slower “Lento” or “Lento Doloroso” and faster “Vivo” or “Presto” sections. The work opens with a “Lento” section that begins with a drone on the pitch “E” in the lower registers of the piano, while the flute has a lyrical theme in the lower register. The piano then responds with a sixteenth note motif that sets up and transitions into the first “Vivo” section that is in a dialogue texture with the piano playing sixteenths on the first half of the measure while the flute responds with fragments from the opening theme on the second half of the measure. Eventually, the texture becomes a steady passage of sixteenth notes passing back-and-forth when the flute switches over briefly. Afterwards, a lyrical and slurred line is played in the flute, which the piano takes over the complete line of sixteenth notes in the right hand and a bass line in the left hand. The next section “Meno mosso” has fragments in the flute with chords responding during their rests, which sets up a return to the “Lento” material. The movement continues alternating between sections with each return presenting new variations, textures, and development of the material. Eventually, there is a quasi-cadenza section where the flute plays a string of sixteenth notes overtop of a drone. The bar lines are now dotted bar lines removing the rhythmic pulse from earlier creating a sense of freedom. The following “Lento” uses aleatoric writing of a fragment in the flute while the piano plays a contrapuntal setting of the material. The second movement “Dolente” presents a lyrical theme that is built around a motif of three step-wise eighth notes leading to a large interval jump to a quarter note. This motif gets expanded into a full phrase as it develops. The piano begins by responding with fragments during the flute’s rests and longer note values but becomes more contrapuntal as it progresses. Eventually, the piano takes over the melodic role, while the flute plays a string of sixteenth notes that begins as two repeated notes moving step-wise that gets expanded outwards as it develops. The roles of the two instruments are then switched. The movement continues in a dialogue texture between the two instruments leading to one final statement played alone by the flute with piano joining in on a chord on the final dotted half note to conclude the movement. The final movement “Vivacissimo” switches between two characters in the flute 1) a dance-like theme with a lilting character leading to virtuosic passages of sixteenth notes and 2) lyrical slurred melodies with a more semplice character. The piano mainly plays an accompanimental role. During the dance-like character they have 1) passages of eighth notes alternating between the hands (bass line and chords) or 2) a bass line on the beat followed by three sixteenth notes in the right hand. As it progresses variations occur such as syncopation of the line of eighth note by adding in some sixteenths in the rhythmic ostinato. There are brief moments when the piano joins in rhythmic unison with the flute at climatic moments. During the lyrical sections the piano plays a bass line in the left hand and arpeggiated sixteenth notes in the right hand.

description: This is a one-movement work with four main sections that reappear throughout in various reiterations in an avant-garde style that explores extended techniques possible on the bassoon combined with virtuosic moments. The first main section “Allegretto” consists of a disjointed theme of staccato eighth notes in large intervals in utilizing twelve tone that rhythmically follows the pattern of note, rest, three notes, two rests. The piano first initially enters with long tones but then joins playing the same row in canon to the bassoon line. The next main section “Allegro barbaro” consists of a sixteenth motif that is in dialogue between the bassoon and piano with accented fragmented interjections throughout. Eventually, this develops in a eighth note with a grace note motif overtop of sixteenths in a scalar motion. The following section “Meno mosso” features a dolce theme that consists of a quarter note that pitch bends a quarter tone flat into an eighth note followed by an arpeggiated group of notes in various groupings such as quintuplet, sextuplet, and nonuplet. The piano in the right hand echoes the theme displaced by a quarter note from the bassoon, while the left-hand plays chords. A reprise of the opening material returns in the piano while the bassoon plays multiphonics. Then, the bassoon joins into the opening theme in cannon to the piano. However, the rhythm becomes more active developing into sixteenths and sixteenth triplets while the piano stays true to the original theme. A short trill section bridges into a return of the meno mosso material but this time in an agitato character. This is followed by a reprise of the Allegro barbaro section before returning again to the meno mosso material in the original texture and character. This leads into a new section of smorzatos in the bassoon overtop of cluster chords in the piano. Finally, one last return to the first part of the opening material returns to conclude the piece.

description: This is Ischenko’s second sonata for flute, which is structured as a one-movement work with a variety of sections that primarily alternate between slow and fast providing a wide range of characters and styles throughout with the incorporation of a few extended techniques to explore different tone colors to showcase a variety of playing capabilities of the flute. The work opens with an “Adagio misterioso” section with a four-measure piano introduction to set a dark and ominous character. The flute then enters with a lyrical slurred theme. The piano is fairly static playing longer note values and fragmented responses to the flute that become more contrapuntal and full phrases. Eventually, the use of glissandos, frullato, and tremolos are introduced to intensify the phrasing. The glissandos are often written at the end of phrases to create a sighing effect. This leads into the first virtuosic display of quintuplet and sextuplet sixteenth notes wandering around the low register of the flute into a frullato passage, while the piano takes over the sixteenths. A return to the calmer texture occurs with the next “Andante” section marked “dolce” consisting of another lyrical theme in the flute overtop of fragments in the piano. Once again the piano texture gets expanded into longer and more contrapuntal writing. Next, a "Pochissimo piu mosso” that is more energetic and rhythmically intricate occurs. It has syncopated eighths in the flute overtop of constant sixteenths in the left hand of the piano and a dotted motif in the right hand that lines up with the flute. This also develops into another virtuosic display of quintuplets and sextuplets. However, this time it extends much longer and into the upper register of the flute. Once again, it leads into a frullato and glissando passage, while the piano takes over the technical line. Next, an aleatoric motif is presented in the flute overtop of the running line of sixteenths. Another “Andante” section occurs bringing back material from earlier but reworking it. This is interrupted by a brief two-measure “Allegro” played alone by the piano. Then an “Andante marciale” section occurs built around a bass line ostianto that changes metrical emphasis creating an unsteady and syncopated feel to the music. The flute enters with a slurred melody that is more disjunct than earlier ones. Next, an “Allegro” occurs comprised of sixteenth notes first in the piano that the flute takes over. A return to the “Andante marciale” occurs afterwards. This is followed by an “Allegro molto” also utilizing a constant stream of sixteenth notes passing around with some trills inserted into the phrase. The work concludes bringin back material from the earlier “Andante” sections with a contrasting “Pochissimo piu mosso” section. The very end of the final “Andante” plays with tone colors by utilizing alternating between ordinary tone, frullato, and glissando in a subdued pianissimo character, which is abruptly interrupted by four fortissimo high C’s to conclude the work.

description: This is a two-movement work that utilizes elements of traditional sonata form combined with modern harmony, rhythm, and textures through extended techniques. The first movement “Andante lirico” opens with a melodic that takes what would be a vocal-like line but inverts smaller intervals to larger ones, such as a minor 2nd being a diminished octave. The rhythm has a vocal quality by only using eighth, quarter, dotted quarter and longer note values. As it progresses, the rhythm becomes more active by next introducing triplet eights, followed by sixteenths and quintuplet sixteenths. The intervals are also being expanded even larger such as 10ths. Next, a repeated note on triplet sixteenths is introduced, which undergoes variation climaxing into accelerando beamed figures. Finally, a final phrase of a slurred vocal-like melody is presented with glissandos added in the final measures leading to a fermata whole note on low “C” to conclude the movement. The second movement “Vivo” opens with sixteenth note key clicks that between a repeated low “E♭” that then intervallicaly expands upwards leading into flourish to a high “A♭” quarter note beginning the main material of the movement. This main material has a scherzo character and undergoes variations. Throughout the movements the key clicks return as a sort of grounding function. The next section features a two-voice contrapoint line which leads back to main material before a return of an extended key click section. Finally, an “Andante” section occurs that is a synthesis of the material of both movements to conclude the work.

description: This is a three-movement work utilizing elements of sonata form combined with a fusion of influences. Fischer’s music often takes inspiration and combines a large amount of influences into his own unique voice. The common influences in his music are his roots incorporating elements of traditional Jewish, Slavic folk music, South American dance music combined with classical influences of French impressionism, Hindemith, and occasionally modernist techniques such as twelve-tone, serialism, and avant-garde. This results in a style that oscillates between styles utilizing polyphonic lines that are interwoven with harsh polyharmony. The first movement “Allegro” is in sonata form opening with a march-like introduction in the piano consisting of a staccato eighth note followed by an eighth rest combined with a dotted eighth and sixteenth. The bassoon enters solo playing an energetic main theme composed of staccato eighth and sixteenth melody leading to long notes, which the march-like occurs underneath. This continues developing with the piano becoming more active with passages of sixteenth notes. As the section continues it is contrasted with a lyrical and vocal-like melody in the bassoon, while continuing in the energetic and staccato character. The second theme is a meno mosso in a more lyrical and calm character in a contrapuntal texture. The development takes fragments from the opening as its basis. This leads back to a full recapitulation that goes attacca into the second movement which is in a cantabile character in ternary form. The A section “Andante” presents a folk-like melody that uses more impressionistic harmonic choices. The B section “Piu mosso” has a sequential two slurred sixteenth note pattern that ascends and descends overtime underneath a vocal-like melody. The return of the A section brings back the opening theme with a new accompaniment texture. In the opening it was chordal and in the return it is more contrapuntal. The movement ends with an accelerando in the piano to attacca into the final movement also in ternary form. The A section “Allegro” has a dance-like character with a lively eighth and sixteenth note theme in the bassoon that is mainly in scalar or arpeggiated motion, often with a lower neighbour motion. The piano plays accompaniment figures and takes over the theme while the bassoon rests. The B section “Meno mosso” features a cantabile slurred theme in the bassoon overtop of chordal accompaniment in the piano. The section accelerandos back into the A material with a much more active piano accompaniment. This is interrupted by a short eight measure “Meno mosso” piano interlude in a chorale-style. The A material returns again with the cantabile theme being incorporated this time leading to a eight measure tutti quarter note chordal passage to an unexpected a B minor augmented 5th chord to conclude the work.

description: This is a three-movement work in a neoclassical style that utilizes elements of sonata form combined with twentieth-century harmonic language in a style similar to Shostakovich. The first movement “Allegro non troppo” is in sonata form and opens with a lyrical main theme consisting of arpeggiated or scalar sixteenths that lead to a longer note value in the bassoon overtop of fragments of sixteenth notes in the right hand and a bass line in the left hand. This develops into the secondary theme based on a sequential passage of staccato sixteenth notes in the bassoon, which the piano echoes. This becomes a fragmented ostinato in the piano that the bassoon plays syncopated quarter notes overtop of before repeating to the beginning. One thing to note about the edition is the repeat is in different spots in the piano score and the bassoon part. It is incorrect in the score and the first ending should only be the last three measures and not the four measures written. The piano score the second time through should play the first measure of the first ending before going to the second ending. The development changes key to Eb minor and begins with a large interval motif in a lyrical style overtop of a chordal piano accompaniment. This is abruptly interrupted with material similar to the secondary theme in a canon-like texture that goes through development stages. The coda brings back material similar to the opening of the development to conclude the movement. The second movement “Andante” begins with a semplice melody in the left hand of the piano consisting of quarter and half notes. Eventually, the bassoon enters with a melody using elements from the opening such as tied quarter notes from beats 3 to 1. As it develops it intensifies, becoming eighth notes and ascending to the upper register of the bassoon. The movement continues developing and recombining the various themes, motifs and fragments of them together leading to a return to the opening material in the piano alone. The final movement “Allegretto” begins with the bassoon attacca overtop of a long note held over in the piano from the previous movement. The bassoon presents the theme by starting slow and accelerando into the allegretto tempo. The theme is a joyful and dance-like character of two slurred eighth notes leading to a staccato eighth. After the bassoon’s presentation the piano enters with the theme while the bassoon plays an accompaniment role of staccato eighth notes on the main beats outlining the harmonic progression. The melody continues passing back and forth until a virtuosic sixteenth note run appears out of nowhere in the piano. This leads into a disjunct and marcato line of eighth notes in the bassoon. The next section is an espressivo and vocal-like melody in the bassoon overtop of chordal eighth notes in the piano. Eventually, this gets combined with the opening theme and motifs, which ritenuendos into a poco meno mosso section that transforms the main theme into a legato and a dream-like quality from the lush harmonies. This is abruptly contrasted with a piano interlude consisting of thick staccato eighth note chords leading into an “Andante” section which has the disjunct eighth notes from earlier in a legato character in the piano that ends on an open fifth. The bassoon enters with a quasi-cadenza moment of rubato eighth notes in the upper register. A final “Allegro” section with marcato eighth notes in dialogue between the bassoon and piano occurs to conclude the work.

description: This is a three-movement work in a neoclassical three-part structure utilizing technical elements from the New Viennese School combined with sonorous effects and modal techniques. The bassoon part was written in a virtuosic manner. The first movement “Introduction” is in an allegro con brio tempo structured around alternation of virtuosic and articulated sections with lyrical and cantabile sections. It opens with a stately motif that is comprised of a pick-up note to a long note in the bassoon combined with chordal responses from the piano during long notes. This develops and becomes more active until it becomes a whole phrase of triplet notes. Eventually, this is briefly interrupted by a more cantabile and legato section of quarter note triplets. The texture consists of constant quarters in an arpeggiated manner in the piano with a more melodic line in the bassoon. It then returns to the original material that becomes more active and virtuosic developing into lines of articulated sixteenth notes. The next main section features the bassoon playing a repeated triplet note bass line while the piano plays a quarter note melody overtop. This then leads into fragmentation of the original material in both instruments before another contrasting lyrical section composed of dotted half notes, half notes and quarter notes in the bassoon with an arpeggiated accompaniment in the piano. Finally, is one last return the original material. The next movement “Passacaglia” is in an andante commodo tempo is a vocal-like melody in the bassoon that goes under slight variations throughout such as becoming augmented or syncopated overtop of a contrast eighth note weaving line in the right hand and chords in the left hand of the piano. The final movement “Rondo - Scherzo” is in an allegro grazioso tempo. It opens with solo bassoon presenting a lilting and dance-like theme built around staccato eighth notes that descend a major third, ascends diminished fourth, and finally a minor second to a quarter note before a quasi-scalar line. This theme continually comes back as the A material in many different tonalities. The piano enters with chords sparsely placed, eventually filling in dialogue with the bassoon. The next main section is a more melodic scalar line in the bassoon overtop of chords in the piano. Eventually, this becomes fragmented and the line trades off every few notes between the two instruments leading back to the A material. The next contrasting section is a long note trills and a chromatic descending bass line. This then develops into a section with material from the virtuosic and articulated material in the first movement. Another return of the A material occurs. Next, is a contrasting lyrical section with singing dotted half notes in the bassoon overtop of arpeggiated-like motif in the piano. Then a return of the first movement material occurs to conclude the piece.
