performace_considerations: The composer describes the work as “the last movement of a drama. The two main characteristics of a sonata can be easily perceived in this composition. Nevertheless, due to an intense development and change of themes there is a sort of “lack of time” illusion which in turn makes an impression of an expromt.” (Kikta, foreword) The work is a grand virtuosic display allowing the flute to effortlessly and lightly soar, while exploring the extremes of dynamics and registers on the flute. The work opens with a “Rubato, improvisation” section consisting of a dialogue between the two instruments with alternating long note values. As it progresses, the rhythmic values become shorter and more notes are added into each statement until the instruments are overlapping. This leads into a “Con moto” where a motif of sixteenth notes leading to a half note tied to an eighth note. This is in a contrapuntal texture and becomes more virtuosic as it develops as the string of sixteenths become longer and eventually, smaller note values into triplet sixteenths. Next, a “Tempo qiusto barbaro” presents a quirky dance-like ostinato accompaniment in the piano while the flute plays a quarter note tied over to a flourish of virtuosic thirty-second notes. As it develops the piano accompaniment changes through to provide variety and interest for the listener. Eventually, the flourishes go from being slurred to articulated in the flute. Then a “Con amarezza” section occurs where the roles reverse with the piano playing the flourishes and a lyrical slurred melody in the flute. After a while, the flute takes the virtuosic role again while the piano plays large rolled chords on each downbeat. Next, a return of previous motifs from earlier come back. The work continues developing these motifs until the piano interrupts with a brief misterioso phrase consisting of a eighth notes that alternate between the low register and upper register.This leads into a “Rubato tranquillo flebile” section comprised of chords in the piano on beat two while the flute plays arpeggiated flourishes. Finally, the coda appears marked “Barbaro” that consists of a syncopated ostinato in the piano and more thirty-second note flourishes in the piano to conclude the work.

description: This is a three-movement work that explores the delicate and sentimental nature of the flute through three contrasting characters. The first movement “Madrigal” contains two main sections both centered around a vocal like melody in the flute built around neighbour-tone motion overtop of chordal accompaniment in a rhythmic pattern of quarter and half notes in the piano. As the melody variates and expands in the flute an echo of fragmentation begins in the piano of the earlier material. This leads into the B section that has a more sweeping and stepwise melodic line in the flute overtop of arpeggiated sixteenth notes in the piano. Near the end of the section the neighbour motion sneaks in to segue to a modulation of the A and B material. The next movement “Intermezzo” is a dance-like character in a major key featuring a staccato quarter followed by an eighth leading to three eighth notes. This leads into a theme consisting of two slurred eighth notes followed by an eighth rest with an accompanimental role in the piano. As it develops the line elongates and connects the fragments into a larger overarching phrase. It is contrasted with slurred lyrical lines in a more mysterious character and minor key character. In the return of the A material sixteenth notes are inserted to make it more virtuosic. The final movement “Serenade” returns to the lyrical and vocal-like melodic line that weaves around and has a character reminiscent of 20th century French woodwind writing. A contrasting B section of repeated staccato sixteenth notes with grace notes occurs to give a more humoresque character. Once again, the piano plays an accompanimental role for the entire movement with the occasional interjection.

description: This is a three-movement work that utilizes elements of sonata form and classical music traditions. The first movement “Allegro moderato" is in ternary form and begins with a theme of eighth and sixteenth notes in the flute overtop of syncopated patterns of chords that become more contrapuntal as it progresses in the piano. Eventually, the piano takes over the theme in a seven-measure interlude before the flute re-enters with it. The movement continues developing and adding in variations to the theme and accompaniment until the “Un poco meno mosso” section, which provides a contrasting character. The flute has an espressivo melody built on a dotted eighth followed by a sixteenth motif leading to either triplets or sixteenth notes that has a vocal-like quality with embellishments reminiscent of an aria. The piano has a contrapuntal texture often with echoes and countermelody like a mini orchestra underneath the flute. The following movement “Andante sostenuto” is also in ternary form, which opens with a four measure piano introduction of a harmonized melody in the right hand and a syncopated bass line in the left hand. The flute then enters with the theme marked “dolce” that is mostly in scalar motion with occasional larger intervals to intensify the phrase. A “Cantando” section in a completely different tonality contrasts. It presents a different theme built around similar principles with four independent voices in the piano accompaniment. The final movement “Scherzo finale” is a fiery display of technique and energy that is also in ternary form. The movement begins with a syncopated motif in the piano that the flute enters overtop with a giocoso theme of eighth and sixteenth notes leading to a tied dotted quarter note primarily in scalar motion. As it progresses, the theme weaves around more. Eventually, the rhythmic pulse is shifted from the triple to duple with a contrasting 2/4 section. This section is more semplice with a simple melody and fragments rotating around the ensemble in a contrapuntal texture. As it develops alternation with passages in 3/4 are introduced to set up a return to the A section.

description: This is a two movement work based on the concept of contrast as described by the composer as “the titles of the movements of the sonata determine the musical content of each movement and of the piece as a whole. The clear contrast between the two movements is the preeminent dramaturgic basis for the sonata.” (Stankovych, foreword) The first movement “Incredible” begins with a short burst of thirty-second notes leading to a longer note value preceded by a grace note. During the longer note the piano responds with grace note figures. After a couple statements the flute line begins getting more and more virtuosic and develops into longer phrases with some melodic content in between the virtuosic moments. During the more melodic moments the piano switches to sweeping arpeggiations. As it develops, the piano then switches to a more chordal accompaniment giving the flute space to play more freely and expressively on their motifs turning them into more of an embellishment of a vocal-like line now in contrast to the earlier incredible virtuosity. The virtuosic nature continues to sneak back in and the movement continues contrasting the two characters. Eventually, on the longer note values frullato is added to create the climax of the movement. A brief piano interlude of chords in a calm texture occurs before a chaotic aleatoric section of disjunct staccato eighth notes takes over. This is followed by a “Piu mosso” section of unison disjunct sextuplets that gets interrupted by frullato on longer note values in the flute turning into a melodic line overtop of accompaniment figures in the piano.This leads in a “Largo” section of a melodic line that is solo in the flute that incorporates material from the opening of the movement. This sets up the character of the second movement “Elegy,” which is attacca with the piano joining in with dotted half note chords. This movement is built around the piano playing the ostinato chords majority of the time with a lyrical and vocal-like theme in the flute consisting of primarily eighth notes leading to a longer note value with occasional triplet embellishments. As it progresses, the melody becomes highly ornamented with flourishes of technique added in. Eventually, the flourishes takes over becoming full passages of various virtuosic motifs. A final “Largo” section occurs with the return of the theme and similar texture occurs. Syncopated half notes are added as a top third staff in the piano overtop of the chords.

description: This is a three-movement work that displays Dorfman’s style combining elements of avant-garde style that explores different timbres through graphic notation and multiphonics that is combined with more neoclassical motifs that are Shostakovich like and Jewish folk and religious music. The first movement is structured on a constantly changing and contrasting section. It begins with an “Allegro” unmetered section, consisting of short fragments that jump between the low and high register of the bassoon. There are notes throughout that interrupt the line with unspecified rhythm with graphic notation for vibrato. The next section “Animato cantabile” begins with a lyrical melody that begins more disjunct through larger intervals and more technical passages incorporated. A short two measure “Allegretto” section of sixteenth notes interrupts before returning to the “Andante.” Another interruption occurs in an “Animato cantabile” section of two measures consisting of septuplet sixteenth notes returning to the Andante again that develops this time into an “Animato assai” featuring material in a similar manner to the opening to conclude the movement. The second movement “Adagio” is in ternary form. It opens with a rhythmic repeated note motif that expands into a melody ornamented with grace notes that leads into unspecified rhythm notes with harmonics, trills, tremolos, and smorzato. This leads into a section with a weaving around melody that builds sequentially. Eventually, the opening material returns with ornamentation and variation. The final movement “Presto” opens with a sixteenth note motif built around the intervals of third, fourth and fifth that is repeated three times before expanding. It ascends and descends the range of the bassoon leading to a fermata low “C”. The motif returns this time staccato as opposed to slurred and expands slowly in a sequential manner. This leads into an espressivo melody built around arpeggios. Next, a couple technical passages in an aleatoric manner consisting of first large intervals and weaving around texture. This returns to the opening material with some slight variations such as a trill added at the top of passage before descending.

description: This work takes folk inspiration combined with a modern approach to harmony and a nod to classical tradition by using the typical three-part form. It is originally written for soprano sopilka, which is a traditional Ukrainian folk instrument similar to a recorder. “However, the composer in private conversations has mentioned that it could be performed by other instruments [piccolo] as well.” (Anibroieva Trans. Gnativ: Sonatina foreward, Kolos Music Publishing). The first movement “Kant” marked “Andante” is inspired by cantus of the 17-18th century that are known for their “syllabic text-setting, homophonic texture, gentle modal harmony, and meditative strophic repetition.” (Anibroieva Trans. Gnativ). Stylistically, this movement’s opening is reminiscent of a Georg Philip Telemann sonata but with modern harmony. The movement opens with a simple lyrical melody in the piccolo with a chordal accompaniment underneath. As it progresses, more ornamentation, complexity, and virtuosity are added into the melody, while the accompaniment becomes more contrapuntal. This leads into a short cadenza to conclude the section. Next, a “Vivo” section occurs with a humoresque and dance-like quality.The melody features strings of eighth (duple or triple) leading to a quarter note, while the accompaniment has ostinato patterns. As well, this becomes more virtuosic with the introduction of sixteenth notes. There are moments of relaxation where the lyrical quality returns briefly to interrupt, such as the 3/4 sections. Otherwise, the movement continues varying the material for the rest of the movement while alternating between the two characters. The next movement “Vyshyvanka” marked “Pittoresco” is “like threads in a pattern, the piccolo’s small ornamental figures and the piano’s “cross-stitch” figuration interweave in intricate metric-rhythmic combinations creating a musical embroidery.” (Anibroieva Trans. Gnativ) The movement opens with an oscillating eighth note line in the piano that the piccolo enters overtop of with a quasi-improvisatory like line consisting of a long note followed by cascading faster note values. The piano is in a dialogue responding back afterwards, which becomes more active as the movement progresses. Next, a “Piu mosso” section with a more dance-like quality reminiscent of a jig occurs. This as well becomes more virtuosic with a string of syncopated runs of sixteenths beginning on the second sixteenth of the measure. This is followed by a return to the original material. This is briefly interrupted by a two-measure “Giocoso” consisting of a chord in the piano and material similar to the earlier “Piu mosso” in the piccolo. The final movement “Kozak-Tanets” (Cossack Dance) when no tempo marking takes inspiration from the folk dance hopak through the “sudden accents, metric ruptures, and contrasting dynamics underscore the warrior nature and irrepressible energy of the hero.” (Anibroieva Trans. Gnativ). This movement is in rondo form. The movement opens with an eight-measure introduction in a grand and declamatory style with unison whole and quarter notes in both instruments. This leads in a fiery dance consisting of virtuosic strings of eighth notes in a sequential motion in the piccolo and chordal accompaniment in the piano. Eventually, this merges into a more vocal melodic line in the piccolo for some contrast, which becomes more virtuosic over time. Next, a return to the A material occurs now in a minor tonality. Various contrasting episodes occur that are alternated with variations on the A material. Eventually, the opening introduction returns to close off the work.

description: This is a short work that presents a theme in a vocal-like style in the middle register of the bassoon consisting of eighth, quarter and half notes in a moderato tempo with seven variations that are all attacca. The first variation “L’istesso tempo” consists of an eighth note followed by a sixteenth rest and note that outline notes from the theme. This develops into a line of consistent triplet eighth notes. The next variation also marked “L’istesso tempo” utilizes a motif of three eighth notes in a syncopated manner beginning on the second eighth note of the beat. The third variation “Andante” is an espressivo character that is slurred in the tenor and upper register of the bassoon. The following variation “L’istesso tempo” features a double dotted eighth note followed by a thirty-second note motif in an arpeggiated manner often with large intervals. The fifth variation “L’istesso tempo” are sextuplet sixteenth notes that weave around the main notes from the theme. The next variation “Allegretto” consists of arpeggiated staccato notes first played as eighth notes, which develops into sixteenth notes. The final variation “Tempo di valse” transforms the theme in a waltz character using two main rhythmic motifs:1) dotted quarter followed by an eighth leading to a quarter note motif throughout and 2) half note followed by a quarter note.

description: This is a three movement work utilizing elements of sonata form in a reduced manner combined with 20th century harmonic languages. The first movement “Allegro non troppo” alternates between a fiery syncopated character of staccato eighth notes and accented dotted quarter notes in contrast to lyrical slurred moments. Often, these lyrical movements appear out of the texture as a surprise. The following movement “Andante molto” is comprised of two different characters that are alternated between: 1) frullato slurred quarter notes leading to a half note and 2) vocal-like slurred melodic lines. These two materials build until a climax of a cascading display of virtuosity through a passage of slurred triplet sixteenth notes that become more disjunct with dotted sixteenth rests inserted into the line. A return to the opening material reworked is presented to conclude the movement. The final movement “Vivo” has a quirky dance character through the rhythm, articulation, and sudden dynamic changes. The rhythmic often features syncopations through the downbeat having rests. Also, the dance gets thrown off through switching between 3/8 and 4/8 meters for each section to break up the patterns being established. The articulation often is very light and staccato with occasional contrasting moments of staccato or slurred passages. Throughout sudden dynamic drops to a quiet dynamic occur to surprise the listener and to rebuild the intensity.

description: This is a one-movement work that is structured around a dialogue between the flute and harpsichord. The work opens with a section marked “Quarter note equals 110”. The flute has a lyrical theme and the harpsichord plays a fragment of disjointed sixteenth notes underneath the flute’s longer note values. As the section develops the harpsichord’s interruptions become closer together and elongated until it creates its own distinct voice in the texture, which the flute then becomes more fragment resulting in a reversal of the roles. The flute is now responding to the harpsichord. Eventually, a return to the original roles occur where the flute plays a motif of slurred sixteenth notes that begins on the second sixteenth of the beat in response to a chord in the harpsichord. Once again the harpsichord’s part becomes more active with longer and more disjointed passages occurring. However, this time the flute switches back to a more lyrical theme again. This dialogue between the two instruments and alternating between the previously presented material continues until the flute emerges with a cadenza-like section marked “poco meno mosso” featuring triplets that ascend to a repeated high F. A final return to the opening material occurs with some small embellishments to conclude the work.

description: This is a short one-movement work depicting a musical picture of the Garden of Paradise (or Eden) through the composer’s use of lush harmonies, contrapuntal lines weaving together, and effortless technique that cascade the registers of the flute. The work opens with a seven-measure organ introduction marked “Andante” with a melodic line and chords underneath. Afterwards, the main section of the work “Moderato” begins with the flute's entrance on a dotted half note trill that blooms into an melody with a quais-improvsitary quality, while the organ sets up a bass line in the lower voice, an ostinato pattern in the middle voice and chords in the upper voices. The flute then takes over the spotlight with a passage of sixteenth notes primarily in scalar motion that cascades around the registers of the flute. The organ then plays an interlude with a semplice quality consisting of a motif of three eighth notes beginning on the second of the measure that is first fragmented then gets slightly developed with each statement, which is overtop of a bass line and chords. Next, a “Piu mosso” section follows that the flute takes over the melodic content from the interlude and expands it into a fuller vocal-like phrase. Eventually, this evolves into another passage of sixteenth notes. Afterwards, a dialogue between the flute and organ occurs passing short motifs back-and-forth. Next, another organ interlude occurs in a more virtuosic manner with a constant stream of sixteenth notes. Eventually, to conclude the work the flute enters with a melodic theme in a vocal-like style comprised of eighth, quarter, and half notes.

description: This is a three-movement programmatic suite that combines elements of traditional and modernist writing. It is in a neo impressionist style with some Spanish folk influence that depicts the composer’s travels and experience in Spain. The first movement “Bells in Twilight” is in an Andante con moto tempo in a ternary form. It reflects a tranquil picturesque evening filled with the sound of distant church bells. The movement is centered around inventive sonorous effects to imitate bells. The A section features accented long tones entering independently throughout the ensemble that occasionally come together creating a layering effect. The meter changes every measure creating an improvisatory nature as if the bells are happening unexpectedly to the listener. The B section “Piu mosso” uses double imitation of a theme that begins as quarter notes and progresses to sixteenths and eventually, tremolos and trills. The movement concludes with an abbreviated reprise of the A section that introduces frullato into the texture. The second movement “Evening Dance” is in an Allegro tempo with a fiery character that utilizes a rhythmic motif of eighth, two sixteenth, four eighths from Coblas, humorous Spanish songs, that is combined with new, modern melodies. In this movement the horn leads the main theme in its upper register. The movement opens with a short homorhythmic introduction of trills and a descending scalar passage before introducing the rhythmic motif and dance elements in a light and staccato character. The final movement “Sounds at Midnight '' is in an Adagio tempo imitating the enchanting sounds of nature at midnight. This is achieved through pedal effects, alternation of solo episodes with tutti ensemble passages, and registrar contrast of melody and accompaniment. The bassoon’s solo episodes reproduces the lyrical atmosphere of a Spanish serenade.

The work is in ternary form that utilizes the flute to convey a sense of unreality and the atmosphere combined with the textured pattern in the piano to create a duet interplay. For example, the piano uses counterpoint in the upper register of the right hand combined with distant chord arpeggiation in the left hand underneath the theme in the flute to give a sense of decorativeness. The piece uses sudden changes in tonality and contrasting it with moments of modality throughout to create a floating quality to the music. It opens with a theme of eighth notes leading to a dotted quarter note tied over the barline, which meanders around tonality. This meanders around to a climax in the middle of the phrase of an octave interval jump before meandering downwards. The B section contrasts by providing a sense of stability through two juxtaposing tonal centers (G major & B minor) being used simultaneously. The texture changes to the flute playing a theme that is more vocal-like with rhythmic contrast, while the piano plays a solely accompanimental role of an oscillating pattern in the right hand and chords moving on the second beat of the measure in the left hand.

description: This is a one-movement work with various short sections that are attacca each with a different character while exploring a variety of extended techniques. The opening section “Annoying but resolute” has an ironic and joking character achieved through a two sixteenth with a large interval jump to an eighth note motif combined with lots of accented notes, grace notes and glissandos. The second section “Pompous, majestic” has a quirky character through constant trading of staccato triplet sixteenths throughout the ensemble in a changing pattern through metered changes and accents. Next, “Shrilly and boring” consists of a short motif that is looped that accelerandos in a short section “Desperately” which sequences the motif higher before arriving at “Dramatically.” This features three disjunct lines based on large intervals that are weaving in and out of one another. Eventually, the parts come together and interact in a call and response manner that gradually becomes one cohesive idea. The next section “Like a bird” is a homorhythmic section with short interjections utilizing extended techniques such as quartertones and frullato imitating a bird call. This is followed by “like an improvisation” which alternates between thick contrapuntal lines and homorhythmic passages featuring the use of trills and vibrato. The next section “Broken organ” is another homorhythmic passage that slowly unravels and becomes more dissonant imitating a machine breaking apart. Then “Love song” occurs which is an oboe solo overtop of long tones in the clarinet and bassoon that explore the concept of pitch by switching between various extended techniques to change the pitch and timbre. This leads into the final section “Love song from the depths” which features a melodic line in the oboe with an intertwined accompaniment of sixteenths in the bassoon and sextuplets in the clarinet with rests interspersed throughout.

description: This is a four-movement suite with a wide range of characters that showcases the flutes lyrical, humoresque, and technical playing. The first movement “Prelude” in ternary form begins with an ominous statement of the minor ninth in the lower range of the piano that a theme which is a vocal-like melody in the right hand joins in on. The flute then enters to play the theme in the low register creating a canon texture passing around voices of the piano.Throughout there are moments of dissonance with clashing semitone passing motion creating a mysterious atmosphere. A timbral-textural exchange occurs between the parts involving the melodic line to shift between the flute and piano with the theme beginning the statement on different pitches in the order of 1) C three times, 2) A and 3) a return to C. The contrasting middle section has a sharp contrast with a faster tempo in D♭ major that plays with the major and minor mode creating an alternation between “F” and “F♭” introducing a tinge of modal instability, which comes across as distant echoes of the preceding sombre image. Rhythmically, it consists of an arpeggiated eighth note line in the left hand of the piano with chords and sixteenth note flourishes in the right hand. The flute plays a lyrical melody with moments of sixteenth note flourishes. The flute’s interplay in the ensemble picks up the first sixteenth note motif from the piano in an unfolding descending-ascending figuration, which results in the piano to repeat the ascending figure. This creates a finely organised interaction between the two instruments as complementary strands of the harmonic process. The gradual transition to the recapitulation is prepared through an increasingly evident return of the original interval motif of the minor ninth demonstrated through the arpeggiated chords in the piano. A new rhythmic motif of two accented eighth notes followed by triplets emerges in the flute that is then echoed by the piano involving the pitches “D♭” and “C” harking back to the opening ostinato. The sixteenth note motif reappears performing an unifying formal function. This is alongside the minor ninth motif being reimagined as a horizontal line as opposed to the chordal structure earlier. This motific transformation prepares the return of the opening section in the form of an abbreviated recapitulation. The theme is presented in two voices: 1) the flute in an inversion and 2) the piano in the original form, which is a reverse of the original presentation in the introduction. In the final measures marked “ritenuto” the piano presents a figuration in eighth notes that refers the listener back to the tonal material of the middle section. This is achieved by the flute reproducing the same pitches one sixteenth later and an octave lower. The sequence D♭ - A♭ - D♭ - E - F - A♭ - D♭ - A alludes to the arpeggiated figurations of the luminous middle episode. Thus, in the coda of the Prelude we witness not simply a return of the initial material but an intonational coupling of the outer and middle sections: a reminiscence of the bright section emerges within the context of the restored sombre image. In the middle section the sombre intonational complex is episodically intruded into the bright tonal environment; in the coda of the Prelude we also observe the reverse process: elements of the bright section appear within the reinstated dark image. As a result, the form is closed not by mechanical repetition but by an internally cohesive outcome, in which the recapitulation proves abbreviated yet semantically condensed. The following movement “Toccata” is cast in a complex ternary form, whose harmonic language synthesises elements of polytonality, extended tonality, modal technique, and free chromaticism. It begins with an ostinato pattern in the piano comprised of staccato eighth notes in the left hand and quarter notes in the right hand. The flute enters overtop with the theme consisting of a line of staccato eighth notes that weave around with chromaticism and large interval jumps. As it develops the composer applies a quartal transposition of the pitch contour, which is a characteristic device of his writing. Subsequently, a redistribution of textural functions occurs when the flute's theme migrates to the right-hand piano part in a high register, while the left hand doubles the original accompaniment pattern an octave higher. At this time the flute presents a new melodic motif of a dotted eight followed by a sixteenth note leading to a quarter note motif is introduced in the flute, while the piano takes over the theme in the upper register.In the next four measures, the right-hand piano part continues to quote the flute's theme exactly, while the left hand exhibits a reduction of the accompaniment that involves every fourth beat to be eliminated. Meanwhile, in the flute part, while preserving the overall pitch collection of the previous phrase, a partial octave transposition is carried out where some of pitches remain in the former ("forgotten") register. This produces a disjointed, leaping melodic line creating an effect of registral stratification. Overall, this achieves a significant timbral and spatial contrast among the textural layers. This leads into a virtuosic display of slurred triplet eight notes cascading across the registers of the flute, while the piano introduces a new motif. The two instruments then switch roles. A brief middle section for contrast occurs with a lyrical melody in the flute that features broken descending chromatic passages in triplets. Underneath this the piano plays staccato eighth notes that vaguely hint at a reinterpretation of the initial theme. As well, the minor ninth motif sneaks back in with a quasi-tremolo figure in the right hand of the piano. As it develops various registral and timbral transformations occur to intensify the sense of latent emotional anxiety through the textural instability. The return of the A section remains virtually untouched form, except for a slight variation in the final measure leading into a final coda. In the coda, the character changes that sonically depicts mechanistic force and pressure through an ascending chromatic staccato passage with accents on the second and fourth beats providing a rhythmic anchor. The flute presents a new lyrical melody that creates a juxtaposition of a vivid imagistic contrast to the piano’s aggressive character. A new polyphonic device of rhythmic augmentation is utilized to allow a textural superimposition to arise against the piano’s playing in the original form. During this the accompaniment undergoes systematic ascending shifts through successive transpositions by a second, then a fourth, again a second, a fourth, a third, and once more a fourth that lead to a powerful fortissimo climax, that alludes to earlier sections. Overall, the characteristic "jagged" line of the piano texture and the flute's grace notes reappear, heralding the final drive toward the cadence. The movement ends with a fortissimo accented half note in unison setting a firm dramatic full stop to this concise, scherzo-like narrative. The third movement “Interlude” marked “Andante rubato” has a quasi improvisatory character and is meditative acting as a contrasting link between the other movements. Harmonically, the movement references the first movement and the minor ninth motif. It is structured around the flute playing a statement solo with the piano responding with an arpeggiated figure. As it progresses the piano’s responses begin to overlap with the flute creating a simultaneous dialogue between the two instruments. Throughout the composer's instruction regarding the precise use of the right pedal prescribes the creation of a deep acoustic reverberation effect, contributing to the maximal fusion of sonorous layers into a single resonating space. In the penultimate measure, a fragment of the flute theme appears in the piano part, but its rhythmic placement is shifted relative to the original presentation by occurring on the third and fifth pitches instead of the first beat. This micro-shift introduces an element of temporal instability on the eve of the denouement. Overall, the harmonic colour of this movement is characterised by a high degree of tension. Although clothed in a meditative, sparse textural presentation there is a dichotomy of the inner tension that creates a specific spirit of restrained unease, concentrating within itself the anticipation of the large-scale and texturally rich events destined to unfold in the final movement of “Rondo.” The final movement “Rondo” marked “Allegro” has a form of ABACA with the A sections having a lighter and playful character of a scherzo-like waltz creating a dance-like buoyancy. Rhythmically, a subdivision of the second note in the triplet groups is used producing a syncopated play. Texturally, the piano uses a significant amount of polyphony with a four-voice texture. In the A section the flute plays a theme built around an eighth note followed by three triplet sixteenth notes in neighbouring motion leading to more eighth notes. The piano plays a contrapuntal role with various staccato and syncopated figures underneath to create forward momentum. This creates an imitative and canonic texture in the music. There are also allusions to the thematic material of the “Toccata.” As it develops the composer uses a registral transformation technique where the flute theme is presented in the piano’s extremely low register that provides a thickening of the material. Afterwards, a three-voice stretto canon occurs in the order of 1) the flute beginning, 2) piano’s left hand in an eighth note delay, and 3) an analogous delay in the piano’s right hand. The contrasting sections, B and C, present a lyrical melody in the flute reminiscent of earlier moments in the piece, while the piano plays a bass line, countermelody and chordal parts. These lyrical sections are in polytonality, meaning the flute and piano are playing in different keys simultaneously, which switch back and forth between them. Particularly, in the B section references the meditative imagery of the “Interlude” creating an arch-like semantic connection within the work’s structure. The ”Rondo” functions as the culminating, synthesising section of the entire suite. In its thematicism and textural solutions there are clear allusions to the preceding movements by references to the minor ninth motif from the “Prelude” combined with harmonic, rhythmic, and characteristic accompanimental passages from the “Toccata”, and the meditative spareness and registral polarisation of the “Interlude.” Thus, the finale not only completes the cyclic form but also carries out a semantic and intonational recapitulation of the entire composition that draws the disparate imagistic spheres together into a single dramaturgical knot.

description: This is a four-movement suite in a neoclassical style that explores both the humoresque and lyrical side of the bassoon, while often utilizing two voice-part writing. The first movement “Allegretto” is centered around a dotted sixteenth followed by a thirty-second note in an ascending interval motif. Throughout the movement this material is expanded into longer phrases. It develops into a section of two-part voice writing with third fourth eighth note of each measure leading to the downbeat in dialogue with two eighth notes in middle of the measure to create one cohesive line. A short return to the opening material occurs leading into another contrasting section of triplet eighth notes in scalar and arpeggiate motion that develops into two-part voice writing of large intervals between the two lines. A final return to the opening material occurs to conclude the movement. The next movement “Tempo di menuetto” features typical rhythmical and melodic motifs of classical waltzes. Throughout the melodic and accompaniment lines are differentiated through two-part voice writing. The third movement “Largo” begins with a vocal like fragment that gets expanded and becomes more virtuosic that leads into an accelerando prompting an Allegro section. This section consists of a return of the first movement’s opening motif now in a virtuosic manner utilizing a two-part voice style. A return to the opening material occurs but now more active using a two-voice part style. The final movement “Allegro” has an energetic dance-like character that features passages of eighth notes leading to a string of sixteenth notes. This is contrasted with material from earlier throughout the work that are recombined and varied in new ways such as inserting elements of the first movement into the main theme of this movement or using material from the largo in a moderato tempo now.

description: This is a four-movement suite that uses neoclassical structure combined with elements of folklorism such as melody, dance elements and harmony. The first movement “Romance” has a Da Capo form. The A section “Allegretto espressivo” features a lyrical main theme in the oboe overtop of half note bass line in the bassoon, and arpeggiated eighth notes in the clarinet. Eventually, the flute joins in on the melody a third above the oboe. This leads into the second theme which is also lyrical, but this time in the bassoon overtop of a falling thirds in eighth notes ostinato that changes harmony throughout, and a countermelody in the flute that joins later on. The B section has a playful staccato eighth note theme in the flute overtop of quarter note accompaniment in the ensemble. A brief chromatic passage of eighth notes in the clarinet bridges a return to the beginning material. The second movement “Waltz” features a spirited waltz-like melody in the lower register of the clarinet overtop of bass line on the downbeats in the bassoon and quarter notes on beats two and three in the flute and oboe. Eventually, the oboe takes over the theme and the flute introduces an espressivo countermelody. The movement continues to develop this material. The third movement “Song” is in an adagio tempo with a folk-like theme that gets passed around the ensemble beginning solo in the oboe. The movement continues providing variations such as different accompaniment figures or changing to a contrapuntal texture throughout, while exploring different key areas. The final movement “Dance” is in an allegretto tempo which consists of texture of a bass line, melodic content and accompaniment figures. Throughout the movement different themes are presented that become more virtuosic as it progresses beginning with an eighth and sixteenth note melody in the clarinet that later is contrasted by a triplet sixteenth melody in the flute. Eventually, fragments of the different themes and motifs are combined together leading to a final accelerando to conclude the work.

premiere: c. 1981 in Winnipeg by Amy Bonham (bsn)
description: This is a six-movement suite in a neoclassical style taking inspiration from Eastern European composers Bartok, Schnittke, Shostakovich, and Silvestrov. The work explores the concept of contrasts through articulation and line. The work is structured by beginning and ending with an unaccompanied solo with a series of duets in between them. The first movement “Tranquillo e espressivo” is a fantasy for solo flute. It begins with a lyrical and slurred melody and as the movement progresses becomes more virtuosic and technical featuring slurred sixteenth passages consisting of scalar and arpeggiated motion. This is contrasted with articulated triplet jumping around the range of the flute. The slurred passages become more disjointed overtime before ending in a sequential passage. Movements two through five are duets. The first one “Energico” features a weaving bass line that is slurred, which uses different one measure motifs as ostinatos. This is combined with a playful melody utilizing grace notes to get a whimsical character. In the opening the flute has the melody and the bassoon the bass line. Eventually, the roles reverse shortly with a lyrical melody in the bassoon before returning to original roles. This leads into a final adagio section in a contrapuntal texture. The next duet “Largo” has a quasi-improvisatory character with the two voices in a dialogue where one instrument plays eighth notes while the other is holding a long note value. Eventually, the voices come into unison playing a homorhythmic passage to bridge into a virtuosic thirty-second note section that weaves around each other. A contrasting section consisting of the flute playing a long note with a slow arpeggiated melody in the bassoon occurs. A return to the thirty-second note material occurs with variations to lead into a reprise of the opening material to conclude the movement. The next duet “Allegro moderato” has a humoresque character through a staccato eighth note line with large intervals in the bassoon underneath a chromatin melody in the flute. As the movement progresses the bassoon begins to fragment the melody in an echo while the flute has long notes developing into its own independent line creating a contrapuntal texture. The final duet “Lento” has an arpeggiated bass line and a vocal-like melody that switches between the two parts. The work concludes with an unaccompanied movement “Allegro marcato” in the bassoon, which is vigorous toccata in a quasi-ternary form. The A section is centered around repeated articulated sixteenth notes showcasing the bassoon’s ability to crisply articulate double-tonguing passages. The B section features slurred arpeggiated triplets that are sequentially exploring a variety of key centers. As the section develops sixteenth notes are introduced one beat at a time into the motif setting up a return to the A section character. However, the reprise of the A section is reduced and in different tonal centers than the opening.

premiere: in summer 2025
key: I (none, D♭ major), II (D major, D minor, none), III (A minor), IV (F major, G major, C Major)
description: This is a four-movement suite that utilizes elements of classical music combined with inspiration from Ukrainian folk music and dance. The first movement “Allegro con moto” opens with chords that weave between consonant and dissonant in the ensemble. The flute then presents the first theme for the introduction based around augmented chords which the oboe joins in a contrapuntal manner while the flute develops the theme. Eventually, the chords in the ensemble become a syncopated ostinato of eighths and sixteenths and a bass line underneath. Next, a cantabile main theme is presented in the flute that throughout the movement undergoes different textures provided by the accompaniment. This is interrupted every so often by a diminished chord forte-piano chord on repeated eighth notes in the ensemble that grows for two measures before returning back to the main theme material. The next movement “Pastorale” features a semplice melody consisting of eighth, quarter, and dotted quarter notes. It is first presented consonant in thirds by the flute and oboe overtop of a major chord drone in the clarinet, bassoon and horn. As the movement progresses the melody passes around the ensemble becoming more virtuosic, while harmonic shifts to more dissonance and folk harmonies such as using the Ukrainian minor scale, while the accompaniment parts become more intricate and contrapuntal. The third movement “Andante” is an arrangement of the Ukrainian folk song “Nich yaka misyachna” (What a Moonlit Evening) that is first presented as a clarinet solo of the melody overtop of a bass line of longer note values in the bassoon. Throughout the movement it undergoes variations such as a chorale section of the melody in homorhythm and a fugal-like section. The final movement “Scherzo and Ukrainian Dance” is in ternary form in an energetic and lively character. The A section is a scherzo that has virtuosic sixteenth note passages that pass around the ensemble overtop of accompaniment figures such as trading eighth notes between pairs of instruments such as the bassoon and clarinet, a three scalar sixteenth notes leading to three repeated eighth notes motif in the flute, and vocal-like melody of eigth, quarter and half notes in pair of instruments such as the horn and bassoon. The B section is a Hopak featuring a bass line in the bassoon, off-beats in the horn, and a melody in the oboe, which the flute joins in on the second phrase of each section exploring a different harmony each time. Eventually, the clarinet enters with a virtuosic line that utilizes glissandos and vibrato that takes over leading into a cadenza to set up a return to the scherzo A section to conclude the work.

premiere: August 15th, 1975 in Toronto, Canada by Christopher Weait on CBC radio broadcast
description: This is a four-movement suite each in a contrasting character with cyclic elements presenting whole-tone motifs throughout the entire work. The first movement “Lento” is a set of continuous variations on a slurred theme consisting of large intervals in an arpeggiated manner. Each new variation becomes more active and virtuosic resulting in a flourish of thirty-second notes up to a high D. Afterwards, the variations wind down becoming more semplice and lyrical. The second movement “Allegro scherzando” consists of staccato quarter and eighth note motifs contrasted with the occasional slurred eighth notes and motif comprised of two beats of dotted eighth and slurred sixteenth note. The following movement “Lento meditativo” is reminiscent of a da capo aria with moments of sincere lyricism contrasted with technical flourishes. The theme returns at the end greatly ornamented with quintuplet and sextuplet sixteenth notes. The final movement “Allegro comodo” loosely resembles sonata form with lively and energetic figures of staccato eighth and sixteenth notes displaying the virtuosic capabilities of the bassoon. There are contrasting lyrical moments such as a “ma espressivo” section with a slurred ocal-like melody ascending to high Eb.

description: This is a two-movement suite in a neoclassical style with clear forms and hierarchy of parts with melodic and rhythmic influence from folk music. The first movement is in ternary form in d minor. The A section “Moderato” opens with a lyrical folk-like theme in the bassoon overtop of syncopated accompaniment figures in the flute and clarinet. Eventually, the clarinet takes over the melody while the bassoon plays a chromatic half note bass line leading into a short homorhythmic section to bridge into the theme being played by the flute while a trading countermelody is passed being the oboe and bassoon to create a more contrapuntal texture. The B section is an “Allegretto” in a folk dance-like character and presents a secondary theme consisting of eighth and sixteenth notes leading to a quarter note overtop of a chromatic quarter note line in the oboe and clarinet. As the section progresses the accompaniment becomes more active. First, a syncopated eighth note motif than passages of scalar and arpeggiated sixteenth notes. The second movement “Allegretto scherzando” is in rondo form. The A section opens with a theme in the flute, accompaniment motifs in the oboe and clarinet, and a bass like in the bassoon. This develops into a dialogue of a fragment of the melody trading between the flute overtop of the original texture. This leads into the B section marked “subito piano” that is a homorhythmic passage of staccato eighth notes beginning tutti amongst the entire ensemble developing into a trading off texture before returning to tutti. The C section is a motif of quarter, two eighths, two quarters in the flute, oboe, and clarinet overtop of a rhythmic variation of this motif in the bassoon. The D section marked “meno mosso” has a lyrical and legato melody in the lower range of the bassoon overtop of an eighth note ostinato in the flute and oboe with a dotted quarter note line in the clarinet. This develops into a cannon of the melody in the flute and bassoon overtop of the ostinato motif. This material then becomes fragmented and developed before a DC al fine returning to the A through C sections.

key: I (C major) II (G major, B♭ major) III (G major), IV (D minor), V (G major) VI (C major, G major)
description: This is a suite of six short movements also in a neoclassical style with folk influence. The first movement “Introduction” in a grave tempo features a dotted eighth followed by a sixteenth motif first introduced in the horn that is echoed by the rest of the ensemble as the horn holds a long note. This texture continues for the rest of the movement with one group playing the motif while the other holds a long note. The second movement “Allegro scherzando” is in ternary form. The A section is mostly a homorhythmic texture of eighth notes and rests with the occasional solo line emerging from the texture. The B section features a solo line that passes around overtop of accompaniment figures in the rest of the ensemble that begin as dotted quarter notes and develop into the opening rhythmic motif of eighth note, eighth rest, eighth note that sets up the return to the A section. The following movement “Ritornello” is in a grave maestoso tempo featuring a motif in dialogue similar to the opening movement with an additional measure of quarter notes leading to a whole note to provide the harmonic functions necessary to conclude the movement. This goes attacca into the fourth movement “Andante con moto” consisting of a folk-like melody, accompaniment figures, and a bass line which the roles pass around the ensemble. The next movement “Ritornello” has a lively character beginning with a four-measure section in an echo texture that then becomes homorhythmic for the rest of the movement. It is centered around an eighth and quarter note motif. The final movement “Finale” is in rondo form with three statements of the virtuosic theme comprised mainly of sixteenth notes is contrasted with episodes that revisit material from the previous movements.

key: I (G minor), II (D minor), III (G major - D♭ major), IV (B♭ minor), V (B♭ major - G minor)
description: This is a five-movement suite that utilizes elements typical of Lyatoshynsky’s writing in the 1940s that was criticized as being formalist. It features introspective melodies that are woven out of short phrases, which emerge out of motifs that use rhythmic and dynamic waves allowing the music to open up as it naturally develops. Another aspect is the incorporation of folk music elements such as melodic and rhythmic ideas that are incorporated into romantic and expressionistic styles. The first movement “Moderato” features a vocal-like melody first presented by a solo oboe, which joined in the middle of the first period of the phrase with a contrapuntal texture. Throughout the movement the melody passes around the ensemble and a driving triplet eighth note motif in arpeggiated and sequential manner is introduced creating rhythmic dissonant against the eighth notes in the melody. Eventually, a return to the opening texture returns with triplet eighth notes introduced into the melody to create a cohesion of the competing motifs to conclude the movement. The next movement “Andante” opens in the same fashion as the previous movement with a vocal-like melody this time in the solo clarinet that gets passed around. The flute and bassoon enter with interjections that develops into a contrapuntal texture. Another driving rhythmic triplet eighth note ostinato is introduced in the middle section. This time the third and first note of each beat tied together featuring the intervals of an octave on the first beat and lower chromatic neighbour on the second beat. The third movement “Allegretto scherzando” is in ternary form. The A section has each of the different parts enter separately allowing the music to build naturally. First, a bass line in the bassoon is presented. Next, a countermelody in the clarinet and flute is added, and finally a melody in the oboe joins in. For the second phrase the flute and oboe switch roles. Next, a fragmented motif of four eighth notes that get traded around and developed into a cohesive new theme. This leads into a rhythmic motif that unwinds into the B section “Meno mosso, tranquillo” featuring two independent lines in a cantabile character that weave in and out of one another in the clarinet and bassoon. Eventually, the flute joins in on these themes with the oboe resting the entire section. A fragment of one of the themes is presented in the clarinet that slowly changes to a staccato character while it accelerandos to prepare the return to the A section. The following movement “Lento ma non troppo” opens with a theme in a period with an espressivo character in the solo clarinet. For the second half of the period the bassoon enters with a countermelody. As the movement continues the theme is passed around with more countermelodies being added creating a thicker texture. After the climax, a chorale section occurs to conclude the movement. The final movement “Allegro” opens with a short fugal section as an introduction with the theme beginning in the bassoon followed by the clarinet, oboe, and finally flute. Afterwards, the main theme of the movement is presented in the clarinet, which is a cantabile and vocal-like melody overtop of a staccato eighth note bass line in the bassoon. Immediately after the second theme is presented in the oboe overtop of the same texture. Throughout the movement these themes are fragmented and combined in different textures. To conclude the movement a virtuosic sixteenth note passage emerges in the clarinet that leads into a chain of sixteenths passing around the ensemble beginning in the low register of the bassoon until it arrives in the upper register of the flute followed by a final G minor chord to conclude the work.

description: The work combines the lyrical and virtuosic sides of the flute into a longing for and depiction of the summer. The work begins with an “Allegro” section marked con anima that starts with a two measure introduction of arpeggiated sixteenth notes in the guitar. The flute then enters with whole notes that then incorporates smaller note values to being a lyrical and vocal-like melody in the low register. The next section features syncopated fragments of sixteenth notes in quasi-arpeggiated motion that alternate between slurred and staccato articulated. It then becomes a full passage of sixteenth notes beginning on the second sixteenth of the measure. The lyrical melodic writing then returns with frullato being added as it develops to create a new texture in the music. The work continues in this manner alternating between lyrical sections and virtuosic sixteenth note passages. Each successive sixteenth note passages gets long and more virtuosic. The next major section “Moderato” marked dolce is a guitar solo written in two voice counterpoint that essentially is a string of eighth notes between two voices. Eventually, the flute enters with a lyrical line based on dotted quarter notes that incorporates glissandos. As it develops slight variations occur between the instruments. This is followed by a “Vivo” section that has a virtuosic sixteenth staccato line in the flute overtop of accented quarter note chords in the guitar. Similarly to earlier, frullato is incorporated later to change the texture and color and the guitar accompaniment becomes more active becoming duple then triplet eighths. This leads the flute back to a lyrical line again. This gets interrupted periodically with accented triplet eighth repeated chords in the guitar and triplet eighths in the upper register of the flute. Next, a “Prestissimo” section occurs consisting of a bass note on the first beat and chords on the section beat of the measure in the guitar while an earlier lyrical theme is played in the flute. A final return to the “Allegro” occurs to conclude the work.

description: This is a short one-movement work in verse-refrain form (ABAB) common in popular and folk music with a naive and joyous character. The A section marked “Andante cantabile” features a vocal-like melody in the flute that wanders by ascending and descending the register of the instrument mainly in stepwise and arpeggiated motion with moments of rhythmic dissonance through duple eighth notes overtop of regular eighth notes in the piano. The piano’s left hand is a dotted quarter note bass line, while the right hand has arpeggiated eighth notes. The piano accompaniment develops for the bass line to become more active. The B section marked “Con anima” has another vocal-like melody rhythmically consisting of quarter notes with the occasional half note or two eighth notes inserted. The piano has accompanimental arpeggiated eighth notes in both hands that highlight the harmonic changes. Eventually, the piano takes over the melody playing a four voice chorale of it in the right hand overtop of arpeggiated triplet eighth notes in the left hand. The flute then re-enters taking over the melodic role again for the rest of the work.

description: Merkhel’s music is in a wide range looking at the creative processes and results from an anthropological perspective by combining elements of conceptualism with performative practices. This is a one-movement work that pushes the technical boundaries of the bassoon virtuosity and extended techniques to create a wide range of textures and tonal possibilities to display the concept of synapse. It consists of two worlds working together to produce one unified result. Often, in the work a contrast and switch between textures occurs. The work begins with a long tone that introduces fast articulated notes briefly in the middle of the note to contrast between a calmer and more frantic texture. This then becomes a short ostinato passage in a chromatic manner that becomes more chaotic through accelerando beaming. This continues to alternate with the opening texture which sequences higher in the bassoon range. Eventually, new material is presented with the introduction of new textures with slap tonguing, frullato and con sordino. As it develops the fragmented motifs return to bring in the contrasting characters and worlds again. However, this time the fragmentations become connected into a longer phrase with no rests in between each iteration becoming more and more virtuosic with each successive return. The work concludes with the longer note value and calmer texture but now interrupted with rests, as if the synapses are breaking down returning to their separate worlds.

description: This is a short one-movement work with a jazz-like feel through the inflections of grace notes, rhythmical feel of syncopation created through eighth note rests and ties, and harmonic exploration of blues scales and harmonies. The piano mainly has a walking bass line in the left hand and accompaniment figures, often echoes of motifs in the right hand. The flute has a melody with a lazy character rhythmically consisting of quarter, eighth and half notes that are often syncopated. The line has a natural rise and fall often beginning in the low and middle register rising to the upper register before returning back down. Dynamically, this is reflected through hair pins of a crescendo upwards and decrescendo downwards. Eventually, triplet eighth notes are introduced to bring variety into the line and create a little more virtuosity.

description: This is a one-movement work and the first of Liashenko’s collection of technema works. This is a style of music that explores different timbres and color schemes to form a melody through micro-motifs and rhythmic displacements. The opening section of this piece features forte, accented dissonant chords with a horn repeated note motif that jumps a diminished fifth that is expanded outwards overtime. As it progresses the entry of each of the notes in the chord become displaced and staggered. Also, a triplet eighth motif that outlines different fourth intervals is introduced in the clarinet. This leads into the next section, which is aleatoric featuring a motif of disjunct sixteenths underneath variations of the motifs introduced thus far in the horn. Eventually, the oboe and clarinet join in on the triplet motif leading into the next section, which is a diminution of this motif on the sixteenth level. This is combined with a melody and a bass line to create a thicker texture. Next, the triplet motif is augmented into quarter notes and combined with fragments of the melodic line to create a new melody through these short fragmented micro-motifs being pieced together. The following section features the introduction of the final motif: two eighth notes in a third interval alternating between major and minor that get passed around the ensemble in a dialogue with unexpected pauses. The rest of the piece takes these micro-motifs continuing to vary and combine them with different possibilities exploring a wide range of timbres, colors and characters in the ensemble through only small changes to the material.

description: This is a one-movement Duo Concerto for oboe and bassoon written in the technema style. The form of the work is not in the typical concerto form. Instead, it has a couple main motifs that develop and come back unexpectedly. The opening texture has a dissonant cluster chord long-tone in the orchestra with two short motifs in the oboe and bassoon that are in dialogue with interjections from the vibraphone. The oboe motif is a legato line that weave around a minor third while the bassoon motif is a staccato arpeggiated line. The section develops and expands these motifs in a larger range and longer statement until it becomes contrapuntal, which the orchestra joins in on. Eventually, this winds down into one cohesive melody in the oboe with a clear accompaniment of counter-melody, inner harmony and bass line. The next section “Allegro moderato” features a trading sixteenth line between the oboe and bassoon that develops into being together while constantly switching between contrary and parallel motion. This is overtop of a homorhythmic accompaniment of fragments of eighth notes with rests in between each statement that eventually join the sixteenth note dialogue. Next, a return to the opening material returns followed by an orchestral interlude in a neoclassical style centered around an eighth note and triplet sixteenth motif. Afterwards, the soloists have improvisatory-like lines that are a beat apart in an echo manner overtop of an active scalar sixteenth note accompaniment. The next section consists of a lyrical line built around large intervals in the soloists overtop of drone texture that becomes more active and involved overtime. Eventually, the accompaniment becomes a line of staccato eighth notes that sets up the next section. The accompaniment has pizzicato string notes and short staccato figures in the winds underneath trading slurred eighth notes in the soloists. The soloists begin to incorporate elements of the accompaniment line until it becomes in unison with it. This leads into a new syncopated quarter note triplet motif in the soloists. As this starts to develop it morphs into a variation of the improvisatory-like lines that echo again, which the accompaniment winds begin to echo with a weaving line played on harmonics in the strings. This texture eventually becomes an orchestral interlude of homorhythmic sixteenth note passages. The piece concludes with a return to a variation of the opening material.

This is a three-movement work combining elements of form and structure of neoclassicism with the language of serialism. The first movement “Introduction” is in an allegro risoluto tempo beginning in a stately character in a homorhythmic texture with an instrument occasionally dropping out of the texture. A “meno mosso” section presents a lyrical melody in the oboe overtop of a syncopated ostinato in the clarinet and bassoon. The accompaniment switches to moments of dialogue throughout as it develops and eventually returning to the homorhythmic material again. The second movement “Pastorale” is in an andante tempo that starts with an espressivo bassoon solo in the middle register. As it develops the material becomes more active progressing to sixteenth notes and becoming more contrapuntal. This eventually leads into moments of homorhythm to ground the music. Next, a “Poco tranquillo” section features a lyrical melody in canon for four measures beginning with the clarinet, followed by the bassoon and then only a fragmentation of it in the flute before a tempo primo in a contrapuntal texture. Another “Tranquillo” follows beginning with a homorhythmic introduction leading to a variation of the opening bassoon solo to conclude the movement. The final movement “Rondo” is in an allegro moderato tempo. The A section features repeated staccato eighth notes in the accompaniment that becomes syncopated with rests underneath a quirky melody first in the oboe. Similar to the previous moments this weaves in and out of homorhythmic moments. The B section features fragmented sixteenth note motifs that get passed around the ensemble to create one cohesive line that eventually join together to leave to the C section “Meno mosso” which consists of eighth note motifs weaving in and out of each out slightly overlapping that become more overlap as it develops. The return of the A section has variations such as the accompaniment figure is now two sixteenths followed by an eighth instead of just eighth notes. The movement continues in this manner with contrasting sections that utilize techniques of connecting or overlapping fragments in different characters that lead to either homorhythmic or contrapuntal textures.

description: This work is inspired by a poem written by Ukrainian poet Lesya Ukraina that is about how the desert breathes in the heat while the golden sand stands still and untouched until a wild wind abandones it. The composer utilizes a wide array of extended techniques to explore unconventional timbres, colors and sounds from the flute to emulate nature to paint an image in the listener’s mind. The work begins with delicate extended techniques of the whistle tone to mimic a light breeze. It then adds in a harmonic note and portamento with a dramatic crescendo to intensity for the scene like the wind is whirling around you now. It then develops into using non-Western scales that wander up and down the register of the flute with pitch bending to allow the wind element to always be incorporated into the phrase as a grounding element to the work. This section of the piece continues in this manner while introducing new extended techniques to allow the wind effects to develop and intensify. Eventually, the wind takes over the main role of the section through air effects occurring. As it progresses more of the conventional flute playing sneaks into the phrases beginning as a fragment and expanding over time. This creates a dialogue and argument between the two textures of wind effects and conventional playing representing the imagery of the desert breathing around a protagonist. The work continues in this manner by reworking and fragmenting the opening conventional playing motifs, which are recombined and reimagined in different textures based on the different effects being incorporated. Near the end of the piece the desert fully comes alive as the performer speaks fragments of text from the poem, while the wind effects completely take over engulfing the listener. The desert gives its final command by the performer saying “dyshe” meaning “breathes” in Ukrainian, which is followed by a harmonic sweep and one last reiteration of the word “dyshe” to demonstrate how the wind is the lifeline of the desert. This composer creates a cyclic effect by beginning and ending with the wind effects as a representation of the importance of the wind in the poem, while taking the listener on a journey through the constant development and variation of the various extended techniques incorporated to have the effects be fluid and changing like the wind does.

description: This is a one-movement work in four main sections that utilizes elements from previously presented sections throughout. The opening section features a slow and soft solo line of half notes in the clarinet which the other instruments enter in counterpoint all moving independently. This first part of this section climaxes to a mf dynamic followed by a subito pp chord leading into a chorale-like texture growing louder until a sixteenth note sextuplet motif is introduced in the flute and horn to lead into the second section. This is an unmeasured section with a string of eighth notes in all of the woodwinds with the melodic content rotating around until arriving at a block-like texture of tutti eighth notes. The third section has the ensemble presenting long tones in different pairings exploring the different timbre possibilities in a wind quintet. This leads back into an unmeasured section similar to the previous one, except this time it is quarter notes. This leads into the third main section that is a measured quarter note accompaniment changing between 5/4 and 6/4 underneath moments of cadenza-like playing in the flute that later the horn and clarinet join, which begins to blur the roles in the quintet with all of the parts be of equal value in the counterpoint. The texture continues to intensify through quicken of rhythm and use of frullato. This leads into the final slower section that combines the various elements introduced in the earlier slower into one cohesive idea.

extended_techniques: This is a short one-movement work that showcases different aspects of the bassoon through lyricism, humoresque character, and virtuosity. The title takes inspiration from two meanings 1) the beginning of new life in the spring after winter, and 2) the birth of the composer’s child this past year. The work is structured in three main sections. The first “Cantabile” marked quarter note equals 110 opens with slurred and vocal-like lines that undergo dynamic hairpins that naturally ebb and flow with a quarter note rest between each statement like a dialogue. As the section develops it is intensified through the rests becoming eighth notes creating one long line, while the hairpins are expanded from one-measure units into two-measure units that dynamically now reach a forte. The next section “Piu mosso” marked quarter note equals 120 consists of staccato eighth notes in an ostinato pattern that undergoes variations throughout the section, such as adding a repetition of each note. The final section “Tempo I” opens with a semitone sixteenth note motif that quickly gets expanded into scalar motion in a virtuosic manner. This leads into a short coda that brings back the lyrical character with motifs from the opening only utilizing eighth, quarter, and half notes now. This coda dynamically fades away into a final pianissimo whole note to conclude the work.

description: The inspiration of this piece is depicting the song and character of a nightingale, which is explained in the signature Zuckert wrote on flutist Suzanne Shulman’s copy “To Suzanne Shulman in the hope you'll make this Nightingale come to life through your mastery, with best wishes from Leon Zuckert Toronto, Apr 10-72'.” Musically, this is exemplified through the majority of the material being written in the upper register of the flute and motifs that have bird-like inspiration. The opening of the work “Lento giusto e capriccioso” consists of short fragmented motifs utilizing quick note values such as triplet sixteenths leading to a long note value in the flute which the piano responds to also with short fragments during the flute’s rests. As it progresses the fragments expand into full phases and the texture becomes more contrapuntal, overlapping one another. This section continues in this manner in a very virtuosic display. The next section “Moderato triste” starts with a lyrical melody that very quickly converts into a virtuosic display of thirty-second sextuplets in the upper register of the flute overtop of an intricate and contrapuntal piano accompaniment. Afterwards, a cadenza in the flute occurs borrowing material from the opening. The piano then plays a brief interlude leading into the concluding section “Lentamente” that begins virtuosic in the flute and unwinds to become a simple melody with some fragments in between rests from the piano as dialogue.

description: This is a one movement work inspired by three quotes by Armenian poet and monk Grigor Narekatsi. The first section of the piece is based on a quote about how he offers his heart that is mourning to God for repentance. The second quote is asking for the Lord to hear the silence of his heart that is crying out and desiring mercy. The third quote is asking for the Lord to hear his prayers and to make him whole again through the sacrifice of salvation. The music is an evolution to depict this transformation in the speak. It begins with slow with contrapuntal lines weaving in and out of each other over top of long tones, which often are quarter tones providing an unstable base. It continues to intensify by increasing tempo, thicker textures, and the use of extended techniques. Eventually, the piece climaxes and a chant-like line emerges in the duduk that is joined by the oboe over drones in the other instruments symbolizing the acceptance of the speaker’s fate.

description: This is a short one-movement work with an upbeat dance-like character that has unexpected harmonies throughout to surprise the listener. The main theme of the work is built on groups of either two or six slurred sixteenth notes leading to a staccato eight note. This gives the work a sense of forward momentum with a light and bouncy character. The piano accompaniment has a bass line ostinato in the left hand and chords on the beat in the right hand. At the end of the phrases is a slight ritardando creating a halting quality to the music like depicting a toy dying and needing to be wound up again to be brought back to life. The second time through the theme the piano plays in homorhythm with the theme in the flute providing a harmony underneath. The secondary theme is a string of sixteenth notes oscillating the interval of a semitone that then arpeggiates up to a destination note. The content then undergoes fragmentation in small two beat units that are syncopated by a sixteenth rest. As it progresses these fragments connect together to form a phrase. A return to the main theme returns to conclude the work.

piece_title: Theme & Variations on a Ukrainian Song
published: Muzychna Ukraina (Kyiv 1975) in “Bassoon Repertoire” pno reduction by Andriy Lazarenko
key: Theme, I, II (C major), III (F minor), IV (D minor), V (E major)
description: This is a one-movement work based on a Ukrainian folk song with five variations. Kozytsky’s music follows in the footsteps of Lysenko and other composers who incorporated folk music and nationalistic elements into their music at the end of the nineteenth century. The work opens with a forte drone on C that decrescendos for the bassoon to enter and presents the theme in the tenor register in an andante maestoso tempo. As the melody proceeds the drone chromatically descends until it arrives back at C. The first variation “Piu mosso” opens with the piano playing theme in unison, which leads into a scalar eighth note passage finally receiving harmonization. The bassoon then enters and plays the theme an octave lower than earlier overtop of chords in the piano. The next variation “Allegretto” puts the melody back in the tenor register but ornaments the majority of the notes with a trill, while the piano plays a string of chordal eighth notes. The third variation “Allegro grazioso” switches into f minor and is built on repeated staccato sixteenth notes with a typical piano accompaniment of bass line and offbeats. There is an interlude where the piano takes over the melody with the bassoon briefly playing the melody in minor in the lowest register before returning to the sixteenth motif. The following variation “Andante molto” returns to major tonality with a cantabile line where the melody starts as a pickup rather than on the beat as originally presented. This is overtop of a triplet arpeggiated piano accompaniment. Eventually, a lengthy and virtuosic bassoon cadenza emerges. It features arpeggiated and weaving sixteenth notes that leads to a disjunct eighth note line with grace notes before the upper notes and mordent on the lower notes. A short piano interlude leads into the final variation “Allegro grazioso” in a dance-like character with lively passages of articulated sixteenth notes. The variation continues developing into a poco stringendo to conclude the work.

description: Overall, the piece is structured in a modern re-interpretation of an aria and recitative structure. The first and third movements emulating an aria and the second movement emulating a recitative. This piece consists of three untitled movements differentiated by their tempo marking. The first movement is marked as the eighth note equals 132-138. It alternates being sections that have a constant rhythmic interplay passing between the bassoon and piano, and quasi cadenza-like character imitating an opera sing doing a dramatic vocal flourish, while the orchestra waits to continue on. The second movement marked quarter note equal 72-76 is in a rubato and free character. The piano has simple aleatoric motifs that resemble a tremolo, acting like a basso continuo typical under an opera singer’s recitative. The bassoon has a vocal-like line with notes of unspecified length thrown in throughout. The final movement marked dotted eighth equals 92-96 opens with a bassoon cadenza that develops into a call and response dialogue with the piano creating a texture of one moving line at a time. This is achieved through either only one instrument having moving notes at a time or both instruments in rhythmic unison.
