description: This is a three-movement work with each being dedicated to a different Ukrainian musician that showcases their instrument. The first movement “Larghetto con moto” is dedicated to Ukrainian flutist Volodymyr Turbovsky, principal of the National Opera of Ukraine. It is in ternary form and begins in a contrapuntal texture featuring descending scalar passages, large intervals and grace notes. However, usually one line is always emerging as the solo line creating an effect of a melody being passed around. The B section “Allegretto” has a virtuosic line that passes from the flute to the oboe overtop of accompaniment motifs consisting of a grace note in a large interval to a quarter note. This is interrupted by a long and virtuosic flute cadenza, before returning. The second time it climaxes into a virtuosic disjunct passage of thirty-second notes in the flute. The second movement “Tranquillo comodo e libero assai” is dedicated to Ukrainian oboist Mykola Densov and opens with an oboe cadenza that weaves around in short fragments. Next, a melodic line is presented in the oboe overtop of accompaniment figures with occasional moments of echoing or interjections in the flute and bassoon. The next section “Piu rubato e pastorale” consists of a quirky theme in the oboe through uneven triplets, accents, and grace notes overtop of a drone in the bassoon. Eventually, the flute and bassoon briefly join in a contrapuntal texture before the oboe plays alone to conclude the movement. The third movement “Vivo” is dedicated to Ukrainian bassoonist, Yuri Dondakov, professor at NMAU. Musically, it is in ternary form and features sixteenth notes in large intervals in the bassoon to create an energetic and humoresque character, while the flute and oboe play accompaniment figures that briefly develop into contrapuntal lines. The B section “Lento cantabile” consists of an espressivo line of triplets in the bassoon that the ensemble echoes. For the reprise of the A section there are moments when the ensemble plays the bassoon theme in unison.

description: This is a three movement work centered around the interplay between the flutist and the harpsichordist by exploring different textures and roles the ensemble can create. The first movement “Moderato” begins with the harpsichord presenting the theme with a lilting character due to the quarter followed by an eighth motif that becomes syncopated combined with a dotted eighth followed by two thirty-second notes. The flute responds alone by expanding on the theme’s motifs as it becomes more virtuosic. This leads into long note values in the upper register in the flute while the harpsichord plays the theme. Next, the B section occurs, which consists of a unison line of arpeggiated sixteenth notes that wander around. Afterwards a new theme is presented by the harpsichord which gets expanded upon in a similar manner until a return to the main theme occurs in the flute with longer note values in the harpsichord underneath. The second movement “Tranquillo” consists of a lyrical melody in the flute with an arpeggiated accompaniment in the harpsichord. As the movement progresses both parts become more virtuosic through diminution of the note values in the harpsichord and ornamentation in the flute. The work returns to a calmer and less virtuosic texture to end the movement. The final movement “A Piacere” opens with a repeated note motif in the flute. This develops into short fragmented motifs between the two voices that are constantly responding to one another. The second section of the movement “Allegretto” has a lilting accompaniment in the harpsichord of an arpeggiated eighth note motif that often has the second of three eighth notes in each beat of 9/8 as a rest. The flute has a virtuosic display of mainly sextuplets, which eventually merge into the harpsichord. Finally, a “Recitando” section returning to the opening’s texture returns that gradually introduces virtuosic motifs from throughout to conclude the work.

description: This work consists of three miniatures with no titles given but is differentiated by metronome marking. The first miniature “quarter note equals 70” features a legato and sorrowful melody that develops and grows over lush harmonies. Through this development a variety of different accompaniment textures such as chordal and contrapuntal are explored to change the character. The second miniature “quarter note equals 85” is a humoresque and ironic waltz. The movement opens with a disjointed trading notes texture amongst the ensemble leading to a waltz-like accompaniment in the bassoons that stumbles onto a dissonant semitone fermata chord twice before being able to successfully continue. The violin then joins in with a sneaky melody that weaves around. Eventually, the first bassoon takes over with a second melody overtop of an arpeggiated accompaniment in the second bassoon. The violin then rejoins with a countermelody before returning to the material similar to the original motifs before arriving at an aggressive and accented coda. The third miniature “quarter note equals 220” has an energetic character through the articulated motifs combined with a constant rhythmic pulse of alternating eighth note and quarter notes that is constantly being thrown off due to the alternating pattern of accents and changing meter.

description: This is a three-movement work as a homage to Spanish artist Pablo Picasso who is known as one of the founders of the Cubism movement. This movement rejected traditional techniques such as perspective and foreshortening in favor of emphasizing the flat, two-dimensional surface of the picture’s plane. This created a new reality that depicted radically fragmented objects. (Britannica “Cubism”) The first movement “Lento” begins with long tones in the winds with the texture of the flute beginning the phrase and the bassoon entering on their second note a perfect fifth below and then moving in between each of the flute’s notes in similar motion. Next, the piano enters a semitone a minor ninth above the bassoon creating dissonance. The piano changes into between the two winds creating a canon-like effect. Eventually, the instruments come together in a homorhythmic texture leading to a fermata half note rest. This is followed by a return to the previous canon-like texture with the piano playing cluster chords in voiced in open spacing. The second movement “Allegro moderato” features a disjunct staccato eighth note ostinato in the piano underneath virtuosic passages of sixteenth notes in the winds. Later, the roles reverse between the piano and the winds. Eventually, a more chordal eighth note accompaniment is introduced. As the movement develops the roles continue to change around in different combinations of instrumentation. The final movement is built around a main motif that slowly gets altered throughout. The opening section “Andante” consists of chords in the piano with a one measure motif of two eighth notes leading to a quarter note followed by an eighth and half note in the flute that starts in the middle of the measure. The next section “Adagio” takes the motif being and slightly compresses it by changing the half note to a quarter note to make it into a one measure ostinato in 7/8 spelling out A major, while the flute plays a lyrical melody overtop of it. Eventually, the metre shifts to 8/8 adding a third eighth note to the beginning of the motif. As it develops and the metre changes to 12/8 the motif becomes expanded in the piano, while the bassoon introduces a countermelody consisting of eight notes weaving around. Eventually, the weaving line becomes staccato in the winds and is played overtop of chords in the piano. A return to the “Andante” section occurs to conclude the work.

description: This is a short three-movement work evoking a scenic picture of the fields in Ukraine for the listener through a calm first and third movements with an improvisatory character that is contrasted by a lively virtuosic second movement. The first movement “Andantino” is in ternary form. The A section opens with a theme similar to a vocalist embellishing a melody with melismas that consists of tied longer note that are connected together though thirty-second note flourishes in a scalar motion. Often the tied note is a chromaticism that is unexpected, creating suspense in the phrase leaving the listener wondering where the harmony will head to next. The B section “piu mosso” switches to 6/8 and has a whimsical character that alternates between slurred and staccato articulated sixteenth notes leading to a tied longer note value. A new disjointed phrase is introduced built on fragmentation of arpeggiation through rests inserted and displaced into different octaves. Eventually,it becomes a cohesive string of sixteenth notes. The second movement “Allegretto spirito” has a more dance-like character featuring different arpeggiated motifs that are often in a staccato articulation. As it develops slurred neighbour tone motion is inserted into the theme. The final movement “Andantino” is very similar in character to the first movement. It has a tied long note followed by a string of thirty-second notes in a sequential manner. The music unwinds becoming calmer as the thirty-second notes become sixteenth notes before one final restatement with thirty-second notes to conclude the work.

description: This is a short three-movement suite that showcases the short articulation, lyrical, and technical capabilities of double reeds. The first movement “Allegro vivace” is an energetic staccato movement consisting mainly of repeated eighth notes. This opens with dissonant repeated eighth notes a semitone apart in the oboes, which the bassoon enters with melodic content. Then a more scalar phrase leading into a contrasting section in a fugal texture before returning to the opening material again but with the melodic content in the first oboe. The second movement “Andante” is a slow contrapuntal texture with whole notes and half notes in the oboes combined with a scalar motif of quarter and half notes in the bassoon. The final movement “Con moto” is a moderate tempo with a weaving texture. The oboes trade sixteenth notes often at unexpected times not in a particular pattern overtop of an eighth note accompaniment in the bassoon.

description: This work consists of three short movements in a neoclassical style. The first movement “Scherzetto” opens with an energetic main theme of staccato eighth and slurred sixteenth notes often using arpeggiated motion of large intervals. The piano accompaniment is mostly chordal eighth notes on the beats. The second theme features staccato eighth notes with graces that outline the harmonic progression. A contrasting middle section follows consisting of a lyrical theme composed of dotted quarter, dotted half notes, and the occasional quarter followed by an eighth. The piano plays a constant stream of eighth notes alternating between arpeggiated and scalar motion. The second movement “Elegy” features a lyrical slurred theme in the tenor register of the bassoon. The piano begins accompaniment and develops into a dialogue with the bassoon and eventually a more contrapuntal role with a countermelody. The final movement “Tarantella” is in ternary form featuring an A section with a stream of staccato eighth notes often in scalar motion in the bassoon overtop of accompaniment figures in the piano. The B section “Poco meno mosso” has a lyrical theme that alternates between triple and duple eighth notes in the bassoon overtop of chords in the piano.

description: These three pieces are from a cycle of five works (two additional unaccompanied works) written for bassoon titled The Bassoonist’s Notebook. It was written throughout Runchak’s studies as a student at NMAU, which is dedicated and premiered by his classmate Taras Osadchiy. This is a three-movement work centered around the concept of contrasting characters throughout. The first movement “Improvvisazione” features a semitone motif based around D flat that develops through dialogue between the piano and bassoon, which later returns throughout the other movements. The work begins with a hyperchromatic piano introduction, presenting a solo chromatic line with minimal motion that gradually carves out motific space by expanding the material to reach an arrival. This arrival at the minor third interval of the pitches “E♭” to “C” becomes an important interval that Runchak uses to tie structural elements throughout the work together, such as to interrupt the rhythmic motif consisting of sixteenth, dotted sixteenth thirty second and tied sixteenths that is being established in the first movement. The movement continues in this dialogue that allows the motif to expand further outwards eventually resulting in the bassoon playing a glissando to the highest possible note they can play. The following movement “Burlesca” is a fast, articulated movement that resembles a dance that gets thrown off constantly by the changing metrical emphasis from the constantly changing meters. This movement is constantly switching between rhythmic motifs of two versus three eighth notes in the bassoon achieved through alternation between 6/8 and 5/8 metres. However, an ambiguity is inserted into the phrasing with the piano’s right hand playing five equal eighth notes slurred together in one connected line that blurs the emphasis of the larger alternating beats. This intentional ambiguity and playing with time continues developing as it becomes a line of quarter notes (or tied eighth notes) in the piano’s right hand and a syncopated line in the left hand. Throughout this movement the development of the sections is achieved through an increasing and organized chaos by having the phrases begin as small fragments, often in a homorhythmic and monophonic texture, but slowly introduces elements to the phrase that adds up over time until it has nowhere further to go and climaxes suddenly at the moment of peak chaos allowing for a restart of the material or introduction of new material. The final movement “Dialogo” features slow monologue-like phrases based on a dotted eighth and sixteenth note rhythmic motif alternating between the bassoon and piano. The movement opens with a cantabile line based around the motif from the opening of the work that expands outwards in the solo bassoon. The piano then provides a brief interlude of new material allowing the bassoon to attempt the opening material again. The movement continues in this manner until the piano concludes with their final interlude dying away.

This is a three-movement that belongs to a collection of works for solo woodwinds. The first movement is structured by a couple main sections with material that returns briefly. The opening section “Allegro moderato” is a virtuosic display beginning with a septuplet sixteenth note flourish. It continues to weave around the range of the instrument in a wide array of rhythmic variety. The next section “Allegro” is a passage of sequential sixteenth notes alternating between half and whole tone steps. The following section “Allegro giocoso” is a playful character of staccato eighth and sequential sixteenth notes. A “Poco tranquillo” section in the low register of the bassoon consisting of fragmented motifs in a dynamic swell leads back to a brief restatement of the opening material that returns to tranquillo material to conclude the movement. The second movement “Andante” is a lyrical melody that becomes more active as it develops with quicker note values and ornamentation supplemented in. When the opening material returns again it undergoes rhythmic augmentation. The final movement “Allegretto” is in ternary form. The A section is energetic and syncopated demonstrating a virtuosic display of technique and articulation through sixteenth notes with various rests inserted. The B section “Meno mosso - tranquillo” consists of a vocal-like melody that becomes more disjunct as it develops.

description: This is a three-movement work centered around the pitch “F”, in which each movement depicts a certain psychological condition of the individual in their interaction with society. The first movement “Andante” has a peculiar philosophical reflection that is reflecting the loneliness of an individual. It opens with a bassoon solo in an espressivo and parlando rubato character where the melody continually returns to fermatas on the pitch “F”. Eventually, the piano enters on this pitch in a dissonance to the bassoon playing a “G”. The two musicians continue in dialogue playing quasi-improvised lines with moments of almost unifying such as the bassoon and left-hand of the piano playing an “F” but the right hand playing a G instead. The movement concludes in a cluster chord around the pitch “F” as commentary on the loneliness one can experience in society despite even being surrounded by others in public. The second movement “Allegretto” is a protest against an aggressive environment and attempts to find a compromise. Texturally, this movement features sections that alternate between a constant and often repeated eighth notes with a changing accent pattern contrasted with quasi-improvised lines that are virtuosic in nature such as arpeggiation or scalar motion. These two characters are in argument throughout, often interrupting one another as the musicians search to find the pitch “F” again. One of the sections is marked “bluesy” and is reminiscent of an improvised saxophone jazz solo with extended techniques such as pitch bending into notes utilized. The movement concludes with a resolution being found through both musicians playing six unison “F” eighth notes. The final movement “Moderato” displays the everyday doubts and hesitations of an individual, which leaves them without answers. Thus, in such a manner the cycle ends as if it is a question mark. Musically, it opens with a weaving sixteenth note line in the piano that has an ominous character, which the bassoon takes over mid-way. This sixteenth motif passes around in different variations throughout the movement. As this motif develops it is often interrupted by a short “Larghetto” homorhythmic section leading to a restart of the ideas like a person contemplating something and their thoughts jumping around while they attempt to make a decision. The final Larghetto section is a dialogue instead with the piano playing ascending syncopated chords, similar to the motif in the other larghettos. This hands off to the bassoon that plays a variation of the weaving sixteenth motif leading to a whole note on the pitch “G” with the piano entering a beat later on a low F in the left hand to conclude the piece without a final resolution.

description: This is a three-movement vocal cycle based on poems by Ukrainian poet Lina Kostenko who was a member of the literary movement “Shistdesiatnyky” (The Sixtiers) during Krushchev’s de-stalinization period. A characteristic of these authors was a renewal of poetic forms, and subjects that included realistic depictions free of the constraints of socialist realism. Kostenko’s poetry often contains intimate and lyricism that discuss social issues such as living in a totalitarian society through diverse rhythms, sophisticated language, a colloquial manner of writing, and a subtle emotivity.86 The first movement “Tsey lis zhyvyi” (This forest is alive) has a texture of controlled aleatoric in the piano underneath a melody in the soprano that is mostly scalar or arpeggiated motion with the occasional large interval. The flute and bassoon provide an accompaniment role often longer note values providing harmonic support or fragmented motifs echoing the vocal line during rests or longer note values. The next movement “Paporot’” (Fern) features ostinato figures that develop in the instruments such as a major fifth interval over two quarter notes in the left hand of the piano, a dotted half note followed by a quarter note on a low E in the bassoon, and a three repeated staccato eighth notes leading to an interval usually major third, perfect fifth or major sixth. The vocal melody incorporates these elements by beginning the phrase with a perfect fifth on the same notes “E” to “B” being played in the piano motif. As the movement develops the material begins to combine together such as the bassoon incorporating the perfect fifth interval, while also adding variations to their ostinato patterns. The final movement “Poslukhayu tsey doshch” (I will listen to this rain) with an accompaniment texture of a constant line of eighth notes that passes around the ensemble with chords in the piano. A middle interlude section where the winds play a more cantabile and lyrical line occurs before a return to the opening melody in the soprano. However, the accompaniment texture changes to a two sixteenth and eighth note ostinato in the right hand of the piano with a countermelody line in the winds. Eventually, the winds take over as the soprano finishes their text and the piano part becomes a constant line of sixteenth notes to conclude the work.

description: This piece includes three untitled movements differentiated by their tempo marking. The first solo has no tempo marking written in a very free and improvisatory style. There is a contrasting ad lib. frullato section on long notes played in the performer’s desired length.

description: This is a three-movement work in a folklorist style using elements from Ukrainian fairy tales as inspiration behind the character of each movement. The first movement “Fairy Clock” is in a moderato tempo opening with the main motif of the movement of descending quarter notes first an octave followed by diminished fifth that are two slurred and two tongued, which leads into the second motif of three eighth notes. It first appears as three repeated notes beginning on the beat but gets transformed to become a syncopated ascending chromatic line. It then continues to undergo various variations throughout the movement. Often the bassoon has bass line figures that feature elements from the main motif but in different variations such as ascending. The movement continues by providing variations on these motifs with the introduction of new material such as arpeggiated eigth notes in the clarinet. The next movement “Music Box” is in an andantino tempo and opens with a contrapuntal texture. It features a lyrical melody with moments of humoresque with staccato eighth notes in the oboe, a playful ostinato consisting of two slurred sixteenths leading to two eighth notes, and a syncopated bass line in the bassoon. This develops into the bassoon taking over the lyrical melodic role, while the oboe and clarinet play the rhythmic ostinato on a repeated note creating a more march-like character. Eventually, a return to the opening material and texture occurs with some variation in the melody by ornamentation of sixteenth notes in the line. This leads into an oboe cadenza in an improvisatory manner leading to a long note, in which the clarinet and bassoon play one final statement of their opening material underneath to conclude the movement. The final movement “Buffoonery” is in an allegro tempo with a Rondo form. It opens with the same texture of the previous movement. The oboe has the melodic material that switches between lyrical and energetic staccato passages overtop of quarter notes in the clarinet and a bass line in the bassoon. The next section consists of fragmented eighth notes that trade between the instruments to create a larger cohesive line. A return to the opening material occurs with some more material added in the clarinet accompaniment line. Next, another contrasting section occurs with more fragmentation of material such as two slurred sixteenth notes combining together in a energetic character. Eventually, the fragments create a full passage by leading to staccato eighth note between each of them. The next contrasting section has a lyrical melodic line in the oboe overtop of the three-note repeated motif from earlier in the work in the clarinet and quarter notes on beats one and three in the bassoon. This develops into a syncopated rhythmic ostinato in the clarinet and bassoon. The following contrasting section utilizes fragmentation of material again. The final contrasting section combines elements from the past sections together creating a synthesis of the material to set up the final A section leading to a short six-measure coda to conclude the work.

description: The piece is based on two musical cryptograms surrounding the bassoon 1) BASS (B♭-A-E♭-E♭) and 2) FAG (F-A-G) short for fagotto. The piece opens with an Andante section introducing the first cryptogram in the bassoon with a chordal accompaniment in the piano. This is then developed as the motif becomes more complex and texture in the piano intensifies and thickens through constantly changing meters leading into an Allegro section. This section features a winding triplet sixteenth passage juxtaposed with the short second cryptogram, with the roles trading between the bassoon and piano throughout. Eventually, a cluster glissando in the piano leads into a “doppio piu mosso” section that is an energetic dance-like section that is a constantly shifting 3 versus 2 note grouping. description: This is a dramatic work that explores the role that the performer has and its connection to the audience. The performance begins with the performer off stage, which after 10-12 seconds enter. The performer then continues playing while moving clockwise around the outside and eventually inside of four dividers that have been placed on stage creating an enclosed space for the performer to interact with. The score is organized by having letter and roman numeral markers that correspond with a guide of where the performer should be standing to perform each segment. Eventually this climaxes into a moment where the performer performs a kind of ritual involving dissembling the flute and lifting it above their head. This is followed by the performer improvising on just the headjoint. The work then concludes with the performer going into the hall with the audience before leaving. Musically, the segments each vary drastically from one another creating a new character for each new location that the performer is at. However, a common recurring motif of a whole note smorzato emerges from the texture often to tie things back together. Eventually this motif is contrasted and becomes in dialogue with a similar motif that utilizes the use of tongue rams to experiment with the different tonal qualities possible on the flute. As the work progresses the material becomes more virtuosic to achieve the climax of the work. Afterwards, it returns to a simpler texture of the smorzato motif. The end of the work imitates a bamboo flute through the use of special fingerings and whistle tones before the final ritual and improvisation as the performer leaves. Throughout the work the concept of silence and how an audience interprets is explored by the use of pauses between segments, the use of exhaling and inhaling instead of playing, and walking to different points to continue playing the following segment.

description: This is a short one-movement work that explores the role the bassoon can have with a string ensemble by creating a wide variety of textures. The piece begins with an “Andante pensieroso” section consisting of staggered entrances of tied whole notes passing around the ensemble that builds up harmonies. Eventually, the bassoon plays a vocal-like line consisting of stepwise and small intervals of a third or fourth. The ensemble begins responding in a polyphonic texture leading into the next section “Meno mosso” that features a descending chromatic line of quarter notes overtop of whole note tremolos. The following section “Con brio” is comprised of a constant stream of sixteenth notes in an ostinato that slowly changes over time. The motif first begins in the second violins with the first violins joining in after four measures. This is overtop of a pedal note on the pitch “E” in the cello and an Alberti bass line in the violas. Eventually, the bassoon enters with a motif of four sixteenth notes leading to an eighth note based around the perfect fourth interval that moves in sequential motion. This develops into a quarter note line and eventually half notes that the rest of the ensemble joins in creating a more chordal texture the cello continues the sixteenth note passage. As it progresses the sixteenths change pattern consisting of oscillating intervals switching between perfect fourth, fifth and major third. Throughout this section the bassoon switches between the roles of providing a pedal point in the low register and more melodic quarter note lines. This section crescendos and climaxes into a final fortissimo E major chord (missing the fifth) to conclude the work.

description: This suite is originally written for a klezmer ensemble with it initially being adapted for the concert hall for violin and clarinet, and later for two bassoons or two clarinets. It includes five movements that elements of klezmer music and extended techniques such as frullato, glissando, and pitch bending to emulate this traditional style. The first movement “March” is a quick, articulated and energetic character where the two bassoons weave in and out of another overtop of a mostly chordal accompaniment piano part. The second movement “Nigun” is a traditional wordless song sung as a means of elevating the soul to God, which often has a solo line that is then repeated in unison and usually quite free in rhythm. In this movement, the first bassoon mostly plays a lyrical melodic line over an accompaniment piano part with the second bassoon joining into the first’s line throughout. The movement climaxes into a short middle tango section before returning to a short reprise of the melody before a first bassoon cadenza to arrive at a short coda to end it. The third movement “Grandmother’s Song” is an adagio that opens with the first bassoon playing a sentimental melody over chords in the piano. Eventually, the second bassoon enters as an echo of the first part type of response to represent a child singing along with their grandmother. The fourth movement “Jewish Tango” is an energetic dance that opens with the first bassoon playing a solo very typical klezmer type melody with rhythmic chords in the piano. Eventually, the second bassoon joins in harmony while playing rhythmic unison of the first. The rest of the movement continues in this fashion with the odd contrapuntal moment between the two parts. There is a small cadenza in the first part near the end. The final movement “Klezmer’s Polka” is in a similar style and structure of the previous movement, except the second bassoon has more independence of part with more contrapuntal writing throughout.

description: This is a suite with eight short movements with direct quotations from Treny-Laments I. The first and sixth movements have no title or character marking. However, it has been given a metronome marking. The first movement “quarter equals 56” is almost identical to Treny-Laments I with three new inserted measures throughout (measures 5 and 8-9) and measure 7 reduced from an 8/4 to a 7/4 measure with the last beat omitted. The second movement “In memoriam Borys Lyatoshynsky” is identical to the fifth movement of Treny-Laments I. The third movement “In memoriam Larysa B.” is identical to the second movement of Treny-Laments and then continues on for eighth more measures that are more virtuosic and cadenza-like. The fourth movement “In memoriam Lidia B.” is identical to the third movement of Treny-Lament I with the final six notes omitted. The fifth movement “Molto agitato” is original material with a very free and virtuosic character with flourishing runs and accelerando beam repeated notes. The sixth movement “Tempo guisto” is original material in a cadenza-like manner consisting of various large arpeggiated and scalar passages. The seven movement “capriccioso e con anima (molto ritmico)”is identical to Treny-Laments I fourth movement. The final movement “Envoi in memoriam Bruce A.” is original material that utilizes material similar to fourth movement evolving into a final arpeggio to a high Ab that is instructed to be held as long as possible ideally achieved through circular breathing that dies away to niente into seven seconds of silence.

description: This is a three-movement work in an atonal, avant-garde style that has motivic material derived from trichord set often using 013, 014, and 015. Three key features throughout the work are the constant meter shifts, two staff style writing and disjunct large interval lines. The switching between the staves denote a polyphonic and contrapuntal manner to the music. The first movement “Inscriptions” is marked in a moderato tenebroso tempo. This movement is based around large intervals that cover the entire range of the bassoon utilizing mainly sixteenth, triplet eighths and sixteenths, quarter, dotted quarters throughout. The second movement “In Accordance” is in a sostenuto aggiustamente tempo that features a repeated sixteenth note motif throughout. It is contrasted with sections of large intervals and shorter, more melodic fragments. Rhythmically, this movement and the final movement are much simpler mainly consisting of eighth, quarter, and sixteenth notes. The final movement “Balletto” is in a lesto grazioso tempo that is centered around the minor ninth interval.

description: This is a three-movement work inspired by medieval and renaissance music combined with elements of modernism. The first movement “Praeludium” begins with each instrument playing their own line in a cantus-firmus style in staggered entrance that develops into a homorhythmic texture. Eventually, the oboe gets a more soloistic role playing a motif of repeated notes on the pitch “A” combined with fragmented arpeggios that develops into a quasi-cadenza like moment. This returns to a brief section of homorhythmic texture before the flute plays quick flourishes of runs overtop of long tones in the oboe and bassoon. The second movement “Intermedius” begins with a flute solo featuring the repetition of a long note tied to triplets with a grace note motif. Eventually, the bassoon takes this motif over playing it solo. As the bassoon is playing this figure the oboe enters with a virtuosic counterpoint. This eventually leads to a section where all three instruments are in dialogue playing a variation of this virtuosic line. Finally, a section of staggered entry of repeated articulated arpeggios occurs before a grand pause, which takes us back to the original motif to end the movement. The final movement “Cantus” a cantus-firmus line that is displaced through large interval jumps transformed into different characters through three main sections. First, a 5:4 sixteenth note motif that gets traded around the ensemble. Then an articulated repeated note arpeggio that gets traded around the ensemble. Finally, thirty-second notes in descending scalar passage played in unison rhythm concludes the work by gradually becoming a slower rhythmic value over time.

description: This is a one movement work that is structured as a theme with seven variations. The opening theme “Morendo” presents the theme in the clarinet consisting of mainly eighth, quarter, half, and dotted half notes. The violin and bassoon provide accompaniment support underneath with short rhythmic motifs. The first variation “Moderato” rhythmically augments and adds virtuosic ornamentation such as sixteenth note sextuplets to the theme played by the violin. The clarinet plays a syncopated ostinato on a repeated pitch, while the bassoon plays the occasional bass note. The next variation “Allegro animato” has a contrapuntal texture with elements of theme weaving between the instruments, while it alternates character from a playful staccato character to lyrical legato. The following variation “Cantabile” turns the theme in a vocal-like line that passes around the ensemble overtop of an arpeggiated eighth note line. Eventually, a syncopated bass line is introduced in the bassoon after its turn at the melody and accompaniment line. Variations four through six have no description marking, but a metronome marking is provided. The fourth variation marked quarter note equals 100-110 turns the theme into triplets in an arpeggiated manner in the clarinet and violin overtop of accompaniment figures in the bassoon. The next variation is marked quarter note equals 70-80, which fragments the theme combining elements together in different combinations. The following variation is marked quarter note equals 80-90 consisting of the theme being passed around by each instrument only playing a couple of the notes at a time before passing off to another. It is also in a more disjunct and staccato character. The final variation “Allegro non troppo” brings back elements from throughout the work such as the syncopated repeated note line combining them once last time to conclude the work.

description: This is a three-movement work that combines elements of neoclassicism and avant-garde by utilizing extended key areas and a method of anagram development, which consists of the repetitions with permutations of its components. The first movement “Toccata” is in an allegretto leggiero tempo that features a repeated staccato sixteenth note motif that gets repeated and passed around the ensemble. As the movement develops it gets recombined with different textures such as trading off, while undergoing slight variations such as becoming tenuto eighth notes. The next movement “Quasi notturno” is in an Andantino molto tranquillo tempo and opens with a homorhythmic passage of quarter and half notes in the flute and bassoon that alternates between dissonant and consonant intervals each note of the phrase. The piano enters with a bass line figure of longer note values moving in step wise motion at the top of the treble clef staff in the right hand. As it develops the bass line becomes larger intervals. Eventually, the piano becomes echoes of the melodic content in the winds to conclude the movement. The final movement “Passacaglia” is in an Allegro moderato tempo, ben misurato following the form of a passacaglia. The movement opens up with a dance-like melody in the lowest register of the piano. This continues to be repeated as the voices enter independently in a contrapuntal texture first with the bassoon followed by the piano’s right hand, and then the flute. As it progresses the tonality becomes more ambiguous with more uses of dissonances and cluster chords. This leads into an “Irato” section featuring a bass line of long note values in the left hand and arpeggiated eighth notes in the right hand of the piano underneath the opening melody in the flute and bassoon. The work concludes with a “Postludio” section that consists of a passage of disjointed eighth notes in the piano leading into an aleatoric section lasting around 17 seconds to conclude the work.

premiere: 1986 in Kyiv by soloists of the Kyiv Camerata
description: This is a one-movement work consisting of various short sections and character changes. The opening is a “Rubato allegretto” that consists of a drone in the bassoon underneath an arpeggiated melody in the clarinet. The next section “Allegretto” is an arpeggiated motif in the piano with the same drone as previous in the bassoon. The third section is an expansion of the melody in the clarinet of the opening section with a drone in the bassoon and piano. The fourth section “Allegretto doloroso” brings back the arpeggiated motif from earlier and expands upon it. Eventually, the bassoon responds with a syncopated motif leading into the clarinet and bassoon taking over the arpeggiated motif together. This progresses into the piano re-entering and introducing a new sort of scalar-like motif, which the clarinet begins to switch between the original and imitating the sixteenths. The next section “cantabile” is a contrapuntal duet between the clarinet and bassoon that is interrupted by marcato sixteenths in the piano. After the second cantabile statement both parts are combined together. The next section “Allegro ma non troppo” brings back the syncopated bassoon motif from the “Allegretto doloroso” that is expanded into a full phrase that the piano and clarinet respond to that eventually comes together in an accented eighth note passage leading into another “Rubato allegretto” that this time has dialogue between the clarinet and bassoon. Then an “Allegretto doloroso” that brings back all of the previous motifs that leads into the final section of the piece. It is a “Rubato moderato” consisting of long tones in the clarinet and bassoon and a disjointed melody in the piano.

description: This is a three-movement work written at the end of her career that combines many different elements of her stylistic elements throughout her life. Musicologist Stefania Pavlyshyn describes that the work “combines neoclassical style with the rigidity of quasi-serial thematism” (Pavlyshyn, 53) with stylistic elements “reminiscent of Schoenberg’s third quartet”(ibid) that “emphasizes the rigidity of textured linearity, which is typical especially, for Hindemith in his “Chamber Music” [Kammermusik].”(ibid) Turkewich also utilizes idioms from an expressionism style through “continuous chromatic harmony”(ibid) with “an emphasis on colorism, even on endearing harmonious colors”(ibid) combined with a “characteristic connection of Turkewich’s works with Ukrainian folklore.”(ibid) through her use of folkloric materials, especially dance elements. The first movement “Moderato” is structured around short sections that contrast characters. It begins with a tutti virtuosic quintuplet passage in a vivo tempo leading into a sostenuto consisting of bassoon solo. The clarinet and flute re-entering independently creating a contrapuntal texture. This continues developing until a virtuosic nonuplet passage in the flute emerges. This leads into a repeated sixteenth with grace note motif before a thirty-second descending sequential passage concludes the section. The next section “Meno mosso” features a vocal-like theme using chromaticism in 5/4 that switches between 3+2 and 2+3 note groupings. The clarinet followed by the bassoon enter in a canon texture. As this section develop the lines become more and more virtuosic until material from the opening vivo returns to interrupt the section. A short variation reprise of the meno mosso material occurs. The following section “Andante mysterioso” features rhythmic dissonance with a quarter note bass line with chromaticism in the bassoon competes against 5:4 eighth notes. Eventually, this develops in triplet eight notes against duple eighth notes. Near the end of the section the ensemble becomes rhtyhmically consonant with sixteenth, quarter, and eighth notes. The next section “affetuoso” is mostly homorhythmic with material that either weaves around or large intervals. This becomes a passage of articulated sixteenths that repeats two notes before changing often using chromatic harmony. The following section “Stretto” is a canon with a quirky theme that leads into the vivo material to conclude the movement. The second movement “Adagio” begins with a disjunct theme in the clarinet with the bassoon entering with a contrapuntal line. The flute enters as it switches to a homorhythmic texture that leads into a virtuosic passage of disjunct sextuplet sixteenth notes. Eventually, it becomes a quasi-improvisatory cadenza in the flute and clarinet in homorhythm but switching between consonant and dissonant intervals, which the flute emerges to finish the cadenza alone. A return to the opening disjunct material then occurs with new variations and development. This leads into a 9/8 section where the flute and clarinet are in a triple grouping while the bassoon begins in duple note groupings creating a rhythmic dissonance that becomes triple note groupings to create a rhythmic consonance that leads to homorhythm. The flute and clarinet harmonically switch between consonant and dissonant intervals as well creating more tension. A short fragment of the opening occurs solo in the clarinet to conclude the movement. The final movement “Allegro” is in ternary form. This features a repeated eighth note motif that expands into an active and syncopated line of eight, sixteenth and tied eighth notes played in a canon texture. New motifs that are more disjunct are introduced as the section progresses, while the texture alternates between canon-like and homorhythmic passages. Eventually, this leads into a texture of a quasi-flute cadenza with tutti interruptions from the clarinet and bassoon. A repeated sixteenth note passage that moves in chromatic harmony leads to a short bassoon cadenza overtop of trills in the flute and clarinet. The B section titled “Andante” is structured around little fragmented solos and tutti homorhythmic passages that leads into a virtuosic cadenza that alternates between the bassoon and flute and clarinet together consisting of thirty-second sextuplets in a chromatic contrary motion. The cadenzas are overtop of tremolos. This leads into a homorhythmic and calmer passage to end the section. A sixteenth note sextuplet leads into a reprise of the A section with variations.

description: This is a three-movement work in a similar style and aesthetic as the wind quintet. The first movement “Sostenuto” begins with a dialogue between the piano and winds alternating roles between a theme and accompaniment figures often longer note values. As it develops the theme becomes more virtuosic and extended. The texture changes from the winds playing the main theme in homorhythm to bassoon playing the arpeggiated bass line originally presented in the left hand of the piano. The next main section takes a scalar thirty-second note passage and passes it around the ensemble in quick succession creating a longer cohesive line. The following section “Allegro” is a virtuosic display of weaving thirty-second notes in the winds overtop of accompaniment figures in the piano, which eventually joins into the winds texture. This eventually develops into a contrapuntal texture climaxing into a moment of rhythmic dissonant where each line is playing a different rhythmic value in contrary motions: 1) thirty-seconds, 2) thirty-second quintuplets, 3) sixteenth note triplets, and 4) sixty-fourths, which ends abruptly. A return to the “Sostenuto” material occurs with new variations in the development. The second movement “Larghetto” begins with a vocal-like melody overtop of a syncopated cluster chord ostinato. Eventually, the bassoon enters with a countermelody. The material develops with the introduction of short aleatoric moments that leads into a virtuosic flute cadenza traversing around the range of the instrument in a sequential manner. A return to the opening material occurs to conclude the movement. The final movement “Allegro scherzando” consists of staccato eighth notes in an energetic character that pass around the ensemble that merge together for moments of tutti playing. Occasional virtuosic solo lines emerge overtop of the texture as little interjections. The movement takes the material and variates it by different textures such as more dialogue-like passages, becoming more active with quicker note values, and changing the time between fragments. It also brings back motifs and textures reminiscent of earlier movements. The movement ends with a final “Presto” section consisting of one last final display of virtuosity leading into trills that become repeated eighth notes that crescendo to conclude the work.

description: This is a three-movement work utilizing elements typical of Avidom’s style. The first movement in ternary form. The A “Andante un poco sostenuto” consists of a melody mainly of eighth, quarter, and half notes utilizing lots of grace notes in the oboe overtop of accompaniment figures in the clarinet and bassoon. The B “Allegro” is a contrapuntal texture of mostly eighth and quarter notes with the occasional longer note value or tied note. As it develops it becomes more rhythmically complex with the introduction of triplet eighth, dotted quarter, dotted eighth, and half notes. The return of the A material is only the second half of the phrase. The second movement “Adagio” features a vocal-like theme that passes around the ensemble in a solo texture that gradually adds in other lines. It develops into a canon of this theme to conclude the movement. The final movement is in ternary form also. The A section “Vivo e leggiero” features an energetic dance-like theme consisting of quarter and eighth notes in a canon texture, which develops into a homorhythmic texture that becomes contrapuntal. The B section “Quasi lento” takes the theme in a contrapuntal texture but now more lyrical and legato.

description: This is a three-movement work with text in old French from three poems by Charles d’Orleans for soprano. Charles d’Orleans was a medieval poet and the Duke of Orleans, who took over after his father’s assassination. On his mother’s deathbed Charles swore a traditional oath of vengeance for his father’s murder. Then after the French-English war he was imprisoned by the English for 24 years. It was during this period that the majority of his poetry was written. The first movement “Priez pour paix, dolce Vierge Marie” is in an andantino tempo is a prayer for peace where the speaker asks the Virgin Mary to bring them peace through the redemption of His blood to grant the end of war, which is ruining everything. Musically, it opens with a flute cadenza with rubato overtop of a cluster chord spaced in opening voicing in the piano. Then the piano introduces an ostinato figure of repeated triplet eighths and duple eighths marked “Chistko” (Evenly). The soprano then enters with the text and melodic content. This is in a dialogue with the flute and bassoon responding at the end of the first phrase. As it progresses the lines between the voice and winds become more interwoven and contrapuntal overtop of chords in the right hand of the piano and the ostinato in the left hand. This texture continues until the end of the movement. The second movement “La temps a laissie son manteau” in an andante tempo. The text is a poem in rondeau form using a repetition of the opening line throughout. It is about the transition from winter to spring and the beauty one encounters and experiences during this process. I believe this could be an analogy for the joy that will come when experiencing freedom from imprisonment and war. Musically, the melody in the voice begins on a repeated pitch “A” that opens up gradually becoming stepwise into larger intervals, mainly the perfect fourth and fifth. The ensemble plays an accompaniment role. The piano mostly plays sweeping arpeggiations leading to chords. Initially, the flute responds to the voice’s melody during rests that becomes a countermelody. The bassoon then enters to take it over, while the flute plays animato ascending trills on dotted quarter notes to create a more energetic and excited character to the music. The bassoon then shifts to an accompaniment role of dotted quarter and dotted half notes as it progresses allowing the flute to return to the countermelody role to conclude the movement. The final movement “Presto” has a lively and dance-like character. The piano plays arpeggiated eigth notes throughout the entire movement however the pattern changes for each section. The flute and bassoon often respond with little motifs during rests and longer note values in the soprano’s line. As the movement develops the wind parts develop into their own contrapuntal lines until they take over for the final coda once the soprano concludes the text.

description: All of Solonskiy’s works are written with a pedagogical purpose in mind to be applied in a concert setting. Each of the pieces were written for a particular student of his to address their particular challenges in their playing. He chooses to use characters from folklore and fairytales to make them approachable and easily understood by the student allowing them to bring their own imagination, emotions and moods into the music based on characters they are familiar with. His goal is to comprehensively reveal the beauty and expressiveness of woodwind instruments through the color, technical, and artistic capabilities. This is a short one-movement work in a folkloristic style with stylistic elements from klezmer. The bassoon part is completely in tenor clef and would be a good educational piece for assisting in a student’s fluency of reading tenor clef. It opens with a “Grandioso bellicoso” section in a quasi-improvised character of a theme that consists of arpeggiated triplets that is first played by the piano alone and then the bassoon overtop of a chord in the piano. The next section “Scherzando” features an energetic and dance-like character. It consists of a melody of two eighth notes followed by a rest than four eighth notes followed by a rest that develops into a virtuosic passage of articulated triplet eighth notes overtop of accompaniment figures in the piano. Then an “Allegretto” section opens with the piano presenting a new eight measure theme, which the bassoon takes over, which prompts the piano to switch to accompaniment figures. This is followed by a “Nobile, serioso” section that consists of legato and vocal-like melody in the bassoon while the piano continues the Allegretto theme. Eventually, a return to the Allegretto returns that develops into a virtuosic display of a sequential sixteenth note passage in the bassoon. The piece continues bringing back the various themes and motifs developing into slightly different variations.

description: This is a one-movement work in three main sections. The first section opens with an ostinato of alternating eighth notes between the pitches “B♭'' and “C” in the left hand with isolated sixteenth note shots in the right hand. Eventually, the bassoon enters with rapid movement in which all the virtuoso possibilities of the modern bassoon are revealed. The second section is in a meditative character with a quiet singing quality through the long cantabile line in the bassoon overtop of the syncopated interjections of the piano. The final section is a stormy, concert finale that unites the main ideas of the first and second sections. It utilizes long rolled chords in the piano underneath the alternating eighth note motif from the opening now in the bassoon. However, this time the motif is very soft and staccato with rests interrupting the phrase to have the motif become shorter and more fragmented as each new statement appears until arriving at tied whole note Bb to conclude the piece.

key: I (Eb major), II (G minor), III (F major), IV (Eb major), V (A minor), VI (F minor), VII (G major), VIII (none used), IX (D minor), X (none used), XI (Ab major), XII (G major)
description: This work consists of 12 short movements each around thirty seconds in a contrasting style and character. Pedagogically, a selection of these could be good for addressing particular issues of an individual student for improvement in their playing. The first movement “Festivo” marked Moderato poco estaticamente is centered around a motif of ascending triplet eighth notes that alternate between stepwise motion and small intervals of a third, fourth and fifth. In between statements of this motif are eighth notes followed by an eighth rest or seven eighth notes in various patterns to bridge together a cohesive phrase. The next movement “Con Minuetto” marked Allegretto innocente has a lilting rhythmic feel featuring a motif of four sixteenths leading to two eighth notes. As the movement develops the strings of sixteenths elongated into a whole weaving scalar passage to conclude the movement. The following movement “Canzonettta” marked Andantino has a legato melody that has a quarter or half note tied over to smaller note values in various rhythmic subdivisions of duple eighths, triple eighths, and sixteenth notes that proceed in stepwise motion leading to a large interval leap. Dynamically the music swells to create a wave-like effect. The fourth movement “Tango Piccolo” marked Con fuoco has a fiery dance-like character from the syncopated rhythms used. Rhythmically, the movement consists of eighth and quarter notes with the occasional sixteenth note flourishes. The fifth movement “Mazurka” marked Grazioso has an elegant and stately character featuring a dotted eighth followed by a sixteenth motif that ascends upwards the flute’s register throughout. This gets contrasted with triplet eighth notes. The proceeding movement “Elegia” marked Triste has a sorrowful and nostalgic character featuring a lyrical and vocal-like melody consisting of eighth, quarter, half and dotted rhythms. The following movement “Movement” marked Con moto is a virtuosic and energetic display of staccato eighth notes leading to a beat of slurred eighth notes. The next movement “Humoresque” marked Con malizia has a quirky character for the alternating of 2+3 and 3+2 note groupings created by the 5/8 meter and the occasional meter change to 6/8 and 7/8 to throw off the pattern. Rhythmically, the movement mainly consists of eighth notes with the occasional longer note value and two sixteenth note pick-ups. Musically, the theme jumps constantly changing the intervals used in the pattern. The ninth movement “Lamento” marked Lagrimoso has a mournful character through a melodic line that features slurred arpeggiated eighth notes leading to a longer note value, which the intervals get longer as it develops to become more dramatic. The next movement “Scherzino” marked Burlando has a joking character through the use of trilled quarter notes throughout followed by little motifs of staccato eighth notes or slurred sixteenth notes. The penultimate movement “Serenade” marked Sensibile features a motif of a dotted eighth note followed by a sixteenth and an eighth often leading to a quarter note and an eighth note. Throughout the melodic content of the motif changes around intervals going between being compact and disjointed. The final movement “Finale” marked Allegro poco dramatico is a virtuosic display of technique with flourishes of sixteenth notes leading to accented sforzando eighth notes. The passage gets fragmented while each statement getting shorter and softer until achieving one note at pianissimo dynamic to conclude the work.

description: This work consists of two short movements each marked “Allegro” with a different pedagogical element that is focused upon. The first focuses on achieving an evenness of articulation across the register and intervals of the flute. The theme is built on a sequence of four arpeggiated staccato eighth notes that begins with an interval that gets expanded larger as it progresses, which is followed by stepwise motion. As it develops it ascends upwards in the flute’s register. This later gets contrasted by a motif of descending slurred arpeggiated eighth notes. The second one focuses on an evenness of slurred intervals. It features a motif of ascending slurred eighth notes that begins as major thirds, which gets expanded larger to become minor sevenths. Eventually, the intervals are flipped to become descending. This is contrasted by arpeggiated staccato eighth notes that become more disjunct as the piece develops.

description: This work consists of two short movements in contrasting characters elegantly displaying the lyrical and virtuosic sides of the flute. The first movement “Improvisacion melancolica” showcases the vocal-like playing capable on the flute with moments of virtuosity through improvisatory embellishments. The first movement begins with a “Lento” section with a harp introduction playing quintuplet sixteenth note arpeggiations cascading across the register. The flute then enters with a lyrical melody of eighth, quarter, dotted quarter, and half notes in the lowest register. It then becomes syncopated with an eighth rest at the beginning and then the use of ties during the phrase. The harp switches to an oscillating eighth note line in the upper voice and chords in the lower voices. As it develops virtuosic flourishes are inserted as embellishments in the flute such as quintuplet sixteenths and eleven-tuplet. The next main section “Allegretto” features a contrapuntal texture between the two instruments with a dance-like character primarily featuring eighth, dotted eighth, and sixteenths. Then a return to the “Lento” occurs that is highly embellished in both instruments. A final return to a fragment from the opening occurs to conclude the movement. The second movement “Improvisacion alegre” marked “Allegretto vivo” begins with an ostinato pattern in the harp consisting of a bass note in the lowest voice and on beats two and three are eighth notes providing the harmony. The flute enters with the main theme that consists of four slurred sixteenth notes that are first scalar then lower neighbour motion leading to an eighth note. Next, the theme introduces a dotted eighth followed by a sixteenth and an eighth motif leading to a string of staccato eighth notes. The harp part briefly becomes more active, switching to scalar sixteenth notes leading to a caesura to reset the music. The original theme and new motif are then combined in the flute. Afterwards, the harp plays a lyrical melody, while the flute plays a long passage of staccato sixteenth notes climbing to the highest register of the flute. A return to the original material with variations occurs. The work continues expanding upon the material for the rest of the movement.

description: This work consists of two short movements that are a virtuosic display of technique that utilizes sequential patterns. The first movement “Moderato”has two main sections. The first section opens presenting the main theme that consists of sixteenth notes that chromatically weave around the pitch “E” in the middle register of the flute. The second phrase expands upon the theme by introducing chromatic lower neighbor tone motion while it expands upwards in the flute’s register. The motif is then repeated a semitone higher and leads into a restatement of the main theme with an extension added to the end leading to a silent pause for the second section. The next section is based on sixteenth note arpeggiations. Eventually, the lower neighbour tone motion from earlier is introduced into this section. It then leads into a passage of arpeggiation marcato eighth notes in descending motion. A final section that becomes more disjunct by wider intervals in the arpeggiation occurs to conclude the movement. The second movement “Quasi toccata” has a similar structure where it presents a motif and expands upon it. The first section uses neighbour motion followed by an ascending interval, then second time a descending interval leading into arpeggiation to set up the next motif on a different harmony that proceeds in a sequential manner. As it develops the material between the neighbour motion gets expanded longer strings of arpeggiation. The work closes with a brief measure and a half Lento using the main motifs of neighbour tone motion and arpeggiation but in a more improvisatory character.

description: This is a short two movement work utilizing elements of folklorism and romanticism following in the footsteps of Lysenko. The first movement “Ukrainian folk song” is in a moderato cantabile tempo featuring a folk melody in the bassoon with accompaniment figures in the piano. There are two small cadenzas consisting of an “ad lib” arpeggio overtop of a fermata chord in the piano. The second movement “Scherzino” is an energetic dance-like character in the form of ABABA Coda. It consists of a melody in the bassoon and quarter note chords in the piano, which become dotted half notes tied to a quarter note in the Coda.

description: These two works are also from The Bassoonist’s Notebook written while he was a student at NMAU. The first one “Lamento” is structured as an improvisation based on an opening arpeggiated motif around the notes C#-G#-D-G-F-E that expands chromatically into a longer singing line, which continues to develop rhythmically increasing in speed. Eventually the motion slows down returning back to the opening motif. The second one “Perpetuo Moto” is an energetic allegro showcasing the bassoon’s rapid staccato articulation. This movement is a rapid string of notes with a constantly changing metrical feel from changing the placement of accents and slurred notes throughout.

description: This is a short two-movement work in a folk style. The first movement “Song” is marked andantino cantabile. It opens with an eight-measure piano introduction that sets up the bassoon to enter with a vocal-like melody that is mostly scalar or arpeggiations in f minor. The melody is completely in the tenor register with one moment where it ascends to a high C. This is overtop of an accompaniment piano with a triplet eighth note counter-melody in the right-hand and chords in the left-hand. The movement has two endings: 1) for performing the first movement alone and 2 ) for continuing on and performing the second movement attacca. The second movement “March” is marked sostenuto and in ABABA form. It also opens with a piano introduction in 2/4 that sets up the character prior to the bassoon entering with the melody. The melody contrasts between staccato eighth notes and tenuto quarter notes to create two different characters within the phrase. The B section “Meno mosso” contrasts with a more vocal-like melody in the bassoon with contrapuntal lines in the piano. The return of the A section omits the piano introduction and has the bassoon playing the motif from the introduction over top of chords before returning to the melody. Next, a return of the B section happens but in a different context of 6/8 now with ornamentation written into the melody overtop of an arpeggiated piano accompaniment. A final reprise of the A section occurs but with the bassoon taking over the last four measures of the introduction before beginning the melody.

description: This work is two untitled movements. The first one “quarter note equals 136” has two main sections. It opens with a dialogue of long tones that begin separated by rests and overtime come together first in dissonance, then consonant interval and finally unison. The second is a rhythmically complex counterpoint that begins contrapuntal and develops into unison. The second movement “quarter note equals 60” takes the pitch “D” and begins as a long tone that ascends and gets more rhythmically intense through shortening values. It begins in a fugal texture that eventually becomes unison. Then it becomes contrapuntal, developing back to unison to end the piece.

description: The basis of this work comes from “the Cossack song “Oy, ne puhay, puhachenku”(Kushnir, foreward) (Oh, don’t scare, owl), which is a lament for fallen warriors” and “of a free, proud people who are fighting and winning.” (Kushnir forward). It takes this folk melody and reimagines it in a virtuosic display for the flute. The piece opens with a “Doloroso” section that presents the theme in a lyrical vocal-like style with grace note embellishment and fermatas emphasizing the arrival points in the phrase. Next, a “Piu mosso” adds more ornamentation to the theme. This is followed by a “Con moto” section where the piece begins to become virtuosic with the introduction of slurred thirty second notes in scalar motion and articulated arpeggiated triplet sixteenth notes. As it progresses the passages of virtuosic ornamentation becomes longer and more disjunct, such as intervals over an octave. Then the “Decisio” section reaches the climax of virtuosity as the phrase becomes completely comprised of those virtuosic motifs. This is followed by a “Meno mosso” that reduces the ornamentation back to a more semplice version of the theme from the beginning in order to conclude the work.

description: This is a one-movement work structured on alternating sections that are inspired by either folk songs or dances. The opening section is an “Andante sostenuto, rubato” that has a vocal-like line based on sixteenths or eighths leading to a longer note centered around A minor. Next, an “Allegretto” section with an alternating 3/8 and 5/8 measures creating a 3+2+3 pattern of eighth notes with the first two notes of the three-grouping slurred creates an energetic dance character. Then the opening section returns now with two voice part writing with the original melody in downwards stems and a countermelody responding in upwards stems. Then a “Allegro marcatissimo” section begins with quarter notes that are jumping between different octaves on the pitch “Bb”. This leads into a slurred sixteenth leading to a eighth note passage that is followed by a syncopated dance-like section achieved through ties over bar lines. This develops into larger interval jumps and the sequence progresses to a high Eb long tone before a descending line of eighth notes to half notes on the pitch “G” to conclude this fiery section. Next an “Un poco meno mosso” section in an espressivo character presents a cantabile vocal-like line in an alternating 2/4 and 3/4 metre pattern. A return to the “Allegro marcatissimo” occurs this time leading to a multiphonic fermata note. A final phrase of the dance-like motif occurs to end the work.

description: This is a six-movement suite that utilizes elements from Hutsul folk songs and dances often using Eastern European scales and tonalities. This work demonstrates Shamo’s ability to write music rich in melody that decorate Ukrainian national musical motifs through its diverse breadth of emotions evoked. The first movement “At the meadow” (Na polonnyni) is in an intrada ad libitum tempo that begins with a bassoon solo in an improvisatory manner, which the other winds respond in dialogue during its long notes. The rest of the movement takes this theme and motifs and develops them alternating between contrapuntal and homorhythmic textures. Eventually, a return to the opening material occurs in the same texture. The second movement “Chabarashky” is an energetic folk dance in an allegro moderato tempo consisting of a fiery melody of eighth and sixteenth notes, syncopated accompaniment figures, and a staccato eighth note bass line with large intervals. Throughout the movement the material develops into tutti passages of staccato sixteenth notes. The next movement “Spivanochky” in an andantino pastorale tempo featuring a cantabile folk-like melody, eighth note arpeggiated ostinato, and chords. As the movement develops a countermelody is added into the texture. The fourth movement “Hahilka” in a moderato leggiero tempo that alternates between two sections 1) a descending staccato eighth note line in cannon leading to trill tied to a virtuosic septuplet in canon, and 2) an ominous folk melody played in harmony overtop of an ostinato. Slight variations occur as the material returns throughout. The following movement “Mountain Stream” (Hirskyi Potik) is in an allegro tempo centered around weaving sixteenth note passages imitating a running stream of water. A sequential eighth note motif interrupts it throughout leading to sixteenth notes being passed around the ensemble before returning to the original weaving line. A folk-like melody is introduced overtop of this texture. The final movement “Hutsulka” is another fiery folk dance in an allegro tempo featuring a syncopated staccato bass line, rhythmic driving repeated staccato eighth notes, and a virtuosic melody consisting of eighth and sixteenth notes with grace notes. Variations to the accompaniment and texture occur throughout such as passages of sixteenth notes in the accompaniment either a single line or passing around.

description: The work has a three-part structure with an introduction and coda that utilizes folk songs as a basis for the themes. All of the instruments have an equal role in the ensemble. However, in the middle section of the work, the piano has a slightly more active role presenting solo material. The bassoon specifically plays an equal role both in the thematic material and participates in creating a variety of timbre colors through musical fragments. The bassoon is used in three main roles throughout the work. First, to present melodic material doubling with the flute two octaves lower in the introduction and a fragmentation of it at the end of the first section in octaves. Secondly, the bassoon is used in a harmonic role in chords with other instruments. Finally, an independent role in the coda presents an ostinato motif.

key: I (C major), II (D major), III (F major)
description: This is a three-movement work that incorporates elements of folk song and dance into neoclassical structures. The first movement “Allegretto '' opens with an ostianto of dissonant articulated eighth notes in the upper winds. The bassoon enters with an energetic folk-like melody. This develops into the ostinato becoming consonant in the horn and clarinet while the oboe has an arpeggiated sixteenth note passage. This leads into a “piu mosso” section which contrasts the opening with a lyrical melody in the horn, a drone on B in the bassoon, and accompaniment figures in the oboe and clarinet. This develops into a homorhythmic passage in the ensemble to wind down into a short three note horn solo. A return to the opening character occurs with variations and fragmentation of the earlier material. After a silence, a final grave in a chorale style ends the movement. The next movement “Moderato con moto” is in ternary form. The first section features a folk-like melody first in the flute then the oboe overtop of accompaniment tenuto quarter notes in the rest of the ensemble. The next section “marcato” has an accented ostinato on the pitch D combined with an accented melody in the rest of the ensemble. The opening material returns with some variations such as the flute and oboe playing the melody at the same time in octaves and a countermelody added in the clarinet. The final movement “Moderato” opens with a canon-like entrance on long tones in the ensemble with a melody in the flute. The next section “marciale” features a dance-like section consisting of a dotted eighth and sixteenth followed by two eighth notes ostinato in horn and clarinet, arpeggiated sixteenths in the flute with occasional interjections from the oboe and bassoon. This develops into the whole ensemble playing a staccato sixteenth passage. Finally, earlier material returns leading conclude the piece

description: The work was written when the composer was completing her Master’s degree at the Amsterdam Conservatory when another student asked her to write a new composition for baroque flute. The title of the work is inspired by her husband having coffee for breakfast as she wrote it.. This piece combines elements of the past with contemporary avant-garde music. This is a short work written for solo baroque flute that has a rich tradition of performance practice and expected technique. However, Azarova pushes the boundaries by incorporating very modern and avant-garde techniques of playing to create new textures and style for this instrument. This is combined with sound effects from electronics to create a new textures and sound world. The work begins with the electronics playing a fragment sampled from a baroque flute that is similar to the music traditionally written from the baroque era for this instrument. The flutist then enters with slap tongued eighth notes and then a statement of the previous fragment from the electronics to create a dialogue. The electronics and flute then are in a contrapuntal texture going back and forth as the fragments get expanded into a full phrase. As it develops it becomes more virtuosic with septuplets and extended passages of quick staccato articulated notes such as thirty-second, quintuplet, sextuplet, and septuplets. The phrases also become much more disjunct leaning into motifs more similar to contemporary and avant-garde music. Also multiple lines are introduced that expands the electronics to three voices to create a quartet texture. This then fades back into a two voice texture to conclude the work.

description: This concerto is based on the dark forest from the beginning of Dante Alighieri’s Divine Comedy. The work opens with an aleatoric motif in the violins that set up the character for the bassoon to enter with a cadenza-like phrase. This leads into quintuplets throughout the soloist and ensemble starting off a rhythmic and energetic section that utilizes pizzicato in the strings creating an accompaniment texture underneath the soloist and lyrical countermelody in the cello. This section develops through a dynamic increase until forte and the range of the bassoon soloist singing up to the high F, while the strings begin to set up the texture of the next section. The third main section is a chordal-like string accompaniment underneath the virtuosic bassoon part. Throughout the section the accompaniment constantly changes providing character and textural contrast such as very rhythmic and disjointed passage of sixteenth notes to quarter note chords. This eventually leads to an orchestral interlude consisting of slowly changing drones. The bassoon re-enters with a syncopated slower motif featuring large interval jumps that evolves into a more melodic line. A sudden shift occurs taking the music back into the disjointed character until arriving at a virtuosic bassoon cadenza exploring the full range of the instrument through articulated large interval jumps and arpeggiated passages. This leads into the final disjointed sixteenth note section with some of the largest interval jumps yet appearing in the bassoon. The concerto then arrives at the final winding down section that features a more lyrical bassoon line with interjection accompaniment figures in the strings.
