description: This is a four-movement programmatic work that follows a story of a unicorn in an avant-garde aesthetic. The work pushes the boundaries of instrumental technique and typical quintet playing through seeking new sounds and forms for musical ideas to settle in, which is achieved through the paradox of characters throughout. The first movement “Unicorn’s Song” is centered around a repeated note motif on the pitch “C” that each instrument is weaving together a different rhythm to create a constant stream of rhythm. This is combined with quartertones surrounding the pitch “C” to create unexpected dissonances creating a melody and effect that sounds like an animal call or cry. The second movement “Unicorn’s defile” has the character of an unbalanced dance with a constant changing of two versus three note grouping of the eighths combined with a melody of eighth notes and quarter notes that do not follow an expected pattern. The opening texture features a melody in the flute, countermelody in the oboe and accompaniment chords in the other voices. This evolves into a string of legato and constant eighth notes before arriving at a more staccato and syncopated eighth note line with the introduction of rests thrown in. This progresses until combining elements of both the legato and staccato motifs together. The movement continues alternating between these characters in the manner of a battle of dominance between the two. The next movement “Unicorn’s dance” is a disjointed line of sixteenths constantly trading off instruments after a couple notes with a couple short motifs emerging. The final movement “Unicorn’s games” features short cells of sixteenth note motifs that weave between the instruments to slowly expand and change over time in order to intensify and climax into the next section.

description: This is a short one-movement work in the same style as the previous work in a ternary form. This also features a long lyrical melodic line in the bassoon consisting mainly of duple and triple eighth notes leading to quarter notes. In the middle of the work this is briefly contrasted with a passage of staccato eighth notes in a sequential manner. The piano accompaniment often plays arpeggiated passages in the left-hand and melodic or counter-melodic lines in the right-hand. This develops into scalar moments of sixteenth and triplet sixteenth notes to create more intensity as the piece climaxes at the end of the middle section. For the return of the A section the accompaniment begins in a chordal role before returning to its original texture. Finally, it provides a virtuosic flourish underneath the bassoon's final long note that leads to a unison staccato eighth note on the tonic to conclude the work.

description: This is a one-movement work in a contrapuntal style that explores a wide variety of keys and harmonies throughout. The character is melancholic due to the minor tonality that sneaks out throughout combined with unexpected harmonies and unprepared shifts of keys to symbolize the spirit of the Ukrainian people constantly pushing through their struggle to fight for their independence despite what unexpected challenges arise. Overall, musically the piece is legato with constant weaving and dialogue between the different instruments to create one long line that appears to never be ending due to two main factors 1) there is never being a rest for everyone at the same time, 2) the cohesion of phrases by one instrument phrase ending colliding with the start of another instrument. The main motif first presented by the flute is two quarters followed by an eighth note on a repeated pitch that then falls into a string of weaving eighth notes. All four of the instruments either play this melody in a fugal style in moments or in a fragmented and variation style.

description: Loginov’s music has a desire to merge together sound ideas and meaning by having a complete openness to any known techniques by turning to theatricality with a synthesis of other art types. An important inspiration in his music is emotion and subconsciousness, which lead to a dream theme. He searches for ways to convey the mutual absorption of dreams and reality with self-reflection. Therefore, according to Loginov music is “primarily about communication, connection with people and the nature of things. In the broadest sense of these words.”60 The work itself utilizes graphic notation to convey various characters and emotions leaving lots of improvisation up to the performer. The score is structured using timestamps to move between the sections. For example, a diagram of circles is used to designate the inhaling and exhaling of air noises. For the multiphonic sections they are denoted with lines that zig zag in desired direction without specifying any specific pitches to be performed. Directions for double tonguing are given with “T-K” syllabus written overtop of the notes. This is also combined with short aleatoric motifs that are written out in between time stamps. All of these extended techniques, improvised sections, and aleatoric motifs are combined overtop of an electronic track. It first begins with static noises that gives the effect of white noise that a person would use to fall asleep to. Next, the track features a low bass drum like effect with animal noises that begin chaotic which become bird chirping. The track continues switching between more ominous noises and more nature-like rainfall to create contrasting characters as if going between a nightmare and a dream. Throughout a return to the static noise occurs to ground the listener.

description: The title of the work translate to “will o’ the wisp” and refers to the ghostly lights seen over marches that represent a lost soul. It is famously referenced in Schubert’s song cycle Winterreise. The work opens with ”Andante, sempre espresivo e liberamente” consisting of a haunting minor melody using long note values, soft dynamics with swells to set a mysterious character for the piece. As it progresses, the melody becomes more active and meanders around with chromaticism entering into the line. The work then explodes into moments of lines of cascading sixteenths to contrast with a livelier character. As it progresses sextuplets are introduced to create an even more virtuosic display. The next section “Presto” features a motif of eighth notes in an upper neighbour and arpeggiated motion in a frantic character. As the line developes it strings together a longer passage of eighth notes that become more disjunct. Eventually, this is interrupted with longer note values using frullato to bring back the earlier mysterious character almost as a reminder like the lost soul trying to find its way back before a return to the frantic eighth notes. The second time, it is interrupted with trills instead. Finally, it finds a way back to sixteenth notes to set up a return to the opening section’s material with some slight variations such as the use of frullato for timbre and rhythmically triplet eighth notes to bring in elements from the middle section like a lost soul bringing along all of its experiences during the course of its life.

description: This is a one-movement work based around a theme with seven variations in a neoclassical style utilizing elements compositional techniques typical of a theme and variations. The theme marked “Singing calmly” is a five-measure vocal-like melody using step wise and arpeggiated motion that is presented solo by the clarinet. The first variation features the theme in canon with the bassoon starting the section with the clarinet entering two beats later. The next variation consists of the theme in the clarinet with a weaving counter melody in stepwise motion consisting rhythmically of eighth and sixteenth notes in the bassoon. The following variation changes key and switches the roles of the part with the bassoon playing the theme and the clarinet playing the counter melody. The fourth variation marked “Freely” divides the theme between the two instruments. The clarinet plays the first measure and then plays a whole note while the bassoon plays the second measure of the theme, which is marked “as an echo”. This same pattern occurs for measures three and four. For the fifth measure the clarinet plays the theme overtop of a dotted quarter in the bassoon that arrives together at a dotted quarter note with a fermata that fades away. The next variation features an eighth note arpeggiated ostinato bass line in the bassoon with the theme being turned into staccato eighth notes followed by an eighth rest. The following variation is polytonal with the bassoon in F major while the clarinet is in C major. The theme is rhythmically different and incorporates grace notes. The final variation is the longest variation within the piece and combines elements from earlier such as syncopation, grace notes, and counter melody motifs.

description: This is a short one-movement work that takes a phrase from a Ukrainian folk song that undergoes six variations. It begins with an introduction section “Moderato” with the main theme in the bassoon. The statement in the bassoon consists of a rhythmic motif of eighth note, dotted eighth, sixteenth and eighth note that is utilized throughout the piece. This is overtop of accompaniment figures in the harp and organ based around arpeggios and various bass line motifs. The first variation rhythmically diminution the theme from the eighth note to the sixteenth note level. It is also fragmented with the introduction of various rests. The next variation removes the rhythmic motif and stretches the theme into quarter and eighth notes with scalar sixteenth and arpeggiated eighth note figures. The third variation brings back the dotted eighth and sixteenth from the opening but extends the phrase longer combining it with more sixteenth and eighth notes. This is combined with quarter note chordal figures in the organ and technical passages in the harp in dialogue with the bassoon theme. The following variation changes the rhythm relation of notes to be three longer notes followed by two shorter notes, first presented as eighth and sixteenths in the harp that is echoed as sixteenths and thirty-seconds in the bassoon. This motif continues to pass around the ensemble. The fifth variation begins the theme as a cantus firmus in a neo renaissance style of quarter and eighth notes. It develops to return to the original dotted eighth and sixteenth rhythmic motif. The final variation “Andante” has a more lyrical character presenting weaving lines of eighth notes in the bassoon and organ with interjections of virtuosic sixteenth note passages in the harp. Once the interjections begin, the bassoon and organ’s left-hand play a more vocal-like line to conclude the work.

recordings: YouTube: 1) 2015 in Kharkiv by composer (cl), Maksym Mikailov (cl), Dmytro Novytskyi (bsn) (https://youtu.be/uuX4ovNwtXk?si=vO1keciTe2YtCgco)
description: This work is a theme and four variations on Ukrainian composer Ivan Karabits (1945–2002) Piano Prelude no. 8. The work opens with four measures of an ostinato of dotted eighth and two sixteenths on the pitch “F#” followed by a dotted eighth rest in the bassoon. The two clarinets then join with the theme in rhythmic unison mostly in contrary motion in a staccato and accented manner. The first variation “Allegro” continues the dotted eighth and sixteenth part of the ostinato now with no rest between iterations in the second clarinet. The first clarinet and bassoon play elements of theme in a dialogue between the two in a risoluto character. The first clarinet has more staccato eighth note responses to a more lyrical bassoon statement consisting of a long note, rhythmic ostinato motif leading to quarter notes. Eventually, the second clarinet and bassoon switch roles. This leads into a homorhythmic passage alternating between the ostinato motif and fragments of the theme. The second variation “Adagio Sostenuto” is in a more chorale character in a contrapuntal texture consisting of quarter notes leading to half and whole notes. The third variation “Andante cantabile” features the theme now in a vocal-like line that is passed around the ensemble overtop of other contrapuntal lines such as a scalar bass line. The final variation “Andante non troppo” brings back the original character of the theme but now with rests inserted within the phrase and ornamentation of sixteenths. This is overtop of constant eighth notes on the pitch “F” switching back and forth between the low and middle octave in the bassoon. As it develops other notes are introduced based on the harmonic progression. Eventually, the bassoon switches to playing sixteenth notes in the inserted rests of the clarinet’s line. A return to the original texture of this variation occurs to conclude the movement.

description: This is a one-movement work based on a theme from Dmitri Shostakovich’s opera Lady Macbeth (1934) and was renamed Katerina Izmailova. This opera ideologically highlighted the corruption created by Marxism in the Soviet Union depicting characters imprisoned by their circumstances. This was a reflection of how Soviet society trapped the average citizen to blindly obey the rules and protocols of the regime, creating a difficult environment to live in. Musically, the opera had Western inspiration from Alban Berg’s opera Wozzeck through the use of integral interludes and passacaglia-based forms as opposed to separate arias and choruses, typical in Russian operas. Komlikova’s piece explores the different characters such as legato vocal-like lines and humoresque staccato passages that the bassoon can achieve through six variations that follow the story of the opera. The opening of the piece, “Epigraph '' presents an introduction solo in the bassoon. Then, for the theme the piano joins in an accompaniment role, mostly providing bass line. The first variation “Rigidly” is a declamatory call and response between the bassoon and the piano. The next variation “Clouding of the mind” opens with a string of eighth notes in the bassoon, which the piano takes over turning it into an accompaniment role while the bassoon presents an elongated version of the theme. The third movement “An unstoppable impulse” is in a quicker tempo utilizing a quarter note followed by an eighth note combined with a string of eighth notes to climax to high Eb in the bassoon that is held for a long time while the piano unwinds into the next variation “Heartfelt.” This variation is a long legato line in a vocal quality in the bassoon with short interjections in the piano. This leads to a quasi-cadenza moment in the bassoon. The fifth movement “Ironically” is typical staccato and humoresque bassoon writing featuring articulated scalar passages and large interval jumps. The final variation “Com improvvisato” is a quasi-improvised section where the bassoon and piano are in dialogue with one another never playing at the same time. This leads into a final “Coda” section is a still and sparse section depicting Katerina’s suicide with only the cold water keeping her story alive. The bassoon mainly plays long notes and short fragments of the original motif while the piano plays open chords in the left-hand and the original motif in the right hand. This texture slowly dies away into just the bassoon blowing air into the instrument with no reed representing the end of her life fading away.

piece_title: Variations on Ukrainian Folk Song “Chy ya va luzi ne layna bula”

instrumentation: ob, bsn, pno [alternative version for cl, bsn, pno]
dedicated: Àngela Lorente Andréu (ob), Olivia del Carmen Alarcón Molina (bsn), Antonio Soria Alemany (pno)
premiere: May 2021 in Spain by dedicatees (ob, bsn), Bohdan Syroyid (pno)
description: The title of the work Vesna is the Ukrainian word for spring and is a three-movement programmatic suite depicting folk Ukrainian life using elements of Ukrainian folklore and folk music throughout. The first movement “Kviten” (April) is an andantino written in a sonata form that has a calm and lyrical character. It opens with a simple melodic line that trades between the oboe and bassoon overtop of chords in an open fifth voicing to depict the past. A contrasting section featuring a constant string of eighth notes trading between the three instruments in a light and leggiero character through staccato articulation in the winds is combined with short, slurred motifs. Then a return to the opening material occurs with the oboe and bassoon in a dialogue creating an echo effect. Next, a trill motif is introduced that rotates around the ensemble while the eighth note staccato motif from the contrasting section returns. Next, a three-quarter note motif is introduced as the earlier material is intertwined together and developed for the rest of the movement. The second movement “Kolyskovsa” is a lullaby in a lento tempo written as a theme with variations. It begins with a contrapuntal duet between the oboe and bassoon, which the piano responds playing the melody in a chorale texture. Next, the melody is individually played by the oboe then the bassoon overtop of an arpeggiated accompaniment in the piano. This eventually leads to fragments of the melody being passed around the ensemble. Eventually this leads to the piano taking over the melodic role with a scalar accompaniment in the winds before. Finally, the movement ends with the oboe and bassoon playing it together in unison overtop of long-tones in the piano. The third movement “Hopak” is an energetic traditional Ukrainian dance by males that is characterized by its high leaps, squatting, and foot stamping. The movement written in a rondo form begins with a six-measure introduction that leads into the A section consisting of a fiery eighth note and sixteenth melody in the winds overtop of accompaniment figures in the piano. Then a contrasting B section consisting of a more lyrical section occurs with a legato melody in the oboe, legato countermelody in the piano, and a bass line in the bassoon. The piece develops and variates these different motifs such as fragmented in a call and response. Overall, this work is structured in a neoclassical form with stylistic elements from folklorism.

description: This is a one-movement work in an unmetered style but with dashed bar-lines throughout to indicate phrases and sections to give a sense of structure to the performer.  Overall, the work features virtuosic passages that often begin as an ostinato that undergoes small changes over time until it reaches a climax. It begins in a calm character with air noise effects before the first fragment of thirty-second notes is introduced which leads to longer note values. As it develops the motifs get stringed together creating a long line allowing for a larger phrase to emerge. Over time the motifs become more disjunct and aggressive through larger intervals and quick repeated and articulated notes, in the manner that a virus would take over as it becomes stronger as it infiltrates its surroundings. Eventually, the motifs begin to break down as rests are unexpectedly inserted without an obvious pattern symbolizing the breakdown caused by a virus. The work continues breaking down in this manner until a rest is between almost every single note allowing for the original air noise texture to return. After the longest rest in the entire work of almost two quarter notes a final fermata air noise note that dies away to niente occurs like a victim taking its final breath before a virus wins.

published: Ortav Music Publications - Centre of Israeli Music (1979)
premiere: unknown
description: This is a four movement suite of back-and-forth contrasting characters and a grand display of virtuosity on the flute through technique and complex rhythms. The first movement “Tempo giusto” is a fiery display of technique featuring quarter notes with frullato leading to a large interval jump, sixteenth and quintuplet arpeggiations and ornamentation such as trills and tremolos creating intensity throughout the lines. This is contrast with calmer “Meno mosso” sections providing a more lyrical and subdued character. They are often in the low register of the flute with a vocal-like melody with embellishments. The final section is a “Tranquillo”that is reminiscent of the “Meno mosso” but incorporates frullato on the longer note values. The next movement “Allegro non troppo” opens with a repeated quintuplet motif leading to staccato eighth notes. An eighth note followed by a sixteenth rest and sixteenth note motif is introduced connecting the statements of the other motif into a larger phrase. As it progresses it develops into groups of sixteenth notes with a sixteenth rest inserted throughout. This is contrasted by a “Poco Tranquillo” marked “Cantando” with similar qualities to the previous movement. A return to the original material occurs leading to a final “Vivo” consisting only of the secondary motif. The third movement “Lento assai” marked “Cantando” has a quasi-improvisatory quality featuring short phrases with hairpin dynamics that lead to either a fermata or a rest. Rhythmically, it begins very semplice with primarily eighth notes leading to dotted quarter notes and as it progresses it becomes more intricate with embellishments of faster note values. The final movement “Allegro con brio” opens primarily with eighth and sixteenth notes with an energetic character created through the use of rests inserted in the line creating syncopations and forward momentum throughout. A contrasting “Andante” section presents another slurred and lyrical line that features expressive large interval jumps. A return to the “Allegro con brio” occurs with variations to the materials, which is then contrasted by a brief two measure “Largo” with a vocal-like line. A final “Vivace” that begins with the opening sixteenth note motif that morphs into a scalar passage of triplet sixteenths leading to a half note trill followed by a final three measure tag to conclude the work.

description: This is a five-movement work that combines elements of neoclassical structure with avant-garde aesthetics and language. It was written after a twenty-year break from composing. The first movement “Scandalous Squabble” is marked very fast using an avant-garde atonal language that is structured around the combination of multiphonic long tones that often enter syncopated and a constant line of disjunct sixteenths that involve a pattern of chromatic intervals often displaced by an octave with perfect fifths that pass around the ensemble. This effect creates constantly changing textures and timbres through the different pairing of instrumentations. Eventually, a 7:4 motif of half notes and quarter notes is introduced that interrupts this chain leading to a cadenza moment in the horn consisting of a large descending glissando to conclude the movement. The next movement “Funeral Interrupted” is marked molto largo, alla marcia funebre structured in a more neoclassical approach. It consists of a typical rhythmic ostinato of quarter, dotted eighth, and sixteenth note in the flute, clarinet, horn, and bassoon that keeps the momentum moving forward. This motif is often in cluster chords rather than the expected minor tonality of a marcia funebre. However, as the work develops this motif expands to have the eighth note and sixteenth three times in a row before returning to a quarter note. Overtop of this texture is a singing, legato oboe solo that plays around with the rhythmic motif often creating syncopation with the accompaniment. The third movement “Supra-Florid Counterpoint” is marked molto largo in a contrapuntal texture. It features five independent lines in an atonal language that are weaving in and out of one another often creating rhythmic dissonance through the combination of different note groupings occurring at the same time such as 3:5 and 4:3 overlapping. The movement has a legato and calm character through tenutos and long slur markings that gets thrown off by the rhythmic dissonance. The next movement “Scattered Mozaic” is marked allegro volatile consists of short fragments that are different rhythmically and pitch-wise in each instrument that connect together to create a larger cohesive phrase. The texture is thinner, usually consisting of only one or briefly two instruments playing at a time when fragments overlap. The final movement “Intimate Chant” is marked lentissimo is homophonic line in the ensemble consisting of longer note values, mainly half notes and whole notes often tied over the bar lines to create a metrical ambiguity. This is combined with the occasional moment of quarter notes to bring a moment of metrical clarity.

description: This is a one-movement work that incorporates elements from various styles such as rhythmic and melodic motifs of folklorism, neoclassical elements of structure and contemporary aesthetics such as rhythmic dissonance of triple and duple subdivisions occurring together. The work opens with a “Rubato” section that consists of a clarinet cadenza overtop of a C drone in the left hand of the piano. Eventually, the bassoon enters in a dialogue with a counter-melody as the piano develops into a chordal texture that is metrically syncopated moving on beats 2 and 4. This leads into the next section “Allegro” features an ostinato eighth note jumping between octaves on the note C in the left hand and a quarter note melody based on the Ukrainian minor scale in the right hand of the piano. Eventually, the clarinet takes over this melody before a variation appears in the bassoon before becoming a bass line. This gives rise to a more active and virtuosic section of arpeggiated passages that are offset by an eighth note in the clarinet and bassoon overtop of chords in the piano. As this section progresses the piano becomes more involved with a syncopated rhythm with dissonance of quarter note triplets and eventually sextuplet eighths overtop of the eighth notes occurring in the winds. This leads to a contrasting “Andante” section that presents a syncopated melody through the use of tied notes, which is first given in the piano alone that the clarinet takes over followed by the bassoon in a contrapuntal manner. This leads into a virtuosic cadenza-like duet between the winds that explores the upper registers. Finally, a return to the opening texture of a drone in the piano and melody in the bassoon occurs. This section brings in different variations than the opening. This leads into a final Allegro that recombines prior material in new ways.

description: The title Vyshyvanka is a Ukrainian word for the traditional embroidered shirts that are worn in Ukraine and the diaspora, which are a proud symbol of culture and identity. I believe the piece is centered around finding a balance between folkloric and avant-garde elements to represent the modern identity of Ukrainians, who are trying to balance the traditional elements of their identity with the complexities of the modern day. The piece opens with a folk like motif that is traded between a solo accordion and solo bassoon. This is then taken over by the oboe and clarinet, with the accordion providing an accompaniment role. However, this accompaniment begins to blur the lines through cluster chords that begin the introduction of atonality and avant-garde stylistic characteristics. This blurring of the texture leads into an unbalanced dance-like section in 5/4 through short staccato passages interacting amongst the ensemble. However, this gets interrupted by the accordion blurring the lines with a weaving chromatic line bringing back the cluster chords and avant-garde elements. The section develops and expands until climaxing into another unbalanced dance-like section for the rest of the piece. The dance is constantly shifting meter and utilizing contemporary techniques such as frullato and multiphonics to juxtapose the two aspects of identity.

description: This a two movement work that depicts a sense of wandering around like a bird taking flight to flutter around above the earth. The first movement “Espressivo” is centered around the pitch D♭ and begins long notes on this pitch that develop from a soft dynamic to a loud dynamic in a sequential fashion. With each reinteration of the pitch there is more wandering around the pitch through short fragmented motifs that are inserted to elongate the phrase. This continues undergoing development to become whole phrases that arrive at different pitches such as C, E♭, and E as it circles around D♭. As the music develops new melodic material and more playful character is introduced to create a more active texture as we begin to lose sight of this pitch center of D♭ like a bird getting high above the ground who is losing sight of the earth. Eventually, it returns to the opening character but does not find the pitch of “D♭” leaving the listener with a search that is uncompleted. The second movement “Trasparente e leggero” follows a very similar structure as the previous movement. It begins with long note values on the pitch C this time with fragmentation added in that builds together to create a full phrase over time. The middle section becomes much more active with the introduction of sixteenth and triplet note passages combined with staccato eighth notes to create a more whimsical character. It then ends in a similar manner in an uncomplete search back to the pitch C by ending on an E♭ this time.

description: Lohin’s compositional approach is focused on educating young performers providing pedagogical aspects to the works. His music draws inspiration from folklore and folk music to paint sound with his feelings and thoughts that appear in his imagination conveyed through melody, rhythm, harmony, and timbre. This work is a short one-movement work in ternary form with an expressive style highlighting the lyrical capabilities of the bassoon. The A section opens with a weaving eighth note line in the tenor register that climbs up to the bassoon’s high D overtop of a chordal accompaniment in the piano. It then develops to become more disjunct through larger intervals in quarter note triplets before returning to the original eighth notes. The B section modulates and features a three-note motif that sequentially climaxes to a the bassoon’s high E♭ underneath a fermata. The piano accompaniment features a constant string of eighth notes providing harmonic support and forward momentum. The music then restarts another attempt at the material, but this time undergoing an accelerando and eventual ritardando before a return to the A material. There is variation in the return of the material with an arpeggiated bass line in the left-hand of the piano and the bassoon’s melody becoming more active with sixteenth notes inserted into the line. A short four-measure coda that consists of a one-measure motif of eighth notes in the bassoon overtop of chords in the piano fades away leading to a final tonic chord to conclude the work.

description: This is a three-movement work that combines structures and techniques from neoclassicism with avant-garde musical language and techniques. The first movement “Allegro umoristico” begins with a theme in the flute that the ensemble interjects with short fragments. It develops into a contrapuntal texture first by the accompaniment becoming independent fragments from one another, which then become their own independent lines. This leads into a motif becoming echoed in all the voices resulting in the flute playing a fermata note alone. The next section consists of a motif that is then either echoed or fragmented in a canon-like texture. This leads into a horn solo that is in dialogue with interjections from the ensemble during longer note values, which develops into a contrapuntal texture. The movement continues in this manner of presenting a theme or motif that develops into a contrapuntal texture ending in the same way the first section ended but with the horn playing the final fermata note. The next movement “Andantino” begins with a lyrical horn solo built on arpeggiation that accompaniment staccato eighth note followed by an eighth rest that are a minor third apart in the flute and clarinet enter in the fifth measure. The bassoon then takes over with a new lyrical theme, with the flute and clarinet entering in the same manner. The rest of the movement continues in this manner switching between the horn and bassoon theme while the accompaniment changes harmonies to create more or less tension through dissonance. There is a “Piu mosso” section that interrupt this consisting of quais-cadenza moments of quintuplet and sextuplet sixteenth notes. This climaxes into an aleatoric section before returning to the original texture. The final movement “Allegro burlesco” has two main sections that alternate. The A sections are a contrapuntal texture that switches characters between dry staccato passages and flowing lyrical lines. It also constantly changes metre creating an unbalanced dance-like character. The B sections “Poco meno mosso” have a lyrical theme in the horn the first time and third time and the oboe the second time overtop of syncopated ostinato motifs. Each time the A material returns it is varied such as it being one homorhythmic line in the ensemble. Eventually, an “Andantino” section occurs to break this pattern, which is reminiscent of the second movement. Then material of the first movement is presented leading into a final “Andantino doloroso” section mainly consisting of longer note values to conclude the work.

description: This quintet is written in a postmodernist style that combines elements from various eras with contemporary languages such as atonality. The first movement “Andante” opens with an offstage horn playing a fanfare type motif typical of the past. The upper winds respond creating a call and response dialogue allowing the horn motif to develop with each successive phrase. Eventually this leads to the bassoon taking over the soloistic role from the horn allowing all the instruments to re-enter beginning to combine their parts together. This leads to a frantic trill section where the horn enters on stage and finally merges their lines together into a cohesive ensemble. The second movement “Fuga” opens with an unmetered dialogue between the upper winds. The next section is a juxtaposition of lyrical line in the bassoon and horn with a quick and staccato line in the upper winds. This concept is contrasted and alternates with aleatoric sections to explore the different possibilities of time within ensemble playing. The third movement “Andante” opens with the clarinet, bassoon and horn each having a soft, independent line that weaves in and out of each other with occasional moments of clarity when the parts line up together. This concept then continues in a duo with the flute and oboe which eventually becomes combined together. Eventually, a solo line in the oboe emerges from this thick texture with the other instruments dropping out. This allows them to re-enter independently one at a time with a new fugal type texture, which develops and expands until we get a more traditional chorale type texture typical of an Andante movement. This leads into the final section which features some elements of earlier like the weaving lines with new material such as fast fragments and short staccato passages. The final movement “Allegro moderato” explores the concept of pulse and time . The opening of the movement has the bassoon and horn still playing in the previous movement’s tempo while the others begin a typical fast and spirited finale movement. This idea continues throughout by having different tempos simultaneously occurring. Eventually, the ensemble solidifies their tempo together leading the final section of the piece. The very end of the piece returns to a variation of the fanfare that opened the piece, which involves the other instruments improvising as they go off stage leaving the horn separated from the ensemble once again.

This is a six-movement suite that combines elements of folk song and dance. Each movement is a different type of Ukrainian folk song. The first movement “Vesnianka” are traditionally sung acapella by young women for games and dances. These songs were originally used to wake nature from its winter sleep, usually depicting new life through bird symbolism. They often have two choruses, the first representing calling the birds and the second identifying the speaker with the birds.42 This movement is in a moderato con moto tempo consisting of a theme in folk-like manner that passes around the ensemble while undergoing variations overtop of accompaniment figures, such frullato eighth notes in the flute that I believe emulate birds. Eventually, the texture becomes more contrapuntal as the theme entrances become closer together and the accompaniment material develops to become more active. The second movement “Hayivka” is in a allegro con spirito tempo that begins with a two-measure motif consisting of two beats of sixteenth notes leading to two eighth notes followed by a quarter note in the bassoon. This is followed by a canon-like texture of a two-note motif descending perfect fourth motif. These motifs come back throughout alternated with contrasting material that is more lyrical with accompaniment figures. The third movement “Rusal’na” is marked sostenuto and consists of a lyrical and folk-like melody with accompaniment figures that become more active and independent as the movement develops. The following movement “Obzhynkova” is a harvest song in an allegro fresco tempo. It begins with a homorhythmic passage of quarter and eighth notes. It then shifts to a texture of a solo melodic line with energetic fragments of eighth notes underneath. Next, a canon-like texture of the melodic content occurs that a contrapuntal texture emerges out of. The next movement “Shchedrivka” is a song for winter solstice featuring a lyrical folk-like melody again with fragmented accompaniment motifs that pass around the ensemble underneath the melody. This texture slowly becomes more contrapuntal overtime. This goes attacca into the final movement “Vesnianka” which brings back the material from the first movement.

description: This is a short one-movement work that explores a variety of characters in a postmodernist language and style. It opens with an introduction that is a call and response between the harpsichord and bassoon. The harpsichord has rhythmic chords, while the bassoon has a syncopated arpeggiated motif or long tone multiphonics. The structure of the piece alternates between dense and thinner texture sections that require immediate character change. The denser sections often consist of an active line of sixteenth notes and chords with unexpected syncopations in the harpsichord that are combined with rhythmically energetic syncopated lines and strings of articulated sixteenths often in large intervals. The thinner sections often are more lyrical and quasi-improvisatory either in a cadenza manner or a simple accompaniment.

description: This is a three-movement work that depicts a magical winter scene of elves through lush harmonies, lyrical themes, and sweeping technical passages. The first movement “Prayer and Magical Extravaganza of Masks” opens with an “Andante moderato” section with a semplice theme in the flute consisting of eighth and quarter notes that melodically either repeat the same note or move in step-wise motion. The oboe and clarinet play a similar rhythmic line to the theme on repeated notes, while the horn and bassoon have longer note values. The theme is then passed to the oboe and the other instruments play contrapuntal lines. As the section progresses the theme becomes fragmented and is passed around the ensemble, while the other contrapuntal lines become more intricate and active. Next, the music changes keys for the next section “Allegro non troppo” that has a more energetic character. The theme of this section first presented by the flute takes the rhythmic elements of the opening section but is now changing chromatically step-wise on each note. The bassoon has a rhythmic bass line to create forward momentum with accompanimental figures in the rest of the ensemble. As the section develops, and fragments of the theme pass around the ensemble, the flute plays sweeping passages of sixteenth notes reminiscent of a wind across the field on a cold winter day. When the theme returns afterwards to the flute it is highly embellished with ornamentation. During the next flurry of sixteenth notes in the flute, a new vocal-like theme emerges underneath. A final return to the opening material with new variations and with incorporation of elements from the middle section such as the cascading sixteenth notes occurs to conclude the movement. The next movement “Winter Fairytale" begins with a “Moderato sostenuto misterioso” section with arpeggiated eighth note theme in the flute with accompanimental figures of quarter and half notes in the rest of the ensemble. This then gets contrasted with a scalar melody on the ascend and thirds on the descend comprised of quarter notes leading to a half note. Next, a “Piu mosso allegretto” section has an alberti bass line in the bassoon and contrapuntal lines consisting of eighth, quarter, and half notes weaving around the ensemble. Afterwards, a “Meno mosso maestoso” has a lyrical theme built on the same rhythmic values in the flute overtop of a bass line in the bassoon with either countermelody or accompaniment figures in the rest of the ensemble. Then the two opening sections return but in reverse order to conclude the movement. The final movement “Harlequin scherzo” opens with a “Con moto” section with a leggiero theme in the oboe using repeated staccato sixteenth notes leading to staccato eighth notes over top of staccato eighth notes on the beat in the ensemble. As it progresses it becomes more contrapuntal with echoes of the material passing around, technical flourishes in the flute, and other new motifs such as slurred oscillating eighth notes in the clarinet. Eventually, the accompaniment becomes a driving repeated eighth note line when a new theme is presented in the flute. A brief two measure “Pesante” in a homorhythmic texture of heavy accented eighth interrupts. The return to the original material offers new variations and reworking of the material to conclude the work.

description: This is a short one-movement work that utilizes melodic, rhythmic, and harmonic elements of folk song and dance. The opening section starts with a drone in an open fifth between the flute and clarinet while the bassoon presents folk vocal-like melody with ornamentation. The flute takes over the melody while the rest of the ensemble plays half note chords underneath to conclude the section. Next, a folk dance-like section occurs with a lively melody of staccato eighth and sixteenth notes first presented by the clarinet with accompaniment figures of staccato eighth notes in the oboe and bassoon. Eventually, the flute brings back the main melody which interweaves with the dance melody. This develops into a quasi-cadenza moment in the flute consisting of a flourish of thirty-second notes overtop of a chord in the ensemble. This is followed by short, fragmented phrases leading to fermatas. Next, two new motifs are introduced alongside the main theme: 1) a triplet quarter notes in stepwise motion and 2) a dotted eighth and sixteenth note oscillating a minor second. The work concludes by combining these various elements together.

description: The title of the work “Zub” is a word coined by the composer deriving from the Ukrainian word that means tooth and the meaning of the word as described by the composer can roughly be expressed as a “quintessence of the dental existence”. The inspiration behind coming up with this concept and image for the piece was a result of the dedicatee’s surname Vilka meaning “fork” in Ukrainian. The opening section of the piece “Prestissimo acuto, con durezza” depicts the sharp aspect of teeth. Musically, it is based around an aggressive accented motif of two eighth notes in a major third leading to an unexpected raised fourth degree. The work first presents the motif leading to a fermata whole note the performer holds for as long as possible. Then the motif gets repeated as an ostinato. The second section “Pesante ma allegro” combines various extended techniques of slap tonguing, key clicks, and multiphonics to create unique textures as contrast. A return to the opening material occurs but now a semitone higher with the introduction of multiphonics in the middle of the long notes. The motif also gets expanded across two octaves of the flute’s register now before becoming an accelerando figure to climax into a high A on the flute. The work continues expanding upon and reinterpreting the motif and material already presented.
